title: Introduction to Data Science
text:
Course Description
This course introduces the concepts and practice of data science: framing a research question that data can answer, preparing and exploring real data, determining what the evidence supports, and communicating the result. Topics progress from exploratory analysis through probability and statistical inference to linear and logistic modeling, where the emphasis is on what a fitted model licenses you to claim.
R is used throughout, with RStudio, RMarkdown, and Git. Every code example in the course notes runs in the browser, with no installation needed to try it.
Students are expected to use AI assistants and to identify when those assistants are wrong. Assignments are graded on that judgment as well as on correctness; see Use of AI Assistants.

Course Prerequisites and Software
You are expected to have a basic understanding of introductory statistics and some exposure to R, whether through prior coursework or online resources. This course does not teach programming from zero.
No class session is spent on R itself. The language is instead covered by the R Primer, a self-paced part of the notes that runs alongside the course from day one: the environment and RStudio, R’s core objects, coercion and missing values, factors and data frames, plotting with ggplot2, reproducible documents, and Git, with browser-based exercises throughout that check themselves and say which misconception you hit. Work through it in the opening weeks and use office hours for anything that will not come right.
The GW bootcamp’s Programming track covers the habits behind it—Git, debugging, and environments—but it is taught in Python, so the R itself is what the Primer is for. The bootcamp’s Math track is the foundation for DATS 6103 rather than for this course.
Install the following before Aug 24:

R—https://www.r-project.org/
RStudio—https://posit.co/products/open-source/rstudio/
Git, and a free GitHub account—https://github.com/
Access to an AI assistant (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, or similar). Free tiers are sufficient; no paid subscription is required.

The Data Science Help Desk exists for exactly this: it is staffed for students in the program or taking DATS classes, in Samson Hall 304—the same stairs as my office, one floor up—and dshelpdesk@gwu.edu will arrange a remote session. Take a setup problem there in the first two weeks rather than to the week an assignment is due.

title: Introduction to Data Science
text:
Course Format
This course is taught as a flipped workshop. Lecture material is delivered as assigned reading; class time is spent on discussion and supervised lab work. Slides are not presented in class, and content is not re-covered from the front of the room. Reading before each session is therefore required.
Each session runs in three modes:

Question triage. Instructor-led, drawn entirely from the questions students posted on the reading.
Reasoning and discussion. Students predict outputs, select tests, and defend conclusions to one another.
Lab. Supervised hands-on work at the keyboard.


Before class: readings and questions
Each class day has an assigned reading, listed in the course schedule. Every chapter of the course notes carries a comment box; students post questions there as they read, and may also answer one another. Questions are due Monday at 12:00 noon, the morning of class. One substantive question earns the week’s credit—a question that identifies what the reading left unclear, rather than a request to restate it. The two lowest weeks are dropped.
The first class is an exception: no reading is due before Aug 24. Students should arrive with R and RStudio installed. Questions and Data is read after that session; assigned reading proper begins with Exploratory Data Analysis, due before Aug 31, with the first questions due Monday, Aug 31 at noon.
The R Primer sits outside this cycle. It is not tied to any session and has no question deadline; post there whenever something does not come right, and those questions are picked up in office hours or at the start of a session.






The first session is ungraded



No work on Aug 24 counts toward the final grade. It is for installing software, registering with the comment system, and becoming familiar with the format.

Students work in a pair for the discussion and a group of three or four for the lab. Project
A team project takes a real dataset through the full life cycle: S.M.A.R.T. questions, acquisition, cleaning, exploration, modeling, and a written and spoken account of the findings.
Deliverables are a GitHub repository, a written report stating what the analysis does and does not support, an AI disclosure statement, and a presentation. Presentation questions are answered individually, so members of one team may receive different grades.

title: R Primer
text:
“It is a capital mistake to theorize before one has data. Insensibly one begins to twist facts to suit theories, instead of theories to suit facts.” – Arthur Conan Doyle, A Scandal in Bohemia

This part is not a week of the course. It runs alongside it.
No session is spent on the material here. Class time starts on Aug 24 with questions and data, and it never comes back to teach you R. That is deliberate: the language is learnable on your own, with feedback, at your own pace—and the two and a half hours a week we have together are worth more spent on the things that are not.
So this part is yours to work through in parallel, from the first day of the term. Most people will want the first three chapters inside the opening two weeks and the practice problems spread across the first month. If you arrive already fluent in R, skim it and go. If you do not, nothing here is optional: every later chapter assumes it.
It does two jobs.
The first is to say what this course is actually about. Not the tool list—R, RStudio, Git, the packages—but the discipline underneath it. Data science is the practice of asking a question you can answer, getting honest evidence to bear on it, and being clear about what that evidence does and does not support. Everything technical in the next fourteen weeks is in service of that last clause.
The second is practical. Your machine should run R, your projects should live somewhere sane, and the R you half-remember from a previous course or a weekend tutorial should be back within reach. That is what chapters R, RStudio, and Your Environment and An R Refresher are for. They are unglamorous and they matter, because a semester spent fighting your own setup is a semester not spent thinking. Plotting with ggplot2 sits here for the same reason: it is the mechanics of a package rather than an idea about data, and the labs assume it from Aug 31 onward, so work through it before then.






If you did the GW bootcamp





The bootcamp covers the habits—Git, debugging, environments, and programming in Python—but it does not cover R. An R Refresher is where the transfer happens, and If you are coming from Python is written for exactly that reader. The set theory and linear algebra from the Math track return in Probability.



A word on how these notes work. The notes are the lecture, in this part and everywhere else in the book. Nothing gets re-covered from the front of the room. For the taught weeks you post your questions at the bottom of the page by Monday noon and that afternoon’s session is built out of them; for this part, post questions whenever you hit something—they get picked up in office hours or at the start of a session. Read with your hands on the keyboard, not with your eyes skimming.
Most code you meet in these notes runs in your browser. There is nothing to install to try it: click into a cell, change a number, press Run, and see what happens. The exercises with a ______ blank check themselves and tell you which misconception you hit, not merely that you were wrong. Use them that way—guess, be wrong, read the feedback.






Objectives





By the end of this part you should be able to:

Say what makes a question answerable with data, and what makes a claim defensible rather than merely plausible.
Explain why cleaning consumes most of an analyst’s time, and why that work is not clerical.
Set up R, RStudio, and a project folder that a stranger could open and run.
Work fluently with R’s core objects—vectors, types and coercion, indexing, factors, data frames, functions—and predict what a line of code does before running it.
Explain how NA propagates and why that behavior is a feature.
Write an RMarkdown document that knits from a clean session, and use the minimum Git workflow your project team will need.










The habit to build





Predict before you run. Every live cell in these notes is an opportunity to be wrong cheaply. Say what you expect the output to be—out loud, or written in a comment—then press Run.
Getting it right after seeing the answer teaches you nothing. Being wrong and understanding why is the entire mechanism by which a mental model gets built, and a good mental model is what lets you catch a mistake that produced a plausible number.
This is also, precisely, the skill the course grades. Code that runs is cheap now; anyone can generate it in seconds. Knowing whether the output means what it appears to mean is not.









Where to get help





No session is spent on this part, but you are not on your own with it.
Office hours, Monday 4:00–6:00 p.m., Samson Hall 313, are the place for setup problems and anything in R, RStudio, and Your Environment or 1.3 that will not come right. Walk in; no appointment. They are shared with DATS 6103, so a Python question is fair game too.
The first session, Monday August 24, is ungraded—the only one all semester. Come with R and RStudio installed if you managed it, and come anyway if you did not.

title: What Data Science Is
text:
The question comes before the data
There is a version of this chapter that lists the tools. R, SQL, Git, a plotting library, a machine-learning library, a cloud thing. It would be easy to write, easy to read, and almost useless, because the tools turn over every few years and none of them is the difficulty.
Here is a better starting point. Data science is the practice of getting evidence to bear on a question, and being honest about how much it bears. Everything else—the cleaning, the plots, the models, the tests—is machinery in service of that sentence. If you finish this course able to write a great deal of R but unable to say what your analysis does not support, you will have learned the easy half.
This chapter sets up the spine of the term. It is not about code, and there is very little of it here. The two live examples exist to make a single point that we will return to in every module: a computation can be perfectly correct and the conclusion drawn from it perfectly wrong.
Beginners tend to work in this order: get a dataset, poke at it, find something, write it up. That order feels productive and it is how most bad analysis gets made, for a reason worth understanding.
A dataset of any size contains an enormous number of comparisons you could run. Ten variables give you forty-five pairwise correlations; add a few subgroups and you have hundreds of things to look at. Some of them will look striking purely by chance—that is not a moral failing of the data, it is arithmetic. If you decide what you are looking for after seeing which comparison came out most strikingly, you have used up the evidence to generate the hypothesis and have none left to test it with. You will meet the formal version of this in the hypothesis-testing module in October. The informal version is available to you now: decide what would count as an answer before you look.
So the first move in any project is to write down a question specific enough that you could, in principle, be wrong about it. Next week we will make this precise with the S.M.A.R.T. framing—specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound. For now, one test does most of the work:
If you cannot, you do not have a question yet; you have a hope. “Does our onboarding email increase 30-day retention?” passes—you can say beforehand what a null result looks like. “Let’s understand our users better” does not. Neither does “show that the redesign worked”, which has already fixed the conclusion and is shopping for support.
The second test is about the data rather than the question: does this dataset contain the thing you are asking about? Transit tap-in records contain times and stations; they do not contain why anyone traveled. Hospital records contain diagnoses that were coded; they do not contain diseases that were never diagnosed. An enormous share of confident wrong analysis comes from asking a dataset about something adjacent to what it recorded, and forgetting the gap.

title: What Data Science Is
text:
Can you name, in advance, the result that would make you abandon your expectation?









 Turning a Vague Request into a Question







A city transit agency hands you three years of tap-in records and asks you to “look at ridership and see what you find.”
You need to turn that into a question you can actually answer. Which of the following is the best candidate?

Is ridership good?Did average weekday ridership on the Red Line fall between 2023 and 2025, and by how much?Why do people ride the train?Does the transit system need more funding?



Did average weekday ridership on the Red Line fall between 2023 and 2025, and by how much?
A question is answerable when you can name, before touching the data, what evidence would settle it—and what evidence would settle it the other way. Here you can: a comparison of weekday tap-ins on one line across two periods, and a difference with an interval around it.
The others fail for different reasons, and the reasons are worth separating.
Is ridership good? has no measurable subject. “Good” is not a quantity, and no computation can produce it. Before this becomes a data question, somebody has to say good compared to what—last year, the projection, a peer city.
Why do people ride the train? is a question about intentions, and tap-in records contain no intentions. They contain times and stations. You could get at motive with a survey, but you cannot get at it with this dataset, and the most common way analyses go wrong is asking data a question about something it never recorded.
Does the system need more funding? is a policy judgment. Analysis can inform it—ridership trends, cost per rider, what happened after the last fare change—but “need” involves priorities and values that no dataset contains. Handing a decision-maker a number and calling it the answer to this question hides the judgment rather than making it.
Notice that the good question is also the least impressive-sounding one. That is normal. Answerable questions are narrow; the interesting part is what you build out of a stack of them.

title: What Data Science Is
section: Most of the work is cleaning, and it is not clerical
text:
Most of the work is cleaning, and it is not clerical
Survey a room of working data scientists on where their time goes and you will hear some version of most of it, on getting the data into shape. The usual figure quoted is 80%. The number is folklore and the exact value does not matter; the shape of it is right, and it surprises people who expected the job to be modeling.
The tempting reaction is to treat cleaning as janitorial—unpleasant preparation before the real work. That reaction is wrong, and it is the source of a great many defective analyses. Cleaning is where the substantive decisions get made, and it looks clerical only because each individual decision is small.
Consider some choices you will genuinely face in S.M.A.R.T. Questions:

A column of ages contains three values above 120. Do you drop those rows, set them to missing, or investigate whether 999 was the data-entry code for “declined to answer”? These give three different datasets and can give three different answers.
Eight percent of respondents have no income recorded. Do you drop them? If people with high incomes decline more often, dropping them biases every income statistic downward—and the analysis will not warn you, because the arithmetic on what remains is flawless.
Two files list the same customers, one as "Smith, Jane" and one as "Jane Smith", and 4% of names fail to match. Whom you fail to match is rarely random.
A date column has both 03/04/2025 and 2025-04-03 in it. One of those is April 3rd. The other might be.

None of these has a correct answer that a tool can supply. Each is a judgment about what the data represents and what your question needs, and each has to be recorded so that a reader can see what you decided. This is why a clean analysis is not merely a tidy one: the log of what you removed and why is part of the evidence.
That is also why cleaning cannot be handed off. The person who decides what counts as a valid age is making a claim about the population being described.

title: What Data Science Is
text:
Plausible versus defensible
Here is the distinction the course is built around.
A plausible claim is one nothing in your output contradicts. A defensible claim is one you can still hold after someone competent and unsympathetic has tried to knock it down. The gap between the two is where analysis lives or dies, and closing it is a skill—not a personality trait, not carefulness, a skill with specific moves that can be taught.
Two demonstrations. Run them, and predict before you do.

Summaries hide the data
The four datasets below are Anscombe’s quartet, constructed by the statistician Francis Anscombe in 1973 to make one point vividly.








To two decimal places, the four datasets have the same mean in x, the same mean in y, the same standard deviation, and the same correlation. Any report that describes them with those numbers describes them identically.
Now look at them.








Set 1 is a cloud around a line. Set 2 is a curve, and a straight-line summary of it is simply the wrong description. Set 3 is an exact line with one outlier dragging the fit. Set 4 has no relationship at all in ten of its points—x is 8 every time—and the entire correlation is manufactured by a single eleventh point. Remove that one observation and there is nothing left to correlate.
The claim “x and y are correlated at 0.82” is true of all four. The claim “y increases with x” is defensible for the first and indefensible for the fourth, and no summary statistic distinguishes them. This is why Module 1 spends a whole session on visualization before we do any inference: look at the data is not a preliminary, it is a control.


Averages can point the wrong way
The second demonstration is nastier, because here the plot will not save you either.








Read the two tables against each other. Among severe cases, A saves 80\% and B saves 75\%: A wins. Among mild cases, A saves 95\% and B saves 90\%: A wins again. There is no third group. Every patient in the study is in one of those two rows.
And pooled, A saves 81.5\% against B’s 88.9\%. B wins comfortably.
Nothing here is a rounding artifact or a coding error—check the arithmetic yourself, that is what the cell is for. What drives the overall gap is that A was given almost entirely to severe patients (900 of its 1{,}000) and B almost entirely to mild ones (1{,}020 of its 1{,}100), and severe patients do worse under either procedure. A’s overall rate is therefore essentially its severe-case rate, and B’s is essentially its mild-case rate. The pooled comparison is not comparing procedures at all. It is comparing who got them.
This pattern is Simpson’s paradox, and the practical lesson is a question to ask before any two-group comparison: what else differs between these groups? If something does, and that something also affects the outcome, the raw comparison answers a question nobody asked. We will spend real time on this when we get to modeling in November, because a regression is, among other things, a machine for holding such things fixed.






 A Reversal in the Subgroups







A hospital compares two surgical procedures on 2,100 patients.




Survived
Died
Survival rate




Procedure A
815
185
81.5%


Procedure B
978
122
88.9%



Splitting the same patients by how sick they were on admission:




Procedure A
Procedure B




Severe cases
720/900 = 80.0%
60/80 = 75.0%


Mild cases
95/100 = 95.0%
918/1020 = 90.0%



Procedure B wins overall, but Procedure A wins among severe cases and among mild cases. Which statement is correct?

One of the two tables must contain an arithmetic error, since a procedure cannot win in every subgroup and lose overall.The subgroup rates are unreliable because some of the counts are small, so the overall table should be trusted.Both tables are arithmetically correct; severity is associated with both the choice of procedure and the outcome, so the overall comparison is comparing different kinds of patient.The overall table is the honest one because it uses all 2,100 patients, and splitting the data is a form of cherry-picking.



Both tables are arithmetically correct. Check them: 720 + 95 = 815 and 900 + 100 = 1000, so Procedure A’s overall rate is 815/1000 = 81.5\%. Nothing is wrong with the arithmetic. This reversal is called Simpson’s paradox, and it is not a paradox so much as a warning about what an average is.
The mechanism: Procedure A was given overwhelmingly to severe cases (900 of its 1,000 patients), and Procedure B overwhelmingly to mild ones (1,020 of its 1,100). Severe cases die more often whichever procedure they get. So A’s overall rate is essentially its severe-case rate (80\%), and B’s is essentially its mild-case rate (90\%). The overall comparison is not comparing procedures; it is comparing patient populations that happen to be labeled by procedure.
Why the other answers are wrong is the useful part.
Small counts are a real concern but not this one—the reversal survives even when every cell is large, and it is not a sampling fluctuation. Nor is subgrouping “cherry-picking”: cherry-picking is choosing a split after seeing which one gives the answer you wanted. Severity is a split you would have written down in advance, because you know before looking that sicker patients do worse.
And using all the data does not make a comparison fair. The overall table uses every patient and is still misleading, because it silently averages over a variable that differs systematically between the groups.
The habit this should build: before comparing two groups, ask what else differs between them. If something does, and that something also affects the outcome, the raw comparison answers a question you did not ask.







The skeptic’s question
Your labs this semester rotate three roles, and one of them—the skeptic—has exactly one job: to ask of every result, what would tell us this is wrong?
That role exists because the question is not natural. When a result agrees with what you expected, the mind stops. When it disagrees, the mind starts hunting for a bug, and often finds one, and often the bug is real—which is precisely what makes the asymmetry dangerous. You debug the results you dislike and accept the results you like, and the process looks like diligence from the inside.
The countermeasure is procedural. Before you believe a number, write down what would have to be true for it to be wrong: a coding error, a subgroup you pooled over, a filter applied earlier than you remember, a sample that is not the population you are describing. Then check the two cheapest of those. It takes five minutes and catches most of what gets caught.

title: What Data Science Is
section: What the analysis does not support
text:
What the analysis does not support
Every project report in this course must contain a section on what your analysis does not support. This is not a humility exercise. It is the part of the report a reader most needs, and the part an inexperienced analyst cannot write, because writing it requires knowing where your evidence stops.
Typical contents:

The population. You studied who responded, not who was asked. If 12% responded, your findings describe a group that chose to respond.
Association versus cause. Almost everything you compute this semester is an association. Saying “increases”, “drives”, or “causes” claims more than a correlation licenses, and the word usually sneaks in during the write-up rather than the analysis.
Precision. A difference of 2.3 percentage points with an interval running from -1.1 to 5.7 is not a difference of 2.3 percentage points. Reporting the point estimate and dropping the interval is the most common way honest analysts mislead.
Generalization. Your model was fitted on 2019–2023 in one city. Whether it holds in 2026 in another is a claim about the world that your data cannot address.

A report that says these things is not weaker than one that does not. It is the only kind whose positive claims are worth anything, because a reader can see they were made by somebody who knows what a claim costs.

title: What Data Science Is
section: What AI changes, and what it does not

title: What Data Science Is
text:
Where this is going
The shape of the semester, in one paragraph. The opening sessions get you set up and get data into shape you can look at, ending with exploratory analysis: describing what is in front of you without misleading anybody, including yourself. The middle of the term is inference—the machinery for saying how much of what you see could be noise, built by simulation first so that you see why it works before you meet a formula. From November it is modeling: linear and logistic models read as statements about evidence, with real attention to when their assumptions fail. The last session carries one analysis from question to written report, which is what your project asks of you.
Underneath all of it is the same question, asked in progressively more technical ways: given this evidence, what am I entitled to say?






Summary






Data science is getting evidence to bear on a question and being honest about how much it bears. The tools are downstream of that.
Write the question before you look, and specify in advance what result would change your mind.
Check that the data actually contains the thing you are asking about.
Cleaning is most of the work and is not clerical—each decision is a claim about what the data represents, and must be recorded.
Identical summary statistics can describe completely different data (Anscombe); an average over pooled groups can point the opposite way to every subgroup (Simpson).
Before believing a result, name what would show it to be wrong, and check the two cheapest possibilities.
AI writes the code; you supply the judgment. The dangerous failure is never the error message—it is the plausible number.




Next: R, RStudio, and Your Environment, which is deliberately practical.

title: R, RStudio, and Your Environment
text:
R and RStudio are two different programs
This chapter is the unglamorous one. It is also the one that decides whether the next fourteen weeks are spent thinking about data or fighting your own laptop.
Nearly every setup problem I see in this course comes from one of four things: not knowing where R thinks it is, not knowing which copy of an object is real, not knowing whether a package is installed or merely loaded, and having a session so full of accumulated state that nothing can be trusted. All four are avoidable with habits that take a week to build.
R is the language and the engine. It is what actually computes. If you launch R directly you get a bare prompt, and everything works.
RStudio is an integrated development environment—an editor, a file browser, a plot viewer, a help viewer, and a console, arranged around R. It does not compute anything itself; it drives R. You can replace RStudio with VS Code or Positron and nothing about your analysis changes.
Two practical consequences. First, install R before RStudio, because RStudio looks for an R installation when it starts. Second, when something goes wrong, ask which of the two is at fault. “My plot does not appear” is usually RStudio. “My mean is NA” is never RStudio.
Install both from the links in the syllabus. Take the current release of each; there is no reason to pin an old version for this course. Then check that R is what you think it is:
If that prints something from several years ago, you have an old R that RStudio found first. Update it before term starts rather than during a lab.

title: R, RStudio, and Your Environment
text:
R.version.string
#> [1] "R version 4.5.0 (2025-04-11)"

title: R, RStudio, and Your Environment
text:
The four panes
RStudio opens with a console and grows three more panes once you open a file. What each is for matters more than where it sits.

Source (top-left). Your scripts and RMarkdown documents. This is the permanent record.
Console (bottom-left). Where R actually runs. Transient.
Environment / History (top-right). Every object currently in memory. Worth glancing at constantly.
Files / Plots / Packages / Help (bottom-right). Where plots and documentation land.

Two keyboard shortcuts pay for themselves in the first week:



Action
macOS
Windows/Linux




Send current line/selection to console
Cmd+Enter
Ctrl+Enter


Insert <-
Option+-
Alt+-


Restart R
Cmd+Shift+F10
Ctrl+Shift+F10


Insert code chunk (RMarkdown)
Cmd+Option+I
Ctrl+Alt+I



That third one is the important one, and we will come back to it.

title: R, RStudio, and Your Environment
text:
Console versus script
This is the distinction that trips up the most people, so it is worth stating flatly.
The console changes the state of your session. The script is the record of how that state was reached.
Both create real objects. An object made in the console is exactly as usable as one made by a script—R does not label them. The difference is that the console leaves no trace in any file. Three hours later your analysis works beautifully and your script, taken on its own, does not run.
You will not notice, because from inside your session everything is fine. Your teammate will notice. So will you, in November, when you reopen the project.
The rule: the console is for looking, the script is for doing. Type head(dat) and summary(dat$age) and nrow(dat) in the console freely—those inspect, they do not create. The moment you write <-, it belongs in the script. Write it there and send it down with Cmd/Ctrl+Enter.






 Works on My Machine







Your script runs perfectly in your RStudio session. You push it to your team’s repository and a teammate reports that line 40 fails with object 'threshold' not found.
You open the script, search it, and confirm: the word threshold appears on line 40 and nowhere else.
What most likely happened?

Your teammate is running a different version of R, which handles undefined variables differently.You defined threshold in the console at some point, so it exists in your global environment but was never written into the script.The script needs to be sourced with source(..., local = FALSE) for the variable to be visible.Git dropped the line defining threshold during the push.



You typed threshold <- ... in the console and never moved it into the script.
This is the single most common failure in a first data science course, and it will happen to you. The console and the script are two different things: the console changes the state of your session, the script is the record of how that state was reached. An object created in the console is just as real as one created by the script—your later lines find it and work perfectly—but it exists nowhere in the file you handed over.
Your session and your script have quietly diverged, and nothing warns you, because from inside the session everything works.
The other options are not plausible. No version of R invents variables; source() evaluates in the global environment by default and does not conjure missing objects; and Git transfers files byte for byte—if a line were missing you would see it in git diff.
The fix is a habit, not a tool. Restart R and run the script from the top, regularly, and certainly before you push. In RStudio that is Session → Restart R (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+F10), which empties the environment, followed by Source. If it runs clean from an empty environment, it will run for your teammate.
The related setting: in Tools → Global Options, turn off “Restore .RData into workspace at startup” and set “Save workspace to .RData on exit” to Never. Otherwise R helpfully reloads yesterday’s objects at every launch, and you can go weeks without discovering that your script has not actually worked since Tuesday.

title: R, RStudio, and Your Environment
text:
Where R thinks it is
R has a working directory: the folder that relative file paths are interpreted against.
getwd()
#> [1] "/Users/dana/projects/transit-analysis"
If the working directory is that folder, then read.csv("data/rides.csv") looks for /Users/dana/projects/transit-analysis/data/rides.csv. Simple enough. The trouble starts with how people set it.
The instinctive move—and the one you will see in older tutorials and in AI-generated scripts—is:
setwd("/Users/dana/Desktop/project final v3")   # do not do this
That line works on exactly one computer. It fails for your teammate, it fails for me when I grade it, and it fails for you when you get a new laptop. It is the single most common reason a submitted analysis does not run.

Use a Project instead
An RStudio Project is a folder with a .Rproj file in it. When you open the project—by double-clicking the .Rproj, or via File → Open Project—RStudio starts a fresh R session with the working directory already set to that folder.
Create one now: File → New Project → New Directory → New Project, and give it a name with no spaces in it.
Because the working directory is handled for you, every path in your code can be written relative to the project root, and those paths work on every machine that has the folder:
dat <- read.csv("data/rides.csv")
saveRDS(model, "output/model.rds")
A layout that scales, and that I would like to see in your project repositories:
transit-analysis/
├── transit-analysis.Rproj
├── README.md
├── data/
│   ├── raw/            <- never edited, never overwritten
│   └── clean/          <- produced by your scripts
├── R/                  <- scripts
├── output/             <- figures, tables, saved models
└── report.Rmd
The data/raw rule is worth taking seriously: never modify a raw data file, not in R and certainly not by opening it in Excel and saving. Cleaning happens in code that reads from raw/ and writes to clean/, so that the transformation is visible, repeatable, and reviewable. A cleaned file with no script behind it is an assertion, not evidence.
One further nicety: file.path() joins path components with the right separator for the operating system, which spares you a class of Windows-versus-everyone-else bugs.






 Exercise: a path that travels





A teammate’s script contains
dat <- read.csv("/Users/dana/Desktop/proj/data/survey.csv")
You have opened the project, so the working directory is already the project root, and the file sits in a data folder inside it. Build the path R should be given—as a character string—using file.path() rather than typing the separator yourself.















file.path(folder, filename)
which gives "data/survey.csv". Writing paste0(folder, "/", filename) happens to give the same string, but file.path() says what you mean and picks the separator for the platform.

title: R, RStudio, and Your Environment
text:
Packages
Base R is deliberately small. Almost everything else arrives as a package, and nearly all of them come from CRAN.
There are two distinct acts, and confusing them causes a specific and very common failure.
Installing downloads the package onto your computer. You do it once per machine, and it is a setup act performed by a person:
install.packages("ggplot2")     # in the CONSOLE, not in your script
Loading makes an installed package’s functions available in the current session. You do it every session, and it belongs at the top of the script:
library(ggplot2)
Put install.packages() in a shared script and you force a reinstall on every run, require a network connection, risk silently upgrading a dependency mid-analysis, and occasionally stop the script dead on a prompt. Keep it in the console.
Two more points.
:: reaches into a package without loading it. stats::median(x) calls median from stats explicitly. This is useful when two packages define the same name—loading dplyr masks stats::filter, and R tells you so at load time in a message most people learn to ignore. When a function behaves nothing like its documentation, suspect masking and qualify the name.
library() errors, require() warns. Use library() in scripts. If the package is missing you want to be told immediately and loudly, not thirty lines later when a function is not found.






 What Belongs at the Top of a Script







A teammate opens a shared analysis script with this at the top:
install.packages("ggplot2")
library(ggplot2)
setwd("/Users/dana/Desktop/project-final-v3")
Which criticism is the most serious for a script that other people have to run?

install.packages should come after library, since you cannot install a package that is not loaded.Both install.packages and setwd will fail or misbehave on anyone else’s computer; the script is not runnable outside Dana’s account.library(ggplot2) should be require(ggplot2), which is the correct form inside a script.Nothing is seriously wrong; the script simply takes longer to run the first time.



Both install.packages and setwd tie the script to Dana’s machine, and each does so in a different way.
setwd("/Users/dana/Desktop/project-final-v3") fails outright for everyone else—that directory does not exist on your computer. A hard-coded absolute path is the most reliable way to make an analysis unrunnable. The alternative is an RStudio Project: open the .Rproj file and the working directory is already the project folder, so every path in the script can be written relative to it, like read.csv("data/survey.csv"). Those paths work on every machine that has the folder, which is the whole point.
install.packages is more subtle, because it does not fail—it does something worse. It reinstalls the package every single run, needs a network connection, can silently upgrade a package to a version that changes your results, and on some systems triggers a prompt or a compile that stops the script dead in the middle. Installing is a one-time setup act performed by a person; loading is what a script does. Keep install.packages() in the console, or in a clearly marked setup file that nobody sources by accident.
The other options are wrong on the facts. install.packages does not require the package to be loaded—loading something you have not installed is the impossible direction. And require() is not the “script” form: it returns FALSE with a warning instead of stopping, so a missing package lets the script continue and fail later, somewhere confusing. In a script you want library(), which fails immediately and tells you why.

title: R, RStudio, and Your Environment
section: The workspace, and why you should refuse it
text:
The workspace, and why you should refuse it
By default, R offers to save every object in memory to a hidden .RData file when you quit, and to reload it when you start. This sounds helpful and is the deepest source of irreproducibility in a beginner’s workflow.
With it on, your session at 9 a.m. contains everything from yesterday. Your script can reference an object it never creates and appear to work indefinitely. You will discover this at the worst possible time.
Turn it off now. Tools → Global Options → General:

Restore .RData into workspace at startup—unchecked
Save workspace to .RData on exit—Never

Then adopt the habit that makes the setting redundant anyway:






Restart R and run from the top





Several times a session, and always before you push or submit: Session → Restart R (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+F10), then run your script from line 1.
Note that rm(list = ls()) is not a substitute. It clears objects but leaves loaded packages, changed options, and anything attached to the search path. Only a restart gives you the session your reader will have.
If it runs clean from an empty session, it will run for someone else. If it does not, you have just found a bug that was going to surface later, in public.

title: R, RStudio, and Your Environment
text:
Getting help
You are allowed the documentation in every lab and exam in this course, so learn to read it.
?mean            # help page for a function you can name
??"linear model" # search help text when you cannot
args(round)      # just the arguments and their defaults
example(seq)     # run the examples from the help page
A help page has a fixed structure, and two sections repay attention out of proportion to their length:

Usage shows the argument order and every default. Most surprises live in a default you did not know existed—mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE) tells you at a glance that missing values are not dropped unless you say so.
Value says what the function gives back, which is exactly what you need to know before writing the next line.

The two functions to reach for when an object surprises you:








str() is the single most useful diagnostic in R. Run it on every object you did not build yourself, and on every data frame the moment you read it in. It answers “what actually is this?” in one line per column, and it is where you catch a numeric column that was silently read in as text.






 Exercise: find it yourself





Below is an object of the sort a modeling function might hand back. Nobody has told you what is inside it. Run str(fit) first, then return the slope coefficient on hours—as a single number.
The point of this exercise is the first step, not the second. Reading an unfamiliar object is a skill you will use every week of this course.















fit$coefficients[["hours"]]
fit[["coefficients"]]["hours"] also works and keeps the name attached. Double brackets drop the name and give you a bare number, which is usually what you want when the value is going into a sentence.

title: R, RStudio, and Your Environment
text:
Errors, warnings, and messages
R has three severities and they are not interchangeable.
An error stops execution. Errors are the friendly ones: nothing further happens, and the message usually names the culprit.
A message is informational—the note about masked objects when you load a package, for instance. Harmless.
A warning is the dangerous category. R tells you something questionable happened and carries on with a value. If you are running a long script or knitting a document, the warning scrolls past and you are left holding a number that was quietly compromised.








Two entries could not be converted, so R produced NA for them and warned. It did not stop. Everything downstream inherits those NAs, and if somebody has written na.rm = TRUE further along, they will silently disappear.






 Exercise: count what you lost





Before dropping anything, you should always be able to say how much you are dropping. Using raw from the setup, return the number of entries that failed to convert to a number.















sum(is.na(as.numeric(raw)))
which is 3. Note that is.na() is the right test here and == NA would not be—that trap gets its own section in An R Refresher.

title: R, RStudio, and Your Environment
section: How people break their own setup
text:
How people break their own setup
A short taxonomy, drawn from previous cohorts. All four are avoidable and all four will happen to somebody in this room.

The script that depends on the console. Covered above. Fixed by restarting R and running from the top.
The absolute path. setwd("/Users/me/Desktop/...") at the top of a script. Fixed by using a Project and relative paths.
The half-installed package. library(x) errors, so the student runs install.packages("x") inside the script, which then fails partway on a machine with no compiler—and the error message is about a C header file, which is genuinely frightening the first time. Fixed by installing in the console, once, and reading which package actually failed.
Two copies of the project. One in Downloads, one in Documents, both open in different windows, edits landing in whichever was clicked most recently. This is what Git prevents, and it is why Reproducibility: RMarkdown and Git exists.

None of this is about being organized as a personality. It is about arranging things so that being disorganised is not fatal.






Summary






R computes; RStudio drives R. Install R first.
The console changes your session; the script is the record. Anything with <- goes in the script.
Use an RStudio Project and relative paths. Never setwd() to an absolute path.
Never modify a raw data file; clean in code, from data/raw to data/clean.
install.packages() once, in the console. library() every session, at the top of the script.
Turn off workspace saving and restoring. Restart R and run from the top, often. rm(list = ls()) is not a restart.
str() on every object you did not build. Read the Usage and Value sections of a help page.
Errors stop you; warnings hand you a compromised value and let you carry on. Warnings are the ones that hurt.




Next: An R Refresher, which is where the real work of this week is.

title: An R Refresher
text:
Everything is a vector
This course does not teach programming from zero, but it does assume that the R you met in a previous course or a weekend tutorial has gone slightly stale. This chapter brings it back, and does so with a particular bias: it spends its time on the places where R does something reasonable that you did not expect.
That bias is deliberate. The syntax you can look up—function names are meant to be looked up, in this course and in professional life. What you cannot look up in the moment is whether the number on your screen means what you think it means. Almost every example below runs without complaint. Several of them are wrong.
Predict before you run. Every cell on this page is live. Say what you expect, then press Run.
There is no scalar in R. What looks like a single number is a vector of length one, which is why the printed output carries an index in brackets.
The [1] at the start of the output is not part of the value; it is the position of the first element on that line. Build a longer vector with c() (for combine) and the point becomes visible:
Some vectors are worth building rather than typing:
The distinction between times and each in the last two lines will come back in a moment, and it matters more than it looks.

title: An R Refresher
text:
Types, and the coercion hierarchy
An atomic vector holds one type only. The four you will meet constantly are:



Type
Example
class()




logical
TRUE, FALSE, NA
"logical"


integer
1L, 47L
"integer"


double
3.14, 2
"numeric"


character
"S", "2019"
"character"



When you combine different types, R does not complain. It coerces everything up to the most accommodating type, along a fixed hierarchy:
\text{logical} \;\rightarrow\; \text{integer} \;\rightarrow\; \text{double} \;\rightarrow\; \text{character}








The rule is worth internalising because of what it means in practice: one bad value in a column of numbers turns the whole column into text. A single "n/a", "—", or "see note" in a spreadsheet column of ages is enough, and R will read the column as character without a word of complaint. Then mean(dat$age) errors, or worse, someone converts with as.numeric(), gets NAs, and drops them.
Coercion the other way is deliberate and is where warnings come from:








as.integer(3.99) giving 3 with no warning is a good one to remember. R does not round; it truncates.
Logical vectors coerce to 0 and 1 in arithmetic, which gives a very common and very useful idiom:








mean() of a logical vector is a proportion. You will use this constantly.






 Coercion and Silent NAs







You read a column of ages out of a spreadsheet where one cell was typed as "42 " with a stray space and another as "unknown". In R you end up with
ages <- c("31", "42 ", "unknown", "28")
mean(as.numeric(ages))
What happens?

An error is raised, because "unknown" cannot be converted to a number.You get NA, with a warning that NAs were introduced by coercion; "42 " converts fine but "unknown" becomes NA, and mean propagates it.You get 33.667, the mean of the three convertible values, since R drops what it cannot convert.You get NA with no warning, because both "42 " and "unknown" fail to convert.



You get NA, plus a warning.
Three separate things are worth pulling apart here.
First, as.numeric does not error on text it cannot parse—it returns NA and emits Warning: NAs introduced by coercion. That is a warning, not an error: the script keeps running, the pipeline keeps going, and if you are knitting a long document the message scrolls past. Warnings in R are the ones that hurt you, precisely because they do not stop anything.
Second, "42 " converts perfectly well. as.numeric tolerates surrounding whitespace, so trailing spaces are not the problem here. The stray space would matter if you had compared strings—"42 " == "42" is FALSE—which is the kind of thing that makes two datasets refuse to join for reasons invisible on screen.
Third, and most important: mean does not ignore missing values by default. One NA anywhere in the vector makes the mean NA. This is a deliberate design choice, and a good one—R refuses to quietly answer a question you did not ask. The mean of “these numbers, and something we do not know” is genuinely unknown.
So the fix is not mean(as.numeric(ages), na.rm = TRUE) typed reflexively. That silently redefines the quantity you are estimating: you are no longer reporting the mean age of your sample but the mean age of the people whose age was recorded. Sometimes those are close. Sometimes the missingness is exactly the point—people decline to state their age non-randomly. Use na.rm = TRUE when you have decided that dropping is defensible, and say in your write-up how many you dropped.

title: An R Refresher
text:
Vectorisation and recycling
Arithmetic in R works element by element, with no loop:








So far so ordinary. Now the part that bites. When the two vectors have different lengths, R does not error. It recycles the shorter one from the beginning until the lengths match:








The shorter vector was reused three times, giving 11 22 31 42 51 62. If the longer length is not a whole multiple of the shorter, you get a warning but still a result:








Recycling is a feature—prices * 1.06 is exactly this rule with a length-one vector—but it is also the mechanism behind a whole family of silent bugs. When the lengths divide evenly, there is no warning at all, and you get a full-length answer built from a mistake.






The dangerous case





length(a) == 6 and length(b) == 2 produces a clean, warning-free, entirely wrong answer if you meant those two values to apply to blocks of three rather than to alternate positions. R cannot tell the difference between the two intentions; only you can.









 Exercise: a discount that runs and is wrong





A shop has six items. The first three are on a 10% discount, the last three on 20%. A colleague wrote
prices * c(0.9, 0.8)
which runs, produces six numbers, and is wrong—it alternates the two discounts rather than applying them in blocks of three.
Produce the correct discounted prices, as a vector of six numbers.















prices * rep(c(0.9, 0.8), each = 3)
giving 10.800 7.650 19.800 12.600 24.000 7.992. Writing c(rep(0.9, 3), rep(0.8, 3)) is equally correct and arguably clearer.
The reason the colleague’s version is dangerous is that it never errors. Six items in, six prices out, all plausible. The only way to catch it is to have predicted what the multiplier vector should look like before multiplying by it.

title: An R Refresher
text:
Indexing
R indexes from 1, and square brackets accept four different kinds of subscript.








Three things here differ from Python and cause specific errors.
x[0] is not the first element and is not an error. It returns a zero-length vector, because position zero exists in R only as “select nothing”:








That silence matters. A loop or a function written with Python’s convention will produce empty results rather than crashing, and empty results propagate quietly.
Ranges include both endpoints. 2:4 is 2 3 4, three elements, not two.
A negative index drops rather than counts from the end. heights[-1] is everything but the first element; it is not the last element. To get the last element, use heights[length(heights)], or tail(heights, 1).
Named vectors add a fourth kind of subscript, which is worth preferring wherever it is available because it survives reordering:









The 1:length(x) trap
This one is worth a moment, because it is the most common source of a loop that runs backwards through an empty vector.








1:length(x) on an empty vector gives 1 0, so a loop over it executes twice with meaningless indices. Use seq_along(x) or seq_len(n). This is not pedantry; it is the difference between a filter that returns nothing and a script that produces two rows of garbage.






 Exercise: trim the calibration readings





A sensor writes a calibration value at the start of every run and another at the end. Both should be discarded before analysis, and the number of readings between them varies from run to run.
Return the readings with the first and last removed—written so that it still works if the run is longer or shorter.















readings[-c(1, length(readings))]
head(readings[-1], -1) also works. What you should not write is readings[-c(1, 6)], which is right by coincidence: the six is a fact about today’s data, not about the problem.

title: An R Refresher
text:
Missing values
NA means we do not know. It is not zero, not an empty string, and not Python’s None. The consequences follow from that reading and are more consistent than they first appear.

NA propagates
Any arithmetic involving an unknown is unknown:








This is a design choice and a good one. R refuses to quietly answer a question you did not ask. The mean of “4, 7, 2, and something we do not know” is genuinely unknown, and a language that returned 4.33 would be inventing an answer.
You override it explicitly:








But be clear about what that line does. It does not compute the mean of x. It computes the mean of the values of x that were recorded, which is a different quantity, and they coincide only if the missingness is unrelated to the value. If high earners decline to state their income more often, mean(income, na.rm = TRUE) is biased downward, and the arithmetic will not tell you. Report how many you dropped, every time.


== NA is always wrong








Is 4 equal to the unknown value? We do not know, so the answer is NA. Even NA == NA is NA, since two unknowns may or may not be the same thing. Use is.na() whenever you want to ask about missingness.
The same trap appears in filtering, where it is easier to miss:








NA > 3 is NA, and an NA used as an index yields an NA element. The first line hands you 4 NA 7 NA—four elements, of which two are phantoms.


%in% never returns NA
When you are testing membership rather than doing arithmetic, %in% is the safer operator, because it treats NA as an ordinary value to compare rather than as an unknown:








Which one you want depends on the question. == "S" says “is this the South?”, and for a missing region the honest answer is we do not know. %in% "S" says “is this one of the values I listed?”, and for a missing region the answer is a definite no. When you are selecting rows to work on, the second is nearly always what you mean.






 Exercise: a filter that does not leak NAs





region has two missing entries. Return a logical vector of length 6 that is TRUE exactly at the positions where the region is "S", and FALSE everywhere else—with no NA anywhere in it.















region %in% "S"
or equivalently !is.na(region) & region == "S".
The reason to prefer %in% is that it cannot silently produce NA, so it cannot silently produce phantom rows when used as an index.










 Why sum(x == NA) Is Not 2







Let x <- c(4, NA, 7, NA, 2). A student wants to count the missing values and writes
sum(x == NA)
What does this return, and why?

2, which is correct—x == NA is TRUE exactly at the missing positions.0, because NA is not equal to anything, including itself.NA, because x == NA is NA at every position, and summing NAs gives NA.An error, because you cannot use == with NA.



NA. And notice the useful thing: the code runs. No error, no warning. It hands back a value that looks like it could be an answer.
NA means we do not know. So the comparison 4 == NA is not FALSE—it is NA, because whether 4 equals the unknown value depends on what the unknown value is, and we do not know. That is true at every position, including the missing ones: NA == NA is NA, since two unknowns may or may not be the same thing. So x == NA is NA NA NA NA NA, and sum of that is NA.
The correct tool is is.na(), which asks a different question—is this entry missing?—and always answers TRUE or FALSE:
sum(is.na(x))   # 2
Two habits follow.
Never compare to NA with ==. Any test that could see a missing value needs is.na. The same applies to filtering: x[x > 3] on our vector returns 4 7 NA NA, quietly carrying the missing values along, because NA > 3 is NA and NA used as an index yields NA. If you want only the known values above 3, say x[!is.na(x) & x > 3].
Treat “it ran” as no evidence at all. This is the theme of the whole course. R’s NA propagation is doing you a favor by refusing to invent an answer—but it can only refuse where you asked a question. sum(x == NA) gives an honest NA; the danger is the analyst who sees NA, adds na.rm = TRUE, gets 0, and reports that the data has no missing values.











 Exercise: above average, honestly





temps has seven daily readings, two of them missing. Return the readings that are strictly above the mean of the recorded values—and only real readings, no NAs in the answer.
Two separate decisions are hiding in that sentence. Find both before you write anything.















m <- mean(temps, na.rm = TRUE)          # 22.36
temps[!is.na(temps) & temps > m]        # 23.0 25.1 22.4
or in one line, temps[!is.na(temps) & temps > mean(temps, na.rm = TRUE)].
Worth noticing: mean(temps) alone is NA, so the version without na.rm fails loudly. The version without the is.na guard fails quietly, returning five values of which two are phantoms. The quiet failure is the one to fear.






NA, NaN, NULL
Three things that are not each other:








NA is a missing value in a vector. NULL is no value at all, and disappears when combined. You will meet NULL mostly as the value of a list element that does not exist.

title: An R Refresher
text:
Factors
A factor stores a categorical variable. Internally it is an integer vector of codes plus a character vector of levels, and knowing that is enough to explain everything factors do.








Levels are sorted alphabetically by default, and that ordering shows up in every table and every plot. When the natural order is not alphabetical, say so:








Two behaviors cause almost all factor trouble.

as.numeric() on a factor gives you the codes








This is the most dangerous single line in the chapter, because mean(as.numeric(year)) returns 2.8—a small, plausible-looking number—instead of 2019.8. Nothing errors. Nothing warns.
The deeper point is that a number stored as a factor is a symptom. It means something went wrong at import, usually a stray "n/a" in a numeric column. Fix the import; do not patch the column downstream.


Dropping rows does not drop levels








An empty level survives filtering and reappears in your tables and plot legends as a category with nothing in it. droplevels() is the fix, and this is exactly the sort of thing to catch by running table() after a filter rather than assuming.






 The Factor That Lies







A survey stores respondents’ ages as a factor, because of how the file was read in:
age <- factor(c(30, 45, 22, 45))
mean(as.numeric(age))
The code runs and prints a number. What number, and is it the mean age?

35.5, the correct mean age—as.numeric recovers the original values.2.25, which is not the mean age; as.numeric returns the integer level codes, not the labels.NA with a warning, because a factor cannot be coerced to numeric.35.5, but only because all the values happen to be whole numbers.



2.25, and it is not the mean age of anybody.
A factor is stored as an integer vector of codes plus a character vector of levels. The levels here are sorted as text and come out as "22" "30" "45", so the codes are 2 3 1 3. as.numeric hands you the codes—2, 3, 1, 3—whose mean is 2.25. The real mean is (30+45+22+45)/4 = 35.5.
This is the most dangerous bug in the chapter, for one reason: the output is a plausible number. If as.numeric had errored, you would fix it in ten seconds. Instead you get 2.25, which looks like a small, well-behaved quantity, and if the surrounding analysis is about something plausibly on that scale—a Likert score, a rating out of 5—it can travel all the way into a report.
The fix is to go through the labels:
mean(as.numeric(as.character(age)))       # 35.5
mean(as.numeric(levels(age))[age])        # 35.5, and faster on large data
The second form is worth reading carefully: levels(age) is the character vector of labels, as.numeric turns it into numbers, and indexing it by the factor itself uses the integer codes to pick the right label for each observation.
The real lesson is upstream of all this. A number stored as a factor is a symptom that something went wrong when the data was read—usually a stray "n/a", "-", or "unknown" sitting in a numeric column, which forced the whole column to be read as text. Fix the import rather than patching the column afterwards, and check str() on every data frame the moment you read it in.











 Exercise: recover the years





year is a factor that should have been a number. Return the mean year as an ordinary number.
If your answer is under 10, you have found the trap rather than avoided it.















mean(as.numeric(as.character(year)))
or mean(as.numeric(levels(year))[year]), which converts each level once rather than each observation.
The failure mode here is not that the wrong answer is hard to spot—2.8 is obviously not a year. It is that in a real analysis the column would be a rating, or a count, or a price, and 2.8 would look entirely reasonable.

title: An R Refresher
text:
Data frames
A data frame is a list of equal-length vectors presented as a table: one column per variable, one row per observation. It is the object almost every analysis in this course operates on.








Note what str() told you: program is chr, not a factor. Since R 4.0 data.frame() and read.csv() leave strings as character by default. Older code and older tutorials assume the opposite, which is worth knowing when you read an example that behaves strangely.
The everyday moves:








Rows are selected with a logical vector in the first position, and this is how nearly all subsetting gets done:








Careful with NA in the condition. If the column you filter on has missing values, the logical vector has NAs, and those become rows of all-NA in the result rather than being dropped:








That phantom row is a genuine hazard: it inflates your row count, and it will survive into a summary as an extra observation with no data in it. subset() handles this for you, and is worth knowing for interactive work:








Adding and modifying columns:








And two summaries that will carry you through Describing a Single Variable:








tapply splits a vector by a grouping factor and applies a function to each piece. aggregate does the same with a formula interface, and note that it drops the NA row silently—another reason to know your missing-value counts before you summarize.






A note on the tidyverse





You have very likely seen dplyr code: students %>% filter(program == "MS") %>% summarize(mean(score, na.rm = TRUE)). It is more readable than the base equivalents above, and we will use it from S.M.A.R.T. Questions onward for real work.
The reason this chapter is base R is that base subsetting is what error messages, help pages, other people’s code, and every AI assistant’s fallback are written in. Being fluent in [ is not nostalgia; it is what lets you debug the tidyverse when it surprises you.









 Exercise: a group mean with a hole in it





Return the mean score among students in the "MS" program. One MS student has no recorded score.
Then—this part is not graded, but do it—decide whether the number you produced is the mean score of MS students, or the mean score of MS students whose score was recorded, and whether the difference could matter.















mean(students$score[students$program == "MS"], na.rm = TRUE)
mean(subset(students, program == "MS")$score, na.rm = TRUE) is equivalent, and tapply(students$score, students$program, mean, na.rm = TRUE)[["MS"]] gets there via the grouped summary.
The un-graded half of the question is the one that matters. 87.25 is the mean of four scores, not five. Whether that is fine depends on why the fifth is missing—and why is a question about the world, which no function will answer for you.

title: An R Refresher
text:
Lists
A list can hold anything, of any type, at any length. It is what you get back from most modeling functions.








The [ versus [[ distinction is the one to remember. Single brackets keep the container; double brackets reach inside it. When a piece of code fails with something like “non-numeric argument to binary operator” on a value you are certain is numeric, you have usually got a one-element list where you wanted a number.

title: An R Refresher
text:
Functions
A function in R is an ordinary object. It returns the value of its last expression, so an explicit return() is optional and mostly used for early exits.








Three things worth stating.
Arguments can be matched by position or by name, and named arguments can come in any order. Once past the first argument or two, name them—round(x, digits = 2) is clearer than round(x, 2) and immune to a change in argument order.
Defaults are evaluated inside the function, so a default can refer to another argument. This is how na.rm = FALSE above works.
Assignment inside a function is local. A function cannot change an object in your global environment by assigning to it:








This is a feature. It means a function’s effect is entirely in what it returns, which is what makes functions safe to reuse. (<<- exists and can reach outward. Do not use it in this course.)






 Exercise: write a small function





The coefficient of variation is the standard deviation divided by the mean—a measure of spread on a scale you can compare across variables with different units.
Fill in the body so that cv() computes it and ignores missing values. The cell ends with a call, so the exercise is checked on the value that call produces.















cv <- function(x) {
  sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}
giving about 0.455. No return() is needed: the last expression evaluated is the value of the function.
A better version would take na.rm as an argument with a default rather than deciding for the caller—hard-wiring na.rm = TRUE inside a function silently discards data on everyone who uses it.

title: An R Refresher
text:
Control flow, briefly
Explicit loops are much rarer in R than in most languages, because vectorised operations cover most of what a loop would do. When you do need them:








Using if where you meant ifelse is a classic error. In current R, if with a condition of length greater than one is an error; in older versions it silently used only the first element, which is why you will find code in the wild that was quietly wrong for years.
And when a loop is genuinely the clearest thing:








Note seq_along, and note that the result vector was allocated first. Growing a vector inside a loop with c() works but is slow and, more importantly, hides how long the answer is supposed to be.






Summary






There are no scalars; everything is a vector, and arithmetic is element-wise.
Vectors hold one type. Mixing types coerces silently along logical → integer → double → character. One bad string turns a numeric column into text.
Recycling repeats the shorter vector. When lengths divide evenly there is no warning, and a wrong answer comes out full-length.
Indexing is 1-based; x[0] returns nothing rather than erroring; ranges include both endpoints; negative indices drop. Use seq_along(x), never 1:length(x).
NA means unknown and propagates. == NA is always NA—use is.na(). %in% never returns NA. na.rm = TRUE changes the quantity you are estimating, so report how many you dropped.
A factor is codes plus levels. as.numeric() on a factor gives the codes; go through as.character(). Filtering does not drop unused levels.
Data frames are lists of equal-length columns. A filter on a column containing NA produces phantom all-NA rows unless you guard it.
[ keeps the container, [[ reaches inside.
A function returns its last expression; assignment inside it is local.




Next: Reproducibility: RMarkdown and Git. Then Practice Problems, which is where you find out how much of this chapter actually stuck.

title: Plotting with ggplot2
text:
Three things, every time
The other chapters in this part draw with base R—hist, boxplot, plot, barplot—because those functions are always there and every cell runs instantly. They are fine for looking. They are poor for building, and they are not what you will be asked to use in a job.
ggplot2 is the standard in the R world. This chapter is the working minimum: enough to build the figures the rest of the course needs, and one idea—faceting— that turns out to be the answer to the hardest problem in the previous chapter.
Every ggplot answers three questions, and the syntax is just those three questions in order.
Read that as a sentence: take d, let hours be horizontal position and score be vertical position, and draw a point for each row.
The aes() call is the part worth slowing down on. It does not set a color or a size—it says which column controls a color or a size. That distinction is the single most common source of confusion for people arriving from base R.
If a legend appears when you did not want one, you set inside aes() when you meant outside. If a legend is missing when you needed one, the reverse.

title: Plotting with ggplot2
text:
What data? — ggplot(data = df)
Which column plays which visual role? — aes(x = ..., y = ..., color = ...)
What marks on the page? — + geom_point(), + geom_col(), + geom_histogram()

title: Plotting with ggplot2
text:
Layers add
The + builds a stack. Each layer draws on what came before, and they share the mapping declared at the top unless a layer overrides it.








labs() is not decoration. An axis labeled hours tells the reader nothing about units; a figure with no title makes the reader guess your claim. Both are graded in your project.

title: Plotting with ggplot2
text:
Faceting is the important idea
facet_wrap() splits one plot into a grid of small plots, one per level of a variable. It costs a single line, and it is the reason this chapter exists.
Recall the trial from Visualization That Does Not Mislead: treatment A beats B among small stones and beats B among large stones, and yet loses when the two are pooled.








Now the same numbers, split:








One line—facet_wrap(~ size)—and the reversal is visible rather than argued.
That is the general lesson, and it is worth more than the syntax: when an aggregate looks surprising, the first move is to break it apart. Simpson’s paradox is not a curiosity that needs detecting by arithmetic. It is what a small multiple shows you immediately, and the reason it goes unnoticed is that nobody drew the small multiple.
Faceting is also how you avoid the dual-axis trap from the previous chapter. Two series on incompatible scales do not need two axes; they need two panels.






 Exercise: one panel per department





Draw score against hours as points, in a separate panel for each department. Complete the plot below.


















facet_wrap(~ dept)
The tilde marks a formula, which here means “split by this”. facet_wrap lays the panels out in a strip that wraps; facet_grid(rows ~ cols) gives you a true two-way grid when you have two splitting variables.
Note what the panels share: the same x-axis and the same y-axis. That is the default, and it is doing real work—panels on different scales cannot be compared by eye, which defeats the purpose.

title: Plotting with ggplot2
text:
Seeing missingness
Where the Data Came From argued that the pattern of missing values matters more than the count. A plot shows the pattern in a way a count never will.








tenure is speckled—missing here and there, no pattern, consistent with MCAR. income is missing in blocks, and the blocks are not random: they are the young respondents. That is the visual signature of MAR, and it is also the good news, because age is a column you have.








A plot that sends you to a number, and a number that confirms the plot. That is the whole method.






 Exercise: inside or outside?





You want every point drawn in red, with no legend. One of these is right. Assign its letter, for example answer <- "A".















B.
A and C map color to the string "red" as though it were data. ggplot2 obliges: it treats the string as a variable with one level, assigns that level its default first color—which is not red—and adds a legend explaining the variable you did not have. The plot comes out pink with a redundant key, which is how you recognize this mistake in the wild.
Inside aes() means “a column decides this”. Outside means “I decide this”.

title: Plotting with ggplot2
text:
What else you will need
You now have enough for most of the course. Four things are worth knowing exist, to be looked up when needed:

scale_* — control axes and color scales. scale_y_continuous(limits =) is how you make the honest choices from the previous chapter deliberate.
theme_* — theme_minimal() alone makes a figure look considered.
geom_col versus geom_bar — col plots values you already computed; bar counts rows for you. Choosing the wrong one is a common silent error.
ggsave() — writes a figure at a size and resolution you specify, rather than whatever your screen happened to be.

Two packages worth installing locally, neither needed here:

GGally::ggpairs(df) — every pairwise scatterplot, correlation and marginal distribution in one figure. The standard first look at a new numeric dataset.
naniar::vis_miss(df) — the missingness map above, without the reshaping.







Check yourself






What is the difference between color = "blue" inside aes() and outside it, and how would you recognize the mistake from the figure alone?
Why is facet_wrap a better answer to Simpson’s paradox than recomputing the pooled rate?
Why do faceted panels share their axis scales by default, and when would you override that?
Your missingness map shows one column missing in blocks aligned with a second column. Which mechanism does that suggest, and what does it let you do?

title: Plotting with ggplot2
text:
Where this goes next
Use ggplot2 for your project from here on. The figures in Practice Problems and in the rest of the course are still base R so that they load quickly, but nothing in them is base-specific—every idea about axes, binning, aggregation and honesty transfers directly, and only the syntax changes.
When we reach modeling, geom_smooth(method = "lm") stops being a decoration and becomes the thing under discussion.

title: Reproducibility: RMarkdown and Git
text:
The two-computer test
Here is the claim this chapter rests on, and it is stronger than it sounds.
An analysis that nobody can rerun is not evidence. It is a report of what somebody says happened on their laptop. It may well be correct; you have no way of finding out, and neither do they.
That is not a moral point about honesty. It is a point about what evidence is. A result becomes evidence when somebody who does not already believe you can follow the path from the data to the number and see for themselves where it came from. If the path exists only as a sequence of clicks, or half in a script and half in a console session that ended in July, there is nothing to follow.
This bears directly on your grade. Forty percent of it is two team projects, each delivering a GitHub repository, and the repository is not packaging around the deliverable—it is part of the deliverable. It is also where the practical trouble lives. Every previous cohort has had at least one team lose a night to two people editing the same analysis, one of them overwriting the other, and neither able to say what the file looked like on Tuesday.
Both problems—“can it be rerun?” and “which version is real?”—have standard solutions, and you can learn the working minimum of both this week.
The test is simple enough to apply honestly:
Nothing else. No email from you explaining that you have to run clean.R first. No “oh, you need the version of the file with the fix in it.” No step that exists only in somebody’s head.
Most beginner analyses fail this test on one of four things:
The first two are R, RStudio, and Your Environment. The third is why raw data is read-only and cleaning happens in code. The fourth is this chapter.

title: Reproducibility: RMarkdown and Git
Reproducibility: RMarkdown and Git
text:
RMarkdown
An RMarkdown document interleaves prose and code in one file, and knitting it runs the code and produces a finished document with the results embedded. The value is not convenience. It is that the numbers in your report are computed by the document rather than typed into it.
A minimal document:
---
title: "Ridership on the Red Line"
author: "Team 4"
output: html_document
---

## Data

We use three years of tap-in records.

```{r}
rides <- read.csv("data/rides.csv")
nrow(rides)
```

The dataset has `r nrow(rides)` observations.
Three parts. The YAML header between the --- fences sets the title and output format. The prose is ordinary Markdown. The chunks, fenced with ```{r}, are R code that runs when you knit.
The last line is the one to look at. `r nrow(rides)` is inline code: when the document is knitted, that is replaced by the actual number. If you clean two more rows out next week, the sentence updates itself.
Compare it with typing “The dataset has 48,213 observations.” That sentence is correct exactly once. Every subsequent edit to the pipeline is an opportunity for the prose and the analysis to drift apart, silently, and they will. Never type a computed number into your prose. This is the single highest-value habit in the chapter, and it costs nothing.

Chunk options
Options go after the r in the chunk header, or on #| lines beneath it. The ones you will actually use:







Option
Effect




echo = FALSE
run the code, hide the code, show the output


eval = FALSE
show the code, do not run it


include = FALSE
run it, show nothing—for setup chunks


message = FALSE
suppress package startup chatter


warning = FALSE
suppress warnings (think before you use this)


fig.cap = "..."
caption a figure



A word about warning = FALSE. It is the right choice for a chunk whose warnings you have read, understood, and decided are noise—library() telling you about masked objects, say.
