It is a very poor choice as a reflex, because R, RStudio, and Your Environment established that warnings are the dangerous category: they hand you a compromised value and let you carry on. Suppressing them by default is how a coerced column full of NAs reaches a finished report.


Knitting runs in a fresh session
This is the mechanism that makes RMarkdown worth using, and it is worth being explicit about.
When you press Knit, RStudio starts a brand-new R session, runs the document top to bottom in it, and throws it away. That session cannot see your Environment pane. It has none of your loaded packages, none of your console objects, none of the three hours of accumulated state your interactive session is carrying.
So a document that knits is a document that stands on its own. A document that only works in your session is one whose results nobody can check, including you in six weeks.
The corollary is a workflow rule: knit early and knit often. Not once, at the end, in a panic. If you have worked for two hours without knitting, you do not currently know whether your analysis runs.






 Why Knit Fails When the Chunks Work







Your RMarkdown analysis prints all the right numbers when you run every chunk by hand in RStudio. When you press Knit, it fails with object 'clean' not found.
You are certain clean exists—it is in your Environment pane right now. What is going on?

Knitting is stricter about variable names and requires objects to be declared before use.Knitting runs the document in a fresh R session, so it sees only what the document itself creates; clean was made in your console or by a chunk you have since deleted or set to eval = FALSE.The Environment pane is shared with the knit process, so this indicates the object was corrupted.You need to add cache = TRUE so that objects persist between chunks.



Knitting starts a brand-new R session and runs the document top to bottom in it.
That is not an inconvenience. It is the single most valuable thing RMarkdown does for you. Your interactive session accumulates history—objects you made in the console, a chunk you ran before editing it, a package you loaded three hours ago, a variable from a completely different project. Any of those can be silently holding your analysis up. The knit session has none of it, so the document either stands on its own or it does not.
A document that knits is a document somebody else can reproduce. A document that only works in your session is a document whose results nobody, including you next month, can check.
The other answers misunderstand the mechanism. Knitting is not “stricter” about names—it runs ordinary R. The Environment pane belongs to your interactive session and the knit process cannot see it, which is the whole point. And cache = TRUE makes things worse here: caching stores chunk output so chunks are skipped on later knits, which introduces exactly the kind of stale state you were trying to escape. Caching is for expensive computations you have already verified, and it is a source of bugs, not a fix for them.
The habit: knit early and knit often, not once at the end. If a document has not been knitted in two hours of work, you do not know whether it still runs.











Caching is not a fix





cache = TRUE stores a chunk’s results so it is skipped on later knits. It is meant for genuinely expensive computations you have already verified.
It is also a reliable way to reintroduce exactly the stale state you were escaping: you change a data-cleaning chunk, the downstream cached chunk does not re-run, and your report mixes old results with new. If a knit ever produces something you cannot explain, delete the _cache directory before you debug anything else.





Randomness needs a seed
Any analysis involving simulation, resampling, random splits, or bootstrapping produces different numbers each run—and from Probability onward, that is most of them. set.seed() fixes the generator’s starting point so the sequence is repeatable:








Set the seed once near the top of the document. Do not sprinkle set.seed() before every random call—that produces a document whose results are stable for a bad reason, and it makes it very easy to accidentally reuse one draw.
And do not choose the seed by trying several until the result looks good. That is a real practice with a real name, and it is fabrication.






 Exercise: reproduce a colleague’s numbers





A teammate reports that their bootstrap produced -0.439 -0.645 1.132. Their chunk was:
round(rnorm(3), 3)
and above it, somewhere in the document, they had set the seed to 6101.
Write code that reproduces their three numbers exactly.















set.seed(6101)
round(rnorm(3), 3)
Note what this does and does not guarantee. It guarantees the same numbers from the same R on any machine. It does not make the result right—a bootstrap with a bug in it reproduces its bug perfectly.










 Exercise: a sentence that updates itself





Your methods section needs a line reporting how many rows were dropped. Someone typed it by hand and it is already out of date.
Build the string from the objects, so that it is correct whatever they contain. It must read exactly:
Dropped 43 of 1200 rows (3.6%).
with the percentage to one decimal place.















sprintf("Dropped %d of %d rows (%.1f%%).", dropped, total, 100 * dropped / total)
%% is how you get a literal percent sign in sprintf. paste0("Dropped ", dropped, " of ", total, " rows (", round(100 * dropped / total, 1), "%).") works too and is uglier.
In an actual RMarkdown document you would not build the string at all—you would write the sentence in prose with `r dropped` and `r total` embedded in it.










 Exercise: make the chunk stand alone





Your report’s methods section says:

We restricted the analysis to respondents aged 18 or over with a recorded income.

The chunk that does this was written in a console session where an object called keep already existed, so it errors on knit. Rewrite it so it stands on its own, and return the number of rows kept.
Look at dat before you write anything. Two of its columns have missing values, and only one of them is mentioned in the methods sentence.















keep <- !is.na(dat$age) & dat$age >= 18 & !is.na(dat$income)
sum(keep)
nrow(dat[keep, ]) gives the same answer, and nrow(subset(dat, !is.na(age) & age >= 18 & !is.na(income))) is the tidier interactive form.
The reproducibility lesson and the correctness lesson are the same lesson here. Defining keep inside the document is what makes the chunk runnable by anyone. Writing the is.na guards is what makes the number it reports true. A chunk that runs in a fresh session and reports 6 is reproducibly wrong—which is better than irreproducibly wrong, but only because now somebody can catch it.

title: Reproducibility: RMarkdown and Git
section: Git, in the amount you need
text:
Git, in the amount you need
Git is a version control system. The mental model that makes it click:
A Git repository is a sequence of labeled snapshots of your whole project, not a backup of one file. Each snapshot—a commit—records the state of every tracked file, who made it, when, and a message saying why. You can return to any of them, compare any two, and see who changed what.
Three places matter, and confusion between them causes most beginner frustration:








Place
What it is
How things get there




Working directory
your files, as they are right now
you edit them


Staging area
changes selected for the next commit
git add


Repository
the committed history
git commit



And a fourth, elsewhere: the remote (GitHub), which you sync with using git push and git pull.

The loop
Ninety percent of your Git use this semester is five commands, in this order.
git pull                         # get your teammates' work BEFORE you start
# ... edit files, run your analysis ...
git status                       # what have I changed?
git add report.Rmd R/clean.R     # stage what belongs in this commit
git commit -m "drop 43 rows with impossible ages"
git push                         # send it to GitHub
Getting started, once per project:
git clone https://github.com/your-team/project-1.git
RStudio has a Git pane that does all of this with buttons, and you are welcome to use it. Learn what the buttons correspond to anyway, because the error messages are written in the command-line vocabulary.


Commit messages, and commit size
A commit message is written for a stranger—which includes you, in November, trying to find where a number changed.
Bad:   "update", "fixes", "asdf", "final", "final2"
Good:  "drop 43 rows with impossible ages (>120)"
       "add logistic model for the readmission outcome"
       "fix: severity was pooled in the group means"
Commit when you finish a coherent piece of work, not on a schedule and not once at the end. A single "final" commit throws away everything a history is for; you have a zip file with extra steps. Ten small commits let you say exactly when a result changed and why.


What does not go in
Git keeps every version of everything, forever. That has two consequences.
Large data files bloat the repository permanently. Deleting the file later does not shrink the history. Commit the script that reads or fetches the data, which is the reproducible part, and keep the data itself out unless it is small.
A committed secret is a leaked secret. An API key or password committed once lives in the history even after you delete the file. If it happens, rotate the credential; do not simply delete it and hope.
Both are handled by a .gitignore file at the project root, listing what Git should never track:
.Rhistory
.RData
.Rproj.user/
*_cache/
data/raw/*.csv
.env
Also skip .Rhistory and .RData for the reason in R, RStudio, and Your Environment: they are session state, and session state is what you are trying to escape.


Conflicts are normal
When two people change the same lines and both push, Git refuses to guess and marks the file:
<<<<<<< HEAD
mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
=======
median(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
>>>>>>> feature-branch
This is not an error and not a disaster. It is Git declining to make a decision that is yours. Open the file, decide which version is right (or write a third), delete all three marker lines, save, git add, git commit.
The way to have fewer of them is procedural: pull before you start working, and commit small. Most conflicts come from three hours of work built on a version that went stale in the first ten minutes.


Branches, lightly
For your projects you can get a long way with everyone committing to main and pulling often. It is worth knowing the alternative exists:
git checkout -b add-logistic-model    # start a branch
# ... work, commit ...
git push -u origin add-logistic-model
then open a pull request on GitHub so a teammate reads the change before it joins main. That review step is where a lot of bad analysis gets caught in practice, and it is a reasonable thing for a team to adopt on the project once the basic loop is comfortable.






 A Team Workflow That Survives the Deadline







Your project team is about to start Project 1. Which working arrangement is the one to adopt?

Each person keeps their own copy and emails the analysis file around; whoever has the newest version merges everything by hand at the end.Everyone commits small, self-describing changes and pulls before starting work; the raw data and any credentials stay out of the repository, listed in .gitignore.One person owns the repository and pushes; everybody else sends them code to paste in, so the history stays clean.Commit everything—data, output, .Rhistory, .RData—in one large commit at the end, so nothing is lost.



Small, self-describing commits; pull before you start; data and secrets out of the repository.
Take the pieces in turn.
Small commits. A commit is a labeled snapshot of the whole project, not a backup of one file. Its value is that you can say what changed and why, and can go back to any point. One commit at the end—"final"—destroys that value entirely; you have a zip file with extra steps. Commit when you finish a coherent piece of work, with a message a stranger could read: "drop 43 rows with impossible ages", not "fixes".
Pull before you start. Most merge conflicts are caused by working for three hours on top of a version that is already stale. Pulling first is a fifteen-second habit that prevents most of them. And when a conflict does happen, it is not a failure—it is Git telling you two people edited the same lines and it will not guess which one you meant. Open the file, delete the markers, keep the right code, commit.
Data and secrets out. Large data files bloat the repository permanently, because Git keeps every version of everything forever. An API key or password committed once is in the history even after you delete the file, and must be treated as leaked. .gitignore is where you list what never goes in: .Rhistory, .RData, *.csv if the data is large, anything with a credential in it. Commit the script that fetches or reads the data instead—that is the reproducible part.
Why the other arrangements fail: emailing files gives you no history, no record of who changed what, and a hand-merge at 2 a.m. before the deadline. A single gatekeeper is a bottleneck, and it also means the history credits one person for everybody’s work—which matters here, because in this course each team member answers questions individually about the project.

title: Reproducibility: RMarkdown and Git
section: What this buys you in the projects
text:
What this buys you in the projects
Concretely, for the team project that makes up a fifth of your grade:

The repository is a deliverable. I will clone it. If it does not run, that is a finding about the analysis, not a technicality.
The history shows who did what. Each team member answers questions individually about the project, so members of one team can receive different grades. A history in which one person made every commit tells a story, and it is rarely the story that team wants told.
Your report’s numbers come from your code. No typed figures, no screenshots of output. If the cleaning changes, the report changes.
Your AI disclosure has to be true. Which is much easier when the history shows what was written when.
You can go back. Somebody will break the analysis two days before the presentation. With a history, that is a ten-minute problem.

None of this requires you to be a Git expert. It requires pull, add, commit, push, and the discipline to write a message somebody else can read.






Summary






An analysis nobody can rerun is not evidence. Apply the two-computer test: could a stranger reproduce every number from the repository alone?
Reproducibility is not correctness—it is the precondition for anyone, including you, being able to check correctness.
RMarkdown puts prose and code in one file so that reported numbers are computed, not typed. Use inline code; never type a computed number into a paragraph.
Knitting runs the document in a fresh session, which is exactly why it catches the hidden state your console hides. Knit early and often.
warning = FALSE and cache = TRUE both hide things you may need to see. Use them deliberately, not by reflex.
set.seed() once, near the top, for anything random. Choosing a seed for the result it gives is fabrication.
A commit is a labeled snapshot of the whole project. The loop is pull, edit, status, add, commit, push.
Keep large data and every credential out of the repository, via .gitignore. Git forgets nothing.
Conflicts are normal and mean Git is refusing to guess. Pull before you start and commit small, and you will have few.




Next: Practice Problems. Bring your answers, and your disagreements, to Monday.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Predicting output
Work these before Aug 24. Nothing here is auto-graded and nothing here is collected—these are the raw material for Monday’s discussion, and several of them are worth arguing about.
Bring at least one of these to class with a question attached. “I do not understand why Problem 9 gives 5” is exactly the kind of thing Monday’s first twenty minutes is for.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Problem 1: coercion





Write down the value and the type of each expression before running anything. Then uncomment them one at a time.








For the last two: why does one of them answer “how many” and the other “what proportion”, when they are applied to the same vector?









 Problem 2: recycling





Predict all four results, including any warnings. One of the four is the dangerous case discussed in An R Refresher; say which and why it is the dangerous one.

















 Problem 3: indexing





x has eight elements. Predict the length of each result first, then its contents.








The last two return things of different lengths for quite different reasons. Explain both. The very last one is recycling appearing somewhere you may not have expected it.









 Problem 4: the empty vector





A filter has removed everything. Predict what each line prints, and then say what a for loop over each would do.








sum and mean of nothing disagree with each other. Is either of them wrong? Defend your answer—this one is worth arguing about on Monday.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Missing values






 Problem 5: what NA does





Predict each, then run.








The last two are the surprising ones and they are not arbitrary. NA & FALSE is FALSE and NA | TRUE is TRUE. Work out why, thinking about what NA means, and then predict NA & TRUE.









 Problem 6: this runs and is still wrong





The analyst wants the mean age of respondents who consented. The cell runs, prints a plausible age, and is wrong.








Start by printing survey$consent == "yes" and comparing it, entry by entry, with the column. Two respondents who plainly consented are being excluded, for two different reasons, neither of which is visible when you look at the data on screen.
Fix it, and you should get 38 rather than 31.5—a difference large enough to change a conclusion.
Then two questions that are not about code:

Respondent 5’s consent is missing. The code silently treats “we do not know” as “no”. Is that the right decision here? What would make it the wrong one?
Your corrected figure of 38 is the mean of how many ages? Write the one sentence that should accompany the number in a report.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Factors






 Problem 7: a plausible number





This is the most dangerous bug in the week, because the output looks entirely reasonable.








The true mean rating is 31/8 = 3.875. Predict what the cell actually prints before you run it, then explain where that number came from and recover the right one.
Now the part that matters: this is a rating out of 5, and the wrong answer is also a number between 1 and 5. Suppose this figure reached a slide deck. What in your workflow would have caught it? Name a specific check, not “be careful”.









 Problem 8: a category with nobody in it





Predict the output of both table() calls.








Then say where this would first become visible in a real analysis, and why a bar chart makes it more embarrassing than a table does.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Data frames






 Problem 9: count the rows





Predict nrow() for each of the three subsets before running. Two of the three agree; one does not.








Then print the first subset rather than counting it. What are those extra rows made of, and where would they cause damage downstream?









 Problem 10: this runs and is still wrong





Each group’s mean score, as a proportion of the overall mean. The code runs and produces two plausible numbers.








Say precisely what quantity the second line computes, why it is not what was asked for, and fix it. Then explain why this bug would survive a test on data where both groups happened to have the same mean.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Reasoning about the claim
The problems above are about code. These are about what the output entitles you to say, which is the harder half and the one the checkpoint discussion will be built on.






 Problem 11: what does this license?





A colleague reports: “Students who attended the optional review session scored 8.75 points higher on the final. The review sessions work.”
Run the cell for the arithmetic, which is correct.








Now list every reason the second sentence might not follow from the first. Aim for at least four, and make them specific to this situation rather than generic. Then answer the harder question: what evidence would you need to say “work”?









 Problem 12: the reversal





Return to the procedure comparison from What Data Science Is. A hospital administrator says: “The subgroup analysis is cherry-picking. Use all 2,100 patients.”








Write the reply. It needs to do two things: explain why using all the patients does not make the comparison fair, and say what would have made the administrator’s objection a good one—because there is a version of “you split the data until you found something” that is a completely legitimate criticism.









 Problem 13: the summary that hides the data





Two pairs of variables, both with a correlation close to 1.








You get about 1.00 and 0.95. On that evidence alone the two relationships look comparably strong. Before plotting, say what you expect each to look like. Then plot both.








Recompute cor(xb, yb) with the tenth point removed. What is the general lesson, and what is the specific habit it implies for every correlation you report this semester?

title: Practice Problems
text:
Reproducibility






 Problem 14: find the four





This chunk appears at the top of a teammate’s RMarkdown report. It knits on their machine. Find four separate reasons it will not knit on yours, and give the fix for each.
install.packages("ggplot2")
library(ggplot2)
setwd("C:/Users/alex/Documents/DATS 6101/project")
dat <- read.csv("survey_cleaned_v3_FINAL.csv")
dat <- dat[dat$age < 120, ]
boot_mean <- mean(sample(dat$income, 500, replace = TRUE))
Then a fifth thing, which is not a knitting problem at all: the fourth line silently changes what population the report describes, and the report does not say so. What sentence is missing?









 Problem 15: two seeds





Predict which of these three lines match each other.








Now the question worth arguing about. A teammate says: “I tried seeds 1 through 20 and seed 14 gave the cleanest result, so I used that one.”
What exactly is wrong with this, and how is it different from the perfectly legitimate practice of setting a seed at all? Where is the line—and is “I ran it once with seed 1 and reported it” on the right side of it?

title: Practice Problems
text:
Bringing it together






 Problem 16: a small analysis, honestly reported





Eight respondents, two variables, one messy column. Get to a defensible statement.








Do the following, in order, and write one sentence at each step saying what you decided and why.

hours came in as text. Convert it, and say how many values you lost.
Compute the mean score in each group.
Compute the difference between the two group means.
Now write the sentence you would put in a report. It should contain the difference, the sample size behind it, and at least one thing the analysis does not establish.

Step 4 is the whole exercise. With four respondents per group, be honest about what a difference of this size tells you—and note that you have not yet been taught the tool that would tell you how much of it could be noise. That tool arrives in September. Saying so is the correct answer for now, and it is a better answer than a confident one.









Before Monday






Post at least one question on the reading, on whichever chapter page raised it, by Monday noon.
Have R and RStudio installed, and a GitHub account created.
Bring your answer to Problem 4, Problem 12, or Problem 15. Those three have no single correct answer and are what the reasoning block is for.
If you got stuck on setup and could not fix it, come anyway and come early. The lab this week is ungraded, and unsticking your machine is exactly what it is for.

title: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them
text:
What is here
Read this part after Monday, August 24. It carries no deadline and no reading questions—post whenever something does not come right, and it gets picked up in office hours or at the start of a session.
The R Primer covers the machinery—R, RStudio, Git, and what this field is for—and runs at your own pace alongside the course. This part is about the two things that actually decide whether a data science project is any good, and neither of them is a model.
The first is the question. Almost every project that goes badly went badly here, in the first week, when somebody wrote down something that sounded like a research question but was not one—because it could not be measured, or because no achievable dataset contained the thing it asked about, or because it had no particular answer that would count as the answer. You cannot fix that later with a better regression. S.M.A.R.T. Questions and The Data Science Life Cycle are about writing a question you can be wrong about, and about the fact that the work loops back and rewrites that question rather than marching forward from it.
The second is the data, in the condition it actually arrives in. Real files have a stray metadata line above the header. Real columns hold -999 where a measurement was not taken, and N/A and n/a and an empty cell in the same column meaning three different things. Real categories are north, North, and NORTH. Real joins drop a third of your rows and tell you nothing. Importing Data and Cleaning and Reshaping are about getting a file into R and finding out what you actually got, before you trust it. Where the Data Came From then asks the question the mechanics cannot: who never made it into the file at all.

title: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them
section: Why this part carries more weight than it looks like it does
text:
Why this part carries more weight than it looks like it does
A fifth of your grade is a team project, proposed and defended on exactly what S.M.A.R.T. Questions asks you to do. The proposal is one page and it is mostly a question. When a project comes apart, the autopsy nearly always ends at that page.
The other half of the week is the part nobody puts in the highlight reel. Surveys of working data scientists put the share of project time spent finding, importing, and cleaning data somewhere between half and three quarters. That number is repeated so often it has become a cliché, and it is still roughly right. If you feel, in Cleaning and Reshaping, that you are doing tedious work rather than data science, the honest response is that this is data science, and the tedium is where most published mistakes come from.

title: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them
section: A theme for the whole week
text:
A theme for the whole week
Watch for the silent failure: the code that runs, returns a number, prints no warning, and is wrong. A join that dropped half your rows. A mean computed over a column of text. A sentinel value averaged in as though -999 were a blood pressure. R will not stop you. Errors are the easy case—an error is R doing you a favor. What you are training here is the instinct to check the things that do not announce themselves.

title: S.M.A.R.T. Questions
text:
The five words
Every data science project starts with somebody being interested in something. That is a good place to start and a terrible place to stay. “I’m interested in housing affordability” is an interest. It is not a question, because there is nothing you could compute that would settle it, and there is no result that would count as being wrong.
The gap between an interest and a question is where most student projects are won or lost. I want to be blunt about this, because it is not what people expect. When a project in this course goes badly, it is very rarely because the regression was misspecified or the plot used the wrong geometry. It is because in the first week somebody wrote a sentence that sounded like a research question, everybody nodded, and six weeks of work went into an activity that could not have produced an answer no matter how well it was executed.
S.M.A.R.T. is a checklist borrowed from project management, and like most checklists it is worth roughly what you put into it. Used lazily it is five words you attach to a question you had already decided on. Used properly it is five separate ways of catching yourself.
Specific. Who or what is being described, and over what population? “Do students who attend office hours do better?” leaves open which students, at which institution, in which course, and in which term. Each of those has to be decided before anyone can compute anything, and if you do not decide them, the data will decide for you and you will not notice.
Measurable. Every noun in the question has to correspond to something you can actually put in a column. “Better” is not measurable. “Final course grade out of 100” is. Notice that making a thing measurable is a substantive decision, not a clerical one: choosing final grade as your measure of “doing better” commits you to a particular and arguable claim about what doing better means, and an honest project says so rather than pretending the choice was obvious.
Achievable. Can you get the data, in the time you have, with the access you have? This is where most ambitious questions die, and it is worth separating two different failures. One is practical: the data exists but is behind an IRB, a paywall, or a six-week request queue. The other is deeper: no dataset of that kind could answer the question. If nobody randomly assigned people to use social media, then no amount of survey data will tell you what social media causes, and a question phrased in causal language is unachievable in principle rather than in practice.
Relevant. Would anyone act differently, or believe something different, depending on the answer? A question whose answer is already known, or whose answer nobody would use, is a fine exercise and a poor project. The test I like: write down both possible answers, and check that they are genuinely different worlds.
Time-bound. Two meanings, and both matter. The question needs a time window in it—“in Fall 2026”, “between 2010 and 2020”—because a relationship that holds in one decade need not hold in another, and a question without a window is quietly claiming to hold in all of them. And the project needs a time budget: you have until the proposal deadline, which is roughly five working weeks, most of which will go on things that are not modeling.
