title: S.M.A.R.T. Questions
text:
Before and after
Checklists are easier to believe once you have watched one do some work. Here are questions students have actually proposed, and what they became.






Example 1



Before. Is Twitter bad for mental health?
After. Among the 1,247 adult respondents to the 2023 wave of the National Health Interview Survey, is self-reported daily social media use (in minutes) associated with the PHQ-2 depression screening score, and how large is the association?


Look at what changed. “Twitter” became a variable that exists in a dataset somebody actually collected. “Bad for mental health” became a specific instrument with a known scale. The population and the year are named. And—this is the part students resist—“is bad for” became “is associated with”, because the data is observational and the honest verb is the weaker one. You have not made the question smaller by doing this. You have made it answerable, which the original was not.






Example 2



Before. We want to predict housing prices.
After. Using the 21,613 King County home sales from May 2014 to May 2015, how much of the variation in sale price is explained by square footage, number of bedrooms, and year built—and does adding location (zip code) improve prediction enough to matter?


The “before” is not a question, it is a genre. Every third project proposal in every data science course in the country is that sentence. The “after” commits to a dataset, a time window, a specific set of predictors, and a comparison that will have an answer. The word “matter” is still soft, and a good proposal would pin it down further: reduce out-of-sample RMSE by more than $15,000, say.






Example 3



Before. Does the minimum wage cause unemployment?
After. In the 12 months after New Jersey raised its minimum wage in April 1992, did fast-food employment in New Jersey change differently from fast-food employment in neighbouring Pennsylvania counties, where the wage was unchanged?


This one is instructive because the “before” is a real and important question that serious economists have argued about for forty years. It fails Achievable for you, this semester—not because it is stupid but because answering it requires a design that lets you say something causal. The “after” narrows to one policy change, one industry, one comparison region, and one window. That is roughly the design of a famous 1994 paper by Card and Krueger, and it is still argued about, which should tell you something about how hard the “before” version is.






Example 4



Before. We will analyze the Titanic dataset and see what we find.
After. Among the 891 passengers in the Kaggle Titanic training set, was passenger class associated with survival after accounting for sex and age, and is the class effect large enough to be visible within each sex separately?


“See what we find” is not a question, and it is the most common thing on a first draft. It is not that exploration is wrong—The Data Science Life Cycle has a whole stage for it—but exploration is what you do, not what you ask. If your proposal contains no sentence with a question mark that names two variables, you do not have a project yet.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: S.M.A.R.T. Questions
section: The tell-tale signs of a bad question
text:
The tell-tale signs of a bad question
Over the years the failures repeat, and they are recognizable from the outside.
A question with the word “best” in it usually has no answer: what is the best predictor of income? depends entirely on what you put in the candidate set, and the answer changes when you add a variable. A question with “impact”, “effect”, or “drives” in it is making a causal claim; ask yourself whether anything in the data design earns that verb, and if not, weaken the verb rather than hoping nobody notices. A question that could be answered by a single number with no comparison in it—what is the average salary of data scientists?—is a lookup, not an analysis. And a question you already know the answer to is not worth five weeks, however comfortable it feels.
The most useful move I know is this: write down the table you would need. Not the data you have—the table. One row per what? Which columns? Then go and see whether such a table exists. Half of all bad questions do not survive that exercise, and they die in ten minutes rather than in week four.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: S.M.A.R.T. Questions
section: Kicking the tires on a question
text:
Kicking the tires on a question
A question is a claim about what your data contains, and claims can be checked. Before you commit to one, check it against the actual file.
Suppose the question is: Among students enrolled in Fall 2026, is the number of office-hour visits associated with the final course grade? It sounds respectable. Here is the roster it would have to be answered from.








Five rows are from Fall 2026, which already makes the question thinner than it sounded. But the question needs visits as well, and visits is missing for much of the file. The number that matters is not how many Fall 2026 rows there are; it is how many Fall 2026 rows have a visit count at all.






Exercise: is the question achievable?



Count the rows that could actually contribute to the question—Fall 2026 and a non-missing visits value.

















sum(roster$term == "2026F" & !is.na(roster$visits))
Two rows. The question is not achievable on this data, and finding that out in ten seconds is worth a great deal more than finding it out in week four. Note that neither condition alone would have told you: five rows are Fall 2026, and six rows have a visit count, and only two are both.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: S.M.A.R.T. Questions
text:
Specific means naming the comparison
The other habit worth building is noticing when a question quietly fails to say what is being compared to what. “Do transit commuters have long commutes?” has no comparison in it, so the natural thing to compute is an average, and an average of one group answers nothing—long compared to what?








Thirty-five minutes. Thirty-five minutes is not an answer to anything, because the question never said what the alternative was. Sharpen it—do transit commuters spend more time commuting than car commuters?—and the quantity you want changes.






Exercise: compute what the sharpened question asks for



Return the difference in mean commute time, transit minus car, as a single number.

















m <- tapply(survey$minutes, survey$commute, mean)
unname(m["transit"] - m["car"])
17.5 minutes. tapply splits minutes by commute and applies mean to each piece, returning a named vector; unname strips the label so you are left with a bare number. Note also that 17.5 is a description of these eight people—what it licenses you to say about commuters in general is the subject of the whole Inference module, which opens with Probability.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: S.M.A.R.T. Questions
section: How this shows up in your grade
text:
How this shows up in your grade
The project—a fifth of the course—is proposed long before it is presented. The proposal is due Oct 19 and the presentation is in December, which gives you weeks to discover that the question you wrote is not answerable. The proposal is short, and it is mostly the question.
What I read for, in that order:

Is it a question? Does the document contain a sentence, with a question mark, naming a population, a time window, and at least two variables?
Does the data exist, and have you looked at it? Not “we plan to obtain”—have you loaded it, run str(), and counted the rows that survive the conditions your question imposes? The exercise above is the whole of this check.
What answer would count as no? If you cannot describe a result that would make you say “no, that is not there”, the question is not falsifiable and the project will end in a paragraph of hedging.
Is the verb honest? Causal language needs a design that earns it.

At the presentation, every team member answers questions individually, and one of the questions is always some version of what would have to be true for your conclusion to be wrong? A team that framed its question well finds that question easy. A team that did not spends the whole answer explaining what they meant.






The uncomfortable part



You will be tempted to pick the question that fits the dataset you already downloaded. Sometimes that is fine—it is called secondary analysis and half of published research works that way. It stops being fine when the question drifts silently to fit whatever the data happened to support, and the report is written as though that had been the plan all along. Changing your question is allowed and normal. Changing it without saying so is not.








 Check yourself







A team submits this project proposal: “We will study whether social media use affects mental health.” They have one semester and a single public survey dataset. Which revision is the strongest S.M.A.R.T. question?

Does social media use cause depression?Among the 1,247 adult respondents in the 2023 wave of this survey, is self-reported daily screen time associated with the PHQ-2 depression score, and how large is that association?Is social media bad for teenagers?We will explore every variable in the survey and report whatever patterns emerge.



The second one. It names the population (adult respondents in the 2023 wave), the sample size it is committing to, the two variables that will be measured (self-reported daily screen time, PHQ-2 score), and the quantity that will count as an answer (the size of the association). Someone else could take that sentence and know exactly what to compute.
The first fails Achievable: a survey that observes people rather than assigning them screen time cannot establish cause, so the question is one this data can never answer no matter how well the analysis is done. The third fails Measurable and Specific: “bad” is not a variable, and no row of the dataset is a teenager unless the survey happens to include them. The fourth is not a question at all—it is a plan to go looking, which is a fine thing to do in the exploration stage but leaves you with nothing to be right or wrong about.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: S.M.A.R.T. Questions
text:
Where this goes next
You now have a question. The next section is about what happens to it—which is that it does not survive contact with the data unchanged, and was never supposed to.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: The Data Science Life Cycle
text:
The stages, honestly
Textbooks draw the data science process as a row of boxes with arrows between them, left to right, and it looks like a factory line:
That picture is useful in exactly one way: it names the stages, and the stages are real. It is misleading in every other way, because the arrows go both directions and most of them go backwards. What actually happens is that you write a question, go looking for data, discover the data is not what you assumed, rewrite the question, clean what you have, discover during exploration that a whole subgroup is missing, rewrite the question again, model, find the model is answering something slightly different from what you asked, and write up the version of the question you ended with rather than the one you started with.
That is not a description of a project going wrong. That is a description of a project going right. The loop is the method.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: The Data Science Life Cycle
text:
Question
S.M.A.R.T. Questions. The thing to add here is that the question is the only stage you will revisit deliberately rather than by accident. Every other stage feeds information back into it: acquisition tells you what exists, cleaning tells you how much of it is usable, exploration tells you whether the pattern you were going to test is even plausible.


Acquire
Getting the data. Downloading a CSV is the easy version; the realistic versions involve an API with rate limits, a government portal that hands you 51 separate files with slightly different column names, a PDF that a human was clearly expected to read, or a colleague’s spreadsheet with the units in a merged cell.
Two things to record at this stage, always, and both take one minute: where it came from (URL, date accessed, version) and what one row means. The second sounds trivial until you have a file where you assumed one row was one patient and it turns out to be one patient-visit, at which point every count you have produced is wrong by a factor you cannot recover after the fact.


Clean
Importing Data and Cleaning and Reshaping, and the majority of your time. Missing values, sentinel values, duplicates, inconsistent categories, types that came in wrong, two tables that need joining and disagree about their keys.


Explore
Summaries and pictures, before any modeling. What is the distribution of each variable? Which pairs move together? Is anything impossible—negative ages, prices of zero, a date in 1900? This is exploratory analysis’s subject, and it is also where cleaning problems that survived the cleaning stage announce themselves, which is one of the backward arrows.


Model
Fitting something: a test, a regression, a classifier. This is the part that looks like data science in the recruiting brochure, and it is usually one afternoon. It is also the part an AI assistant can now do for you in about fifteen seconds, which is exactly why the rest of the loop is where your value is.


Communicate
A report, a plot, a presentation, a number in a meeting. The stage where you say what you found and what you did not find, and where the honest sentence about the 78% missing variable goes.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: The Data Science Life Cycle
text:
Where the time actually goes
Ask a working data scientist how their week broke down and the modeling is a rounding error. The widely quoted figure is that something like 50–80% of project time goes to finding, importing, and cleaning data. That statistic has been repeated so often it has become a cliché, and the specific number is softer than people pretend, but the shape of it is right and matches what you will experience.
A rough and honest allocation for a five-week course project:








Stage
Share of your time
What it feels like




Question and re-question
10%
Frustrating, and the highest-leverage 10%


Acquire
10%
Tedious, occasionally impossible


Clean
40%
Tedious, and where the mistakes come from


Explore
20%
Enjoyable, and where you learn the most


Model
10%
Fast, and the part everyone budgets for


Communicate
10%
Always underestimated



If your team’s plan allocates four weeks to modeling and three days to cleaning, the plan is wrong, and it will be wrong in the specific way that produces a presentation on the Sunday night before it is due.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: The Data Science Life Cycle
text:
The week-three discovery
Here is the situation this section exists for.
It is week three. Your question is fixed, your teammates have divided the work, and you finally sit down with the file to fit the model. You need three variables: price, sqft, and built. Individually each one looks fine—each is missing for only two or three rows out of twelve. Then you ask how many rows have all three.








Three missing prices, two missing areas, two missing build years, out of twelve rows. Nothing alarming. Now the number that matters:








Five. Not eleven, not nine—five, out of twelve. Missingness in different columns lands on different rows, so it accumulates, and it accumulates faster than anyone’s intuition. On a real file with eight predictors this is how a 50,000-row dataset becomes a 4,000-row dataset without anybody deciding that it should.






Exercise: how bad is the worst single column?



Return the largest number of missing values in any one column of housing.

















max(colSums(is.na(housing)))
Three. The gap between this number and the five surviving rows is the whole point: reporting per-column missingness is standard, comforting, and by itself misleading.







Exercise: what fraction of the data survives?



Return the proportion of rows that are complete on price, sqft, and built—a number between 0 and 1.

















mean(complete.cases(housing[, c("price", "sqft", "built")]))
Roughly 0.417. mean() of a logical vector is the proportion of TRUEs, because TRUE counts as 1—a small idiom worth keeping, since it turns any yes/no question about rows into a percentage in one call.
This is the number that belongs in your report, next to a sentence about who the seven missing homes were. If they are missing at random, dropping them costs you precision. If they are all the cheap ones, dropping them costs you the truth.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: The Data Science Life Cycle
section: What to do when the data cannot answer the question
text:
What to do when the data cannot answer the question
You will hit this. Somebody in your team will hit it in week three of Project 1. The variable is not there, or it is there and 80% empty, or it turns out to be self-reported when the question needed it measured, or the years you need are the years the agency stopped publishing.
The instinct is to feel that the project has failed and to start hiding it. Both halves of that instinct are wrong.
It is a finding. “The 2019–2023 county-level data cannot support a comparison of rural and urban outcomes, because rural counties are suppressed for privacy whenever the count is under ten, and 62% of rural counties are suppressed” is a genuine, reportable, useful result. Someone reading it now knows not to spend their own five weeks on the same road. Negative results about data are, if anything, more reusable than negative results about hypotheses.
Revising the question is the process, not an admission. The loop exists precisely so that what you learn in the cleaning stage can rewrite the question stage. What is not allowed is revising silently—presenting the new question as though it had always been the plan, with no mention of what you found. That is where a normal course correction turns into a misrepresentation.
A workable move, in order:

Quantify it. How many rows, exactly? Missing for whom? Is the missingness related to the outcome you care about?
Ask what question the surviving data can answer. Often it is a narrower version: one state instead of fifty, one year instead of a decade, an association instead of an effect.
Check that the narrower question is still Relevant. Sometimes it is not, and you should change datasets. That is allowed too.
Write down both. The report says what you asked, what you found out about the data, and what you asked instead. One paragraph. It costs you nothing and it is the difference between a project that reads as honest and one that reads as lucky.







In this course specifically



A project that reports “we could not answer our original question, here is precisely why, and here is the narrower question we answered instead” can earn full marks. A project that reports a clean result and turns out to have quietly dropped 60% of its rows to get there cannot. Every presentation includes individual questions, and how many rows did you start with and how many did you model on? is one I ask often.








 Check yourself







Three weeks into a project you discover that the variable your question depends on is missing for 78% of the rows, and that the rows where it is present are mostly from one large city. Which response is the honest one?

Impute the missing 78% from the observed 22% and proceed with the original question as written.Delete the incomplete rows, analyze the remaining 22%, and report the result as a finding about the full population.Revise the question to one the surviving data can actually answer, and report both the missingness and what it rules out.Quietly switch to a different dataset and present the project as though the first attempt never happened.



The third. The missingness is itself a result: you now know something true about the data that you did not know three weeks ago, and a reader deserves to know it too. Revising the question in response is the life cycle working as designed, not a failure of planning.
Imputing 78% of a variable means the analysis is mostly reporting your model of the missingness rather than anything the respondents said. Deleting the incomplete rows is sometimes reasonable, but describing what is left as a finding about the full population is false when the survivors are concentrated in one city—that is a claim about that city wearing a national label. Switching datasets silently is not wrong because switching is wrong; it is wrong because the discarded attempt is evidence, and hiding it is hiding evidence.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: The Data Science Life Cycle
text:
A note on version control
Because the loop revisits stages, the state of your analysis changes in ways that are hard to reconstruct from memory three weeks later. This is what Git is for, and it is why last week set it up before there was anything to commit. Commit after each stage, with a message that says what changed and why—“drop rows with suppressed rural counts; n falls 4,812 → 1,840” is a useful message, “update” is not. When you write the report, your commit history is the record of what you actually did, and it is much more reliable than anyone’s recollection.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: The Data Science Life Cycle
text:
Where this goes next
The next two sections are the cleaning stage in detail: getting a file into R (Importing Data), and finding out what is wrong with it (Cleaning and Reshaping).
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Importing Data
text:
The simplest possible import, and what it already got wrong
Importing looks like the least interesting thing in this course. One function call, one line, done. In practice it is where a surprising share of wrong analyses are born, because read.csv makes a series of guesses about your file—where the header is, what separates the fields, what each column’s type is, what counts as missing—and it does not tell you what it guessed. It just hands you a data frame that looks fine.
The discipline of this section is short and it is not negotiable: after every import, look at what you got, before you use it.
Here is a small file and a plain read.csv.
That looks perfect. It is not.
id came in as int, and the values are 7, 8, 9. The leading zeros are gone, permanently, and R did not consider this worth mentioning. If those ids are keys you later join on, or zip codes, or account numbers, or anything else where 007 and 7 are different strings in some other system, the damage is done at line one and shows up in week four as a join that silently drops rows.
The general shape of the problem: read.csv infers the type of each column from its contents. If every value in a column parses as a number, you get a number, and any information carried by the text form—leading zeros, a distinction between 01 and 1, a phone number’s formatting—is discarded.
You fix this by telling it what you want:
colClasses accepts a named vector, so you only have to name the columns you care about; everything else is still inferred. It is worth using for every identifier column in every file, as a reflex.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Importing Data
text:
What read.csv actually does
read.csv is read.table with some defaults pre-set. The ones worth knowing:



Argument
Default in read.csv
What it controls




header
TRUE
Is the first line column names?


sep
","
Field separator


quote
"\""
What wraps a field containing a comma


dec
"."
Decimal mark


na.strings
"NA"
Which text becomes NA


stringsAsFactors
FALSE
Do text columns become factors?


strip.white
FALSE
Trim spaces around unquoted fields


comment.char
""
Text after this is ignored


check.names
TRUE
Make column names syntactically valid


colClasses
NA
Force column types


skip
0
Lines to discard before the header


nrows
-1
Stop after this many rows


fileEncoding
""
Character encoding of the file



Two of these deserve their own paragraphs.

stringsAsFactors
Before R 4.0.0, released in April 2020, this defaulted to TRUE, and every text column silently became a factor—R’s type for a categorical variable, stored internally as integer codes plus a lookup table of levels. This caused so much grief that changing the default was one of the headline items in that release.
You are on a modern R, so text stays text and you may reasonably wonder why this matters. It matters for two reasons. First, a great deal of code and a great many Stack Overflow answers on the internet were written before 2020, and an AI assistant trained on that corpus will occasionally hand you code that assumes the old behavior. Second, factors have not gone anywhere—you will create them deliberately, and read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = TRUE) still exists—and the classic factor trap in Cleaning and Reshaping is one of the sharpest silent failures in R.


check.names
R makes column names syntactically valid by default, which means anything that is not a letter, digit, or dot becomes a dot, and names starting with a digit get an X in front.








Median Income ($) has become Median.Income...., which is ugly but usable. The reason to know about it is that check.names = FALSE preserves the originals, and you then have to refer to them with backticks, as in d$`Median Income ($)`, which is why most people accept the mangling and rename the columns explicitly instead:








Renaming to short, lower-case, underscore-separated names on import is a habit worth forming. It costs one line and it makes the next three weeks pleasant.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Importing Data
section: What a messy file actually looks like
text:
What a messy file actually looks like
Real exports are not four tidy lines. Here is a file of the sort that arrives from a survey platform or an agency portal: a couple of provenance lines above the header, a missing value written as N/A, and an empty cell.








Read that again. No error. No warning. A data frame with six rows and two columns, and a straight face.
Here is what happened. comment.char is "" in read.csv, so # is not special—it is just a character. The first line therefore became the header, and because that line happens to contain a comma (“survey, export”), R concluded the file has two columns. The data rows have three fields each, so R decided the extra leading field must be row names, and quietly used the city names for that purpose.








Every value in the file is still on screen somewhere, which is what makes this so dangerous: nothing looks empty. It looks like data. If your next line had been nrow(bad) you would have got 6, which is even close to the truth.
This is the whole argument for the inspection ritual below. Skip the two junk lines and the file parses properly:








Now look carefully at what you have.

respondents is int, and Denver’s empty cell became NA. Correct: an entirely empty field in a numeric column is read as missing.
mean_score is chr. It is text, because N/A is not in the default na.strings and so the column is not entirely numeric.

And here is the silent failure:








NA, with a warning. Trace it: there are no NA values in mean_score—it is text throughout—so na.rm = TRUE removes nothing. mean receives three strings, declines, and returns NA. The na.rm = TRUE you carefully typed was pure decoration.
Fix it at the point of import, which is where it belongs:








Now the column is numeric, the missing value is genuinely NA, and na.rm has something to do. Note that I passed a vector of strings: real files frequently use several spellings of missing in the same column, because several different people exported them.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Importing Data
text:
Delimiters that are not commas
CSV is a family, not a format. European exports often use ; because the comma is the decimal mark; tab-separated files are everywhere in bioinformatics; and pipe-delimited files turn up in banking.








One column named city.pop, with values like "Austin;961855". Nothing errored. If you had not looked, you would have a data frame with the right number of rows and one useless column.








R also ships read.delim (tab-separated) and read.csv2 (semicolon separator, comma decimal mark) as pre-configured wrappers, but read.csv with an explicit sep and dec is clearer about what you assumed.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Importing Data
text:
Encodings, briefly
A text file is bytes; an encoding is the agreement about which bytes mean which characters. When the agreement breaks you get Ã© where é should be, or a column name that starts with an invisible character and never matches names(d) == "city".
Three things worth knowing.
UTF-8 is the modern default and what you should ask for whenever you control the export. read.csv(f, fileEncoding = "UTF-8") states it explicitly.
Excel on Windows writes a BOM. Files exported from Excel as “CSV UTF-8” begin with three invisible bytes marking the encoding. R reads them as part of the first column name, so names(d)[1] looks like city and is not equal to "city". The cure is fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM". If a name comparison is mysteriously failing on the very first column, this is why—check with nchar(names(d)[1]).
Older exports are often Latin-1. fileEncoding = "latin1" handles most Western European legacy files.
The diagnostic habit: if any text in your data frame looks wrong on screen, the problem is almost certainly encoding and almost certainly at import, not something to patch downstream with gsub.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Importing Data
text:
The inspection ritual
Five calls, every time, before you trust anything.








































What each one is for:

dim—do you have the number of rows and columns the source claimed? A file that should have 50 states and has 51 has a “United States” total row in it, and every mean you compute will be wrong.
str—the single most useful function in R. Types, and the first few values of each column. This is where you catch chr where you expected num.
head—do the first rows look like data, or like a second header line?
summary—ranges. This is where -99 in the score column is visible as a minimum, and where you notice an age of 999 or a price of 0.
sapply(d, class)—a compact list of types when there are too many columns for str to be readable.

summary(big) above shows Min. :-99.00 for score, on a variable that is otherwise between 2.9 and 5.0. That is a sentinel value, it is Cleaning and Reshaping’s subject, and you found it in four seconds because you looked.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Importing Data
text:
Exercises






Exercise: get past the metadata



The file f has two provenance lines above the header. Read it correctly and return its dimensions.

















d <- read.csv(f, skip = 2)
dim(d)
skip discards lines before R looks for the header, so the third line becomes the column names. An alternative here is comment.char = "#", which works because these particular junk lines happen to start with #; skip works regardless of what the junk looks like.







Exercise: make missing actually missing



The file f writes missing scores as N/A. Read it so that mean_score comes back as a numeric column, and return its mean over the non-missing values.

















d <- read.csv(f, na.strings = c("NA", "N/A", ""))
mean(d$mean_score, na.rm = TRUE)
About 4.067. Listing the empty string as well is defensive: it changes nothing for a numeric column, where an empty field already becomes NA, but it matters enormously for text columns, where an empty field otherwise arrives as ""—a perfectly valid string that is.na() will never flag. Cleaning and Reshaping has more on that.







Exercise: keep the leading zeros



f holds a zip code column. Read it so the zip codes survive as written, and return the first one.

















d <- read.csv(f, colClasses = c(zip = "character"))
d$zip[1]
"02134". The failure this prevents is nasty because it is geographic: zip codes with leading zeros are concentrated in the Northeast, so an analysis that loses them does not lose a random 8% of rows—it loses New England, and any regional comparison it then reports is wrong in a patterned way that looks like a finding.







 Check yourself







A CSV has a column score whose three values are 4.1, N/A, and 3.7. You read it with read.csv(f) using every default, then run mean(d$score, na.rm = TRUE). What happens?

It returns 3.9, silently and correctly.It returns 3.9 together with a warning that one value was dropped.It returns NA together with a warning that the argument is not numeric.It stops with an error, because a character column cannot be averaged.



It returns NA and warns argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA.
The chain of events is worth tracing. read.csv scans the column, finds the text N/A, and concludes—correctly, given what it was told—that this column is text. Nothing in the column is an NA value, so na.rm = TRUE has nothing to remove and does exactly nothing. mean is then handed three strings, declines to average them, and returns NA.
Notice which part is dangerous. The warning is not the danger; the warning is R being helpful. The danger is that a script with fifty lines in it prints warnings you scroll past, and NA then flows into everything downstream. The fix is at import: read.csv(f, na.strings = c("NA", "N/A", "")) turns the text into a real NA, the column comes back numeric, and na.rm = TRUE finally has something to do.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Importing Data
text:
Beyond CSV, in one paragraph
Base R reads delimited text and .RData; everything else needs a package. Excel files: readxl. Stata, SPSS and SAS: haven. JSON: jsonlite. Databases: DBI with a driver. Large CSVs where read.csv is too slow: data.table’s fread, or readr’s read_csv, which also declines to mangle your column names and prints the types it guessed. We will meet readr when we get to the tidyverse; for now, everything you need is in base R, and knowing what read.csv does with a file is the foundation for understanding what the fancier readers are doing differently.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Importing Data
text:
Where this goes next
You have the file in R and you have looked at it. Cleaning and Reshaping is about everything you found when you looked.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Cleaning and Reshaping
text:
Three kinds of nothing
This is the longest section of the week and the one most likely to feel like drudgery. I want to reframe it before we start.
Cleaning is not preparation for the analysis. Cleaning is analysis—it is a sequence of decisions about what your data means, each of which changes your answer, and each of which you are responsible for. Deciding that -999 is missing rather than a very low blood pressure is a decision. Deciding that north and North are the same site is a decision. Deciding to keep only the rows that matched in a join is a decision. None of them are announced by R, all of them move your final number, and the ones you make without noticing are the ones that end up in a correction notice.
Throughout this section, one small messy table:
Six rows. Four separate problems.
The single most useful idea in this section is that “missing” is not one thing in a data file. There are at least three, and R treats them very differently.
NA is R’s actual missing value. It propagates: any arithmetic involving NA is NA, and functions like mean refuse to give an answer unless you tell them what to do about it. That refusal is a feature. It is R declining to make a decision on your behalf.
"", the empty string, is a perfectly ordinary character value that happens to have zero characters in it. It is not missing. is.na("") is FALSE. It counts as a category in table(). It is the fifth-most-common “site” in your study.
A sentinel like -999, -99, 9999, or 1900-01-01 is a real number that somebody’s software wrote to mean “not recorded”, usually because the file format had no way to represent missingness. It is not missing either. It is a number, and R will happily average it.
Zero missing values in bp, according to R, and a mean blood pressure of −246. The first number is a lie you were told by your own code, and the second is what happens when you believe it.
The tool that catches this is summary, because it prints the range:
A minimum of −999 on a blood pressure variable is not subtle. Once you know, you convert the sentinel to a genuine NA and then compute, and the honest version reports how many observations it used:
130.5, over four patients. Not −246 over six. And notice the second number in that output: “mean 130.5” alone is not a result, because it does not say what it is a mean of. na.rm = TRUE silently discards observations, and a report that uses it without saying how many were discarded has hidden something.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Cleaning and Reshaping
text:
na.rm = TRUE is a decision, not a fix



It is not wrong—usually it is what you want—but it changes what your number means. mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) is the average among those we observed, and it equals the average of everyone only if missingness is unrelated to the value. Blood pressures are often missing precisely for the patients who were too unwell to be measured. Whenever you type na.rm = TRUE, ask who is missing and whether they are missing for a reason connected to the thing you are measuring.








Exercise: the honest mean



clinic$bp uses -999 for “not recorded”. Return the mean blood pressure over the real measurements only.






bp <- clinic$bp
bp[bp == -999] <- NA
mean(bp, na.rm = TRUE)
130.5. bp == -999 produces a logical vector, and using a logical vector on the left of <- assigns only to the TRUE positions—one of base R’s most useful idioms.
In a real project you would do this at import instead, with read.csv(f, na.strings = c("NA", "-999")), which handles every column that uses the sentinel at once and leaves a record of the decision at the top of the script where a reader will see it.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Cleaning and Reshaping
text:
"" is not missing
Now the site column.








One NA, in row F. Row C, whose site is "", is reported as present. That is correct—"" is a string—and it is also not what you meant. If you tabulate sites, the empty string gets its own column and quietly becomes a category:








Five distinct non-missing values, plus one real NA, for what is really two sites. north and North differ by a capital and a trailing space; south and SOUTH differ by case; and the empty string sits at the far left of that table masquerading as a site called nothing.






table() hides NA unless you ask



By default, table() drops NA entirely and does not mention that it did. So does prop.table() on its output, which means your percentages are percentages of the non-missing—computed on a different denominator than you think. useNA = "ifany" is worth typing every single time.


The standard repair for text categories is: trim whitespace, unify case, and promote the empties to real NAs.








Two sites and two missing values, which is the truth. trimws removes leading and trailing whitespace; tolower unifies case. Notice the order does not matter here but the combination does—either one alone leaves you with three categories.






Exercise: count the usable sites



How many rows of clinic have a site value that is genuinely usable—not NA, and not blank or whitespace-only?

















sum(!is.na(clinic$site) & trimws(clinic$site) != "")
Four. The order of the two conditions matters more than it looks: & in R is not short-circuiting element-wise, so both sides are evaluated for every element, and trimws(NA) gives NA—which is why you need !is.na() in the conjunction rather than relying on it to guard the second test.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Cleaning and Reshaping
section: Type coercion, and the factor trap
text:
Type coercion, and the factor trap
R’s atomic vectors hold one type. When you combine types, R does not complain; it finds the most permissive type that can hold everything and converts silently.








TRUE quietly became the number 1, and then a single string turned the whole thing into text. The hierarchy is logical → integer → double → character, and R always slides to the right, never to the left. A single string anywhere in a column turns the whole column into text. That is the mechanism behind the N/A problem in Importing Data, and it is also what happens when someone types “n/a” or “see note” into one cell of a spreadsheet with 40,000 rows.
The sharper trap involves factors. A factor stores categories as integer codes plus a table of levels. If a numeric column accidentally becomes a factor—which happens with old code, with stringsAsFactors = TRUE, and with several data-reading packages—then converting it back is where people get hurt.








Two things to notice. The levels are sorted as text, so "12" comes before "23" before "7". And the underlying storage is 1, 2, 3—positions in that list. So:








1 3 2 3. Not 12 7 23 7. R has given you the level codes, and it has given them to you without a warning, because from R’s point of view you asked for the numeric representation of a factor and that is what a factor’s numeric representation is.
The values 1 3 2 3 are numbers. They have a mean. They will go into a regression. They will produce coefficients and p-values, and every one of those numbers will be about the alphabetical ordering of your labels.








as.character first recovers the labels, and then as.numeric parses them. This detour is one of the most-repeated pieces of advice in R, and this is why.






Exercise: rescue the numbers



scores is a factor that should have been numeric. Return the sum of the actual values.

















sum(as.numeric(as.character(scores)))

The wrong answer, 9, is the dangerous one precisely because it is a perfectly reasonable-looking number. Nothing about it says “this is the sum of four alphabetical positions”.

The habit that prevents this entirely: run str() after import, and if a column you expect to be numeric says Factor, fix it there rather than downstream.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Cleaning and Reshaping
text:
Duplicates
Duplicates come in two flavours and they need different treatment.








Six rows. Order 102 appears twice, identically—almost certainly an export or join artifact. Order 104 also appears twice, but with different amounts, 50 and 55, which is not an artifact; it is a data quality problem, and deleting one of them at random is a decision about which number is true.








duplicated() returns TRUE for every occurrence after the first. On the whole data frame it finds one row (the second 102). On the key alone it finds two, because 104 is repeated as a key even though the rows differ.








unique() on the whole frame removes exact repeats and leaves five rows, which is safe: nothing was lost. Deduplicating on the key is different:








Four rows—and the 104 that survived is the one with amount = 50, purely because it appeared first in the file. Nobody decided that. The file’s row order decided it.






The right move when keys repeat with different data



Do not silently take the first. Find out why. Are these two genuine orders that were assigned the same id? Two versions of one order, of which the later is correct? A join upstream that inflated the table? Each has a different fix, and !duplicated(key) implements none of them—it implements “trust the file’s sort order”, which is a decision you would never make deliberately.








Exercise: how many distinct orders?



Return the number of rows left after keeping only the first row for each order_id.

















nrow(orders[!duplicated(orders$order_id), ])
Four. nrow(unique(orders)) gives five instead, and comparing the two is a good diagnostic: if they disagree, some key repeats with conflicting data, and you have a question to answer rather than a row to drop.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Cleaning and Reshaping
text:
Wide and long
The same data can be laid out two ways, and which one you want depends entirely on what you are about to do.
Wide puts one row per unit and one column per time point or measurement:








Long puts one row per observation, with the thing that used to be a column name now a value in its own column:








Same six numbers, six rows instead of three. reshape is base R’s tool for this and its argument names take some getting used to: varying names the columns that are really repeated measurements, v.names is what the stacked values should be called, timevar and times name and fill the new column that records which measurement each row is, and idvar says what identifies a unit. (row.names(long) <- NULL is cosmetic—reshape builds row names like Austin.2024, which are harmless and ugly.)
Going back is the same function with a different direction:









Why the shape matters
Wide is for humans. It is compact, it fits on a slide, and comparing 2024 to 2025 for one city is a glance across a row.
Long is for computers, and specifically for anything that has to treat “year” as a variable. Group by year, plot rate against year, fit a model with year as a predictor—every one of those needs a column called year, and in the wide layout there isn’t one, because the year is hiding in the column names, where no function can reach it.
The tell that you need long format: you find yourself writing the same operation once per column, or naming columns in a formula. In long format:








One call, and it would still be one call with forty years instead of two.






The tidyverse version



You will hear the terms pivot longer and pivot wider, from the tidyr package, which does the same job with much friendlier arguments (pivot_longer(wide, cols = c(y2024, y2025), names_to = "year", values_to = "rate")). We will meet it later in the course. It is genuinely nicer, and it does not do anything reshape cannot—so the concept you are learning here transfers unchanged, which is the point of learning it here.








Exercise: a summary that needs the long shape



long is already built for you. Return the mean rate for each year.

















tapply(long$rate, long$year, mean)
2024 gives 3.3 and 2025 gives 3.5. tapply returns a named vector, and those names come from the grouping variable—which is one more reason the year had to be a variable rather than part of a column name.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Cleaning and Reshaping
text:
Joining two tables
Almost every real project needs data from more than one file, and joining them is where rows go to die quietly.








Two rows. You started with four stores and you have two, and R said nothing at all, because merge defaults to an inner join: keep a row only if its key appears in both tables. S3 and S4 have no region; S5 has no sales; all three are gone.
Now the part that should make you uneasy:








Total units fell from 56 to 35. If the next line of your report is “total units sold were 35,000”, you have just published a number that is 37% too small, and nothing in your session told you so.
The other join types are one argument away:








all.x = TRUE is a left join: keep every row of the first table, fill region with NA where there is no match. All four stores survive, and the NAs are visible—they are the point. This is usually what you want when one table is your data and the other is a lookup.








all = TRUE is a full join: every key from either side, five rows, with NA where a side had nothing. S5 appears with NA units, which tells you your region table knows about a store your sales table has never heard of—often a genuine finding about your pipeline.

The other direction: rows multiplying
The opposite failure is less famous and just as damaging. If the key repeats in the second table, rows multiply.








S1 now appears twice, and units = 10 appears twice with it. Sum units on this table and you have counted store S1’s sales once for each price plan it offers. The rule: merge gives you every combination of matching rows, so a key that is unique on the left and duplicated on the right inflates the left table’s numbers.


Keys that do not match for stupid reasons








One row. "S2 " and "S2" are different strings. The same happens with case ("s2"), with a zip code that is "02134" in one file and 2134 in the other, and with an id read as numeric in one file and character in the other. Clean your keys—trimws, tolower, and a deliberate as.character—before you join, not after you notice.






The join checklist



Every single time you join, in three lines:

nrow() of each input, and sum(duplicated(x$key)) on each—if the key is not unique on at least one side, you will inflate.
The join.
nrow() of the output, compared with what you expected. For a left join it should equal the left table’s row count. If it is smaller, something went wrong; if it is larger, the right-hand key was not unique.

Then colSums(is.na(result)) to see how many rows failed to match. Ten seconds, and it converts the most common silent failure in data science into something you can see.








Exercise: count the casualties



How many rows of sales are lost by the default merge with regions?

















nrow(sales) - nrow(merge(sales, regions, by = "store"))
Two: S3 and S4. An equivalent and arguably better answer is sum(!sales$store %in% regions$store), which also tells you which ones—and naming the casualties is usually more informative than counting them, because it is how you notice that all the dropped stores are in one region.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Cleaning and Reshaping
text:
complete.cases and the shrinking sample
One last tool, and one last warning about it.








Rows C and F are incomplete—C is missing visits, F is missing site. But look at what complete.cases says about rows C and F’s blood pressure:








Five of six rows are “complete” on bp and visits, even though two of those five have a blood pressure of -999. complete.cases looks for NA and nothing else. It cannot see a sentinel, an empty string, or an impossible value.
That is the shape of this whole section. R’s missingness tools are excellent, and they only work on missingness you have already told R about. Everything before this point—the sentinel conversion, the empty strings, the type fixes—exists so that by the time you reach complete.cases, it is telling you the truth.






 Check yourself







A clinic file records blood pressure, and the extraction tool wrote -999 wherever the reading was not taken. You did not know that. Which single check, run before you computed anything, would most likely have caught it?

sum(is.na(clinic$bp))complete.cases(clinic)summary(clinic$bp)nrow(clinic)



summary(clinic$bp). It prints the minimum, and a minimum of -999 on a blood pressure variable is not a subtle clue.
The first two options both look for NA, and -999 is not NA—it is an ordinary number that R will happily average. sum(is.na(clinic$bp)) returns zero and you conclude the column is complete. complete.cases agrees with it, for the same reason. nrow tells you how many rows there are, which was never in doubt.
The general lesson is that missingness has to be represented as missing before any missingness tool can see it. Your first pass over a numeric column should always ask whether its range is physically possible: minimum, maximum, and a glance at whether some improbable round number appears far more often than chance allows. -999, -99, 9999, 0, and 1900-01-01 are the usual suspects.











 And one more







sales has one row for each of four stores, S1 through S4. regions has three rows, for S1, S2, and S5. You run merge(sales, regions, by = "store"). What do you get, and what does R tell you?

Four rows; S3 and S4 are kept with NA in the region column.Two rows; R prints a warning that two rows were dropped.Two rows; R prints nothing at all.Five rows; every store from either table appears once.



Two rows, and complete silence.
merge defaults to an inner join: a row survives only if its key appears in both tables. S3 and S4 have no region, S5 has no sales, and all three vanish. R does not warn, because from its point of view nothing went wrong—you asked for the intersection and it gave you the intersection.
This is the single most common way a correct-looking analysis quietly becomes false. Half your stores left the building and every summary you compute afterwards is a summary of the survivors. The habit that catches it is boringly simple: record nrow() before the join, record it after, and look at the difference on purpose. If you wanted the unmatched sales rows kept, that is all.x = TRUE; if you wanted everything from both sides, all = TRUE.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Cleaning and Reshaping
text:
A cleaning log
The last thing, and it takes two minutes per project. Keep a list, in your README or at the top of your script, of every decision you made in this section:


bp: -999 treated as missing (142 rows affected)
site: trimmed, lower-cased; 38 empty strings converted to NA
orders: 4 exact duplicate rows removed; 2 ids repeat with conflicting amounts, kept the later timestamp
joined to regions on store; 2 of 4 stores unmatched, kept via left join


Every line of that is a judgment call that changed your answer, and a reader who disagrees with one of them can now say so. That is what separates an analysis from an assertion—and in this course it is also a substantial part of what your project report is graded on.

title: Where the Data Came From
text:
The aircraft that came back
Every table you will analyze is a subset of something larger. Some rows made it in and some did not, and every method in the rest of this course assumes—quietly, and usually without anyone checking—that the rows which made it in resemble the rows which did not.
When that assumption fails, nothing downstream repairs it. A larger sample does not help. A better model does not help. The confidence interval you compute in The Standard Error of a Mean will be narrow and wrong, which is worse than wide and wrong.
So there is one question to ask of a dataset before any of the others, and it is the question this chapter is about:
During the Second World War, the U.S. military studied the bullet holes on aircraft returning from missions over Europe. The damage was concentrated on the wings and fuselage; the engines were comparatively clean. The apparent conclusion was to add armour where the holes were.
Abraham Wald, working for the Statistical Research Group, pointed out that the sample consisted entirely of aircraft that had returned. Planes hit in the engines were not underrepresented in the data because engines were rarely hit. They were underrepresented because they were at the bottom of the Channel.
Armour the engines.
The story survives because the error is so easy to make and so hard to see from inside the data. Nothing in the table is wrong. Every bullet hole was recorded accurately. The table simply answers a different question from the one being asked—not where are aircraft hit, but where are aircraft hit given that they survived being hit.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Where the Data Came From
section: Three ways a sample goes wrong
text:
Three ways a sample goes wrong
Survivorship. The sample was filtered by the outcome you care about. The aircraft is the classic case, but the modern ones are everywhere: companies that have lasted ten years share these three habits, which cannot distinguish a habit that causes survival from a habit that survivors adopt; our users love the redesign, measured among the users who stayed.
Selection. The process that put a row into the table is related to the thing you are measuring. Volunteers for a trial are not like non-volunteers. People who click a feedback link are people with an opinion strong enough to click.
Convenience. Whoever was easy to reach—the lobby at two o’clock on a Tuesday, the students in your own program, the first thousand rows the API returned. Convenience samples are the most common and the hardest to argue about, because the bias is real but its direction is unknown. You cannot say which way the answer is wrong, only that you have no grounds to say it is right.






The diagnostic





Describe, in one sentence, the process that decided whether a row exists in this table.
If you cannot write that sentence, you do not yet know what your sample is, and every number you compute from it is provisional.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Where the Data Came From
section: Missing data is a mechanism, not a gap
text:
Missing data is a mechanism, not a gap
The same reasoning applies one level down. A row can be present while a value is absent, and the reason the value is absent matters far more than the fact that it is.
Statisticians name three mechanisms, and the names are worth learning because they tell you what you are allowed to do next.
MCAR—missing completely at random. Whether a value is missing has nothing to do with anything, observed or not. A sensor dropped packets at random; a page of forms was lost in the post. Dropping the incomplete rows costs you precision and nothing else. This is the case everyone assumes and almost nobody has.
MAR—missing at random. Whether a value is missing depends on something you did observe. Younger respondents skip the income question more often, and you recorded age. The name is unfortunate—nothing here is random in the ordinary sense—but the situation is the hopeful one: because the thing driving the missingness is in your data, you can use it to recover the answer.
MNAR—missing not at random. Whether a value is missing depends on the missing value itself. The highest earners decline to state their income; the sickest patients drop out of the study. No amount of cleverness recovers this from the data alone, because the information you would need is precisely the information that is absent. You need an assumption from outside the dataset, and you need to say out loud what it is.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Where the Data Came From
text:
Seeing MAR happen
Below, twelve employees in three departments. salary is the truth, which you would not normally have. reported is what the survey collected: two engineers declined, and nobody else did.








The survey says 97.0 when the truth is 103.3—a shortfall of six, entirely because the best-paid department is the one that answered least. Nothing was mistyped. na.rm = TRUE did exactly what it promised, and the promise was the problem.
This is MAR, not MNAR: within engineering the two who declined were not the two highest earners, so knowing somebody’s department tells you everything about their chance of answering. That is the opening the next exercise uses.






 Exercise: recover what dropping destroyed





Estimate the overall mean salary by averaging the three department means computed from reported. Return a single number.


















mean(tapply(staff$reported, staff$dept, mean, na.rm = TRUE))
Exactly 103.33, against the naive 97.0.
The bias vanished because the departments are equally sized in the population and averaging their means restores that balance—the two missing engineers stop counting as an absence of engineers and start counting as an absence of two observations from a group you can still see.
This is what “MAR is recoverable” means in practice. It is also why the answer depends on having recorded dept at all. Had the survey collected income and nothing else, the same missingness would have been indistinguishable from MNAR, and the six-point error would have been permanent.







 Exercise: name the mechanism





A survey asks for household income. People with very high incomes decline to answer noticeably more often than everyone else. The survey records nothing else that predicts income.
Assign the letter of the correct answer, for example answer <- "A".















C. The probability of answering depends on income itself, and income is exactly what is missing.
D is the tempting one, and it is wrong in an instructive way. You can impute from the other respondents—the software will not stop you—but the other respondents are systematically poorer than the people who declined, so the imputed values inherit the bias and then wear the appearance of data. You have not fixed the problem, you have hidden it.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Where the Data Came From
section: Imputation, and why it is not free
text:
Imputation, and why it is not free
Filling gaps in is a large subject and this course does not teach it. Two things are worth knowing now.
Mean imputation—replacing every gap with the column average—is almost always the wrong move. It does not merely fail to add information; it actively destroys some, because every imputed row now sits exactly at the center. The variance shrinks, the standard error shrinks with it, and the analysis reports more confidence than the data can support. A method that makes you more certain by discarding information should be treated with suspicion.
Principled methods exist—multiple imputation is the standard one—and they work by imputing repeatedly and letting the disagreement between the versions carry the uncertainty forward. They assume MAR. Under MNAR they are as stuck as everything else.
The honest minimum for this course, and for the project:

Report how many rows you lost, not just the ones you kept.
Say what you believe the mechanism was, and why.
Say which direction it would push your answer if you are wrong.

The third is the one that separates an analyst from a technician. You will often not be able to quantify the bias. You can nearly always sign it.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Where the Data Came From
text:
Four situations
Take these one at a time. For each, name who is missing, and say whether their absence pushes the answer up, down, or in a direction you cannot determine.

“We surveyed the users who clicked the feedback link.”
“We studied the habits of companies that have lasted ten years.”
“We dropped every row with a missing income value.”
“We asked people in the lobby at two o’clock on a Tuesday.”

Post your answers in the comment box below. Disagreement is the useful outcome here—two of these have a clearly signed direction and two do not, and arguing about which is which is the whole exercise.






Check yourself






What was wrong with the aircraft data, given that every bullet hole in it was recorded correctly?
Which of MCAR, MAR and MNAR can be corrected using the data you already have, and what does the correction require you to have recorded?
Why does mean imputation make a confidence interval too narrow?
Your analysis drops 18% of rows. What three things belong in the write-up?
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Where the Data Came From
text:
Where this goes next
Importing Data and Cleaning and Reshaping are about the mechanics—getting a file open, getting the types right, deciding what na.rm = TRUE should mean in a particular line. Read them with this chapter in mind, because the mechanics will happily produce a clean, tidy, fully documented table that answers the wrong question.
The idea returns twice more. When we reach modeling, confounding is this same problem wearing different clothes: a comparison contaminated by a difference between the groups being compared. And the project asks you to state what your analysis does not support, which is usually a sentence about who was not in your data.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Practice Problems
text:
Predict the output
These are not graded and nothing here is auto-checked. They are the raw material for Monday’s reasoning block, where you will argue about them in pairs and one of you will be asked to defend an answer to the room.
crumbs: Questions, and Data That Can Answer Them

title: Practice Problems
text:
A1. Four ways to count








Predict all five before running. In particular: are the last two the same number, and if not, why not?







Discussion





NA, 2.667, NA, 2, and 3.
The first four behave as advertised: NA is contagious through arithmetic and through sum, and na.rm = TRUE switches that off.
The fifth is the interesting one. x > 2 is FALSE NA TRUE TRUE, and subsetting a vector with a logical vector containing NA does not drop that position—it returns NA for it. So x[x > 2] is NA 3 4, of length three. R’s reasoning is defensible: it does not know whether the missing value exceeds 2, so it will not claim the element belongs and it will not claim it does not.
The practical consequence is that length(d[d$x > 2]) and sum(d$x > 2, na.rm = TRUE) count different things, and if you use them interchangeably—as almost everybody does—one of your row counts is wrong.






A2. The phantom row








Two ways of doing the same thing. Do they return the same data frame?







Discussion





No. d[d$x > 2, ] returns three rows, one of which is entirely NA with a row name of NA. subset(d, x > 2) returns two.
Same mechanism as A1, now with visible consequences: bracket subsetting keeps a phantom row for every NA in the condition, and subset was written to treat NA as “not selected” and drop it.
Neither is wrong. What is wrong is not knowing which one you used. If your analysis filters with [ and then reports nrow(), your denominator includes rows that contain no data at all, and every proportion you compute from it is slightly too small.






A3. Percentages of what?








Five responses. What denominator do those proportions use?







Discussion





Three. table() silently drops NA, so prop.table divides by 3, and you get 0.333 and 0.667.
If you report “67% said yes”, that is 67% of the people who answered, and you have written a sentence about five respondents that is true of three of them. Two out of five is 40%, and which of 67% and 40% is the honest number depends entirely on why those two are missing—which is a question about the study, not about R.
table(v, useNA = "ifany") shows all three categories. Type it every time.






A4. A perfectly reasonable number








What comes out, and what is it the mean of?







Discussion





2.25, which is the mean of 1, 3, 2, 3—the positions of each value in the alphabetically sorted level list "12", "23", "7".
The real mean is 12.25. Nothing about 2.25 announces itself as wrong; it is a plausible number in a plausible range, and if the variable had been something like a satisfaction rating it would look entirely at home in a results table.
as.numeric(as.character(f)) is the fix, and str() after import is how you notice you need it.






A5. ifelse and the third possibility








ifelse takes a condition, a value for TRUE, and a value for FALSE. There are only two branches. What happens to the NA?







Discussion





"low", NA, "high", "high". ifelse propagates NA rather than sending it down either branch, which is the right thing to do and is not what most people assume when they write a line like this to bin a variable.
The trap is the version people actually write:
band <- ifelse(x > 2, "high", "low")
table(band)
which then quietly reports on fewer rows than you have, for the reason in A3. If missing values should be their own category, say so explicitly: band[is.na(x)] <- "unknown".






A6. Sorting















Discussion





"10" "100" "9". Character sorting compares position by position, so "1" beats "9" at the first character and nothing after that matters.
You will meet this whenever an id, a version number, a zip code, or a survey-round label was read as text—which, per Importing Data, is exactly what you asked for when you passed colClasses = c(id = "character"). Both types have a cost. The point is to know which one you have, and to convert deliberately when you need ordering.

title: Practice Problems
section: This runs and is still wrong
text:
This runs and is still wrong
Every cell in this part executes without error. Some print a warning; several do not. In each case, say what the output should have been and what the reader of a report containing this number would be misled about.

B1. Which summaries survive a sentinel?








The mean is absurd on sight. Are the other two safe?







Discussion





The mean is −285.8, which nobody would publish. The max is 74, which is correct—sentinels below the data cannot affect the maximum. The median is 69, and the true median of the four real readings is 70.5.
So the median is wrong, and it is wrong by 1.5 degrees: small, plausible, invisible. That is the pattern worth internalising. The summaries a sentinel destroys loudly are the ones you catch. The ones it nudges are the ones that get published.
This is also the argument for summary() over mean() as your first look at a numeric column: summary prints the minimum, and the minimum is where sentinels live.






B2. Stacking two files








Two months of data, stacked. The mean comes out at 2.5. What is wrong with it?







Discussion





Several things at once, and they compound.
rbind found a numeric v and a character v, coerced the whole column to character, and said nothing. as.numeric then turned "oops" into NA with a warning, and na.rm = TRUE dropped it. The 2.5 you see is the mean of 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5—arithmetically correct, and a mean of three quarters of your data presented as though it were all of it.
The reader is misled about the sample size, and nobody ever asked what "oops" was. It might be a code the vendor uses for “instrument failed”, in which case those readings are missing not at random and dropping them biases the mean.
The habit: after any rbind, run str(); after any as.numeric on a character column, run sum(is.na(new)) - sum(is.na(old)) and look at the values that failed to parse before you throw them away.






B3. A join that made you richer








Every store matched. Nothing was dropped. Total units went from 56 to 66.







Discussion





S1 offers two plans, so it has two rows in prices, so merge produces two rows for it—each carrying units = 10. Summing units on the joined table counts S1’s ten units twice.
This is the mirror image of the dropped-rows failure in Cleaning and Reshaping, and it is harder to spot because the join looks successful: no NAs, no missing stores, every key matched. The only symptom is that the row count grew, and 5 is not an alarming number when you were expecting 4.
The check that catches it is the one from the join checklist: before merging, sum(duplicated(prices$store)). If the key is not unique on the right-hand side, any left-hand quantity you sum afterwards is inflated.
The deeper issue is that the joined table’s row is no longer “a store”. It is “a store-plan”. Once the unit of observation changes, quantities defined per store—like units—stop being summable, and no amount of careful arithmetic on the joined table fixes that.






B4. The average of the averages








A district reports its average score as 70.







Discussion





70 is the average of two school averages. The average student scored 61, because 200 of the 210 students are at the school scoring 60.
Nothing here is a coding error. mean(schools$mean_score) is exactly what it says. The mistake is a mismatch between the unit of observation in the data—one row per school—and the unit in the claim—“the average student”. Aggregated data has this property constantly, and it is the source of a large fraction of misleading statistics in the press.
Ask, of every mean you compute: a mean over what population? If the answer is “over rows of this table”, check that a row is the thing you meant to average over.






B5. The zip code join








Three zips on each side, all three the same places. How many rows come back?







Discussion





One.
merge coerces to a common type, so the numeric 2134 becomes the string "2134", which is not "02134". Only 20052—the one zip with no leading zero—matches. R does not warn, because as far as it is concerned you asked it to match on a key and it matched what it could.
Now look at what survived. Leading-zero zips are concentrated in New England and the mid-Atlantic. The join did not lose a random two-thirds of the data; it lost northeast and kept south. Any regional comparison built on the result is not merely underpowered, it is systematically wrong, and it will look like a finding.
This is the concrete cost of the leading-zero issue from Importing Data, and it is why identifier columns get colClasses = c(zip = "character") on every file in the project, not just the one you happened to think about.






B6. Dates that are not dates















Discussion





sort gives November first and March second, and max claims the latest date is July 15. Both are correct string operations and both are chronological nonsense, for the reason in A6.
sort(as.Date(dates, format = "%m/%d/%Y"))
gives March, July, November. Dates are the single most reliable source of silent errors in real data, partly because of this and partly because 3/1/2026 is March 1st in the United States and January 3rd almost everywhere else—a file that mixes conventions cannot be repaired at all, only detected. (The tell: a day-first file read as month-first has no dates with a first component above 12, which is a check you can actually run.)
Convert dates at import, with an explicit format, and check the range afterwards.

title: Practice Problems
section: What does this license you to claim?
text:
What does this license you to claim?
No code here. For each, decide what the analyst may write in the report, and what they may not. Bring your answer.

C1.
A team joins 4,812 sales rows to a store lookup table with merge, gets 3,104 rows, does not notice, and reports: “Average units per store were 17.5.”
What, precisely, is the claim they are entitled to make instead? Note that “average units per store among stores appearing in both tables” is technically accurate and probably still misleading—why?


C2.
From S.M.A.R.T. Questions: eight commuters, four by transit and four by car, and transit commutes averaged 17.5 minutes longer.
Which of these are supported? (a) In this sample, transit commuters averaged 17.5 more minutes. (b) Transit commuting takes about 17.5 minutes longer. (c) Switching from car to transit would add about 17.5 minutes to your commute. (d) Transit commuters live further from work.


C3.
A housing dataset has 12 rows. Three variables are needed; each is missing for two or three rows; five rows are complete on all three. The team fits a model and reports an R^2 of 0.91.
What has to appear in the report alongside that number, and what would you ask the team at the presentation?


C4.
A team cleans a site column by lower-casing, trimming whitespace, and converting empty strings to NA. They now have two sites where the raw file had five distinct values.
Under what circumstances is that cleaning step wrong? Give a concrete example of a dataset where North and north are genuinely different things.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Bring to class

Take one of the four “before” questions in S.M.A.R.T. Questions and write a fifth pair of your own: a vague question you have actually been curious about, and a S.M.A.R.T. version of it. Be ready to have the room attack the second one.
Find a real CSV—any open data portal, any Kaggle dataset—load it, and run the five-call inspection ritual from Importing Data. Come with one thing you found that you would not have found by opening it in Excel, and one thing Excel showed you that R did not.
For the same file: how many rows, how many columns, what does one row mean, and what proportion of rows are complete on the three variables you would most want to use? If any of those four questions is hard to answer, that is the interesting part—bring the difficulty rather than a number.
Argue one of these, either side:

“Dropping rows with missing values is almost always the wrong default, and the fact that R does it automatically inside modeling functions—without printing how many it dropped—is a design mistake.”

You will be assigned a side in class, so prepare both.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
What this week covers
Monday, August 31
Last week you got data into shape. This week you look at it.
That sounds like the easy part, and it is where most of the damage gets done. Exploratory data analysis is where you form the beliefs that everything afterwards is built on: which variables matter, which relationships look real, which observations are strange. If you form those beliefs badly, no amount of careful modeling downstream will save you—you will simply get a very precise answer to the wrong question.
The awkward fact about EDA is that it has no right answer to check yourself against. A regression coefficient is either computed correctly or it is not. A histogram is not wrong; it is a choice, and a different choice would have shown you something else. So the skill this week is not “which function makes the plot.” It is judgment: knowing what each summary throws away, noticing when two honest-looking pictures of the same data tell opposite stories, and being able to say out loud what you are claiming and what you are not.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Describing a Single Variable



Center, spread, quantiles, skew, and outliers. Why the mean and the median disagree and what that disagreement is telling you. Why the variance formula divides by n-1—stated honestly, not waved at. Histograms and boxplots, and what each of them hides.








Relationships Between Variables



Two-way tables, scatterplots, covariance and correlation. What a correlation coefficient cannot see. And the difference between association and cause, stated carefully rather than as a slogan you repeat and then ignore.








Visualization That Does Not Mislead



Truncated axes, aspect ratio, bin widths, dual axes, and aggregation that hides a reversal in the subgroups. The through-line: the same data supports several pictures, and choosing one is an argument you are making.








Alongside this week: Plotting with ggplot2



The tool you will actually be asked to use: data, an aesthetic mapping, a geom, and layers that add. It lives in the self-paced R Primer rather than in this week’s reading, because it is the mechanics of a package rather than an idea about data. Work through it whenever you need it—the labs assume it from Aug 31 onward.








Practice Problems



Predict-before-you-run, and code that runs perfectly and is still wrong. Not graded—bring your answers and your disagreements to class.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Where this is heading
