\text{raining}) is nearly 1; P(\text{raining} \mid \text{wet}) is not, because sprinklers exist. Getting from one to the other requires knowing how common rain and wetness are in the first place—and that requirement is Bayes’ rule.
Write the joint probability two ways using the multiplication rule:
P(A \cap B) = P(B \mid A)P(A) = P(A \mid B)P(B)
and divide:
\boxed{\;P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}\;}
The denominator is usually expanded by the law of total probability—B can arrive either with A or without it:
P(B) = P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid A^c)P(A^c)
That is the whole of Bayes’ rule: two lines of algebra from the definition. Nobody finds the derivation hard. What people find hard is believing the answer.






 Which way round is it?







An analyst reports: “80% of the customers who canceled last month had contacted support in the 30 days before canceling.”
The head of product proposes acting on it: flag every customer who contacts support as a churn risk and route them to a retention offer.
What is the problem with that reasoning?

There is no problem—80% is a strong signal and acting on it is exactly what the number is for.The report gives P(\text{contacted} \mid \text{canceled}), but the proposal needs P(\text{canceled} \mid \text{contacted}), and converting between them requires knowing how common contacting support is among all customers.The number is only valid if contacting support and canceling are independent, which has not been checked.One month of data is too small a sample to support any conclusion.



The two conditional probabilities point in opposite directions and have different denominators. The report divides by the cancellers; the proposal needs to divide by the contacters.
Put numbers on it. Suppose there are 50,000 customers, 500 of whom canceled, and 400 of those (80%) had contacted support—the reported figure exactly. Now suppose 20,000 customers contact support in any given month, because that is simply what customers do. Then
P(\text{canceled} \mid \text{contacted}) = \frac{400}{20{,}000} = 2\%,
against a baseline churn rate of 500/50{,}000 = 1\%. Contacting support does double the risk, which is worth knowing—but the retention team would be chasing 20,000 people to reach 400 of them, and 98% of everyone they contact was never going to leave. That is a very different program from the one “80%” suggests.
Change one number and the conclusion changes completely: if only 1,000 customers contact support, then 400/1{,}000 = 40\% and the proposal is excellent. The missing quantity is the base rate of the conditioning event, and it is missing from the report entirely.
This is the same structure as the medical-test problem, and the same structure as the courtroom error of confusing “the probability of this evidence if the defendant is innocent” with “the probability the defendant is innocent given this evidence”. Whenever you read a conditional probability, say out loud what is on each side of the bar before you act on it.
Independence is not the issue here—the whole point is that the two events are related. And sample size is a real concern in general but not the flaw in this argument: with ten years of data the reasoning would be equally wrong.

title: Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
The medical test problem
This is the centrepiece of the chapter. If you take one thing from Probability, take this.






The setup



A disease affects 5 in 1,000 people—a prevalence of 0.5%.
A screening test is good:

Sensitivity 99%. If you have the disease, it comes back positive 99% of the time.
Specificity 95%. If you do not have the disease, it comes back negative 95% of the time.

Your test comes back positive. You have no symptoms; you were screened because it was on the routine panel.
How worried should you be?
Write your answer down before you read on. Most people—including most doctors, in studies that have been repeated for forty years—say something in the region of 95%.


We are not going to argue about it. We are going to build the population and count.








Read the table before doing any arithmetic.

514 of the 100,000 simulated people have the disease. The test caught 510 of them and missed 4. It is, as advertised, an excellent test.
99,486 do not have the disease. The test correctly cleared 94,413 of them—and wrongly flagged 5,073.

So 5,583 people got a positive result, and only 510 of them are ill.








About 9%.
Nine percent. Not 95%. A positive result on a 99%-sensitive test for this disease leaves you more than ten times more likely to be healthy than sick.

Why, in one sentence
The healthy group is 200 times larger than the sick group. Its 5% error rate is applied to a vastly bigger population than the test’s 99% success rate is. Five percent of a huge number beats 99% of a tiny one, and it is not close.
The number doing the work here is the one nobody was given prominently: the prevalence, 0.5%. The two impressive-sounding percentages describe the test. The prevalence describes the world, and the world wins.


Now the algebra, and watch it agree
With D = has the disease and + = tests positive:
P(D \mid +) = \frac{P(+ \mid D)\,P(D)}{P(+ \mid D)P(D) + P(+ \mid D^c)P(D^c)}
= \frac{0.99 \times 0.005}{0.99 \times 0.005 + 0.05 \times 0.995}








0.0905, against the simulation’s 0.0913. They agree to within simulation noise, which is what should happen—the algebra is a shortcut for the counting, not a separate source of truth.
The same thing in whole people, per 100,000 screened, which is the version to use when explaining this to somebody:








495 true positives against 4,975 false positives. Ten false alarms for every real case, from a test that is right 99% of the time when it matters and 95% of the time when it does not.






 The interview question







A disease affects 1 person in 1,000. A screening test is very good: it flags 99% of the people who have the disease, and it correctly clears 99% of the people who do not.
A patient with no symptoms is screened as part of a routine check-up and tests positive. Roughly how likely is it that this patient has the disease?

About 99%, since that is the accuracy of the test.About 90%.About 9%.It cannot be estimated without knowing how many people were screened in total.



Think in counts, over 100,000 screened people.

100 of them have the disease. The test flags 99 of those.
99,900 do not. The test wrongly flags 1% of them: 999 people.

So 1,098 people test positive and only 99 of them are ill: 99 / 1098 \approx 0.09, or about 9%.
The reason this feels wrong is that “99% accurate” is a statement about P(\text{positive} \mid \text{disease}), and the patient is asking about P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive}). Those are different conditional probabilities over different denominators, and Bayes’ rule is the bookkeeping that converts one into the other:
P(D \mid +) = \frac{P(+ \mid D)\,P(D)}{P(+)}
= \frac{0.99 \times 0.001}{0.99 \times 0.001 + 0.01 \times 0.999} \approx 0.09.
The healthy group is a thousand times larger than the sick group, so even its 1% error rate produces ten times more positives than the disease itself does. That is base-rate neglect: the prevalence is doing most of the work and it is the number people leave out.
The last option is a real temptation and it is wrong: nothing here depends on the size of the screened population. The counts above are a device for thinking; the answer is a ratio, and 100,000 cancels out.
One thing that changes the answer completely: why the patient was tested. All of this assumes a routine screen of someone drawn from the general population. A patient tested because they had suggestive symptoms is not from that population, their prevalence is far higher than 1 in 1,000, and the same positive result then means something much more serious.

title: Conditional Probability and Bayes
section: Base rates, and why the intuition fails
text:
Base rates, and why the intuition fails
The technical name for what just happened is base-rate neglect: when given vivid, specific evidence, people weigh it heavily and quietly discard the background rate.
It is not stupidity, and knowing about it does not cure it. The pull is structural: the test result is about you, and the prevalence is about a faceless population, so the mind treats one as evidence and the other as trivia. But the prevalence is your prior, and Bayes’ rule says the answer is a compromise between the prior and the evidence, weighted by how strong each one is.
Watch how completely the same test changes character as the base rate moves:
















The test never changed. Its sensitivity and specificity are properties of the assay and they are fixed. But a positive result means 2% at a prevalence of 1 in 1,000, 9% at 5 in 1,000, 51% at 5%, and 95% at 50%.






The practical consequence, which is not about medicine



A test’s accuracy is not a property you can quote on its own. What a positive result means depends on who you tested.
This is why mass screening of healthy populations is genuinely controversial: at low prevalence the false positives swamp the true ones, and the resulting biopsies, anxiety, and follow-up procedures are real harms borne mostly by healthy people.
And it is why the same argument transfers, unchanged, to everything you will build:

Fraud detection. Fraud is rare. A 99%-accurate model flooding an investigations team with false positives is the normal outcome, not a bug.
Rare-disease and rare-event models. Same arithmetic.
Alerting and monitoring. An alert that fires on a rare condition with a 1% false-positive rate will be ignored within a fortnight, and then it will be ignored on the day it is right.
Hiring screens, security screening, content moderation, spam filters. Every one of them is this problem.

When someone reports a classifier as “99% accurate”, the only useful reply is: out of the ones it flagged, how many were real? That number is called precision, and it is the same quantity as P(D \mid +).



The same four numbers, under two sets of names
This is worth pinning down now, because you will meet these quantities again in DATS 6103 and in every interview that touches classification, and the two fields that use them most do not use the same words.



Conditional probability
Medicine and screening
Machine learning




P(+ \mid D)
sensitivity
recall, true positive rate


P(- \mid \text{no } D)
specificity
true negative rate


P(D \mid +)
positive predictive value
precision


P(\text{no } D \mid -)
negative predictive value
—



They are the same four numbers. Read the table by which side of the bar the test result sits on: sensitivity and recall condition on the truth and describe the test, so they do not move when the disease becomes rarer. Precision and PPV condition on the result and describe what a flag is worth, so they collapse when the base rate falls—which is the whole content of the previous section.
That is also why a model can be reported as having 99% recall and be nearly useless. Recall is a property of the classifier; precision is a property of the classifier and the population you deployed it into, and only one of those is in the paper.


The other conditional, for completeness
A negative result, on the other hand, is enormously reassuring—precisely because the disease is rare:








About 4 in 100,000. The same low prevalence that made the positive result nearly meaningless makes the negative result almost conclusive. Both facts come from the same base rate, and if only one of them surprises you, that is worth sitting with.

title: Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
Exercises

Exercise: the conditional, from the simulated population















mean(disease[positive == 1])
About 0.091. Equivalently mean(disease & positive) / mean(positive), or sum(disease == 1 & positive == 1) / sum(positive == 1).



Exercise: the same table, the other way round















mean(positive[disease == 1])
About 0.992. This is the number the test manufacturer advertises. The previous exercise is the number the patient cares about.



Exercise: Bayes without the simulation















sens * prev / (sens * prev + (1 - spec) * (1 - prev))
0.0905.



Exercise: the same test, a different clinic















sens * 0.05 / (sens * 0.05 + (1 - spec) * 0.95)
0.510. Ten times the prevalence turns a 9% posterior into a 51% one. This is also the honest answer to “but surely my doctor ordered the test for a reason”—if you were tested because of symptoms, you are not in the 0.5% population any more.



Exercise: what do you tell the patient?















answer <- "B"
The full picture needs both numbers: the posterior (9%) and the update (0.5% to 9%, an eighteen-fold increase). Reporting only the first makes the test sound useless; reporting only the second makes it sound damning.

title: Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
Summary

Conditioning is subsetting. P(A \mid B) is computed by discarding everything outside B and counting what remains: mean(a[b == 1]).
P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B) / P(B). Most errors are denominator errors, so always ask “out of what?”
Multiplication rule: P(A \cap B) = P(B)P(A \mid B). Plain multiplication is the independent special case, and sampling without replacement is not it.
Bayes’ rule reverses a conditional, and it needs the base rate to do so. P(A \mid B) \ne P(B \mid A), and they can differ by an order of magnitude.
A 99%-sensitive, 95%-specific test for a disease with 0.5% prevalence gives a positive predictive value of 9%. That is not a paradox; it is what happens when a small error rate is applied to a much larger group.
Base-rate neglect is the habit of weighing the vivid evidence and forgetting the prior. It is why “99% accurate” is not a reportable property of a classifier and why “precision” exists as a separate word.
The same arithmetic governs fraud detection, alerting, screening, and every rare-event classifier you will ever build.

Next: random variables, which is what you get when you stop asking whether an event happened and start asking for a number.

title: Random Variables
text:
Discrete and continuous
So far, events. An event happened or it did not, and we counted. But data is not made of yes/no answers—it is made of numbers, and to reason about numbers we need one more object.
Roll two dice. The outcome is a pair like (6, 1). From that one outcome you can compute many different numbers, and each rule is a different random variable:
X = \text{the sum}, \qquad Y = \text{how many sixes appeared}
One column of outcomes, two columns of numbers computed from them. d1 + d2 is the function; X is what it returns. Notice that (d1 == 6) + (d2 == 6) adds two TRUE/FALSE values as 1 and 0—an event is a random variable that only takes the values 0 and 1, which is why the mean() trick has been working all along.
Notation. Capital letters (X, Y) are the random variable; lower-case (x, y) is a particular value it might take. So P(X = 7) is the probability that the sum comes out 7, and P(X \le 7) is the probability it comes out 7 or less. Getting the case right is not pedantry; it is the difference between “the rule” and “a number”.
Random variables come in two kinds, and which one you have determines what questions are answerable.
A discrete random variable takes values you can list: 0, 1, 2, \dots. Counts are discrete. Number of sixes, number of clicks, number of defective units, number of support tickets today.
A continuous random variable takes any value in a range. Measurements are continuous. Height, time, temperature, concentration. Between any two possible values there are infinitely many others.
The line is blurrier in practice than in theory—money is technically discrete (there are only so many cents) and heights are recorded to the nearest centimetre—and that is fine. The question is never “what is it really?” but “which set of tools describes it usefully?” Salary in dollars has so many possible values that treating it as continuous is more useful than listing them.

title: Random Variables
text:
Discrete: the probability mass function
For a discrete variable, each value carries a lump of probability. The probability mass function is the rule that says how much:
p(x) = P(X = x), \qquad \sum_x p(x) = 1
You already know how to estimate one—it is a table of proportions:
















It sums to 1, because every roll produced exactly one value and they all got counted. That is not a coincidence to be checked; it is what “probability distribution” means.








The familiar triangle. Seven is the most likely total because it has the most outcomes producing it—six of the 36 pairs—while 2 and 12 have one each. The shape of a distribution comes from the process that generated it, and this is the smallest example of that principle.
Compare the pmf of Y, the number of sixes:








Three values, and their exact probabilities are 25/36, 10/36, 1/36—0.694, 0.278, 0.028. The simulation gives 0.699, 0.272, 0.028. Same 100,000 rolls, a completely different distribution, because it is a different function of the same outcomes.

title: Random Variables
text:
The cumulative distribution function
The pmf breaks down for continuous variables, for a reason we will get to. The CDF does not, which makes it the more fundamental object:
F(x) = P(X \le x)
It is defined for every random variable of either kind, it starts at 0, it never decreases, and it ends at 1.








For a discrete variable the CDF is a staircase: flat between the possible values, jumping at each one, and the height of each jump is exactly that value’s probability mass. The picture and the pmf carry identical information.
The reason to care is that the CDF answers interval questions by subtraction:
P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)








0.6657, against the exact 24/36 = 0.6667. Every p-function you meet in the next chapter—pnorm, pbinom, ppois—is a CDF, and this subtraction is how you get an interval probability out of one.






Watch the inequality signs. F(9) - F(4) excludes 4 and includes 9. For a discrete variable that matters: P(X \le 9) - P(X \le 4) is not the same as P(X \le 9) - P(X \le 5), and off-by-one errors here are the most common source of quietly wrong probabilities in applied work. For a continuous variable it makes no difference at all, for reasons that are about to become clear.

title: Random Variables
text:
Continuous: density instead of mass
Now the part that trips people up.
Take heights of adults, in centimetres:








Ask for the probability that someone is exactly 180 cm tall:








Zero. And not “zero because our sample is finite”—exactly zero, in the true distribution. There are infinitely many possible heights, and if every one of them carried a positive lump of probability the total would be infinite. So each individual value must carry none.
That sounds like a defeat, but it is only a redefinition. Probability for a continuous variable lives in intervals, not points:








The probability density function f(x) is what you integrate over an interval to get its probability:
P(a < X < b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx
so f(x) is probability per unit of x, not probability. Its units are “probability per centimetre”. A histogram with freq = FALSE is an estimate of it—bar heights scaled so that total area is 1:














A density is not a probability, and it can exceed 1



dnorm(0, mean = 0, sd = 0.1) returns about 3.99. Nothing is broken. Squeeze a distribution into a narrow range and the curve must get tall to keep the area at 1. A uniform distribution on [0, 0.5] has density exactly 2 everywhere inside it.
The practical version: read heights of a density as relative, and read areas as probabilities. Density × width ≈ probability, for a narrow enough width:








0.02283 predicted against 0.02289 counted. The density did its job; it just was not itself a probability.


The CDF, meanwhile, needs no such apology. It means the same thing for continuous variables as for discrete ones—it is simply smooth instead of a staircase:








And the interval rule is unchanged:








0.1068 against 0.1056. That is the entire relationship between a simulation and a formula: same question, two ways of answering it, and if they disagree by more than noise you have found a bug in one of them.






 Density versus probability







A continuous random variable X has probability density f(0.3) = 2.4.
Which statement is correct?

Something is wrong: a probability cannot exceed 1, so f is not a valid density.Nothing is wrong. f(0.3) is a density, not a probability. P(X = 0.3) = 0; probabilities are areas under f, and an area can stay below 1 while the curve above it is tall and narrow.It means X takes the value 0.3 about 2.4 times as often as any other value in the sample.It means P(X \le 0.3) = 2.4, which is impossible, so X must be discrete.



Densities have units of probability per unit of x, not probability. Squeeze a distribution into a narrow range and the curve has to get tall to keep the total area at 1. A uniform distribution on [0, 0.5] has density exactly 2 everywhere inside that interval; dnorm(0, mean = 0, sd = 0.1) in R returns about 3.99. Neither is a bug.
For a continuous variable, P(X = 0.3) = 0 exactly—there are uncountably many values it could take and no single one carries any mass. That sounds like a technicality until you meet it in practice: mean(x == 0.3) on a sample of continuous measurements returns 0, and it always will. What you can ask for is P(0.29 < X < 0.31), which is an area, roughly f(0.3) \times 0.02 = 0.048.
The third option describes something a density nearly does—the curve being higher at 0.3 than at some other point does mean values land near 0.3 more often than near that point—but “2.4 times as often as any other value” is not what the number 2.4 says. The height is only comparable to other heights of the same density, not to 1, and never to a count.
The practical rule: read heights of a density as relative, and read areas as probabilities. The function that gives you areas directly is the CDF, and in R that is pnorm, punif, pbinom, and their relatives.

title: Random Variables
text:
What comes next, and why
You now have a distribution: a complete description of what values a random variable takes and how often. A complete description is often too much description. Eleven numbers for the dice sum, a whole curve for heights—you cannot put that in a sentence, and you cannot compare two of them at a glance.
So next week compresses a distribution into two numbers:

Expectation, E[X]—the long-run average value, the balance point of the distribution. It is the mean from Describing a Single Variable, promoted from a fact about a sample to a property of the process that generated it.
Variance, \operatorname{Var}(X)—how far the variable typically strays from its expectation.







Why The Standard Error of a Mean is the hinge of this course



Those two summaries would be mildly useful on their own. What makes them the center of the term is a single fact about how they combine:
For independent random variables, variances add.
Everything downstream follows from that one line. Apply it to a sample mean \bar X and you get \operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \sigma^2/n, so the standard deviation of a sample mean is \sigma/\sqrt{n}—the standard error. That formula is why bigger samples are better, exactly how much better, and by what rate. Confidence intervals are built on it. So are p-values, sample-size calculations, and every A/B test you will ever run.
Notice the word independent in the statement. That is the concept from Probability, and it is load-bearing: when observations are not independent—repeat visits from the same user, students within a classroom, days within a week—\sigma/\sqrt{n} is wrong, your interval is too narrow, and you are more confident than the data entitles you to be. This is one of the most common real errors in applied statistics, and by The Standard Error of a Mean you will be able to say exactly which step it breaks.
We are not deriving any of that here. Arrive next week solid on two things and it will be a short evening: a random variable is a function of a random outcome, and independence means P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B).

title: Random Variables
text:
Exercises

Exercise: a different function of the same rolls















mean(abs(d1 - d2) == 0)
Or simply mean(d1 == d2). The exact value is 6/36 = 1/6 \approx 0.1667.



Exercise: reading a CDF















Fx(9) - Fx(4)
About 0.6657. For an integer-valued variable, “at least 5” means “not at most 4”, so the subtraction point is 4 and not 5. The same off-by-one shows up whenever you use pbinom or ppois for a tail probability.



Exercise: a tail probability for a continuous variable















mean(h > 185)
About 0.031, and pnorm(185, 170, 8, lower.tail = FALSE) gives 0.0304.



Exercise: which kind of variable















answer <- "A"
Counts and yes/no outcomes are discrete; times and measurements are continuous. The binary case is worth flagging because it is the one people forget: TRUE and FALSE are a perfectly good random variable, and treating them as 1 and 0 is what lets mean() compute a probability.

title: Random Variables
text:
Summary

A random variable is a function from outcomes to numbers. The rule is fixed; only the outcome is random. Several different random variables can be defined on the same outcomes, and the same simulation supports all of them.
Discrete variables take listable values (counts, categories, 0/1); continuous ones take any value in a range (times, measurements).
The probability mass function p(x) = P(X = x) describes a discrete variable, and table(x) / length(x) estimates it.
For a continuous variable P(X = x) = 0 for every x. Probability lives in intervals, described by a density f(x) whose area is the probability. Densities are not probabilities and may exceed 1.
The CDF F(x) = P(X \le x) works for both kinds, and interval probabilities are F(b) - F(a). Mind the endpoints for discrete variables.
Next week: expectation and variance, and the fact that variances of independent quantities add—which gives \operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \sigma^2/n and everything built on it.

Next, though: the handful of distributions that describe most of the data you will ever meet, and how to tell which one you are looking at.

title: The Distributions We Actually Use
text:
R’s four-letter alphabet
There are hundreds of named probability distributions. You will use about five.
They earn their place not because they are mathematically convenient—though they are—but because each one is the answer to a kind of question about a process. A named distribution is a compressed description of a mechanism: “independent yes/no trials with a fixed success rate” is a binomial, and once you have said that, every probability about it is already determined.
That is the skill this chapter trains, and it is why “which distribution would you use for X?” is such a common interview question. The bad answer squints at a histogram. The good answer describes the process that generated the data and reads off the distribution that matches.
Before the distributions, the interface. Every distribution in R comes with four functions, distinguished by a single prefix letter. Learn the pattern once and you know it for all of them.
p and q are inverses of each other: p takes a value and returns a probability, q takes a probability and returns a value. Mixing them up is the most common error in this chapter, and the way to catch it is to ask what the units of your answer should be. A cutoff has units of the data; a probability does not.

title: The Distributions We Actually Use
text:
Prefix
Gives you
Normal
Binomial
Poisson




d
density or mass at a point, f(x) or P(X = x)
dnorm
dbinom
dpois


p
cumulative probability, P(X \le x)
pnorm
pbinom
ppois


q
quantile: the x with P(X \le x) = p
qnorm
qbinom
qpois


r
random draws from the distribution
rnorm
rbinom
rpois










Every one of these takes the distribution’s parameters as further arguments— pnorm(x, mean, sd), pbinom(q, size, prob), ppois(q, lambda). If you forget them, R silently uses defaults (mean = 0, sd = 1), which is a real source of wrong answers that look fine.

title: The Distributions We Actually Use
text:
Bernoulli: one yes/no trial
The simplest random variable there is. X = 1 with probability p and X = 0 otherwise.
The generating process: one trial with two outcomes. A coin flip, a click, a conversion, a default, a patient recovering.








Twenty draws with a true rate of 0.3 gave a sample mean of 0.4. Nothing went wrong—that is Probability’s whole theme in one line, and quantifying how far off it is allowed to be is The Standard Error of a Mean’s job.
The Bernoulli is not a curiosity. Every logical vector you have taken the mean of in these notes was a sample of Bernoullis, and every proportion you will ever estimate—conversion rate, click rate, mortality rate, accuracy—is the mean of one.

title: The Distributions We Actually Use
section: Binomial: how many successes in n trials
text:
Binomial: how many successes in n trials
Add up n independent Bernoulli trials that all share the same p, and you have a binomial.






The three conditions, all of which can fail



X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p) requires:

a fixed number of trials n, decided before you start;
the trials are independent;
the success probability p is the same for every trial.

When someone hands you count data and asks whether it is binomial, these are the three questions. In real data, condition 3 is the one that usually fails, and we will simulate exactly that failure at the end of the chapter.


An email campaign sends 20 messages to each recipient list, and each message has a 30% chance of being opened. How many opens per list?








The parameters mean what they say: n = 20 is how many chances there are, and p = 0.3 is the chance each one comes off. The distribution is centered at np = 6.








Simulation against formula, as always:
















0.1925 against 0.1916; 0.2398 against 0.2375. The d and p functions are doing in closed form what 100,000 simulated lists did by brute force.
And q runs it backwards—what open count is the 95th percentile?








Nine. So a list that produced 12 opens is genuinely unusual under this model, and that sentence—this outcome is unusual under this model—is the seed of every hypothesis test you will meet later in the term.

Exercise: a tail probability, and the off-by-one















1 - pbinom(14, size = 20, prob = 0.5)
0.0207. Equivalently pbinom(14, 20, 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE) or sum(dbinom(15:20, 20, 0.5)). The endpoint rule for an integer-valued variable: P(X \ge k) = 1 - P(X \le k-1).



Exercise: simulate it, then check it















mean(opens >= 8)
About 0.229. The exact answer is pbinom(7, 20, 0.3, lower.tail = FALSE) = 0.2277—and note the 7 rather than the 8, the same off-by-one as the last exercise.

title: The Distributions We Actually Use
section: Normal: the one everybody has heard of
text:
Normal: the one everybody has heard of
The Normal (or Gaussian) distribution is continuous, symmetric, and defined by two parameters that are exactly what you would want them to be: \mu the center and \sigma the spread.
The generating process: a quantity built from many small, independent contributions added together. Adult height is genetics plus nutrition plus childhood illness plus a hundred other things, none dominant. Measurement error is the accumulation of many small imperfections. That is the mechanism, and it is why the Normal turns up as often as it does.














The 68–95–99.7 rule



For any Normal distribution, the proportion within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean is fixed:








68%, 95%, 99.7%. It does not depend on \mu or \sigma—rescaling a Normal gives another Normal, which is why one table used to serve for all of them.
Worth memorizing because it makes you fast: an observation two SDs out is noticeably unusual, three SDs out is rare. And the multiplier for a 95% interval is not exactly 2 but qnorm(0.975) = 1.96, a number you will type roughly a hundred times between here and December.


The three non-random functions, on a test scored with mean 100 and SD 15:








Read them as four different kinds of question. The density is a curve height and means little on its own. pnorm answers “what fraction score below 115?”—84%. lower.tail = FALSE answers “what fraction above 130?”—2.3%. And qnorm answers “what score puts you in the top 2.5%?”—129.4, which is in points, not in probability.

Exercise: a cutoff, not a probability















qnorm(0.9, mean = 100, sd = 15)
119.2. Equivalently qnorm(0.10, 100, 15, lower.tail = FALSE).

title: The Distributions We Actually Use
section: Poisson: counts of events in a window
text:
Poisson: counts of events in a window
The generating process: events arriving independently at a constant average rate over a fixed interval of time or space, with no fixed number of trials and no natural upper bound.
Support tickets per hour. Emergency calls per shift. Typos per page. Website visits per minute. Defects per square meter. Earthquakes per decade.
One parameter, \lambda, which is the expected number of events per window.














The Poisson’s fingerprint: mean equals variance











For a Poisson, E[X] = \operatorname{Var}(X) = \lambda. Both come out at about 3.19 here.
This is a genuinely useful diagnostic. Given count data, compute the mean and the variance. If the variance is much larger than the mean—which happens constantly—your counts are overdispersed, the constant-rate assumption is wrong, and a Poisson model will understate your uncertainty. That usually means the rate is not constant: some hours are busier, some pages have more typos, some users click far more than others.


The relationship to the binomial is worth one line: a binomial with huge n and tiny p, holding np = \lambda, converges to a Poisson. That is why the Poisson is sometimes called the law of rare events, and it is why “many chances, each unlikely” and “a steady arrival rate” describe the same data.

title: The Distributions We Actually Use
section: Uniform: no value preferred over any other
text:
Uniform: no value preferred over any other
The generating process: every value in a range is equally likely, and nothing in the mechanism favours any part of it.








Genuinely uniform real-world data is rarer than students expect—“I have no information, so everything is equally likely” is a statement about you, not about the world. Where the uniform earns its keep is as the raw material of simulation: runif is the engine underneath sample(), and under the hood every other r-function is a transformation of uniform draws. You will also meet it later in the term as the distribution of a p-value when the null hypothesis is true, which is a fact worth arriving pre-warned about.






A continuous uniform on [0, 0.5] has density 2 everywhere inside the interval— dunif(0.3, 0, 0.5) returns 2. Densities above 1 are ordinary, as Random Variables insisted.

title: The Distributions We Actually Use
section: Exponential: the time until the next event
text:
Exponential: the time until the next event
The Poisson counts how many events fall in a window. The exponential measures the gap between consecutive events. Same process, two questions—if arrivals are Poisson at rate \lambda, the waiting times are Exponential(\lambda).








Two features are worth carrying away. The mean and the standard deviation are both 1/\lambda, so an exponential is always as spread out as it is large—a distribution with a mean of twenty minutes routinely produces gaps of an hour. And it is memoryless: having already waited ten minutes tells you nothing about how much longer you will wait.








The two numbers agree. This is the formal version of the intuition that a bus which is already late is not therefore “due”—and it is the assumption that fails most often in practice, because real machines wear out and real customers give up.

title: The Distributions We Actually Use
text:
Log-normal: positive, skewed, and everywhere
The Normal arises when many small effects add. When they multiply, you get the log-normal—because the logarithm of a product is a sum, and a sum of many small independent things is Normal.
That covers a great deal of the data you will actually be handed: incomes, revenue per customer, response latency, session durations, file sizes, claim amounts. All are positive, all have a long right tail, and none of them are Normal.








The mean sits well above the median, which is the signature you met in Describing a Single Variable—now with a mechanism attached rather than just a shape.
There is a trap here that catches people who ought to know better. meanlog is the mean of the logarithm, not of the variable:








exp(meanlog) is the median, not the mean; the mean is larger by a factor of e^{\sigma^2/2}. Reporting the wrong one understates an average revenue or latency by a third here, and by more as the spread grows.
The practical move is to work on the log scale—take logs, do the ordinary Normal-theory analysis, and transform back while remembering that the back-transformed center is a median. Nearly every “our average response time is fine but users are complaining” story is a log-normal being summarized by its mean.

title: The Distributions We Actually Use
section: Choosing a distribution: ask what made the data
text:
Choosing a distribution: ask what made the data
Here is the decision, stated as a set of questions about the process, not about the shape of a histogram:







If the process is…
reach for




a single yes/no outcome
Bernoulli(p)


a count of successes out of a fixed number of independent trials sharing the same p
Binomial(n, p)


a count of events in a fixed window, arriving independently at a steady rate, with no fixed n
Poisson(\lambda)


a continuous quantity built from many small independent contributions that add
Normal(\mu, \sigma)


a positive quantity built from many small independent contributions that multiply
Log-normal(\mu, \sigma)


the waiting time between events arriving at a steady rate
Exponential(\lambda)


every value in a range equally likely, by the mechanism
Uniform(a, b)









 Which distribution, and why







You are modeling the number of emergency calls a dispatch center receives in a given 10-minute window. Calls arrive independently from a large population at a roughly steady average rate, and there is no fixed upper limit on how many could arrive.
Which distribution is the natural starting point, and why?

Binomial, because each call either happens or does not, so the count is a sum of successes.Poisson, because the quantity is a count of independent events arriving at a constant rate in a fixed window, with no fixed number of trials and no natural maximum.Normal, because counts of many small independent contributions are approximately Normal.Uniform, because with no information favouring any particular count, all counts should be treated as equally likely.



Choose a distribution by asking what process generated the number, not by looking at the shape of a histogram.
The Poisson description fits this generating story exactly: events, independent of one another, arriving at a constant average rate \lambda over a fixed window, with the count unbounded above. That is what the Poisson distribution is, and its single parameter \lambda is the expected number of calls in the window.
The binomial answer fails on a specific point: a binomial needs a fixed number of trials n, and here there is none. There is no roster of, say, 200 potential callers each of whom flips a coin. (The connection is real, though: a binomial with huge n and tiny p and np = \lambda converges to a Poisson, which is why the Poisson is sometimes described as the law of rare events.)
The Normal answer is a statement about a limit, not about a generating process. For large \lambda the Poisson does become roughly Normal, and using a Normal approximation may be fine for computation—but it is continuous, unbounded below, and will happily assign probability to -3 calls. As a model of the mechanism it is wrong even where it is numerically convenient.
The uniform answer is the one to watch for, because it sounds principled. “No information, so all outcomes equally likely” is a statement about your ignorance, not about the world—and it is factually wrong here: 3 calls in ten minutes is far more likely than 300. Uniform is right when the mechanism genuinely has no preference, such as a random draw from a range, not as a default for not knowing.






When the assumption fails: overdispersion
The binomial’s third condition—the same p for every trial—is the one that breaks in real data, and it breaks quietly.
Twenty ad impressions per user. Suppose you are told the overall click rate is 30% and you model clicks as \text{Binomial}(20, 0.3). But users are not interchangeable: half are casual browsers who click 5% of the time, half are engaged users who click 55%. The overall rate is still exactly 30%.








Identical means—6.00 against 5.99. And a standard deviation of 5.28 against the model’s 2.05, more than two and a half times too small.








One distribution has a single hump; the other has two, and the model’s center sits in the valley between them—the same failure mode as the commute data in Describing a Single Variable, arriving now with a probability model attached.
The practical damage:








The model says 0.7% of users click at most once. The reality is 37%. If you built an alerting rule on “fewer than two clicks is anomalous”, you would have flagged more than a third of your users as anomalies and had no idea why.






The lesson, which is the point of the whole chapter



Every number you would have reported about the average was right. The mean was exactly correct. What was wrong was the spread, and therefore every statement about how surprising an observation is—which is to say, every p-value, every confidence interval, every threshold.
Choosing a distribution is not a formality you perform before the real analysis. It is a claim about the mechanism, and when the claim is wrong the analysis is confidently, quietly wrong in exactly the direction that makes you overconfident.
The diagnostic is cheap: compare the variance you observe with the variance the model implies. For a binomial that is np(1-p) = 4.2; we observed 27.9. For a Poisson it is \lambda. When the observed spread is much larger, some parameter you assumed constant is not.




Exercise: which process is which















answer <- "A"
Fixed n with a shared success probability gives a binomial. A rate over a window with no fixed n gives a Poisson. A measurement built from many small independent contributions gives a Normal. One yes/no trial gives a Bernoulli.

title: The Distributions We Actually Use
text:
Summary

A named distribution is a compressed description of a generating process. Choose one by describing the mechanism, not by looking at a histogram.
R gives every distribution four functions: d (density or mass), p (cumulative, P(X \le x)), q (quantile, the inverse of p), and r (random draws). Check the units of your answer to catch p/q confusion.
Bernoulli(p): one yes/no trial. Every proportion you estimate is a mean of these.
Binomial(n, p): successes in a fixed number of independent trials with a constant p. All three conditions can fail.
Normal(\mu, \sigma): a continuous quantity built from many small independent contributions. 68–95–99.7, and qnorm(0.975) = 1.96.
Poisson(\lambda): counts of independent events at a steady rate in a fixed window. Its fingerprint is \text{mean} = \text{variance}, and a variance much larger than the mean is evidence the rate is not constant.
Exponential(\lambda): the gap between Poisson arrivals. Mean and standard deviation are both 1/\lambda, and it is memoryless—waiting longer does not make the event more due.
Log-normal: positive quantities built from effects that multiply—income, revenue, latency, durations. exp(meanlog) is the median, not the mean. Work on the log scale.
Uniform(a, b): every value equally likely by the mechanism—not as a default for ignorance. Mostly seen as the raw material of simulation.
When a distributional assumption fails, the mean often survives and the spread does not. A mixture of two click rates matched the binomial’s mean exactly and had a standard deviation two and a half times larger, turning a 0.7% event into a 37% one.

Next: the practice problems, and then The Standard Error of a Mean turns these distributions into two numbers apiece and shows you what those two numbers buy.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Predict before you run
None of these are graded and none of them are auto-checked. They are here so you arrive on Monday with something to argue about.
Work them in order. Most of the first section comes in two parts: predict, then run. The prediction is where the learning happens. Probability is the topic where skipping straight to the answer is most tempting and most useless, because every output looks reasonable once you have seen it.
Write your prediction down. On paper, in a comment, in a note on your phone. Then run it.

title: Practice Problems
text:
A1. Twenty flips
Predict all four numbers before running.








Then answer: the fair coin came up 1 sixteen times out of twenty. Is this evidence that sample() is broken? Write down what you would need to compute to decide, without computing it—you will have the tools in three weeks. Then say what the longest_run figure would have to be before you started to worry, and why “that looks non-random” is a bad instinct.


A2. Two events on one die
Predict all four numbers, and in particular predict whether the last two will be equal.








Then answer: A and B are events on a single roll of a single die, and they are independent. Explain how that is possible when they are computed from the same number. Then construct a third event C on the same die that is not independent of A, and say how you would know before simulating.


A3. The screen, at a different prevalence
Do not run this yet. Write down your guess for the second number first.








Then answer: state, in one sentence each, which of the two numbers a test manufacturer would print on the box, which one a patient is asking for, and which one a hospital deciding whether to run the screen at all should care about. They are not all the same.


A4. The Normal, checked
Predict all four before running.








Then answer: the last two numbers do not match exactly. Which one is “right”? Say precisely what each of them estimates, and which you would report if these 100,000 values were real measurements rather than draws from a distribution you chose yourself.


A5. Same mean, different world
Predict which pair of numbers will match and which will not.








Then answer: the variances differ by a factor of about seven. Name a business decision that would be identical under both models and one that would be badly wrong under the first. Then say which single plot would have revealed the difference in two seconds.

title: Practice Problems
section: This runs, and it answers a different question
text:
This runs, and it answers a different question
Every cell below executes cleanly and prints a correct number. Each one is attached to a stated task that it does not answer. Find the mismatch, say what question the code actually answers, and write the code that answers the one asked.
This is the harder skill and the more valuable one. Code that crashes tells you it is broken.

B1. At least one six

Task: you roll four dice. What is the probability of getting at least one six?















Hint, once you have a guess





What is mean(sixes == 2)? Should that outcome count toward the task’s question?



Fix it, then compute the exact answer with the complement rule and check that the two agree.


B2. The reassuring number

Task: a patient tests positive on the screen in problem A3. Report the probability that they have the disease.









The number printed is correct and it is not the answer. Say which conditional probability it is, compute the one that was asked for, and then write the sentence you would actually say to the patient—including both the posterior probability and the size of the update from the prior.


B3. Two flights

Task: you have a connection with a two-hour layover. Flight A and flight B each run late about 20% of the time. What is the probability that both legs are late?









Every marginal probability here is correct. The final line is not. Compute the right answer from the same three vectors, state the ratio between the two, and name the variable in the code that is the reason. Then give two more examples from your own field where the same shared-cause structure would break a multiplication.


B4. Two children

Task: a family has two children. You learn that at least one of them is a girl. What is the probability that both are girls?









The answer printed is about 0.5. The answer to the task is not 0.5.
Find the line that conditions on the wrong event, fix it, and explain the gap in terms of denominators: how many families are in each of the two conditioning sets, and which families are in one but not the other. This is a famous problem and the argument about it is usually about the wording, not the arithmetic—so also state one plausible way of learning “at least one is a girl” that would genuinely make 0.5 the right answer.


B5. The alert threshold

Task: an error-logging service sees about 7 errors an hour. Set an alert threshold so that it fires on roughly 1% of normal hours.









The threshold was computed correctly from a Poisson with the correct mean. The alert fires on 11% of hours, not 1%.
Diagnose it using a comparison the chapter told you to run on every count variable. Then propose a fix, and say what the fix costs—there is more than one defensible answer here, and “use the empirical quantile instead” is only one of them.


B6. The classifier that is 97% accurate

Task: a fraud model flags transactions. Report whether it is any good.









Accuracy of 0.97 sounds excellent. Compute two further numbers from the same vectors: the proportion of flagged transactions that are actually fraud, and the proportion of fraud that gets flagged. Then compute the accuracy of the model that flags nothing at all, and say what that comparison tells you about accuracy as a metric for rare events.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Judgment
No code. Bring written answers; we will disagree about these out loud.

C1.
You are asked in an interview: “Are mutually exclusive events independent?”
Write the answer you would give out loud, in under thirty seconds, including one concrete example. Then write the follow-up question you would expect next, and answer that too.


C2.
A public health agency is deciding whether to screen the whole adult population for a disease with a prevalence of 1 in 2,000, using a test with 99% sensitivity and 98% specificity.
Make the strongest case for the program and the strongest case against it, each in three sentences, using numbers you compute yourself. Then say which single additional piece of information would settle it for you.


C3.
Your A/B test assigns visitors to a variant and records whether they convert. The analysis treats the visitors as independent.
List three concrete ways that assumption can fail in a real product, and for each one say whether it makes your reported uncertainty too small, too large, or unclear. (You will be able to prove the direction after The Standard Error of a Mean; for now, argue it.)


C4.
Conditional Probability and Bayes showed that a positive result on an excellent test can leave you at 9% probability of illness, and also that the same result raises your risk eighteenfold.
Both statements are true of the same number. Write a short paragraph—the kind you would put in a report—that conveys both without leaving the reader with a false impression in either direction. Then write the version a journalist would print from it, and say what you would do differently to prevent that.


C5.
Everything this week was about a process you chose: you knew the true probability, so you could check the answer.
Real data does not come with the true probability attached. Pick any one quantity from these chapters—the 9% posterior, the 0.30 chance of at least one six, the click rate of 0.3—and answer: if you only had the data and not the generating process, how would you know your distributional assumption was wrong?
Bring your list of checks to class. Some of them are standard-error and hypothesis-testing material, and I would rather you wrote them down first.

title: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error
text:
What is here
Monday, September 21
Post your questions on any of these pages by Monday at 12:00 noon, the morning of class.
This is the most important week of the course, and I would rather say so plainly than let you discover it in November.
Everything from confidence intervals onward, hypothesis tests, A/B tests, the standard errors printed next to every regression coefficient you will ever read—rests on one result, and that result is derived here, in The Standard Error of a Mean, in about four lines. If those four lines are solid, the rest of the term is bookkeeping around them. If they are not, you will spend the next ten weeks manipulating formulas whose origin you cannot reconstruct, and you will not be able to tell when software has handed you a number that does not mean what its label says.
The result is this. Take a sample of size n from a population with standard deviation \sigma, and compute the sample mean. That mean is itself random—a different sample would give a different value. How much would it move?
\operatorname{SE}(\bar X) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
That is the whole of inference in one line. It says the wobble in your estimate is knowable, that it shrinks as you collect more data, and—the part that costs money—that it shrinks only like \sqrt{n}.
Describing a Single Variable ended by asking: if the data collection were repeated from scratch, how different would your number be? This is the week you can answer it.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error
text:
Expectation



E[X] as the number a long-run average settles down to, watched settling. The discrete and continuous cases. Linearity, including the fact that E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] whether or not X and Y are independent. And the distinction that trips people for years: expectation is a property of a distribution, the sample mean is a statistic computed from data.








Variance and Standard Deviation



\operatorname{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2] as average squared distance. Why we square, and why we then take a root. \operatorname{Var}(aX+b) =
a^2\operatorname{Var}(X), and the b vanishing. And the key fact: for independent X and Y, variances add—standard deviations do not. We simulate a case where the rule holds and a case where it fails spectacularly, so that “independent” reads as a condition rather than as a word in the way.








The Standard Error of a Mean



The payoff. \operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \sigma^2/n derived from the two rules in Expectation and Variance and Standard Deviation, then demonstrated by simulation at n = 4, 16, 64, 256. What 1/\sqrt{n} costs you in practice. And the difference between the standard deviation of the data and the standard error of the mean, which is the most reliably muddled pair of numbers in applied statistics.








Practice Problems



Predict-before-you-run, code that executes cleanly and is still wrong, and questions with no code at all. Not graded and not auto-checked—bring answers and disagreements to class.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error
text:
How to read this week
Simulation before formula, every time. Nearly every rule in these three chapters is stated, then checked by generating data and looking. That is not decoration. A formula you have verified yourself, on numbers you watched appear, is a formula you can reconstruct in an interview or a meeting three years from now. A formula you accepted is one you will misremember.
So when a cell is about to demonstrate a rule, predict the output first. If the chapter says variances add, write down what you think var(x + y) will print before you press Run. Being wrong once, deliberately and cheaply, is worth more than reading the correct statement five times.






Due this week



HW 2 is due at the start of class, and Monday’s lab is Watching \sigma/\sqrt{n} emerge by simulation—so arrive having read 5.3.
Post your reading questions by Monday noon. This is the week to ask small, embarrassing questions: why the square, why the square root, why independence, why \sqrt{n} and not n. Every one of those is a good question, and the session is built out of what you post.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Expectation
text:
Watching it settle
Last week you met random variables and the distributions we actually use. A distribution is a complete description of a random quantity: every value it can take and how often. That is more information than anyone can hold in their head, so we do to distributions exactly what Describing a Single Variable did to columns of data—replace them with a couple of numbers.
The first of those numbers is the expectation, E[X]. It is the center of the distribution in the same sense the mean was the center of a dataset: the balance point.
But the definition worth carrying around is the operational one.
The cleanest way to believe this is to watch it happen. Roll a fair die ten thousand times and track the running average after every roll.
After 10 rolls the running mean is 3.30. After 100 it is 3.51, after 1,000 it is 3.556, and after 10,000 it is 3.4909. Now look at the whole path, with E[X] =
3.5 drawn as a dashed line. The horizontal axis is on a log scale, because otherwise the first thousand rolls are squeezed into an invisible sliver at the left:
Two things are worth noticing, and the second one is the one people miss.
It settles. The early wobbling is violent—after five rolls the running mean can easily be 2 or 5—and then it calms down and hugs the line. That convergence has a name, the law of large numbers, and it is the reason a casino with enough customers has no risk at all while any individual customer has plenty.
It settles slowly. Look at the axis: it took a log scale to make the picture readable, because the improvement from 100 rolls to 1,000 rolls looks about the same as the improvement from 1,000 to 10,000. Getting one more decimal place costs a hundred times the data. You have just seen 1/\sqrt{n} without being told about it, and in The Standard Error of a Mean we will pin the rate down exactly.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Expectation
text:
Computing E[X]

The discrete case
For a discrete random variable, weight each value by its probability and add:
E[X] = \sum_{x} x \cdot P(X = x)
That is a weighted average, and the weights are the probabilities. Here is a scratch card. It costs $2, and the prize table is:



Prize
$0
$1
$5
$20




Probability
0.70
0.20
0.08
0.02











The expected prize is exactly $1.00. The card costs $2. So the expected profit per card, from your side, is -\$1.00: every card you buy costs you a dollar on average, forever, regardless of how you feel about the one that paid $20.
Believe the arithmetic, then check it anyway:








Half a million cards give a mean prize of 0.9967 and a mean profit of -1.0033. The formula and the simulation are computing the same thing by two routes, which is exactly the habit this week is trying to build: when a formula surprises you, simulate it.






Note the scale at which the expectation becomes a fact rather than a tendency. Sell 100,000 of these cards and the operator’s take is close to $100,000 with very little uncertainty. Buy one, and the expectation tells you almost nothing about your evening. Same number, two completely different kinds of usefulness.





The continuous case
For a continuous random variable the sum becomes an integral, weighted by the density f(x) instead of by point probabilities:
E[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, f(x)\,dx
You will not be asked to evaluate integrals in this course. What you do need is that it is the same idea—every possible value, weighted by how much probability sits near it—and that for the distributions you met last week the answer is already known:



Distribution
E[X]




Bernoulli(p)
p


Binomial(n, p)
np


Normal(\mu, \sigma)
\mu


Uniform(a, b)
(a+b)/2


Exponential(rate \lambda)
1/\lambda


Poisson(\lambda)
\lambda



Check one of them. An exponential with rate 0.4 should have expectation 1/0.4 = 2.5:








2.5029 against 2.5. Close, and not exact—which is the subject of the next section.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Expectation
text:
E[X] is not \bar{x}
This distinction is worth more to you than any formula in the chapter, and it is the one that quietly confuses people for years.
Draw 30 observations from that same exponential, six separate times, and compute the sample mean each time:








2.869, 3.329, 2.356, 3.123, 2.298, 2.147. Six numbers, all of them the “average” of an exponential with expectation 2.5, none of them 2.5, and the spread between the largest and the smallest is over a full unit.






Two objects, two kinds












E[X], or \mu
\bar{x}




What it belongs to
the distribution
a sample


Is it random?
no—it is a fixed number
yes—a different sample gives a different value


Do you know it?
usually not
always, you computed it


How do you get it?
from the model, by formula
from data, with mean()



\bar{x} is an estimate of \mu. It is right on average and wrong in every particular sample. The question “how wrong, typically?” is not answerable from anything in this chapter—it needs the variance, which is 5.2, and then the derivation in The Standard Error of a Mean.


Notation helps and is worth adopting now: Greek letters (\mu, \sigma) for population quantities you do not know, Latin letters (\bar{x}, s) for things you computed from data. When you see a formula with both in it, it is telling you something about how the second relates to the first.






 Expectation versus sample mean







You simulate 30 draws from an exponential distribution whose expectation is exactly 2.5, and mean() of your draws returns 2.869.
What is the relationship between the 2.5 and the 2.869?

The 2.869 is the better number, since it came from actual data rather than from a formula.Something is wrong with the simulation: with a correct random number generator the sample mean should reproduce 2.5.E[X] = 2.5 is a fixed property of the distribution and does not change. The 2.869 is a statistic computed from one sample; a different 30 draws would give a different value, and the whole of Week 5 is about how different.They are the same quantity with different names, so either may be reported.



These are two different kinds of object and keeping them apart is most of what this week is for.
E[X] is a number attached to the distribution. It is not random, it does not depend on any data, and no amount of sampling changes it. For an exponential with rate 0.4 it is 1/0.4 = 2.5, full stop.
\bar{x} is a number attached to a sample. It is computed from data, and because the data are random, \bar{x} is itself a random quantity. Run the same simulation six times and you get six different values—in the chapter, 2.869, 3.329, 2.356, 3.123, 2.298, 2.147.
Nothing is broken. \bar{x} is an estimate of E[X]: correct on average (that is what E[\bar{X}] = \mu says) and wrong in every individual sample. The question the rest of the course answers is “wrong by how much, typically?”—and the answer, derived in 5.3, is \sigma/\sqrt{n}.
Notation is a real help here. Greek letters (\mu, \sigma) are population quantities you do not know; Latin letters with bars and hats (\bar{x}, s) are things you computed from data.






Exercise: reading a payout table















sum(payout * prob)
R multiplies the two vectors elementwise, so payout * prob gives the five contributions and sum() adds them: -0.55 + 0 + 0.30 + 0.40 + 1.00 = 1.15.



Exercise: what is a fair price?















sum(prize * p)
The expected prize is $1.00, so $1.00 is the fair price. Every cent above that is the operator’s expected margin per card.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Expectation
text:
Linearity
Now the property that makes expectation genuinely useful, as opposed to merely meaningful.

Constants pass straight through
E[aX + b] = a\,E[X] + b
If you double every value and add ten, the balance point doubles and moves by ten. This is not deep; it is what “balance point” means. But it is worth verifying once so you trust it later:








mean(x) is 4.9992, and both routes to E[3X+10] give 24.9976. Identical, not approximately identical, because the rule holds for the sample mean exactly as it holds for the expectation.
The practical use is unit conversion. If waiting times average 14 minutes, then in seconds they average 60 \times 14 = 840, and nobody has to re-derive anything.


Sums add, and independence is not required
E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]
This one deserves your attention. It holds always. It does not care whether X and Y are independent, correlated, or one is a deterministic function of the other.
Most people, having been told all term that independence matters, assume it must be lurking here. It is not. Watch: let Y be X^2, which is about as dependent on X as anything can be.








E[X] \approx 4.999, E[Y] \approx 29.009, and both the mean of the sum and the sum of the means come out at 34.0079. To the last printed digit.
Now the contrast that shows independence does matter somewhere. Try the same thing with a product:








185.20 against 145.02. Not close, and not noise—E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] is a different rule and it genuinely requires independence, which X and X^2 spectacularly lack.






The line to remember



Sums are free. Products are not.
E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] needs no assumptions at all. E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] needs independence.
This is why you can compute the expected value of a total—revenue across regions, total delay across the legs of a journey, the sum of n observations in a sample—without knowing anything whatever about how the pieces move together. In 5.3 that is precisely what lets us find E[\bar X] in one line.
And then in Variance and Standard Deviation, variance will turn out to behave like the product rule, not the sum rule. That asymmetry is the whole reason independence is a condition worth checking.








 Sums versus products







Let X be tomorrow’s high temperature and Y the number of ice creams a seaside kiosk sells tomorrow. These two are about as dependent as two variables get.
Which of the following are you entitled to write down?

Neither, because X and Y are dependent and both rules assume independence.E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always holds, dependence or not. E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] does not, and here it will fail badly.Both, because expectation is linear and linearity covers products as well as sums.E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] always holds; it is the sum rule that needs independence.



Sums are free. Products are not.
E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y] is unconditional. There is no independence assumption anywhere in it, and this is genuinely surprising the first time you meet it—the average of a total is the total of the averages, no matter how tangled the two variables are. Averaging simply does not notice how the two variables move together.
E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] is a completely different statement, and it does require independence. On a hot day both X and Y are large at the same time, so the product is large exactly when both factors are, and the average product comes out well above the product of the averages.
The practical consequence: you can compute the expected value of any sum or any weighted total—revenue across regions, total delay across legs of a journey, the mean of a sample—without knowing anything at all about how the pieces are related. That is what makes the derivation in 5.3 possible. Variances are the ones that will demand independence, and that is exactly where 5.2 gets careful.







Exercise: linearity without re-simulating















1.8 * mean(x) + 32
mean(x) is 4.99919, so the answer is 1.8 \times 4.99919 + 32 = 40.99855. Try mean(1.8 * x + 32) afterwards and confirm it agrees to every printed digit.



Exercise: a sum of dependent variables















mean(u + v)
It returns 95.0036. By linearity E[V] = 100 - 2E[U] = 90, so E[U+V] = 95, and the dependence between U and V is irrelevant to the calculation.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Expectation
text:
A worked fair-game problem
Expectation questions in interviews are almost always one of these two shapes, and both are the same shape underneath.
Shape one: is this bet worth taking? A friend offers: roll a fair die, they pay you the face value in dollars, and you pay $4 to play.
E[X] = 3.5 for a fair die, so the expected profit is 3.5 - 4 = -0.50 per roll. Decline.








-0.5027 over 200,000 rolls, against the exact -0.50.
Shape two: what is the edge? American roulette, straight-up bet on a single number. There are 38 pockets. You stake $1; if your number comes up you win $35 in profit, otherwise you lose your $1.








-0.052632 per dollar staked. That is the famous 5.26% house edge, and it is the entire business model: a number small enough that no individual player notices it and large enough that, multiplied by the law of large numbers you watched in the first figure, it builds a building.
Notice the structure both problems share. List the outcomes, attach probabilities, multiply, sum, compare to the price. Insurance premiums, warranty pricing, the value of a coupon campaign, and whether to run an expensive experiment are all the same computation wearing different clothes.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Expectation
text:
Summary

E[X] is the number a running average settles down to. Watch it settle, and notice that it settles slowly—that slowness is 1/\sqrt{n}, and it is what The Standard Error of a Mean is about.
Discrete: E[X] = \sum x P(X=x), a weighted average with probabilities as weights. Continuous: the same idea with an integral. For the standard distributions the answer is a known formula.
E[X] is not \bar{x}. The first is a fixed property of a distribution; the second is a random quantity computed from one sample. Six samples gave six different means and none of them was the truth.
E[aX+b] = aE[X]+b. Constants pass straight through, which is why unit conversion is free.
E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] always, independent or not. E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] requires independence. Sums are free; products are not.
Fair value equals expectation. Every “should I take this bet” problem is: list outcomes, weight by probability, sum, compare with the price.

Next: the second summary number. If the expectation says where a distribution sits, the variance says how far it typically strays—and it is the variance, not the expectation, that will make independence matter.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Variance and Standard Deviation
text:
Why squared, and why then a root
The expectation tells you where a distribution sits. It tells you nothing about how far the values stray from there, and two distributions with the same expectation can be nothing alike—a bet that pays $1.00 every time and a bet that pays $0 or $100 with the right probabilities both have E[X] = 1, and only one of them will end your month badly.
The second summary number fixes that.
\operatorname{Var}(X) = E\!\left[(X - E[X])^2\right]
Read it inside out and it is a sentence you already understand: take the distance from each value to the center, square it, and average. Variance is the average squared distance from the expectation.
Describing a Single Variable computed s^2 from a column of data. This chapter is about \operatorname{Var}(X), a property of a distribution—the same relationship the last chapter drew between \bar{x} and E[X]. The formulas look alike on purpose.
The obvious first attempt is to average the raw deviations X - E[X]. It fails instantly, and it is worth seeing it fail:
Zero, to ten decimal places, and not by luck. The mean is the balance point, so the positive and negative deviations cancel exactly, by construction, for every dataset that has ever existed. An average deviation of zero is not a measurement of anything.
You need to stop the canceling, and there are two ways to do it: take absolute values, or square. Both are used. Squaring won, for three reasons:
Here is the calculation, all three quantities side by side:
The mean squared deviation is 4.0168, and var(x) is also 4.0168.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Variance and Standard Deviation
text:
It penalizes large deviations more. A point twice as far away contributes four times as much. That is often what you want—being off by 100 is usually worse than being off by 10 twice.
It is smooth. |x| has a corner at zero, which makes calculus awkward. x^2 does not, and every optimization you meet later (least squares, maximum likelihood, gradient descent) leans on that.
It adds. This is the real reason, and it is the subject of the second half of this chapter. Variances of independent quantities add; mean absolute deviations do not. Without that additivity there is no \sigma/\sqrt{n} and there is no inference at all.










A note on the divisor, not a repeat of it



Strictly, var() divides by n-1 and mean((x - mean(x))^2) divides by n, so those two numbers are not identical—they differ by a factor of (n-1)/n = 199999/200000, which does not survive rounding to four places.
Describing a Single Variable explained why the n-1 is there: the sample mean was fitted to this very sample, so deviations measured from it are systematically too small. That argument is about estimating a variance from data. This chapter is about the variance itself, \operatorname{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2], which is defined with the true \mu and has no divisor to argue about at all.
Two different objects, and the n-1 belongs only to the first.



Back to the original units
The variance here is 4.0168 what? The data are in some unit—say millimetres—so the variance is in squared millimetres, which is not a quantity anyone has an intuition about. So we take the square root:
\operatorname{SD}(X) = \sigma = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
sd(x) returns 2.0042, and that number is in millimetres. It is the one you put in a sentence: values are typically about 2 mm from the center.






So why not work with the SD throughout and skip the variance? Because the SD does not obey nice rules and the variance does. Every derivation in this course happens in variance, and the square root is taken at the very end, purely so that a human can read the answer. Watch for that pattern in The Standard Error of a Mean—it is exactly what happens there.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Variance and Standard Deviation
text:
Rescaling: \operatorname{Var}(aX + b)
\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2 \operatorname{Var}(X)
Two claims in one line, and students distrust both.
The b vanishes entirely. Adding a constant to every value slides the whole distribution sideways. No distance between any two points changes. Variance is built out of distances, so it cannot possibly notice.
The a is squared. Variance lives in squared units, so a factor applied to the data is applied twice to the variance.
Predict all five of these before you run it:








4.0168, 4.0168, 36.1513, 36.1513, 36.1513.
Adding 100 changed nothing—not approximately nothing, nothing. Multiplying by 3 multiplied the variance by 9, and 9 \times 4.0168 = 36.1513 exactly. Multiplying by -3 gave the identical answer, because (-3)^2 = 9: flipping a variable’s sign does not make it less variable.
In standard deviations the rule loses the square:
\operatorname{SD}(aX+b) = |a| \operatorname{SD}(X)








2.0042 and 6.0126, which is exactly three times it.






 Shifting and scaling







A variable X has \operatorname{Var}(X) = 25.
What is \operatorname{Var}(4X + 10)?

110, because the 4 multiplies the variance and the 10 is then added on.100, because the 4 multiplies the variance and adding a constant does nothing.410, because the 4 is squared and the 10 is still added on.400, because the 4 is squared and adding a constant does nothing at all.



\operatorname{Var}(aX+b) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X), so \operatorname{Var}(4X+10) = 16 \times 25 = 400.
Two separate things are going on, and both are worth being able to say out loud.
The b disappears. Adding 10 to every value slides the whole distribution ten units to the right without changing any distance between any two points. Variance measures spread, and spread is built entirely out of distances, so it cannot see a shift. This is the part students distrust until they run var(x + 100) and get back exactly var(x).
The a is squared. Variance is in squared units, so a factor applied to the data gets applied twice to the variance. If you want the rule with no squaring, use the standard deviation: \operatorname{SD}(aX+b) = |a|\operatorname{SD}(X), here 4 \times 5 = 20—and indeed 20^2 = 400.
The absolute value matters: \operatorname{Var}(-4X) = 400 too. Flipping a variable’s sign does not make it less variable.






Exercise: rescaling without recomputing















25 * var(g)
Or 5^2 * var(g). Both give 628.4032, and so does var(5 * g - 3).



Exercise: changing units















2.54 * sd(h)
sd(h) is 3.0445 inches, so the answer is 7.7329 cm. The variance, by contrast, goes from 9.2688 in² to 2.54^2 \times 9.2688 = 59.7984 cm².
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Variance and Standard Deviation
text:
The key fact: variances add
Here is the result the whole week is built on.






Variances of independent quantities add



If X and Y are independent, then
\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y)
Standard deviations do not add. You must go to the variance, add there, and come back with a square root.


Two independent variables, one with SD 3 and one with SD 4:








25.003 against 25.013. The rule holds, up to the noise you get from 200,000 draws.
Now look at what that means in standard deviations:








5.000 versus 7.003. The SD of the sum is 5, not 7. If you had added the standard deviations you would have overstated the spread of the sum by 40%.
The 3-4-5 triangle is not a coincidence: \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5. Adding independent variability is Pythagorean, not arithmetic. And it is always in this direction—\sqrt{a+b} < \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}—so adding SDs always overstates the answer. The reason is cancellation. Some of the time a is high while b is low, and the two partially cancel; the 5 is the arithmetic of that cancellation.






 Do standard deviations add?







Two measurement errors are independent, and each has a standard deviation of 5 units. You add the two measurements together.
What is the standard deviation of the sum?
