The Standard Error of a Mean

title: The Standard Error of a Mean
text:
Where this goes
You now have the result the rest of the course quotes:
\operatorname{SE}(\bar X) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad \text{estimated in practice by } \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
In real work you do not know \sigma, so you substitute the sample standard deviation s. That substitution introduces extra uncertainty of its own, which is small when n is large and not small when n is small—and it is exactly why the t distribution exists, with its n-1 degrees of freedom, the same n-1 Describing a Single Variable argued about.

Confidence intervals. You know the sampling distribution is centered at \mu with width \sigma/\sqrt{n}; the central limit theorem will tell you it is roughly Normal. Put those together and \bar{x} \pm 2\,\text{SE} becomes an interval with a stateable success rate. There is nothing else in it.
Hypothesis tests. A test statistic is (\text{estimate} - \text{claim})/\text{SE}—“how many standard errors away is what I saw from what you claimed?” The SE is the denominator of every test in this course.
A/B testing. How long to run the test is the sample-size calculation you just did, with a difference of two means in place of one mean.
Regression. Every coefficient in every model output comes with a standard error beside it, and it means precisely what it means here: how much would this number move if I collected the data again.

If you take one thing from The Standard Error of a Mean, take this: every “give or take” in statistics is a standard error, and every standard error is a variance divided by n with a square root taken at the end.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error
The Standard Error of a Mean

title: The Standard Error of a Mean
text:
Summary

E[\bar X] = \mu: the sample mean is centered on the truth, by linearity, with no assumptions required.
\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \sigma^2/n, and so \operatorname{SE}(\bar X) = \sigma/\sqrt{n}. Four lines, using only the scaling rule and the addition rule.
Independence is used exactly once, in the step where variances add. When observations are clustered or repeated, that step fails, the covariances are usually positive, and the reported SE is too small.
Simulation confirms it: at n = 4, 16, 64, 256 the spread of 5,000 sample means came out 5.99, 2.97, 1.49, 0.76 against a predicted 6, 3, 1.5, 0.75. It works for skewed populations too—the derivation never mentioned shape.
Quadruple the sample to halve the error. n = (\sigma/\text{SE})^2. Early data is cheap and valuable; late data is expensive and marginal.
A tiny standard error says nothing about bias. Two million self-selected respondents give a beautiful SE and can still be badly wrong.
SD of the data describes people and does not shrink with n. SE of the mean describes your estimate and shrinks like 1/\sqrt{n}. Say which one your error bars are.
A proportion is a mean of zeros and ones, so \operatorname{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n} with no new theory. Rare rates have small absolute errors and large relative ones, which is why they need so much traffic.

Next: practice problems, and then—next week—what shape that sampling distribution has, and what you are allowed to claim once you know.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error
The Standard Error of a Mean

title: Practice Problems
text:
Predict before you run
None of these are graded and none of them are auto-checked. They exist so that you arrive on Monday with something to argue about.
Work them in order. Most of the first section comes in two halves: predict, then run. The prediction is the half that teaches you anything. Pressing Run first and nodding at the output feels like learning and is not—output you expected and output you did not expect look identical after the fact.
Write the prediction down somewhere before you run the cell. On paper, in a comment, in a note on your phone.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Practice Problems
text:
A1. Shifting and scaling
Predict all six numbers. You need mean(q) and sd(q) from the first two, and the rules from Expectation and Variance and Standard Deviation for the rest—do not run it and then explain the output.








Then answer: the mean responded to both transformations and the SD responded to only one. State the two rules, and then explain—in terms of what variance is—why subtracting 20 cannot possibly change it.


A2. Two dice
Predict all four numbers, at least to the nearest whole number.








Then answer: d1 + d2 and 2 * d1 both have twice the expectation of a single die, and their variances differ by a factor of two. Explain the difference in one sentence that a non-statistician would understand. Then say which of the two is a better model for “the total score after two rolls” and which is a better model for “a game that pays double on one roll”, and why the distinction is not pedantic.


A3. The two numbers again








Then answer, without running anything else: you collect 22,500 more heights from the same population, for 25,000 in total.

What will sd(h) be, roughly?
What will the standard error be, exactly?
Which of the two changed, and what is the one-sentence reason?



A4. Does independence matter here?
Predict which two of these three are equal before running.








Then answer: one rule survived the dependence and one did not. Which is which, why, and what is the general rule that covers the case that failed?


A5. Where the \sqrt{n} comes from








Then answer: the sample size quadrupled twice. Write down the ratio of consecutive standard errors, and then answer this: if the standard error went like \sigma/n instead of \sigma/\sqrt{n}, what would these three numbers have been? Which step of the derivation in The Standard Error of a Mean would have to be different for that to happen?
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Practice Problems
section: This runs, and it is still wrong
text:
This runs, and it is still wrong
Every cell below executes without an error or a warning, and every one produces a number that is wrong, misleading, or answers a question nobody asked. Find the problem, then fix it.

B1. The impressive precision

Task: 900 customers rated a product from 1 to 5. Report the average rating and how precisely it has been estimated.









The analyst writes: “Mean rating 3.25, ± 0.89.”
Which number did they report, which one did the task ask for, and what is the factor between them? Then write the two sentences that use each number correctly, and say which one belongs in an executive summary and which in a methods appendix.


B2. The diversified portfolio

Task: two assets, each with an annual return standard deviation of about 0.99. You hold half your money in each. Report the standard deviation of the portfolio return.









The analyst reports a portfolio SD of 0.699 and calls it a 29% risk reduction from diversification. Now compute the truth:








Then answer: where exactly in the first cell was independence assumed, and what is it about the two lines generating r1 and r2 that makes the assumption false? By what factor was the risk understated? Finally: give the general formula that would have produced the right answer, and say which single extra quantity the analyst would have needed to compute.


B3. The standard error that is too good

Task: 200 students sat an exam. Report the standard error of the mean score.









The number is 0.056. Two questions: what is the correct value, and—more usefully—what should have made you suspicious of 0.056 before you checked the formula? Answer the second one in terms of what the number is claiming about the world.


B4. The average of the averages

Task: four laboratories each measured the same compound. Report the overall mean concentration and its standard error.









Two independent errors here, one in each line.
For the first line, compute the correct overall mean and say why it differs. For the second, the analyst used n = 4 in the standard error. Say what population that standard error is describing, whether that is the population the task asked about, and what you would need in order to do it properly.


B5. More data, same problem

Task: estimate the mean household income in a city. A web panel returns 250,000 responses.









The standard error is about $105 on a mean of about $79,300—roughly an eighth of one percent. The analyst reports the city’s mean household income as “$79,300, with a margin of error of ±$210”.
The arithmetic is correct. Say what the standard error is and is not measuring, and construct a specific, plausible way in which this estimate could be wrong by $15,000 while the standard error stays at $105. Then answer the practical question: what would you spend the next $10,000 of project budget on—more responses, or something else?


B6. The repeated measurement

Task: estimate the mean resting heart rate of a population. Ten volunteers each wore a monitor that recorded their heart rate once a minute for 100 minutes.









The reported standard error is about 0.21 beats per minute, from n = 1000.
Then answer: which step of the 5.3 derivation does this violate, and where in the data-generating code can you point to the violation? Roughly what is the effective sample size here—10, 1000, or something in between—and why? Then compute a defensible standard error from these same data with one line of code. (Hint: what are the ten quantities you actually have independent information about?)
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: Practice Problems
text:
Judgment
No code. Bring written answers; we will disagree about these out loud.

C1.
A colleague says: “Our A/B test needs to detect a 0.5% lift. We ran it for a week and got 40,000 users per arm, and the confidence interval is still too wide. Let’s run it another week.”
Using only \sigma/\sqrt{n}, explain what a second week buys them, as a factor. Then say how long they would need to run it to halve the width of the interval, and give one reason why running an A/B test for that long is a bad idea for reasons that have nothing to do with statistics.


C2.
You read a paper reporting “mean tumour volume 340 mm³ ± 25”. The methods section does not say whether the 25 is an SD or an SE, and the sample size is n = 9.
Work out what the other quantity would be in each case. Then say which interpretation makes the paper’s conclusion look stronger, and why an author with a result to sell has an incentive here that a reader should be aware of.


C3.
Variance and Standard Deviation showed three sums with identical marginal distributions whose variances came out 0, 18, and 36 depending only on the dependence structure.
Invent a real situation—not a mathematical one—where two quantities you might add together are strongly negatively dependent, so that the total is far less variable than either part. Then explain why someone would deliberately build such a pairing. (Every hedging strategy, every redundant system design, and a good deal of portfolio theory is an answer to this question.)


C4.
Here is a claim you will hear: “With big data, statistics doesn’t matter any more. The standard errors are so small that everything is significant.”
The first sentence of that is wrong and the second is nearly right. Separate them. Say what genuinely does become easy with a very large n, what does not improve at all, and what new problem the second sentence is actually pointing at. Then give one concrete example of a question that a billion rows cannot answer and a randomized experiment on two hundred people can.


C5.
Go back to the list you wrote at the end of Describing a Single Variable—if the data collection were repeated from scratch, how different would my number be?—and answer it, for the number you chose then.
You now have the machinery. Write the actual sentence you would put in a report: the estimate, the give-or-take, and the assumption you had to make to be entitled to the give-or-take. That last clause is the part most people leave out, and it is the part this week was for.
crumbs: Expectation, Variance, and the Standard Error

title: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals
text:
What is here
Monday, September 28
Post your questions on any of these pages by Monday at 12:00 noon, the morning of class.
Everything so far has described a sample. This is the week the description turns into a claim about the world.
You already have the two numbers that make it possible. The Standard Error of a Mean established that the sampling distribution of \bar X is centered at \mu with spread \sigma/\sqrt{n}. What was missing was its shape, because without a shape you cannot convert “give or take 0.28” into “and here is how often that works”.
The central limit theorem supplies the shape, and the confidence interval is what you get by rearranging one line of algebra. The difficulty of this week is not the arithmetic—the interval is a mean, a standard error, and a \pm. The difficulty is saying precisely what the resulting pair of numbers claims, and resisting the three or four more satisfying things it does not.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals
text:
The Central Limit Theorem



Why the mean of almost anything goes Normal, watched happening rather than asserted. How large “large enough” really is—not 30, but whatever your simulation says. And the case where it fails outright: with infinite variance, averaging a thousand observations is no better than averaging ten.








Confidence Intervals



The construction, and then the careful part. A hundred studies produce a hundred different intervals, a few of which miss the truth and none of which look wrong from the inside. What 95% attaches to, what it does not, and the four misreadings worth being able to name.








When \sigma Is Unknown



We have been substituting s for \sigma and pretending nothing happened. At n = 5 that pretense turns a 95% interval into an 88% one. Student’s t, why its degrees of freedom are n-1, and the one thing it does not fix.








Intervals for a Proportion



Conversion rates, click rates, defect rates. The obvious interval covers 80% of the time at a 3% rate, which is exactly where commercial data lives—and the fix is one function call.








Practice Problems



Predict-before-you-run, code that runs and is still wrong, and six statements to judge against a single interval. Not graded—bring your disagreements.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals
text:
A habit for this week
Check the coverage. Every claim in these chapters is of the form “this procedure works x% of the time”, and every one of them can be verified in about four lines: simulate a population where you know the answer, run the procedure many times, count how often it was right.
That is not a pedagogical device. It is what you should do whenever you are unsure whether a method applies to your data—far more useful than remembering whether the rule was 30 or 10, and it is how the two failures in this week’s material were found.






Due this week



HW 3 is due at the start of class. And as always, post your questions on these pages by Monday noon—that afternoon’s session is built out of them.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
What it says
The Standard Error of a Mean told you where the sampling distribution of \bar X sits and how wide it is: centered at \mu, with spread \sigma/\sqrt{n}. Two numbers, derived in four lines, with no assumption about the population beyond having a finite variance.
What it did not tell you is the shape. And without the shape you cannot turn those two numbers into a statement, because “the estimate is 31.4 with a standard error of 0.28” does not yet say how often the truth is within half a point.
The central limit theorem supplies the shape, and it supplies it in a form so convenient that it is worth being suspicious of.
Read what is not in that sentence. There is no condition on the shape of the population. It may be skewed, bimodal, discrete, bounded, or something with no name. Provided the variance is finite and the draws are independent, the means go Normal.
That is a genuinely surprising claim, so watch it happen rather than believing it.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text: For independent observations from a population with finite mean \mu and finite variance \sigma^2, the sampling distribution of \bar X approaches a Normal distribution with mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma/\sqrt{n}, as n grows.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
Watching it happen
The exponential distribution is about as un-Normal as a common distribution gets: it starts at zero, falls away immediately, and has a long right tail. Its mean and standard deviation are both 1 when the rate is 1.








Now take samples of size n, average each one, and look at the distribution of those averages.








At n = 1 you are looking at the population itself. By n = 5 the worst of the skew is gone. By n = 30 it is nearly symmetric, and at n = 100 you would not guess the parent distribution from the picture.
Put numbers on it. Skewness measures asymmetry: zero for a symmetric distribution, positive for a long right tail.








Two things at once. The center and spread are exactly what the previous chapter predicted—0.1 at n = 100, against 1/\sqrt{100}. And the skew falls from 1.91 to 0.19, roughly like 1/\sqrt{n}, which is the central limit theorem doing its work.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
How large is large enough?
Textbooks say n = 30. Treat that as folklore rather than a theorem.
The honest answer is that the required n depends on how skewed the population is. A symmetric population is close to Normal at n = 5; the exponential above is respectable by 30; a distribution with a rare enormous value—insurance claims, revenue per customer, time on site—may still be visibly skewed at n = 1{,}000.








The population’s skew is about 8.9. At n = 30 the means are still more skewed than the exponential population was to begin with, and it takes n = 1{,}000 to reach the symmetry the exponential had at n = 30. The rule is not a sample size; it is to check. Simulating from a plausible population takes one line, and it is the only defensible way to answer the question for data you actually have.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
What it does not say
Three misreadings, in order of how often they appear.
It does not say your data become Normal. Nothing happens to the data. The 20,000 exponential values in the first histogram are just as skewed as they ever were. It is the distribution of the mean that goes Normal, and the mean is a different object.
It does not say every statistic goes Normal. The theorem is about sums, and the mean is a sum divided by n. A median, a maximum, a correlation, a ratio— none of them are covered by it. This is the gap Why Resample exists to fill.
It does not license a Normal model for individual observations. If you need to say where the next single value will fall, the CLT is silent. It describes the estimate, not the world.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
Where it fails
The theorem has one condition worth respecting: the population must have a finite variance. Distributions without one exist, and they are not merely pathological—financial returns, network traffic and file sizes are all modeled with heavy tails.
The Cauchy distribution is the standard example. It looks like a bell curve with fat tails, and it has no mean and no variance at all.








A hundredfold increase in sample size and the spread does not move. For a Cauchy population, the mean of 1,000 observations is no more precise than the mean of 10—averaging accomplishes nothing, because the occasional enormous draw dominates whatever the other 999 do.
You will not meet a true Cauchy. You will meet data with tails heavy enough that convergence is slow and the sample mean is a poor summary, and the practical signal is the same: if the mean of your data lurches around when you add observations, averaging is not working and no interval built on it will be honest.






 Exercise: what the theorem claims





A dataset of 5,000 customer transaction amounts is strongly right-skewed. Assign the letter of the correct statement, for example answer <- "A".















B.
A is the misreading to guard against—it is what leads people to quote \bar x \pm 2s as the range of individual transactions, which for skewed data is wrong at both ends.
C mistakes the theorem’s content for its condition: a non-Normal population is the situation the theorem is about, not an obstacle to it.
D is wrong for a reason worth keeping: the theorem is a statement about sums, and a median is not a sum. Its sampling distribution does become roughly Normal under conditions, but not by this argument, and there is no simple formula for its standard error—which is exactly why Why Resample exists.







 Exercise: how skewed are the means?





The population is rexp(n, rate = 1). Return the skewness of 5,000 sample means at n = 25, using the function skew() provided.


















skew(replicate(5000, mean(rexp(25, rate = 1))))
About 0.4, against a population skew of 2. The reduction is a factor of \sqrt{25} = 5, which is the general rate: skew falls like 1/\sqrt{n}.
That rate is the useful form of the “is n big enough” question. It tells you that a population twice as skewed needs four times the sample to reach the same symmetry—and that no sample size fixes a population with infinite variance, because there the argument does not start.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
Summary

The CLT supplies the shape that The Standard Error of a Mean was missing: \bar X is approximately Normal, centered at \mu, with spread \sigma/\sqrt{n}.
It requires independence and finite variance, and nothing at all about the shape of the population.
Convergence was visible by n = 30 for an exponential population and incomplete at n = 1{,}000 for a heavily skewed log-normal. The number 30 is folklore; simulate instead.
Skew of the sampling distribution falls like 1/\sqrt{n}.
It is about the mean, not the data and not every statistic. Medians, maxima and correlations are outside it.
With infinite variance it fails outright: averaging 1,000 Cauchy draws is no better than averaging 10.

Next: what these two numbers and a shape let you actually say—the confidence interval, and the careful sentence that goes with it.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Confidence Intervals
text:
Building one
You have everything you need. The sampling distribution of \bar X is centered at \mu, has standard deviation \sigma/\sqrt{n}, and is approximately Normal. A Normal distribution puts 95% of its mass within 1.96 standard deviations of its center. Therefore:
P\left(\left|\bar X - \mu\right| < 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \approx 0.95
Rearranged so that \mu sits in the middle, that is the confidence interval:
\bar x \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
That is the entire derivation. There is nothing else in it, and the rest of this chapter is about what the resulting number does and does not entitle you to say.
Two numbers you already knew how to compute, and a \pm. The difficulty was never the arithmetic.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Confidence Intervals
text:
What “95% confident” means
Here is the sentence that costs students marks, and practitioners credibility:

The interval is random. The parameter is not.

\mu is a fixed number. It does not have a distribution, it is not more likely to be here than there, and it is either inside your particular interval or it is not. What varies from study to study is the interval—a different sample gives a different center and a different width.
So “95% confidence” is a statement about the procedure, not about the interval in front of you:

If you repeated the whole study many times and built an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain \mu.

That is testable, which is the good news. Build a hundred and count.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Confidence Intervals
text:
The coverage experiment








Every interval is a different length and sits in a different place. The vertical line—the truth—does not move. A handful of intervals miss it entirely, and nothing about those intervals looks wrong from the inside. They were built by the same correct procedure as the others; they simply came from unlucky samples.
That is what a confidence level is: the long-run fraction of the gray ones.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Confidence Intervals
section: Four things it does not mean
text:
Four things it does not mean
“There is a 95% probability that \mu is between 29.6 and 33.2.” No. Both numbers are fixed and \mu is fixed; the probability is 0 or 1, you just do not know which. The 95% attached to the procedure before you saw the data, and it does not transfer to the particular answer afterwards.
“95% of the data lie in this interval.” No, and the size gives it away. With n = 200 the interval above is about four minutes wide while commutes scatter over fifty. That is the SD-versus-SE confusion in interval form, and it is the most common one in student reports.
“95% of future sample means will fall in it.” Also no—that is roughly 83%, not 95%, because a future mean has its own sampling error to add. If you want an interval for a future observation you need a prediction interval.
“The result is significant because the interval is narrow.” Narrow means precise, not correct. As Where the Data Came From argued, a large biased sample produces a narrow interval around the wrong number—and the narrowness makes it more persuasive, not less wrong.






The sentence to write





“We estimate the mean commute at 31.4 minutes (95% CI: 29.6 to 33.2).”
Then, if the reader needs it: “an interval constructed this way contains the true mean about 95% of the time.” That is defensible, and it is short.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Confidence Intervals
text:
What controls the width
The half-width is 1.96 \cdot s/\sqrt{n}, so exactly three things move it.








Sample size, through \sqrt{n}—so quadrupling the data halves the width, the same k^2 rule as before. Confidence level, which buys certainty with width: going from 95% to 99% costs about a third more interval. And the variability of the data, which is a property of the world rather than a choice.
There is no fourth lever. In particular there is no way to have a narrow interval and a high confidence level on a small noisy sample, and an analysis that appears to manage it has made an error somewhere.






 Exercise: measure the coverage yourself





Run 10,000 studies. Each draws n = 40 from a skewed population— rexp(40, rate = 1/31), whose true mean is 31—and builds the usual t-interval. Return the proportion of intervals containing 31.


















```{r}
mean(replicate(10000, {
  x  <- rexp(40, rate = 1/31)
  ci <- mean(x) + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, 39) * sd(x) / sqrt(40)
  ci[1] <= 31 && 31 <= ci[2]
}))
```
About 0.932—not 0.95.
The procedure promises 95% and delivers 93.2%, because at n = 40 the central limit theorem has not finished converting an exponential population into a Normal sampling distribution. The interval is slightly too narrow and slightly off-center, so it misses more often than advertised.
This is worth more than the number. A confidence level is a claim that can be checked, and checking it by simulation is the honest answer to “is my sample large enough”—far better than consulting a rule about 30.







 Exercise: which statement is legitimate





A study reports a mean satisfaction score of 7.2 with a 95% confidence interval of 6.9 to 7.5. Assign the letter, for example answer <- "A".















C.
A treats \mu as random. It is the interpretation almost everyone intends, and there is a framework where it is legitimate—a Bayesian credible interval says exactly this—but it is not what a confidence interval says.
B confuses the interval with the spread of the data. With a few hundred respondents this interval is many times narrower than the range of individual scores.
D asks for a prediction interval, which is wider still.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Confidence Intervals
text:
Summary

\bar x \pm 1.96 \cdot s/\sqrt{n}, and the derivation is one line from the central limit theorem plus the standard error.
The interval is random; the parameter is not. Confidence is a property of the procedure across repetitions, not of the interval you are holding.
Simulation makes this concrete: 100 studies gave 100 different intervals, a few missed, and the misses looked exactly like the hits from the inside.
Coverage is checkable. For a Normal population the recipe delivered 95%; for a skewed population at n = 40 it delivered 93.2%.
Width is controlled by n, the confidence level, and the variability of the data. There is no fourth lever.
A narrow interval is precise, not correct. Bias is invisible to it.

Next: what to do about the fact that we substituted s for \sigma and carried on as though nothing had happened.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: When \sigma Is Unknown
text:
How much it costs
The derivation used \sigma, the population standard deviation. You have never had one and you never will. Every interval you have built substituted s, the sample standard deviation, and carried on as if nothing had happened.
Something did happen. s is itself an estimate, computed from the same handful of observations, and it wobbles. Replacing a known constant with a noisy estimate and keeping the same 1.96 quietly claims a precision you have not earned.
Measure it. Build intervals with the Normal critical value 1.96, using s in place of \sigma, and see how often they cover.
At n = 200 the damage is negligible. At n = 5 an interval advertised as 95% covers 88% of the time—it misses more than twice as often as it claims. The population here is exactly Normal, so nothing is wrong with the central limit theorem. The error is entirely from pretending s is \sigma.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: When \sigma Is Unknown
text:
The fix
t = \frac{\bar X - \mu}{s/\sqrt{n}}
does not follow a Normal distribution. It follows Student’s t with n - 1 degrees of freedom—the same n-1 that appeared in the variance divisor, for the same reason: one degree of freedom was spent estimating \bar x before s could be computed.
The t looks like a Normal with heavier tails. Heavier tails mean a larger critical value, which means a wider interval—which is precisely the extra allowance you owe for not knowing \sigma.
















With four degrees of freedom you need 2.776 standard errors rather than 1.96—an interval 42% wider. By df = 29 it is 2.045, and by 199 it is 1.972, which is 1.96 for any practical purpose.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: When \sigma Is Unknown
text:
Does it work?








95% at every sample size, including n = 5. The t distribution is not an approximation that improves with n—for a Normal population it is exact, and the convergence to 1.96 is the correction becoming unnecessary rather than becoming accurate.






In practice





Use t.test(), which does all of this and prints the interval:
```{r}
t.test(x)$conf.int
```
Use t always. At large n it agrees with the Normal to three decimals, so there is no situation in which choosing the Normal is worth the risk of being wrong at small n.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: When \sigma Is Unknown
section: The assumption you have now taken on
text:
The assumption you have now taken on
The t interval is exact for a Normal population. That is a stronger requirement than the central limit theorem needed, and it bites in exactly the case where you reached for t in the first place.








The t correction fixes the unknown-\sigma problem and does nothing about skew. On a skewed population at n = 8 the interval still under-covers badly, and there is no critical value that rescues it—the sampling distribution is not symmetric, so no symmetric interval can be right.
Small n and skewed data is the case where the formulas have nothing to offer. It is one of the situations Why Resample was written for.






 Exercise: the critical value





A study has n = 12. Return the critical value for a 90% confidence interval for the mean—a single number.















qt(0.95, df = 11)
= 1.7959. The two traps are df = n-1, not n, and 0.95 rather than 0.90, because a two-sided 90% interval leaves 5% in each tail.
Against qnorm(0.95) = 1.645, the correction costs about 9% of extra width—the price of not knowing \sigma with twelve observations.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: When \sigma Is Unknown
text:
Summary

Substituting s for \sigma adds uncertainty that the Normal critical value ignores. At n = 5 a nominal 95% interval covered 88%.
(\bar X - \mu)/(s/\sqrt{n}) follows a t distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom, whose heavier tails give a larger critical value and a wider interval.
qt(0.975, 4) = 2.776 against 1.96; by df = 199 it is 1.972. Use t always—at large n the choice does not matter, and at small n it does.
The t interval is exact for a Normal population, not an approximation that improves with n.
It corrects for unknown \sigma and nothing else. Small n with skewed data under-covers no matter which critical value you use, because a non-symmetric sampling distribution cannot be captured by a symmetric interval.

Next: the same construction for a proportion, where the standard recipe fails in a way that matters for every conversion rate you will ever report.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Intervals for a Proportion
text:
Checking it the way we checked the others
A conversion rate, a click-through rate, a defect rate, a poll result. These are the quantities you will be asked about most often, and The Standard Error of a Mean already gave you their standard error, because a proportion is the mean of a column of zeros and ones:
\operatorname{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}
So the obvious interval is the obvious one:
\hat p \pm 1.96 \sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}
This is the Wald interval. It is what every introductory course teaches, what most people reach for, and it is unreliable in precisely the situations that matter commercially.
The method from Confidence Intervals applies unchanged: fix a true p, simulate many studies, count how often the interval covers.
At p = 0.5 it is close enough. At p = 0.03—a perfectly ordinary conversion rate—an interval sold as 95% covers about 80% of the time. One in five such intervals is wrong, and there is no warning anywhere in the output.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Intervals for a Proportion
text:
Why it breaks
Two failures compound, and both get worse as p approaches 0 or 1.
The standard error is estimated from \hat p. When the true rate is 3% and n = 100, a study that happens to observe zero conversions gets \hat p = 0, hence \operatorname{SE} = 0, hence an interval of zero width that is certainly wrong. Less extreme versions of the same thing happen constantly: an unluckily low \hat p produces an unluckily small SE, so the interval is too narrow exactly when it is most badly centered.
The Normal approximation is poor near the boundary. The sampling distribution of \hat p is discrete and skewed when np is small, and a symmetric interval cannot describe it. The interval also runs off the end—








—a lower limit below zero, for a quantity that cannot be negative.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Intervals for a Proportion
section: The fix, which is one function call
text:
The fix, which is one function call
Rather than estimating the standard error at \hat p and inverting, the Wilson interval asks which values of p are consistent with the data and solves for them directly. It is not more complicated to use:








Nonnegative, asymmetric, and it does not collapse. Its coverage:








Around 95% across the board, including the case where the Wald interval was catastrophic.






What to do





Use prop.test() or binom.test() for a proportion. They are one call, they are in base R, and they do not fail quietly.
If you must compute by hand, the Agresti–Coull rule is a good approximation and easy to remember: add two successes and two failures, then apply the Wald formula to the adjusted counts. Two conversions in 100 becomes four in 104.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Intervals for a Proportion
section: The rule of thumb, and why it is not enough
text:
The rule of thumb, and why it is not enough
The traditional check is n\hat p \ge 10 and n(1-\hat p) \ge 10. Here n\hat p = 3, so the rule does flag this case—which is a point in its favor.
The difficulty is that the rule uses \hat p, the very quantity whose unreliability is the problem. A study that observes 3 conversions out of 100 when the truth is 12% passes nothing and looks fine. And the rule offers no guidance at all on what to do instead.
Using prop.test() unconditionally is simpler than remembering the rule, and it is right in the cases where the rule would have said the Wald interval was fine.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Intervals for a Proportion
section: Why this matters more than it looks
text:
Why this matters more than it looks
Rare events are the commercially interesting ones. Conversion, churn, fraud, click-through, adverse reactions—all sit at a few percent, which is exactly where the Wald interval is worst.
Combine that with the relative-precision arithmetic from the standard error chapter:








To pin a 3% rate down to within a tenth of itself you need tens of thousands of observations. That is the honest answer to “can we call the experiment yet”, and it is why the interval being correct matters: at these sample sizes the decision often hinges on whether the interval includes the current rate.






 Exercise: the two intervals, side by side





A trial converts 7 of 250 visitors. Return the width of the 95% Wilson interval from prop.test(7, 250, correct = FALSE)—a single number.















diff(prop.test(7, 250, correct = FALSE)$conf.int)
About 0.0430, running from 0.0136 to 0.0567 around \hat p = 0.028.
The interval is not symmetric—the upper arm is longer than the lower one. That is correct behavior: a rate near zero has more room to be larger than it has to be smaller. A Wald interval is symmetric by construction and therefore cannot represent it, which is the same defect that lets it produce negative lower limits.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Intervals for a Proportion
text:
Summary

A proportion is a mean of zeros and ones, so \operatorname{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n} and the Wald interval is the obvious construction.
It is unreliable when p is near 0 or 1: at p = 0.03 with n = 100 a nominal 95% interval covered 80%.
It fails two ways at once—the standard error is estimated at \hat p, so an unlucky sample gets a too-small SE, and a symmetric interval cannot describe a skewed sampling distribution. It also produces impossible negative limits.
prop.test(x, n, correct = FALSE) gives the Wilson interval, which held near 95% everywhere tested. Use it unconditionally.
Agresti–Coull—add two successes and two failures—is the hand version.
This is not an edge case. Conversion, churn and fraud all live at a few percent, which is where the standard recipe is worst.

Next: practice problems, and then a term of putting these intervals to work.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Practice Problems
text:
Predict the output
None of these are graded and none are auto-checked. They exist so that you arrive on Monday with something to argue about. Several have no single right answer; those are the useful ones.
Say what each prints before you run it. Getting it wrong and understanding why is the point.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Practice Problems
text:
Discussion





1. Essentially zero. With a million degrees of freedom the t is indistinguishable from the Normal. This is why “use t always” costs nothing.
2. The 99% interval is wider, by a factor of qt(0.995, 8)/qt(0.975, 8) \approx 1.45. Buying certainty costs width, and at small n it costs a lot.
3. The standard error at p = 0.5 is larger than at p = 0.05—0.050 against 0.022. In absolute terms a rare rate is easier to pin down. In relative terms it is far harder: 0.022 is 44% of 0.05, while 0.050 is 10% of 0.5.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Practice Problems
section: This runs and is still wrong
text:
This runs and is still wrong
Each of these produces a number. Each number is wrong, or right for a question nobody asked. Find the error.































Discussion





4. The interval describes the mean, not the students. It is about a point wide while scores scatter over forty. To describe students you want roughly \bar x \pm 2s, which is a different number entirely and is not a confidence interval at all.
5. One conversion in forty. n\hat p = 1, so the Wald interval has no business being used; it returns a lower limit below zero. prop.test(1, 40) gives a sensible answer instead.
6. The interval is beautifully narrow—about 0.07 wide—and it excludes the truth of 6.4 entirely. Precision is not accuracy. No sample size fixes a sampling frame that never contained the people you care about, which is the argument from Where the Data Came From arriving with a confidence interval attached.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Practice Problems
section: What does this license you to claim?
text:
What does this license you to claim?
For each statement, decide whether it is defensible from a 95% confidence interval of [2.1, 5.7] for a mean difference. Write a sentence for each.

“The difference is between 2.1 and 5.7.”
“There is a 95% chance the difference is between 2.1 and 5.7.”
“The difference is not zero.”
“The difference is probably around 3.9.”
“A difference of 5.6 is consistent with our data.”
“If we ran the study again we would get an interval between 2.1 and 5.7.”








Discussion





7. Overstated—it drops the uncertainty entirely. Say “we estimate the difference at 3.9, 95% CI 2.1 to 5.7.”
8. The classic error. The interval is random, the parameter is not. This is a credible interval’s claim, not a confidence interval’s.
9. Defensible, and the most useful thing the interval says. The whole interval lies above zero, so zero is not among the values consistent with the data at this confidence level.
10. Reasonable, if “around” is doing honest work. 3.9 is the point estimate; the interval is what stops “around” from being a lie.
11. Defensible. 5.6 is inside the interval, so it is consistent with the data—which is a much weaker claim than saying the difference is 5.6.
12. No. A repeat study gives a different interval. About 95% of such intervals contain the truth; that says nothing about them containing each other.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Practice Problems
text:
Bring to class

The coverage you can measure. Pick a population shape you think your project data resembles—skewed, bimodal, heavy-tailed, bounded. Simulate it, build 10,000 t-intervals at the sample size you expect to have, and report the actual coverage. Bring the number. If it is not close to 0.95, bring an opinion about what to do.
An interval in the wild. Find a reported confidence interval in a news article, a company blog post, or a paper. Bring it, and answer: is it an interval for a mean, a proportion, or a difference? Is the sample size given? Does the surrounding text interpret it correctly?
Argue about this. A colleague says: “We have 40,000 users in the experiment. The sample is so large that confidence intervals are pointless —every difference will be significant.” They are partly right and mostly wrong. Work out which part is which, and be ready to defend it.
crumbs: The Central Limit Theorem and Confidence Intervals

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
What is here
Monday, October 5
Post your questions on any of these pages by Monday at 12:00 noon, the morning of class.
Last week produced an interval and a careful sentence about what it claims. This week narrows the question: is the data compatible with this particular claim?
The machinery is small—one statistic, one tail area—and you have already built most of it. What the week is really about is the gap between what a test computes and what people report it as having computed. That gap is where a large share of published findings that later fail to replicate came from, and it is worth understanding as a mechanism rather than as a scandal.
Two of these chapters cover material that is usually left out of an introductory course. Power determines what a non-significant result means and is the reason underpowered studies overstate every effect they publish. Multiple comparisons explains why an honest analyst, making defensible choices one at a time, arrives at a finding that is not there. Neither is advanced. Both are asked about in interviews, and both will decide whether your project’s conclusions hold up.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
The Logic of a Test



Assume the claim, measure surprise. The test statistic as a standardized distance, the p-value as a tail area you can simulate rather than look up, and the exact correspondence between a two-sided test and a confidence interval.








What a p-value Licenses



Under a true null, p-values are uniform—which explains both why 0.049 and 0.051 are the same evidence and why small p-values are guaranteed if you look enough times. Then the five misreadings, and why significance is not importance.








Power



The half of the picture nobody reports. How many observations you need, what “we found nothing” is worth, and the winner’s curse: at 25% power, the studies that reached significance overstated a true effect of 0.3 as 0.57.








Multiple Comparisons



Twenty tests, a 64% chance of a false positive. Where it really happens— subgroups, outcomes, peeking, specification hunting—and what Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg each cost you.








Practice Problems



Including three analyses that run, return a number, and mislead: an underpowered null result, a peeked A/B test, and the subgroup that worked.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
A habit for this week
Report the interval, then the p-value if you must. The interval carries the effect size, the precision, and the p-value’s information; the p-value alone carries the least of the three and is the one most likely to be misquoted back at you.






Due this week



HW 4 is due at the start of class. And as always, post your questions on these pages by Monday noon—that afternoon’s session is built out of them.

title: The Logic of a Test
text:
The four steps
A confidence interval answers how big is it, and how precisely do we know? A hypothesis test answers a narrower question: is the data compatible with this particular claim?
The second question is more often asked and more often misunderstood, and almost all of the misunderstanding comes from one structural feature that this chapter exists to make unmissable. A test assumes the claim is true and then measures surprise. It never evaluates whether the claim is true; it evaluates the data, on the supposition that it is.

title: The Logic of a Test
text:
State a null hypothesis H_0—a specific claim precise enough to compute with. “The mean is 100.” “The two groups have the same rate.”
Choose a test statistic—one number summarizing how far the data sits from that claim, in units of its own standard error.
Work out how that statistic behaves if H_0 is true. This is the part the whole term has been building towards, and it is where the standard error and the central limit theorem get used.
Ask how often that behavior would produce something at least as extreme as what you saw. That proportion is the p-value.

title: The Logic of a Test
section: The statistic is a standardized distance
text:
The statistic is a standardized distance
Step 2 is always the same shape:
t = \frac{\text{estimate} - \text{claim}}{\operatorname{SE}(\text{estimate})}
How many standard errors away is what I saw from what you claimed? Every test in this course is that expression with different things substituted in.








The sample mean is about 2.7 standard errors below the claim. Whether that is surprising depends on how often a t of that size arises when the claim is true—which is step 3, and which you already know: it follows a t distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom.

title: The Logic of a Test
section: The p-value is a tail area
text:
The p-value is a tail area








t.test() does all of it and reports the confidence interval alongside, which is worth noticing: the interval excludes 500, and the p-value is below 0.05. Those are the same fact stated twice. A two-sided test at level \alpha rejects exactly when the 1-\alpha confidence interval excludes the claimed value.






Prefer the interval





Given the choice, report the interval. It contains the p-value’s information and adds what the p-value omits—the size of the effect and the precision of the estimate. “Mean fill 495.9 g, 95% CI 492.8 to 499.0, against a claimed 500” says everything “p = 0.010” says, plus the two things a reader actually needs.

title: The Logic of a Test
text:
Seeing the null distribution
Nothing about step 3 requires trusting a formula. Simulate the world in which H_0 holds and look at what it produces.








The simulated proportion matches t.test()’s p-value. A p-value is a frequency in a world you constructed, and that is the whole of its meaning.

title: The Logic of a Test
section: What the p-value is a probability of
text:
What the p-value is a probability of
Write it precisely, because the order of the conditioning is where everything goes wrong:
p = P(\text{data at least this extreme} \mid H_0 \text{ true})
It is not P(H_0 \text{ true} \mid \text{data}). Those are different quantities, and swapping them is the same inversion as Conditional Probability and Bayes warned about with medical tests—where the two conditionals differed by a factor of thirty.
A small p-value says: if the claim were true, data like this would be rare. Rare things happen. And a claim being incompatible with the data does not identify which of your assumptions is at fault—the null is one assumption among several, alongside independence, the sampling frame, and the measurement.

title: The Logic of a Test
section: Rejecting, and what the two errors are
text:
Rejecting, and what the two errors are
Choosing a threshold \alpha before looking converts the p-value into a decision, and creates two ways to be wrong.




H_0 true
H_0 false




Reject
Type I error, rate \alpha
Correct


Do not reject
Correct
Type II error, rate \beta



\alpha is chosen. \beta is not—it follows from the sample size and the size of the effect, and it is the subject of Power.
The asymmetry matters. “Do not reject” is not “accept”. A test that fails to find evidence has not produced evidence of absence, and the difference between those is entirely a question of how much power the study had.






 Exercise: compute a p-value from scratch





x holds 25 measurements. Test H_0: \mu = 12 against a two-sided alternative without using t.test(). Return the p-value.


















```{r}
tstat <- (mean(x) - 12) / (sd(x) / sqrt(25))
2 * pt(-abs(tstat), df = 24)
```
About 0.030. t.test(x, mu = 12)$p.value gives the same number.
Two details worth keeping. -abs(tstat) gets the lower tail regardless of sign, and doubling it covers both directions. And df = 24, not 25, for the usual reason.

title: The Logic of a Test
text:
Summary

A test assumes H_0 and measures surprise. It never evaluates whether H_0 is true.
The statistic is always (\text{estimate} - \text{claim})/\operatorname{SE}—how many standard errors away.
The p-value is P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0), and it can be obtained by simulation as easily as by formula. It is not P(H_0 \mid \text{data}).
A two-sided test at level \alpha and the 1-\alpha confidence interval agree exactly. Report the interval—it carries the effect size and the precision too.
\alpha is chosen; \beta is inherited from the design. “Do not reject” is not “accept.”

Next: what a p-value licenses you to say, and the four claims it does not support.

title: What a p-value Licenses
text:
Under the null, a p-value is uniform
The p-value is the most reported and least understood number in applied statistics. This chapter is short because its content is mostly subtraction: here is the one thing it says, and here are the five things people take it to say.
Start with a fact that makes everything else easier to reason about.
Flat. When the null is true, every p-value is as likely as every other: 5% below 0.05, half below 0.5, and so on. That is not an accident; it is the definition working. A threshold of 0.05 produces false positives 5% of the time precisely because the distribution is uniform.
Two consequences follow immediately.
A p-value of 0.049 and one of 0.051 are the same evidence. Nothing happens at the boundary. The distribution has no feature there, and the only thing that changes is which side of a convention you land on.
Under the null, small p-values are guaranteed to occur. Run twenty honest tests of true nulls and you should expect one below 0.05. That is the whole of Multiple Comparisons, visible already in this histogram.

title: What a p-value Licenses
text:
The five misreadings
“p = 0.03, so there is a 3% chance the null is true.” The p-value is P(\text{data} \mid H_0), not P(H_0 \mid \text{data}). Getting from one to the other requires a prior, which is what Conditional Probability and Bayes was about. Without one, the second quantity is simply not available.
“p = 0.03, so there is a 97% chance the effect is real.” Same inversion, wearing a hat.
“p > 0.05, so there is no effect.” A non-significant result is compatible with no effect and with a real effect the study was too small to detect. Which of those you are in is a question about power, and the p-value cannot answer it. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
“p = 0.001, so the effect is large.” The p-value confounds effect size with sample size. A trivial effect measured on a million users produces a tiny p-value; an enormous effect measured on nine people may not.








The first result is “highly significant” and describes an effect of 0.01. The second is a hundred times larger and less significant. Significance is not importance, and the only way to tell them apart is to look at the estimate and its interval.
“The result replicated, because both studies had p < 0.05.” Two studies agreeing on which side of a threshold they fall is a weak form of agreement. Compare the intervals instead.






What a small p-value does license





“If the null were true, data like this would be uncommon.”
That is it. It is a real thing to know and it is worth reporting—but it is a statement about the data under an assumption, not about the assumption.

title: What a p-value Licenses
section: Effect size, and why it is not optional
text:
Effect size, and why it is not optional
Every test in this course has an effect size sitting next to it, and it is usually the number the audience actually wanted.








Report the difference and its interval first. Cohen’s d—the difference in standard deviations—is useful when the units are not meaningful to the reader, with the usual rough anchors of 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. Treat those as vocabulary rather than law; a d of 0.1 on a mortality outcome is enormous.






 Exercise: which conclusion is available





A study of a new onboarding flow reports: mean time to first action fell by 0.4 seconds, 95% CI [-1.9, 1.1], p = 0.60, n = 5{,}000.
Assign the letter, for example answer <- "A".















C.
A turns “no evidence of an effect” into “evidence of no effect”, which is the most common error in the list and the reason underpowered studies are dangerous rather than merely useless.
B is the inversion again.
D asserts the effect is real, which the data do not support either.
The interval is doing all the work here. It contains zero, so the null survives; it also contains -1.9, so a substantial improvement survives too. Reporting the interval makes that visible; reporting p = 0.60 hides it.

title: What a p-value Licenses
text:
Summary

Under a true null, p-values are uniform. Five percent fall below 0.05 by construction, and 0.049 versus 0.051 is not a distinction.
A p-value is P(\text{data} \mid H_0). It is not the probability the null is true, nor the probability the effect is real.
Non-significant is not null. That distinction is a question about power.
The p-value confounds effect size with sample size: 0.01 on 100,000 people beat 1.2 on nine.
Report the estimate and its interval. Add the p-value if you like; it is the least informative of the three.

Next: the missing half of every non-significant result.

title: Power
text:
Two questions it answers
\alpha is chosen. It is the false positive rate, it is set at 0.05 by convention, and everyone reports it.
\beta is inherited. It is the false negative rate, it follows from the sample size and the size of the effect, almost nobody computes it, and it is the reason most published findings that fail to replicate ever got published.
Power is 1 - \beta: the probability that a study finds an effect that is really there.
\text{power} = P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ is false})
Both are asked constantly, and neither has any other route to an answer.
“How many observations do we need?” — the sample-size calculation, before the study.
“We found nothing. What does that mean?” — the interpretation, after it. A non-significant result from a well-powered study is informative. The same result from an underpowered study is not evidence of anything.

title: Power
text:
Measuring it by simulation
Power is a probability, so simulate it: build worlds where the effect is real, run the test, count how often it fires.








About 75%. So a quarter of studies run this way will miss a real, medium-sized effect and report nothing—and nothing in their output will indicate that this is what happened.
R also computes it directly.

title: Power
text:
The three levers
Power rises with the effect size, the sample size, and \alpha. Only two of those are yours to choose.








The dashed line is 80%, the conventional target. Read off where each curve crosses it:








Halving the effect quadruples the sample. That is the same k^2 relationship as everywhere else this term, and it is why detecting small effects is expensive and why claims of small effects from small samples deserve suspicion.

title: Power
text:
The winner’s curse
This is the part with consequences beyond your own study, and it is best shown rather than described.
Suppose a real effect of 0.3 exists, and studies of 20 people go looking for it.








Three numbers worth sitting with.
Power is 25%. Three quarters of these studies find nothing.
Averaged over all studies, the estimate is unbiased—0.30, exactly right.
Averaged over the studies that reached significance, the estimate is 0.57— nearly double the truth.
That is not a coding error and it is not a bias in the estimator. It is selection. To clear p < 0.05 on twenty observations, a study needs a large observed effect; studies that happened to see the true 0.3 do not qualify. So the significance filter systematically passes overestimates.






Why replication fails





The published literature is the significant subset. In an underpowered field, that subset overstates every effect it contains, so the next team powers their replication using the inflated number, is underpowered again, and finds nothing.
The original was not fraudulent. It was underpowered, and being underpowered guarantees that whatever you do publish is exaggerated.

title: Power
section: Post-hoc power is not the fix
text:
Post-hoc power is not the fix
Having found nothing, it is tempting to compute power using the effect size you observed. Do not. That quantity is a deterministic function of the p-value—it tells you nothing the p-value did not, and it is always low when the result was non-significant, which makes it look like an explanation while being a restatement.
The useful version is the confidence interval. If the interval is [-1.9, 1.1], then effects up to 1.9 remain consistent with your data and you say so. If it is [-0.05, 0.04], you have genuinely ruled out anything large, and that is evidence of absence.






 Exercise: how many do we need?





You are planning an A/B test on a continuous outcome. The smallest difference worth acting on is 0.25 standard deviations. You want 80% power at \alpha = 0.05, two-sided, with equal group sizes.
Return the required number per group, rounded up.















```{r}
ceiling(power.t.test(delta = 0.25, sd = 1, power = 0.8, type = "two.sample")$n)
```
253 per group, 506 in total.
Two things to carry into your project. Two-sample designs cost roughly twice per group what one-sample designs do, because a difference carries both groups’ sampling error—the variance addition rule from Variance and Standard Deviation, showing up as a budget.
And the calculation requires you to name the smallest difference worth acting on before collecting anything. That is a business question rather than a statistical one, and being forced to answer it is most of the value of doing the calculation at all.

title: Power
text:
Summary

Power = 1 - \beta, the chance of detecting an effect that is really there. It follows from the design; it is not chosen.
Simulate it in four lines, or use power.t.test().
Halving the effect quadruples the sample. Detecting d = 0.5 takes 34 observations; d = 0.2 takes 199.
The winner’s curse: at 25% power, significant studies overstated a true effect of 0.3 as 0.57. The estimator is unbiased; the filter is not.
Underpowered research does not merely fail to find things. It guarantees that what it does publish is exaggerated, which is the mechanism behind failed replication.
Post-hoc power is not diagnostic. Report the confidence interval, which says which effects remain on the table.

Next: what happens when you run not one test but forty.

title: Multiple Comparisons
text:
The arithmetic
A test at \alpha = 0.05 produces a false positive one time in twenty. That is not a defect; it is the specification.
It becomes a defect the moment you run more than one test, because the guarantee was per test and the claim people make is about the collection.
If m independent tests are run and every null is true, the chance that at least one comes out significant is 1 - 0.95^m.
Twenty tests and it is more likely than not. A hundred and it is essentially certain. Twenty is not a large number of tests—it is one outcome across twenty subgroups, or five outcomes at four time points, or a dashboard.
Nothing is different between any of these groups. Report only the smallest p-value and you have a finding, a plausible story to explain it, and no way for a reader to tell.

title: Multiple Comparisons
text:
Where it actually happens
Rarely as an explicit set of twenty tests. Usually as one of these:
Subgroup hunting. The treatment did not work overall, so you check men, women, under-40s, over-40s, each region, each product line. Twelve subgroups is twelve tests.
Outcome hunting. Revenue did not move, so you look at sessions, retention, clicks, time on page, support tickets.
Peeking. Checking an A/B test daily for three weeks and stopping when it crosses 0.05 is not one test. It is twenty-one opportunities, and the false positive rate is far above 5%.
Specification hunting. Trying the analysis with and without outliers, with and without a covariate, logged and unlogged, and reporting the version that worked.
The last is the hardest to see from the inside, because each individual choice is defensible. The problem is not any one decision; it is that the decisions were made after seeing which way they pushed the answer. No p-value in the final write-up records the paths not taken.

title: Multiple Comparisons
text:
Two corrections
Bonferroni controls the probability of any false positive: compare each p-value to \alpha/m instead of \alpha. It is exact, it is one line, and it is brutally conservative—with 100 tests each must clear 0.0005.
Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate: the expected proportion of your rejections that are false. It is the right tool when you are screening many candidates and can tolerate some duds in the shortlist.








Averaged over 2,000 runs of that setup, the pattern is stable:

9.3
4.4


Bonferroni
4.4
4.3
0.05


Benjamini–Hochberg
7.2
6.8
0.4



Read the trade honestly. Uncorrected, a third of your findings are false. Bonferroni removes essentially all of them and finds fewer than half the real effects. BH finds two-thirds of the real effects at the cost of about one false one in twenty reported.






Which to use





Bonferroni when a single false positive is expensive—a clinical claim, a regulatory filing, a public statement.
Benjamini–Hochberg when you are generating a shortlist for follow-up and the cost of a dud is another experiment.
Neither, if you can instead pre-register the one comparison you care about. That is not a correction; it is not needing one.

title: Multiple Comparisons
section: Correction is not the real fix
text:
Correction is not the real fix
Adjusting p-values assumes you know m. The dangerous case is the one where you do not—where a dozen analytic choices were made fluidly while looking at the data, and no one, including you, could reconstruct how many comparisons were implicitly made.
Three habits work better than any adjustment.
Decide the primary analysis before seeing the outcome. One outcome, one comparison, written down. Everything else is explicitly labeled exploratory.
Report everything you ran. A table of twenty p-values, uncorrected, is more honest than one corrected p-value from an unstated twenty.
Treat exploratory findings as hypotheses. They are the input to the next study, not the conclusion of this one. Held to that standard, subgroup hunting is a good use of data.






 Exercise: how bad does it get?





You run 12 independent tests, all of them null, at \alpha = 0.05. Return the probability that at least one is significant.















1 - 0.95^12
About 0.46.
Twelve is not an unusual number—four regions by three product lines gets you there without anyone feeling they are fishing. Nearly half of such analyses produce a significant subgroup when nothing at all is happening.
Note the tempting wrong answer, 12 \times 0.05 = 0.6. That overcounts, because it adds the probability of every test firing without subtracting the overlaps. The complement rule from Probability avoids the problem entirely, which is what it is for.

title: Multiple Comparisons
text:
Summary

The 5% guarantee is per test. Twenty tests give a 64% chance of at least one false positive; a hundred give 99%.
It arrives as subgroup hunting, outcome hunting, peeking, and specification hunting—rarely as an explicit list of tests.
Bonferroni (\alpha/m) controls any false positive and is conservative. Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate and finds more.
In the 100-test simulation: uncorrected found 13.7 things of which 4.4 were false; BH found 7.2 of which 0.4 were false.
Correction requires knowing m, and the worst cases are the ones where you do not. Pre-specify the primary comparison, report everything you ran, and treat exploratory results as hypotheses.

Next: the practice problems, and then a term of deciding which test the question actually calls for.

text:
Predict the output

title: Practice Problems
text:
Discussion





1. Roughly 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9—the quantiles of a uniform. Under the null the p-value carries no information about anything.
2. A p-value around 0.02 for an effect of 0.05. Highly significant, utterly trivial. Significance tracks \text{effect} \times \sqrt{n}, and with n=2000 the second factor does all the work.
3. 64% chance of a false positive across twenty tests, and Bonferroni’s answer is to demand 0.0025 from each.

title: Practice Problems
section: This runs and is still wrong
text:
This runs and is still wrong































Discussion





4. The p-value is above 0.05 and the interval is enormous—it comfortably contains both zero and a 25-point difference. The study did not find no difference; it found nothing at all, because twelve per group has almost no power against a difference of this size. Compute the power and see.
5. Twenty looks at data with no effect whatsoever. If any of them crossed 0.05 and you had stopped there, you would have shipped a change that does nothing. Fixing the sample size in advance is the whole defense, and it is why Power has to be computed before the experiment rather than during it.
6. Twelve subgroups, no effect anywhere, and the smallest p-value will often be under 0.05. Written up as “the effect was concentrated in enterprise customers in the West”, it is a finding with a story attached and no way for a reader to know that eleven other cells were examined.

title: Practice Problems
section: What does this license you to claim?
text:
What does this license you to claim?
A trial reports: treatment reduced average recovery time by 1.2 days, 95% CI [0.1, 2.3], p = 0.03, n = 180.

“The treatment works.”
“The treatment reduces recovery time by 1.2 days.”
“There is a 3% chance the treatment has no effect.”
“A reduction of 2 days is consistent with these data.”
“The effect is clinically important.”
Now suppose the same trial reported p = 0.03 for one of nine outcomes it measured, and the other eight are not shown. What changes?








Discussion





7. Defensible but vague. Better: the data are inconsistent with no effect, and the plausible effects run from 0.1 to 2.3 days.
8. Overstated—1.2 is the estimate, and the interval says the truth could plausibly be a tenth of that or twice it.
9. The inversion. P(\text{data} \mid H_0), not P(H_0 \mid \text{data}).
10. Yes. 2 lies inside the interval, so it is consistent with the data.
11. Not a statistical question. A tenth of a day is likely irrelevant and 2.3 days may matter a great deal; the interval spans both, which is the honest report.
12. Nearly everything. Nine outcomes at \alpha=0.05 give a 37% chance of at least one significant result under a complete absence of effect. Without knowing whether this outcome was pre-specified, p = 0.03 is close to uninformative.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Bring to class

Power for your project. Name the effect you would care about, guess the standard deviation, and compute the sample size you would need for 80% power. If your project data are already collected, compute the power you have instead. Bring the number, and be ready to say whether the study can answer its question.
Find a p-value in the wild. A news article, a press release, a paper. Bring it and answer: how many comparisons could plausibly have been made? Is an effect size reported alongside? Would the interval have told a different story?
Argue about this. “We should lower \alpha to 0.005 so that fewer false findings get published.” Work out what that costs, who pays it, and whether it addresses the mechanism in Power or merely moves it.

title: Experiments and Causal Claims
text:
What is here
Monday, October 19
Post your questions on any of these pages by Monday at 12:00 noon, the morning of class.
Everything so far has described data you were handed. This week is about data you cause to exist, and about the reason that distinction is worth a session of its own.
Every question anyone actually wants answered is causal—does this work, should we ship it, did the change help—and no amount of care applied to observational data answers one. Randomization does, and it is the only thing that does. This week is what it buys, how to run one properly, and the specific ways a well-designed experiment still ends up producing the wrong answer.
The machinery is small, because you already have it: a proportion and its standard error from Intervals for a Proportion, and power from Power. What is new is the design, and the discipline of writing it down before the data exists.

title: Experiments and Causal Claims
text:
What Randomization Buys



Self-selected groups differed by 1.62 on an unrecorded variable; randomized groups by 0.046. Why that matters more than any adjustment you could make, what randomization does not buy, and why you randomize the user rather than the session.








Designing an A/B Test



Six decisions, all made before any data arrives: one primary metric, guardrails, the smallest effect worth acting on, the sample size that follows from it, a stopping rule, and the analysis written down in advance.








What Goes Wrong



Sample ratio mismatch, checked before any outcome and invalidating the experiment when it fires. Then novelty and primacy, interference in marketplaces and social products, and a 0.05 percentage point lift with a p-value of 3 \times 10^{-7}.








Choosing a Test



The decision table, the paired test that found an effect the unpaired test missed on identical data, chi-squared for categorical association, and an honest note on why ANOVA is not in this course.








Practice Problems



Including an experiment that looks clean and is broken, and a design that randomized sessions when it should have randomized users.

title: Experiments and Causal Claims
section: The sentence this week is aiming at
text:
The sentence this week is aiming at
“We ran an experiment, and here is what it licenses us to claim.”
Half of that sentence is design and half is honesty about scope. A randomized experiment gives you a fair comparison among the people you ran it on—and that is a genuinely strong thing to have, provided you do not quietly extend it to people who were never in the study.
November takes up the harder case: what you can say when randomizing was never an option.






Due this week



Your project proposal. One page, mostly a question—see S.M.A.R.T. Questions. And as always, post your questions on these pages by Monday noon.

title: What Randomization Buys
text:
The problem, stated honestly
Every question anyone actually cares about is causal. Does the new onboarding flow increase retention? Does the drug work? Should we ship this? None of those are questions about association, and all of them are routinely answered with an association and a hopeful tone.
This chapter is about the one procedure that closes the gap, why it works, and what it costs.
You want to compare outcomes under treatment with outcomes without it. For any individual you observe exactly one of those. The other is not missing data in the sense of Where the Data Came From—it is unobservable in principle, because that person either got the treatment or did not.
So every causal claim is a comparison between different people, and it is only as good as the claim that those groups were otherwise alike.

title: What Randomization Buys
text:
Why “otherwise alike” almost never holds
Suppose there is some characteristic that affects the outcome—motivation, severity, prior spend, whatever. Call it a confounder. Now compare groups formed by letting people choose.








The groups differ by 1.62 units on a variable nobody recorded. Any difference in outcome will be a mixture of the treatment and that gap, and the data cannot separate them.
Now assign at random instead.








Centered on zero, with a spread of 0.046—thirty-five times smaller than the self-selected gap, and shrinking like 1/\sqrt{n} in the familiar way.






The claim randomization actually supports





Randomization does not make the groups identical. It makes them identical in expectation on every variable at once—including the ones you did not measure, did not think of, and could not have measured.
That last clause is the whole value. Statistical adjustment can only control for variables you have. Randomization handles the ones you do not, which are the ones that ruin observational studies.

title: What Randomization Buys
text:
What it does not buy
It does not fix a bad outcome measure. Randomizing perfectly and then measuring the wrong thing yields a clean estimate of something irrelevant.
It does not license generalization. A randomized experiment on your existing users tells you about your existing users. Randomization gives you internal validity—the comparison is fair. External validity is a separate question, and it is the Where the Data Came From question again.
It does not survive interference. The arithmetic assumes one person’s assignment does not affect another’s outcome. In a social product, a marketplace, or anywhere users interact, that fails—and it fails in the direction of making the treatment look better or worse than it is depending on which side of the market you touched.
It does not make the result large enough to matter. That is Practical significance.

title: What Randomization Buys
section: Randomize the unit that is independent
text:
Randomize the unit that is independent
The commonest design error is randomizing the wrong thing.
If one user makes twenty visits and you randomize visits, the same person appears in both arms, the arms are correlated, and your standard error is too small for the reason The Standard Error of a Mean gave: n is the number of independent units, and fifty measurements on ten patients is not n = 50.
Randomize the user, not the session. If users interact in teams, randomize the team. The unit of randomization should be the unit you are willing to call independent, and it is usually larger than the unit you would like it to be.






 Exercise: what does the comparison support?





A company emails all customers offering a new premium tier. Three months later, customers who took it have 40% higher retention than those who did not.
Assign the letter, for example answer <- "A".















B.
C is the sample-size fallacy. A larger sample makes a biased estimate more precise, not more correct—it narrows the interval around the wrong number.
D is the more sophisticated error, and it is the one worth arguing about. Controlling for age, region and tenure handles those three. It does nothing about the reason a customer upgraded, which was not recorded and probably could not be.
