That gap is what Model checking returns to in November, and it is why the honest form of the sentence is “customers who upgraded retained better”—which is true, and is not a claim about the tier.

title: What Randomization Buys
text:
Summary

Every causal question compares outcomes you cannot both observe, so it becomes a comparison between different people.
Self-selected groups differed by 1.62 on an unrecorded variable; randomized groups differed by 0.046. Randomization balances every variable in expectation, including the unmeasured ones.
It buys internal validity only. Generalization, measurement, and interference are separate problems it does not touch.
Randomize the unit you are willing to call independent—usually the user, sometimes the team, rarely the session.

Next: turning that into an experiment somebody can actually run.

title: Designing an A/B Test
text:
1. One primary metric
An A/B test is a randomized experiment with a marketing name. Everything in What Randomization Buys applies, and this chapter is the checklist that turns it into something you can run on Monday.
The order matters. Every decision below is made before any data arrives, and writing them down is what separates an experiment from an exercise in finding something.
Name the single number that decides the question. Not a dashboard—one number, chosen in advance.
The reason is Multiple Comparisons. Five metrics at \alpha = 0.05 give a 23% chance of a false positive under a complete absence of effect, and the write-up will report whichever one moved.
Secondary metrics are fine and useful. They are labeled secondary, they do not decide the ship, and they are reported whether or not they moved.

title: Designing an A/B Test
text:
2. Guardrails
Guardrail metrics are the ones you are not trying to improve and are not willing to break: latency, error rate, unsubscribes, support tickets, revenue.
They exist because optimizing one number almost always costs another. A change that lifts click-through by making the button misleading will lift click-through. The guardrail is how you find out what it cost, and the decision rule is asymmetric—you need evidence of improvement on the primary metric and absence of harm on the guardrails.

title: Designing an A/B Test
section: 3. The smallest effect worth acting on
text:
3. The smallest effect worth acting on
Before computing any sample size you have to answer a business question: how big would the effect have to be for us to do anything differently?
This is the hardest step and the one most often skipped, because it is not a statistical question and there is no formula for it. It is also where most of the value of the exercise is—teams frequently discover at this point that no plausible effect would change the decision, which means the experiment need not be run at all.

title: Designing an A/B Test
text:
4. Sample size, from power
Now it is arithmetic. A conversion rate is a proportion, so power.prop.test() does the work.








Detecting a lift from 5% to 6% takes 8,158 per group. Halving the target effect, to 5.5%, takes 31,234—almost four times as many, which is the same k^2 relationship as everywhere else this term.
This is where the previous step earns its keep. If your traffic is 5,000 users a week and you need 62,000, the experiment takes three months, and that is worth knowing before you start rather than in week six.






Guess the baseline honestly





power.prop.test needs the baseline rate, which you usually know from historical data. Take it from the same population, the same days of week, and the same measurement definition you will use in the test. A baseline borrowed from a different segment is the most common reason a carefully computed sample size turns out to be wrong.

title: Designing an A/B Test
section: 5. A stopping rule, fixed in advance
text:
5. A stopping rule, fixed in advance
Write down the sample size, and stop there.
The Oct 5 problems showed twenty looks at data with no effect whatsoever crossing 0.05 along the way. Checking daily and stopping when it looks good is not one test; it is as many tests as you took looks, and the false positive rate is far above the 5% you think you are paying.
There are legitimate sequential designs—group sequential methods, always-valid inference—that let you look repeatedly with the arithmetic adjusted. Use one, or fix n in advance. What is not available is looking repeatedly with the arithmetic of a single test.

title: Designing an A/B Test
section: 6. Analysis, written down before the data
text:
6. Analysis, written down before the data
The analysis is two lines and there is no reason not to write them first.








A lift of 0.375 percentage points, p = 0.056, with an interval running from -0.009 to +0.76 percentage points.
Report it that way. “Not significant” is a poor summary—the interval says the data are consistent with no effect and also with a lift of three quarters of a percentage point, and whether that ambiguity matters depends on the decision threshold you set in step 3.






 Exercise: how long will this take?





Your checkout page converts at 12%. The product team will act on an improvement of one percentage point or more. You want 80% power at \alpha = 0.05.
Return the required number per group, rounded up.















```{r}
ceiling(power.prop.test(p1 = 0.12, p2 = 0.13, power = 0.8)$n)
```
17,169 per group, about 34,000 in total.
Try it again with p2 = 0.125—half the effect—and the requirement goes to roughly 67,500 per group. Small effects are not slightly more expensive to detect; they are four times more expensive for every halving, and that is the single most useful fact to have in your head when someone proposes testing a change they expect to move the needle by a fraction of a percent.

title: Designing an A/B Test
text:
The checklist



Before you start





Primary metric
One, named in advance


Guardrails
What you refuse to break


Minimum effect
The smallest difference worth acting on


Sample size
From power, using an honest baseline


Stopping rule
Fixed n, or a sequential method


Analysis
Written down before the data exists



If you cannot fill in every row, the experiment is not ready to run—and the row that is usually blank is the third one.

title: Designing an A/B Test
text:
Summary

One primary metric, chosen in advance. Everything else is secondary and reported regardless.
Guardrails catch what the improvement cost, with an asymmetric decision rule.
Name the smallest effect worth acting on before computing anything. It is a business question, and answering it sometimes cancels the experiment.
Sample size follows from power: 5%→6% needs 8,158 per group, 5%→5.5% needs 31,234.
Fix the stopping rule. Peeking with single-test arithmetic is not a slightly optimistic analysis, it is a different false positive rate.
Report the difference and its interval, not “significant” or not.

Next: what goes wrong once it is running.

title: What Goes Wrong
text:
Sample ratio mismatch
The design is correct, the randomization is correct, and the experiment still produces the wrong answer. This chapter is the short list of ways that happens, in roughly the order you should check for them.
Check this first, before looking at any outcome.
You assigned users 50/50. Count how many actually landed in each arm. If the split is off by more than chance, something in the pipeline is broken, and the outcome comparison is worthless no matter how good it looks.
The first is ordinary sampling noise. The second is a 2% imbalance and its p-value is 2.5 \times 10^{-10}—at this scale, a discrepancy far too small to notice by eye is overwhelming evidence that assignment is broken.
That sensitivity is the point. SRM is the cheapest diagnostic you have and it catches the expensive failures: a redirect that drops users before logging, a bot filter applied to one arm, a caching layer serving control to returning visitors, an assignment hash that is not uniform.

title: What Goes Wrong
text:
An SRM invalidates the experiment





It does not mean “be careful interpreting this”. It means the mechanism that was supposed to make the groups comparable did not run as specified, so you no longer know what the groups are. Find the cause, fix it, and rerun.
The tempting move—dropping the excess users to restore balance—makes it worse, because whatever selected them is now doing the selecting.

title: What Goes Wrong
text:
Novelty and primacy
Users react to change, not only to the change.
Novelty: a new interface gets clicked because it is new. The effect decays. Measured in week one and extrapolated to a year, it is a fantasy.
Primacy: the opposite. Existing users are slowed down by an unfamiliar layout and the treatment looks worse than it is, until they adapt.
Both are diagnosed the same way: plot the effect over time, and look at new users separately from established ones. If the treatment effect is large on day one and gone by day fourteen, you have measured a reaction to novelty. If it is negative on day one and positive by day fourteen, you have measured primacy and should run longer.
This is also why “run the experiment for a full week” is standard advice—weekday and weekend users differ, and an experiment ending on a Wednesday has an unbalanced mix.

title: What Goes Wrong
text:
Interference
The arithmetic assumes one user’s assignment does not affect another user’s outcome. Common situations where it plainly does:
Marketplaces. Show treatment users better search results and they buy the scarce inventory, so control users see less of it. The treatment looks good partly by making control worse, and the measured difference overstates what happens when everyone gets it.
Social features. A user in treatment posts more; their friends in control see more content. The effect leaks into the control arm and the difference understates the truth.
Shared resources. A treatment that increases server load slows everyone down, including control.
The fix is to randomize a larger unit—by market, by region, by time period—so that interference happens within an arm rather than between them. It costs enormous power, because the number of independent units collapses from millions of users to a handful of markets, and that trade is the whole difficulty of experimentation in marketplaces.

title: What Goes Wrong
text:
Practical against statistical significance
The last failure is one of reporting rather than mechanism.








A lift of 0.05 percentage points, with a p-value of 3 \times 10^{-7}. It is real, it is precisely measured, and it is almost certainly not worth the engineering cost of shipping it.
Statistical significance answers “is it there?”. Practical significance answers “does it matter?”. The second question is settled by the threshold you wrote down in step 3 of the design, before the data existed—which is the reason that step is not optional.






 Exercise: check for SRM





An experiment intended a 50/50 split and observed 12,412 users in control and 12,088 in treatment. Return the p-value of a chi-squared test against a 50/50 expectation.















chisq.test(c(12412, 12088), p = c(0.5, 0.5))$p.value
About 0.038.
An imbalance of 1.3% is invisible on a dashboard and unlikely enough here to stop and find out why. The right response is to investigate the assignment pipeline, not to discard the surplus—dropping users to restore balance substitutes your selection for the randomizer’s, which is the thing the experiment existed to avoid.

title: What Goes Wrong
text:
The order to check things

SRM. Before any outcome.
The metric definition, computed identically in both arms.
Effect over time, for novelty and primacy.
Guardrails.
The primary metric, with its interval.
Practical significance, against the threshold you set in advance.

Everything above the primary metric is a check on whether the experiment ran. Only once those pass does the estimate mean anything.

title: What Goes Wrong
text:
Summary

Sample ratio mismatch invalidates an experiment. A 2% imbalance on 100,000 users gives p = 2.5 \times 10^{-10}; check it first, and never fix it by dropping users.
Novelty and primacy are diagnosed by plotting the effect over time and splitting new from established users.
Interference breaks the independence assumption in marketplaces, social products and shared infrastructure. The fix—randomizing markets or regions—costs most of your power.
Significant is not important. A 0.05 percentage point lift on twenty million users had p = 3 \times 10^{-7} and is probably not worth shipping.

Next: the machinery, and a decision table for choosing among tests.

title: Choosing a Test
text:
The decision
Every test in this course is (\text{estimate} - \text{claim})/\operatorname{SE} with different things substituted in, so choosing among them is not deep. It is a question about what kind of variables you have, and it gets asked in interviews because a surprising number of people cannot answer it.
Two questions get you to the row: what kind of thing is the outcome, and how many groups are being compared. Everything else is detail.

title: Choosing a Test
text:
Outcome
Comparison
Test
In R




Numeric
One group against a claimed value
one-sample t
t.test(x, mu = )


Numeric
Two independent groups
two-sample t
t.test(x ~ g)


Numeric
Same units measured twice
paired t
t.test(x, y, paired = TRUE)


Numeric
Skewed, or a statistic with no formula
permutation
Permutation Tests


Binary
Two proportions
two-proportion
prop.test(x, n)


Categorical
Association between two categorical variables
chi-squared
chisq.test(table(a, b))


Categorical
Small expected counts
Fisher’s exact
fisher.test(table(a, b))

title: Choosing a Test
section: Paired is a different test, not a nicer one
text:
Paired is a different test, not a nicer one
The most consequential row is the third, because getting it wrong throws away most of your power.








The same data, the same 3-unit effect. Unpaired, the subject-to-subject spread of 20 swamps it and the test finds nothing. Paired, each subject serves as their own control, that spread cancels, and the effect is unmissable.
If the same unit appears in both groups, the observations are not independent, and the paired test is not an optional refinement—it is the one that respects the design.

title: Choosing a Test
text:
Chi-squared, for categorical association
The chi-squared test compares a table of counts with the counts you would expect if the two variables were unrelated.








The statistic is the same idea as always—observed minus expected, standardized and squared—and the expected counts assume independence.








The rule of thumb is that every expected count should be at least 5. Below that, the approximation degrades and fisher.test() is the honest choice; R warns you when it happens, and the warning is worth reading rather than suppressing.
A two-proportion test is the two-by-two special case. prop.test and chisq.test on the same 2×2 table give the identical p-value, which is worth seeing once:








Prefer prop.test: it reports the difference and its confidence interval, which chi-squared does not, and by now you know why that matters.

title: Choosing a Test
text:
What about ANOVA?
You will meet it, so here is the honest position. ANOVA tests whether several group means are all equal. It is the natural extension of the two-sample t test to three or more groups.
It is not taught in this course because a linear model with a categorical predictor does the same job and more: it gives you the individual group differences and their intervals rather than a single “something differs” verdict, it extends to covariates, and it is where November goes anyway. If you need it, aov() exists and summary(lm(y ~ g)) tells you more.






 Exercise: which test





Forty participants each rate a website before and after a redesign, on a 1–100 scale. You want to know whether the redesign changed ratings.
Assign the letter, for example answer <- "A".















B.
A treats forty people measured twice as eighty independent observations, which is the independence failure from The Standard Error of a Mean.
C confuses a numeric scale with categories. Ratings from 1 to 100 are numbers you can average; treating them as 100 unordered categories throws away their order and their spacing.
D is not wrong so much as wasteful. Dichotomising a numeric outcome at an arbitrary cut discards information and power, and the cut point is a researcher degree of freedom of exactly the kind Multiple Comparisons warns about.

title: Choosing a Test
text:
Summary

Two questions choose the test: what kind of outcome, and how many groups.
Paired when the same unit appears twice. In the simulation the unpaired test found nothing and the paired test found the effect easily, on identical data.
Chi-squared for categorical association, with expected counts of at least 5; Fisher’s exact below that.
A two-proportion test is chi-squared on a 2×2 table. Use prop.test, because it reports the difference and its interval.
ANOVA is a linear model with a categorical predictor, and the model tells you more.

Next: the practice problems, and then a month of modeling.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Predict the output
Not graded, not auto-checked. Bring your answers and your disagreements.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Discussion





1. Near zero against about 1.6. The second is not a bug in the code—it is what selection does, and it is the entire reason experiments exist.
2. 17,169, then 67,496, then 267,611. Each halving of the target effect quadruples the sample. Anyone proposing to detect a quarter-point lift should be shown this before they estimate a timeline.
3. Identical. A two-proportion test is chi-squared on a 2×2 table, and the only reason to prefer prop.test is that it hands you the difference and its interval.

title: Practice Problems
section: This runs and is still wrong
text:
This runs and is still wrong































Discussion





4. p \approx 7 \times 10^{-6}. A 2.25% imbalance, invisible on a dashboard, and decisive evidence that assignment is broken. Nothing downstream of this is interpretable, and dropping 900 users from the larger arm makes it worse.
5. The session-level standard error is far too small, because 2,000 sessions are really 200 independent users and the per-user variation is doing most of the work. This is the n-is-not-what-you-think failure from The Standard Error of a Mean, arriving as an experimental design error rather than an arithmetic one.
6. A 0.1 percentage point lift, p \approx 0.52, interval running from about -0.20 to +0.40. “No significant difference” is a bad summary: the experiment is consistent with a meaningful gain in either direction and has settled nothing. Whether that is a failure depends entirely on the minimum effect you named before starting.

title: Practice Problems
section: What does this license you to claim?
text:
What does this license you to claim?
A team reports: users in the treatment arm completed onboarding 8% more often, p = 0.01, over one week, with a 50.4/49.6 split across 90,000 users.

“The new onboarding causes an 8% lift.”
“We should ship it.”
What would you check before believing any of it?
The effect was +14% on day one and +2% by day seven. What is that, and what does it do to the headline number?
The team also reports that support tickets rose 6%, “but not significantly.” How should that enter the decision?








Discussion





7. Defensible on internal validity if the randomization held—but check the split first. 50.4/49.6 on 90,000 gives an SRM p-value of about 0.016, which is enough to want an explanation before trusting anything.
8. Not a statistical question. It depends on the minimum effect named in advance, the guardrails, and the cost of shipping.
9. SRM, metric definition identical across arms, effect over time, guardrails, and whether the unit of randomization was the user.
10. Novelty. The one-week average overstates the steady state, and the honest move is to run longer and report the later window—or to report both and say which one you believe.
11. Carefully. “Not significant” on a guardrail is the weakest possible reassurance: guardrails are usually underpowered, so a 6% rise that failed to reach significance may well be real. Ask for the interval. This is the asymmetry from Designing an A/B Test—you need evidence of improvement on the primary metric and evidence of absence of harm on the guardrails, and the second is much harder to obtain.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Bring to class

Design one. Take your project question, or invent a product change. Write the six rows of the design checklist: primary metric, guardrails, minimum effect worth acting on, sample size, stopping rule, analysis. Bring the sample size and how long it would take at a realistic traffic level.
Find an experiment in the wild. A company engineering blog, a paper, a press release. What was randomized? What was the primary metric? Can you tell how many metrics were examined?
Argue about this. “We cannot randomize—it would be unfair to give some users a worse experience.” Work out when that objection is right, when it is an argument for randomizing sooner rather than later, and what Where the Data Came From says about the alternative.

title: Linear Models
text:
What is here
Monday, November 2
Post your questions on any of these pages by Monday at 12:00 noon, the morning of class.
Every week so far has ended with a number and an interval around it. A model does the same thing, several times at once, for questions of the form how does this outcome differ across values of that variable, among cases alike in these other respects?
The mechanics are one function call. This part is about the output, because a regression table is the most over-interpreted object in applied statistics and almost every misreading of one is a version of forgetting that its numbers are estimates.
Two ideas run through all four chapters. A coefficient has a sampling distribution, so it comes with a standard error meaning exactly what standard errors have meant since September. And a coefficient describes a comparison among cases that agree on the other predictors in the model—which is a precise and limited claim, and which the phrase “holding everything else constant” flatters.

title: Linear Models
text:
Fitting a Line



Least squares, lm(), and how to read every column of summary(). Residuals that sum to zero because the fit forces them to, and why an intercept is only interpretable when x = 0 is a value your data contains.








A Coefficient Is an Estimate



Five thousand refits give a slope distribution with a spread of 0.0975; one fit reports a standard error of 0.0979. That is what the column means. Then intervals, the test against zero, and why spread in x buys precision as effectively as sample size.








More Than One Predictor



The study-hours effect reads 8.55 against a truth of 1.5 until the confounder is added. Omitted-variable bias, categorical predictors and their baseline, interactions, and why “holding the others constant” means only the others you put in.








R^2, and What It Does Not Tell You



Anscombe’s four datasets share a slope, an intercept and an R^2 to three decimals and look nothing alike. Eight columns of noise raise R^2 and sink adjusted R^2. Low is not bad and high is not good.








Practice Problems



Including a coefficient that is biased rather than noisy, an excellent-looking fit controlled by one row, and a housing model whose bedroom coefficient is negative for a good reason.

title: Linear Models
text:
The sentence to practice
“Among homes of the same age and bedroom count, an extra square foot is associated with about $142 more, give or take $22.”
Every clause is doing work: among homes of the same… names what was held fixed, associated with declines the causal claim the data cannot support, and give or take is the standard error. Write your coefficients that way all term and most of the errors in this part become impossible.






Due this week



HW 5 is due at the start of class. And as always, post your questions on these pages by Monday noon—that afternoon’s session is built out of them.

title: Fitting a Line
text:
The model
Everything so far has compared groups. A model does something more flexible: it describes how an outcome changes with one or more other variables, and it does it in a form you can interrogate.
The mechanics are two lines of R. The whole difficulty is in what the output means, which is why this part spends four chapters on a function you will call once.
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i
Three objects, and it is worth keeping them apart from the start.
That distinction is the content of the next chapter, and half the errors people make with regression come from losing it.

title: Fitting a Line
text:
\beta_0, \beta_1 are parameters—properties of the population, unknown, fixed.
\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1 are estimates—computed from your sample, and therefore random in exactly the sense The Standard Error of a Mean established.
\varepsilon_i is the part of y_i the line does not explain.

title: Fitting a Line
text:
Least squares
Among all possible lines, choose the one minimizing the sum of squared vertical distances to the points.








The gray verticals are the residuals, y_i - \hat y_i. Least squares makes the sum of their squares as small as any line can.
Squared rather than absolute for two reasons, one good and one historical. The good one: squaring makes the solution a projection, which is what the linear algebra in DATS 6103 is for and what makes a closed-form answer exist. The consequence to remember is that squaring makes least squares sensitive to outliers, since a point twice as far away contributes four times as much.

title: Fitting a Line
text:
Reading the output








Take it a piece at a time.
Estimate — the fitted coefficients. The intercept 4.10 is the predicted y when x = 0; the slope 1.765 says y rises by 1.765 for each one-unit increase in x.
Note that the true slope was 2.0. The estimate is not the parameter, and the gap here is ordinary sampling variation rather than a mistake.
Std. Error — how much each estimate would move if you collected the data again. This is the subject of A Coefficient Is an Estimate and it is the most useful column in the table.
t value and Pr(>|t|) — the estimate divided by its standard error, and the p-value for the null hypothesis that the coefficient is zero. The same (\text{estimate} - \text{claim})/\operatorname{SE} as always, with the claim fixed at zero.
Residual standard error — the typical size of a residual, an estimate of \sigma. It is in the units of y, and it is what a prediction interval is mostly made of.
R-squared — the share of variance the model accounts for. It gets its own chapter, mostly to say what it does not mean.

title: Fitting a Line
text:
Fitted values and residuals








The residuals sum to zero and are uncorrelated with x—not as a property of your data, but as a consequence of how the line was chosen. They are guaranteed, so they tell you nothing about whether the model is any good. Checking that a model fits requires looking at residuals in ways that are not forced, which is Nov 9.

title: Fitting a Line
text:
Prediction








Predicting inside the range of the observed x is interpolation and is what the model is for. Predicting outside it is extrapolation, and the model has no information about that region—it will answer anyway, confidently, in a straight line that nothing in the data supports.






 Exercise: fit and read





cars is built into R: speed in mph, dist the stopping distance in feet. Fit dist ~ speed and return the slope—a single number.


















coef(lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars))[2]
3.932 feet per mph.
The intercept is -17.6, a negative stopping distance for a stationary car. That is not a flaw in the fit—it is the line doing its job over the range where data exists (speeds of 4 to 25 mph) and being meaningless outside it. An intercept is only interpretable when x = 0 is a value the data actually contains.

title: Fitting a Line
text:
Summary

y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon. Parameters are fixed and unknown; estimates are computed and random.
Least squares minimizes the sum of squared residuals, which makes it sensitive to outliers.
summary(lm()) gives estimates, standard errors, t statistics and p-values; the p-value tests the coefficient against zero.
Residuals summing to zero and being uncorrelated with x are guaranteed by the fit and are not evidence of anything.
Interpolate freely, extrapolate never, and check whether x = 0 is in your data before interpreting an intercept.

Next: the standard error column, which is where the inference lives.

title: A Coefficient Is an Estimate
text:
The sampling distribution, measured
The slope printed by lm() is not the relationship. It is one draw from a distribution of slopes you would have got from other samples, and the whole of regression inference is the observation that everything you already know about a sample mean applies to it unchanged.
Collect the data again and again from the same population, refit each time, and look at the slopes.
Centered on the truth, roughly Normal, with a spread of 0.0975. Now compare that against what a single fit reports:
Std. Error on the slope is 0.0979, against the simulated 0.0975.
That is the entire meaning of the column. The standard error is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of that coefficient, estimated from one sample rather than from five thousand—which is what The Standard Error of a Mean did for \bar X, arriving now with a model attached.

title: A Coefficient Is an Estimate
text:
The interval, and the test
Once you have an estimate and its standard error, the rest is machinery you already own.








The interval for the slope runs 1.57 to 1.96, and it covers the true value of 2.00—just. Read it the way you read any confidence interval: the procedure captures the truth 95% of the time, and this is one run of it.
The t statistic in the summary is \hat\beta / \operatorname{SE}, testing \beta = 0. That null is a genuine question—is there any relationship at all?—but it is rarely the interesting one, and it is the default only because software has to pick something.






The interval carries more than the test





A coefficient of 1.765 with an interval of [1.57, 1.96] says the relationship is real and pins it down to about a fifth of a unit.
A coefficient of 1.765 with an interval of [-0.4, 3.9] has the same estimate and a p-value above 0.05, and says almost nothing—the data are consistent with a strong positive relationship, no relationship, and a mild negative one.
Reporting “p = 0.41” for the second makes it sound like evidence of no effect. It is not; it is absence of evidence.

title: A Coefficient Is an Estimate
section: Where the standard error comes from
text:
Where the standard error comes from
You do not need the formula, but the shape of it explains what makes a coefficient precise:
\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}}
Three readings.
More data helps, since the denominator grows with n—the familiar 1/\sqrt{n}.
Spread in x helps. The denominator is the total variation in the predictor. Measuring y at ten values of x ranging over 0 to 100 pins the slope down far better than measuring it at ten values ranging over 49 to 51. If you are designing data collection, push x to its extremes.
Noise hurts, through \sigma. A tighter relationship gives a tighter coefficient.








Same sample size, same noise, and the coefficient from the wide design is about eight times more precise. How you collect x matters as much as how much of it you collect.






 Exercise: a coefficient with its interval





Using cars, fit dist ~ speed and return the width of the 95% confidence interval for the slope—a single number.


















```{r}
diff(confint(lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars))["speed", ])
```
1.671, from an interval of [3.097, 4.768].
Worth saying out loud: the estimate is 3.93 feet per mph and the data cannot distinguish 3.1 from 4.8. That is a fifty percent range on the quantity of interest, from fifty observations—which is a useful calibration for how much data a precise coefficient actually takes.

title: A Coefficient Is an Estimate
text:
Summary

A coefficient is an estimate with a sampling distribution. Simulated over 5,000 datasets its spread was 0.0975; the single fit reported 0.0979.
confint() gives the interval; the printed t and p-value test the coefficient against zero, which is the default question rather than the interesting one.
Report the interval. The same estimate with a wide interval and with a narrow one support entirely different claims.
Precision improves with more data, more spread in x, and less noise. A wide design was ten times more precise than a narrow one at identical n.

Next: what happens when there is more than one predictor, and what “holding the others constant” is really claiming.

title: More Than One Predictor
text:
What a coefficient means now
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \varepsilon
Adding predictors is one more term in a formula, and it changes what every coefficient means. That change is the most important idea in this part and the one most often stated as a slogan without being understood.
In a single-predictor model, \beta_1 is the average change in y per unit of x.
With several predictors, \beta_1 is the average change in y per unit of x_1 among cases that agree on all the other predictors in the model. The usual phrasing is holding the others constant, and the phrase is accurate provided you read the last five words: the others that are in the model.
Watch what that does.
The true effect of an hour of study is 1.5 points. The naive regression reports 8.55—nearly six times too large—because students who study more are also more skilled, and the model has no way to tell the two apart. Add skill and the coefficient snaps to 1.52.
This is omitted-variable bias, and note the direction: the coefficient is not noisy, it is systematically wrong, and no amount of extra data fixes it. A bigger sample gives you 8.55 with a tighter interval.

title: More Than One Predictor
text:
The honest reading





“Holding the others constant” is a statement about arithmetic, not about the world. The model held constant the variables you gave it. It could not hold constant the ones you did not measure, and in the simulation above the unmeasured one was doing almost all of the work.
That is why a regression coefficient is not a causal effect, and why Oct 19 spent a week on the one procedure that does balance the variables you never thought of.

title: More Than One Predictor
text:
Categorical predictors
A factor with k levels enters as k-1 indicator variables. One level becomes the baseline and every coefficient is a comparison against it.








The intercept, 50.17, is the mean for free—the baseline, chosen as the first level. planpro at 7.40 is the pro-minus-free difference; planent at 14.37 is ent-minus-free.
Two consequences worth knowing.
There is no coefficient for the baseline, because it is the reference point rather than a comparison. A reader who does not know which level is the baseline cannot interpret any of the others, so say it.
The baseline is a choice. relevel() changes it, which changes every coefficient and every p-value in the block without changing the model at all. Pick the level that makes the comparisons you actually want to report.
This is also the answer to what about ANOVA: this model is the one-way ANOVA, and it tells you the individual differences and their intervals rather than a single verdict that something differs somewhere.

title: More Than One Predictor
text:
Interactions, briefly
y ~ x1 * x2 fits both main effects and their product, which lets the slope on x_1 depend on x_2.








hours is the slope for the baseline group (basic). hours:tierpremium is how much more the slope is for premium users. Adding them gives the premium slope.
Interactions are the honest way to say “it depends”, and they cost power—you are estimating a difference of differences, which carries the sampling error of both. Include one because you have a reason to expect it, not because you went looking.

title: More Than One Predictor
text:
Adding predictors is not free
Every additional predictor spends a degree of freedom, and predictors correlated with each other inflate one another’s standard errors. Two nearly duplicate predictors cannot be told apart by the data, and the model says so by widening both intervals enormously while the fitted values barely move—which is multicollinearity, and it is a diagnostic topic for Nov 9.
The practical rule for now: put a variable in because you can say why it belongs, not because it improved a number.






 Exercise: does the coefficient move?





mtcars is built into R. Fit mpg ~ wt, then mpg ~ wt + hp, and return the change in the coefficient on wt—the second model’s minus the first’s.


















```{r}
coef(lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars))["wt"] -
  coef(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars))["wt"]
```
About +1.47: the coefficient moves from -5.34 to -3.88.
Heavier cars tend to have larger engines, so in the simple model weight was being charged for part of horsepower’s effect. Neither coefficient is wrong. They answer different questions—how does mpg differ across cars of different weight, and how does mpg differ across cars of different weight but the same horsepower—and which you want depends on what you are going to do with it.
The habit worth building: when a coefficient changes on adding a predictor, that is information, and it is the first thing to look at rather than something to tidy away.

title: More Than One Predictor
text:
Summary

With several predictors, each coefficient describes a comparison among cases that agree on the others in the model—and only those.
Omitted-variable bias is systematic, not noisy. The study-hours effect read 8.55 against a truth of 1.5 until the confounder was added, and more data would not have helped.
A factor enters as k-1 indicators against a baseline you choose; there is no coefficient for the baseline, and this model is the one-way ANOVA with more detail.
Interactions let a slope depend on another variable, cost power, and should be motivated in advance.
Add predictors because you can justify them, not because a statistic improved.

Next: the statistic people quote most and understand least.

title: R^2, and What It Does Not Tell You
text:
What it is
R^2 is the share of the variance in y that the model accounts for. It runs from 0 to 1, it is easy to quote, and it is the number most likely to be reported in place of thinking.
This chapter is what it is, followed by the four things people take it to mean.
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2}{\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2}
The numerator is the squared error your model makes. The denominator is the squared error a model that predicts \bar y for everyone would make. So R^2 is the proportional reduction in squared error relative to using the mean, and in simple regression it is exactly the squared correlation between x and y.
crumbs: $R^2$, and What It Does Not Tell You

title: R^2, and What It Does Not Tell You
section: It does not say the model is right
text:
It does not say the model is right
Anscombe’s quartet is four datasets built to make this point, and it is built into R.
















Identical to three decimal places: slope 0.5, intercept 3.0, R^2 0.67. One is a reasonable linear relationship, one is an obvious curve, one is a perfect line with a single outlier dragging it, and one is a vertical stack plus a lone point that determines the entire fit.
A summary statistic cannot distinguish them. Plot the data.
crumbs: $R^2$, and What It Does Not Tell You

title: R^2, and What It Does Not Tell You
text:
It always goes up
Add any predictor—including pure noise—and R^2 cannot decrease.








R^2 climbs from 0.029 to 0.071 as eight columns of pure noise are added. Nothing was learned; the model simply gained freedom to fit the sample.
Adjusted R^2 charges for that freedom, and here it falls steadily to -0.169—correctly reporting that every one of these predictors made the model worse.
Use adjusted R^2 when comparing models with different numbers of predictors. Neither statistic is a model-selection procedure on its own.
crumbs: $R^2$, and What It Does Not Tell You

title: R^2, and What It Does Not Tell You
section: It is not accuracy, and low is not bad
text:
It is not accuracy, and low is not bad
R^2 is relative to the variance of y, so it depends on the population as much as on the model.








The same relationship, the same residual standard error of 1.90, and R^2 of 0.22 against 0.90—purely because the second population has more spread in x.
So an R^2 of 0.3 is not evidence of a poor model, and 0.9 is not evidence of a good one. In fields where outcomes are genuinely noisy, 0.1 can be a real finding; in a physical measurement, 0.95 may be a disappointment.
If you want to know how accurate predictions are, report the residual standard error, which is in the units of y and answers the question directly.
crumbs: $R^2$, and What It Does Not Tell You

title: R^2, and What It Does Not Tell You
text:
The four misreadings

“High R^2 means the model is correct.” Anscombe sets 2, 3 and 4.
“Adding this predictor improved R^2, so it belongs.” Noise improves R^2.
“Low R^2 means no relationship.” The coefficient and its interval answer that; a small, precisely estimated effect in noisy data is a real finding with a small R^2.
“R^2 is prediction accuracy.” It is variance explained in this sample, with no holdout involved. Out-of-sample accuracy is a different quantity, and it is DATS 6103’s subject.







 Exercise: what does adding noise do?





Using mtcars, fit mpg ~ wt, then add a column of random noise as a second predictor. Return the change in R^2—the second model’s minus the first’s.


















```{r}
summary(lm(mpg ~ wt + junk, data = mtcars))$r.squared -
  summary(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars))$r.squared
```
A small positive number, and it is positive no matter what noise you generate —the fit can always set the new coefficient to zero and do no worse, so it never does worse.
Run the same comparison on adj.r.squared and it typically goes the other way. That difference is the entire reason the adjustment exists, and it is why “R^2 went up” is not an argument for a variable.
crumbs: $R^2$, and What It Does Not Tell You

title: R^2, and What It Does Not Tell You
text:
Summary

R^2 is the proportional reduction in squared error relative to predicting the mean; in simple regression it is \operatorname{cor}(x,y)^2.
Anscombe’s four datasets share slope, intercept and R^2 to three decimals and look nothing alike. Plot the data.
R^2 cannot decrease when a predictor is added; eight columns of noise took it from 0.029 to 0.071 while adjusted R^2 fell to -0.169.
It depends on the spread of x: the same relationship gave 0.22 and 0.90. Low is not bad and high is not good.
For accuracy, report the residual standard error, which is in the units of y.

Next: the practice problems, and then a week on whether the model deserves to be believed at all.
crumbs: $R^2$, and What It Does Not Tell You

title: Practice Problems
text:
Predict the output
Not graded, not auto-checked. Bring your answers and your disagreements.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Discussion





1. They agree because the reported standard error is an estimate of the standard deviation of the sampling distribution—the thing the simulation measures directly. One sample suffices; you never need the 3,000.
2. -5.34 becomes about -3.8. Weight is correlated with horsepower and displacement, so the simple coefficient absorbs part of their effect. Both are correct answers to different questions.
3. All 0.67. Then look at the four scatterplots and decide what a summary statistic is worth.

title: Practice Problems
section: This runs and is still wrong
text:
This runs and is still wrong































Discussion





4. The coefficient is about 8.5 with a tiny p-value—the opposite of “barely matters”, and also nearly six times the truth of 1.5. Significance is not the problem here; the estimate itself is biased because skill is missing.
5. R^2 stays very high and the slope has been dragged by a single row. High R^2 is compatible with a fit that one observation controls, which is Anscombe set 3 arriving in the wild. Influence is a Nov 9 topic and this is the preview.
6. Plain R^2 rises from 0.002 to 0.077, because five extra indicator columns always let the model fit the sample better. Adjusted R^2 falls, from -0.019 to -0.052. Nothing about region matters; the data are pure noise, and only one of the two statistics says so.

title: Practice Problems
section: What does this license you to claim?
text:
What does this license you to claim?
A housing model reports: price ~ sqft + bedrooms + age, with sqft = 142 (SE 11), bedrooms = -4{,}800 (SE 2,100), R^2 = 0.71, n=900.

“Each extra square foot adds $142 to the price.”
“Adding a bedroom reduces a home’s price by $4,800.”
“The model explains 71% of what determines house prices.”
What would you need to believe for 8 to be a claim about renovation?
The client asks for a price estimate for a specific 2,000 sq ft home. Which interval do you give them?








Discussion





7. Almost. It is an association among homes that match on bedrooms and age, and “adds” is causal language the data do not support. Say “associated with about $142 more, comparing homes of the same age and bedroom count”, and give the interval: 142 \pm 22.
8. The sign is real and it is a classic. Holding square footage fixed, more bedrooms means smaller rooms. The coefficient is answering “among homes of the same size, is it better to divide the space into more rooms?”—which is a sensible question and not the one the sentence asks.
9. No. R^2 is variance explained in this sample, and it depends on the spread of the predictors as much as on the model. See R^2, and What It Does Not Tell You.
10. That the homes differing in bedroom count are otherwise comparable in every way that affects price—including the ones not in the model, like layout quality and neighbourhood. Almost certainly false, which is why this is a description rather than a renovation recommendation.
11. A prediction interval, not a confidence interval. See Inference for a Fitted Model—the client is asking about one house, not about the average of all such houses.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Bring to class

Fit a model on your project data. One outcome, two or three predictors you can justify. Bring the coefficient table and one sentence per coefficient, written the careful way.
Find the omitted variable. For your own model, name a variable you did not measure that plausibly affects the outcome and correlates with a predictor. Say which direction it biases the coefficient.
Argue about this. “We should include every variable we have—more information can only help.” Work out what it costs, using More Than One Predictor and R^2, and say when the advice is actually right.

title: Model Checking
text:
What is here
Monday, November 9
Post your questions on any of these pages by Monday at 12:00 noon, the morning of class.
Last week you fitted a model and read its coefficients. This week asks whether it deserved to be believed.
lm() does not object to curved data, does not notice when the spread grows with the prediction, and does not know that one of your rows is a typo. It reports a standard error computed under assumptions it never checks. Checking them is the analyst’s job, and it is almost entirely visual—the failures live in the residuals, and no summary statistic reports them. The clearest demonstration in the part is a model with R^2 = 0.81 and p = 10^{-43} that is fitting a straight line to a parabola.
The last chapter is the one the term has been building towards. October answered the causal question with randomization. Most of the time you cannot randomize, and “what would license a causal claim anyway?” is the question your project and your job will actually put to you.

title: Model Checking
text:
Reading Residuals



The four assumptions, in order of how much they matter, and the one plot to always draw. A smile means the form is wrong; a funnel means the standard errors are. Plus why a check that is guaranteed to pass is not a check.








Leverage and Influence



Outlier, leverage and influence are three different things and only the third matters. One row in thirty-one halves a slope—hat value 0.61 against an average of 0.065, Cook’s distance 17.4 against a next-largest of 0.11—and the summary table says nothing.








When Predictors Overlap



Two near-duplicate predictors inflate a standard error sevenfold while R^2 moves by 0.0005. Collinearity damages coefficients, not predictions—which decides what you should do about it.








What Would License a Causal Claim



Confounder, mediator, collider: control for the first, usually not the second, never the third. Controlling for a mediator took a true effect of 6.17 to -0.09; controlling for a collider turned no relationship into -0.93 with p \approx 0. Then what you can honestly say when randomizing was never an option.








Practice Problems



Including a hospital study whose fourth control is the problem, and an author who reports that adding a variable “strengthened the result”.

title: Model Checking
section: The habit this week is aiming at
text:
The habit this week is aiming at
Fit the model, then try to break it. Draw the residuals. Compute Cook’s distance. Refit without the influential row. Refit with a different set of controls and look at the range.
A coefficient that survives all of that is worth reporting. One that has never been tested is a number your software produced, and the reader has no way to tell the difference unless you say.






Due this week



HW 6 is due at the start of class. And as always, post your questions on these pages by Monday noon—that afternoon’s session is built out of them.

title: Reading Residuals
text:
What the model assumes
lm() fits a line to anything. It does not object to curved data, it does not notice when the spread grows, and it reports a standard error computed under assumptions it never checks.
Checking them is your job, and it is almost entirely visual. The residuals are where the model tells you what it could not explain, and that is the only place the failures show.
Four things, in decreasing order of how much they matter.
The first three are checked by looking at residuals. The fourth barely matters for coefficients at any decent sample size, because of the central limit theorem —but it matters a great deal for prediction intervals, which describe individuals rather than averages.

title: Reading Residuals
text:
The relationship has the form you fitted. Linear in the predictors, or whatever you specified.
Constant variance. The spread of the errors does not depend on the fitted value.
Independent errors. The residual of one observation says nothing about another’s.
Roughly Normal errors. Least important, and the one everybody worries about most.

title: Reading Residuals
section: The one plot to always draw
text:
The one plot to always draw
Residuals against fitted values. If the model is adequate, it is a featureless cloud.








R^2 of 0.81 and a p-value of 10^{-43}. Every number in the summary looks excellent, and the model is wrong.








The residual plot is a smile. High at both ends, low in the middle—which is what a straight line through a curve always produces, and which no summary statistic reports.
A pattern in this plot means the model is missing something. A curve means the functional form is wrong; a funnel means the variance is not constant; a drift means something structural is unaccounted for.

title: Reading Residuals
text:
Non-constant variance








The fan is unmistakable in the residual plot and easy to miss in the data plot.
What it costs: the coefficient estimates stay unbiased, but the standard errors are wrong, so intervals and p-values are wrong. Inference for a Fitted Model measured it— the formula reported 0.1242 where the truth was 0.1463.
What to do: bootstrap the coefficient, use robust standard errors, or model the outcome on a scale where the variance is stable. Taking logs often does it, which is not a coincidence—positive skewed quantities are frequently log-normal, and on the log scale they behave.

title: Reading Residuals
text:
R’s four plots
plot(fit) gives the standard set. Two are worth your time, one is worth a glance, and one is worth knowing you can ignore.








Residuals vs Fitted — the plot above. Look for curvature and funnels.
Scale-Location — the same information with the sign removed, which makes a trend in spread easier to see. Rising means non-constant variance.
Normal Q-Q — residual quantiles against Normal ones. Deviations in the tails are common and mostly harmless for coefficients. Worry when it is severe and n is small, or when you intend to quote prediction intervals.
Residuals vs Leverage — the influence plot, which is the next chapter.

title: Reading Residuals
text:
Independence
There is no plot for this in the standard four, because the check depends on what could link your observations. Two habits cover most cases.
If the data have a time order, plot residuals against time. A drift or a run of same-signed residuals means serial correlation, and the standard errors are too small.
If observations are grouped—multiple rows per user, per school, per store—the independence assumption fails by design. This is the failure from September appearing in a model: n is the number of independent units, and the fit will happily treat 2,000 sessions from 200 users as 2,000.






 Exercise: does the fit have a problem?





Fit dist ~ speed on cars and return the correlation between the residuals and the fitted values.


















cor(resid(fit), fitted(fit))
Zero, to machine precision—and it is zero for every least-squares fit with an intercept, however wrong the model is. Least squares chooses the line that makes it so.
That is the point of the exercise. A correlation of zero here is not evidence of anything, and any check that is guaranteed to pass is not a check. Correlation measures linear association, and the two failures you are hunting— curvature and a funnel—are both invisible to it. Draw the plot.

title: Reading Residuals
text:
Summary

Linearity, constant variance and independence are checked by looking at residuals; Normality matters least, except for prediction intervals.
Residuals against fitted is the plot to always draw. A curve means the form is wrong; a funnel means the variance is not constant.
The curved example had R^2 = 0.81 and p = 10^{-43} with a completely wrong model. Summary statistics do not detect misspecification.
Non-constant variance leaves estimates unbiased and standard errors wrong. Bootstrap, use robust errors, or change scale.
Residuals summing to zero and being uncorrelated with the fit are forced, so they are never evidence.

Next: the observations that decide your coefficients by themselves.

title: Leverage and Influence
text:
One point, half the slope
Least squares minimizes squared error, so a point twice as far from the line counts four times as much. One observation can therefore decide a coefficient, and the summary table will not mention it.
Three words get used interchangeably and mean different things.
A point can be a wild outlier with no influence, and a point sitting almost on the line can have enormous influence. Only the third matters.
The slope falls from 2.09 to 1.03. One observation out of thirty-one halved the estimate.
Notice that the red point does not look absurd. Its y of 20 is inside the range of the other y values. What makes it dangerous is its x: sitting at 25 when everything else is under 10, it acts as a lever.

title: Leverage and Influence
text:
Leverage, measured
The hat value h_i measures how far observation i sits from the center of the predictor space. It runs from 1/n to 1, and averages p/n where p is the number of coefficients.








The point has a hat value of 0.613 where the average is 0.065—it alone accounts for 61% of the fit’s freedom.
The usual flag is h_i > 2p/n. Treat it as a prompt to look, not a verdict.

title: Leverage and Influence
text:
Influence: Cook’s distance
Leverage says a point could matter. Cook’s distance says whether it actually does, by measuring how much every fitted value moves when the point is dropped.








17.36 against a next-largest of 0.11. A common rule of thumb flags values above 1; this is seventeen times that, and the plot needs no rule at all—one spike, everything else at the floor.






What to do about an influential point





Not delete it. In order:

Check it is real. Influential points are disproportionately data-entry errors—a decimal misplaced, a sentinel value like -999 that survived cleaning, a unit mix-up.
If it is real, understand it. A genuine observation with high leverage is often the most informative row you have, and sometimes the finding itself.
Report the fit both ways. “With and without this observation the slope is 2.09 and 1.03” is an honest sentence, and far more useful than either number alone.

Silently dropping it and reporting one number is the thing not to do, because the reader cannot tell it happened.

title: Leverage and Influence
section: Why this is not just about outliers
text:
Why this is not just about outliers
The cars data have no dramatic point, and influence still varies:








Observation 49—a car at 24 mph stopping in 120 feet—has the largest influence, and it is a perfectly plausible measurement. Nothing needs doing about it. The point of looking is that you now know which row your slope depends on.






 Exercise: how much does one row matter?





Using cars, fit dist ~ speed, then refit without the single observation with the largest Cook’s distance. Return the change in the slope—the refit’s minus the original’s.


















```{r}
fit <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)
i   <- which.max(cooks.distance(fit))
coef(lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars[-i, ]))[2] - coef(fit)[2]
```
About -0.29: the slope moves from 3.932 to 3.640, a change of roughly 7%.
That is the reassuring outcome, and it is worth as much as the alarming one. The check is two lines, and the answer is either “no single row is running this” or “one row is, and you need to say so.”

title: Leverage and Influence
text:
Summary

Outlier, leverage and influence are three things. Only influence—unusual in x and off the line—changes your answer.
One point of thirty-one halved a slope, with a hat value of 0.613 against an average of 0.065 and a Cook’s distance of 17.4 against a next-largest of 0.11.
Rules of thumb: h_i > 2p/n, Cook’s > 1. Both are prompts to look, not verdicts.
Do not delete influential points. Verify them, understand them, and report the fit both ways.
A quick influence check on a well-behaved dataset moved the slope by 7%. Knowing that is the point.

Next: what happens when two predictors are telling you the same thing.

title: When Predictors Overlap
text:
The symptom
A coefficient describes a comparison among cases that agree on the other predictors. If two predictors move together almost perfectly, there are barely any such cases, and the data cannot tell you what you asked.
The model does not refuse. It answers, with enormous standard errors, and the symptom is easy to misread as “the variable does not matter”.
The predictors correlate 0.989. Adding x2 leaves the estimate on x1 roughly where it was and inflates its standard error from 0.070 to 0.478—a factor of seven—so a coefficient that was overwhelmingly significant alone becomes non-significant beside its twin.
Nothing is broken. The data genuinely cannot separate two variables that are nearly the same variable.

title: When Predictors Overlap
text:
Fitted values are fine
The critical point, and the one that decides what to do:








R^2 moves from 0.7997 to 0.8002 and the residual error is unchanged.
Collinearity damages the coefficients, not the predictions. The model predicts as well as ever; it simply cannot apportion credit between two predictors that carry the same information. If you want prediction, ignore it. If you want to interpret a coefficient—which is what this course is about—it matters a great deal.

title: When Predictors Overlap
section: Measuring it: the variance inflation factor
text:
Measuring it: the variance inflation factor
\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R^2_j), where R^2_j comes from regressing predictor j on all the others. It is the factor by which the variance of that coefficient is inflated, so \sqrt{\text{VIF}} is the factor on the standard error.








A VIF of 47 predicts the standard error is 6.9 times larger than it would be with an uncorrelated predictor—which is exactly the inflation observed above.
Conventional flags are VIF above 5 or 10. As always, they are prompts.






How to recognize it without computing anything





Three signs, any of which should send you to look:

The overall model is highly significant, but no individual coefficient is.
A coefficient has a sign you know is wrong.
Adding or dropping one predictor swings another’s coefficient wildly.

The third is the most common in practice, and it is also the honest way to report the problem.

title: When Predictors Overlap
text:
What to do
Drop one. If two predictors mean nearly the same thing—height in inches and height in centimetres, revenue and revenue-per-day at fixed days—keep the one you can interpret.
Combine them. An average or an index of several correlated measures is often what you meant anyway. Principal components does this systematically, at the cost of interpretability, and is DATS 6103’s territory.
Accept it and say so. If both variables genuinely belong in the question, report that the data cannot separate them. “Advertising spend and store footfall are collinear here, so we can estimate their combined effect but not their individual contributions” is a real finding.
Do not drop the one with the larger p-value and present the result as though you had always intended that model. That is specification hunting and the reported uncertainty no longer means anything.






 Exercise: compute a VIF





Using mtcars, compute the VIF for disp in the model mpg ~ disp + hp + wt. Return a single number.


















```{r}
1 / (1 - summary(lm(disp ~ hp + wt, data = mtcars))$r.squared)
```
About 7.3, so \sqrt{7.3} \approx 2.7 times the standard error.
Heavy cars have large engines and large engines make horsepower, so the three predictors are largely the same information wearing different units. The model will still predict fuel economy well. What it cannot do is tell you whether economy is really about weight, displacement or power—and reporting the individual coefficients as though it could is the mistake.

title: When Predictors Overlap
text:
Summary

Collinearity means there are too few cases that differ on one predictor while agreeing on the others, so the comparison a coefficient describes is barely observed.
It inflates standard errors and leaves predictions alone: SE went from 0.070 to 0.478 while R^2 moved from 0.7997 to 0.8002.
\text{VIF} = 1/(1-R^2_j); the standard error is inflated by \sqrt{\text{VIF}}. A VIF of 47 gave the observed factor of 6.9.
Recognize it by a significant model with no significant coefficients, a wrong sign, or a coefficient that swings when another is added.
Drop, combine, or report that the data cannot separate them—but do not quietly keep the version that came out best.

Next: the chapter this whole part has been building towards.

title: What Would License a Causal Claim
text:
“Controlling for” is not “intervening”
In October the answer was randomization, and it was a good answer. Most of the time you cannot randomize—the data already exist, the intervention is impossible, unethical, or was decided years ago—and the question is still causal.
This chapter is about what you can say then. It is the most useful hour in the course and the one with the fewest formulas.
Adding a variable to a regression asks: among cases that agree on this variable, how do outcomes differ? That is a comparison. Intervening asks: if we changed this, what would happen? That is a different question, and a coefficient answers the first while people quote it as the second.
The gap between them is entirely a question of which variables you controlled for, and whether that set was the right one. There is no way to check this from the data. It is an argument about the world, made before fitting, and the regression cannot help you make it.
crumbs: What Would License a Causal Claim

title: What Would License a Causal Claim
section: Three roles a third variable can play
text:
Three roles a third variable can play
This is the practical content of the chapter. A variable you might add to a model is one of three things, and adding it is right for one, wrong for another, and catastrophic for the third.

Confounder — a common cause. Control for it.
A confounder causes both the predictor and the outcome, so it creates an association that is not causal. More Than One Predictor showed it: skill drove both study hours and score, and the coefficient on hours read 8.55 against a truth of 1.5 until skill was added.
Adding a confounder removes bias. This is the case everyone knows, and it is why “control for more things” feels like it must be safer.


Mediator — on the causal path. Usually do not control for it.
If the treatment works through the variable, controlling for it removes the very effect you were trying to measure.








The total effect is 6.17. Control for the mediator and it becomes -0.09—the treatment appears to do nothing, because you asked what does the treatment do among people whose mediator is the same, and the answer is correctly nothing.
Both numbers are right. They answer different questions, and only one of them is “does this treatment work”.


Collider — a common effect. Never control for it.
The dangerous one, because it runs opposite to intuition: controlling for a variable can create an association that does not exist.








x and y are independent by construction. The plain regression correctly finds nothing: coefficient -0.02, p = 0.53.
Add z, and the coefficient becomes -0.93 with a p-value of essentially zero. A strong, highly significant, entirely fictitious relationship, created by adding a control.
The intuition: among cases with the same z, a high x must be offset by a low y, because z is their sum. Conditioning on the total manufactures a negative relationship between the parts.






Why “control for everything” is bad advice





It is right for confounders, destroys the effect for mediators, and invents effects for colliders. Since the data cannot tell you which role a variable plays, throwing every available variable into a model is not caution—it is three different mistakes with equal probability.
The set of variables to control for follows from a claim about what causes what. That claim comes from you, and it should be written down before the model is fitted.
crumbs: What Would License a Causal Claim

title: What Would License a Causal Claim
section: What you can honestly say without an experiment
text:
What you can honestly say without an experiment
Four things, in ascending order of strength.
1. Describe the association, and say it is one. “Among homes of the same age and size, an extra bedroom is associated with $4,800 less.” Always available, always defensible, and often all anyone needed.
2. Name what would have to be true. “This is a causal estimate if the only things affecting both X and Y are the ones I controlled for.” Stating the condition lets a reader disagree with something specific instead of with your conclusion.
3. Name the most likely violation, and sign it. “The obvious omitted variable is prior interest, which would push this coefficient up—so 8.5 is probably an overestimate, and the true effect is smaller.” You usually cannot quantify the bias. You can nearly always say which direction it runs, and that is far more useful than silence.
4. Show the conclusion survives disturbance. Refit with different plausible control sets and report the range. If the coefficient sits between 1.2 and 1.6 across every sensible specification, that is worth much more than one number from one model—and if it swings from -2 to +5, you have learned the important thing.








The estimate ranges from 8.59 to 1.74 depending on what is controlled for. That spread is the finding: without knowing whether skill belongs in the model, the data support anything from a modest effect to an enormous one.






 Exercise: should it go in the model?





You want the effect of a job-training program on earnings. You have data on motivation before applying, hours of training completed, and whether the person was hired within six months.
Assign the letter, for example answer <- "A".















B.
Motivation causes both enrollment and earnings: a confounder, and it belongs in the model.
Hours completed is how the program works: a mediator. Controlling for it asks what the program does among people who completed the same number of hours, and the honest answer is very little.
Being hired is caused by training and by earning potential: a collider. Conditioning on it creates an association between the two, in the manufactured way the simulation above showed.
A is the instinct this chapter exists to break. D is defeatist—adjustment cannot deliver what randomization does, but “describe the association and name what would have to be true” is a real and useful output.
crumbs: What Would License a Causal Claim

title: What Would License a Causal Claim
text:
Summary

Controlling for is not intervening. A coefficient compares cases; an intervention changes them, and only an argument about the world connects the two.
A third variable is a confounder (control for it), a mediator (usually do not), or a collider (never). The data cannot tell you which.
Controlling for a mediator took a true effect of 6.17 down to -0.09. Controlling for a collider turned no relationship into -0.93 with p \approx 0.
“Control for everything” is three mistakes at once, and the set of controls has to be argued before the model is fitted.
Without an experiment you can still: describe the association honestly, state the assumption that would make it causal, sign the likely bias, and show the range across specifications.

Next: the practice problems, and then a term of applying all of it to your own data.
crumbs: What Would License a Causal Claim

title: Practice Problems
text:
Predict the output
Not graded, not auto-checked. Bring your answers and your disagreements.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Discussion





1. The first is zero by construction and tells you nothing. The second— absolute residual against fitted—is a crude test for a funnel and is not forced, so it can actually detect something.
2. The standard error inflates sevenfold while R^2 barely moves. Collinearity damages coefficients, not predictions.
3. From -0.02 to -0.93. The “control” is a collider, and adding it invented a strong relationship between two independent variables.

title: Practice Problems
section: This runs and is still wrong
text:
This runs and is still wrong































Discussion





4. R^2 = 0.81, p = 10^{-43}, and the residual plot is a smile. Every number endorses a model that has the wrong functional form. Only the plot detects it.
5. One mistyped row at 60 mph with a stopping distance of 40 feet flips the conclusion, and Cook’s distance flags it immediately. The right response is to check the row, not to report the p-value.
6. Model A gives 6.17, model B gives -0.09. B controls for the mediator, so it is asking what the program does among people it already worked on. “No effect” is a claim about model B that nobody would make if they had written down what the model was comparing.

title: Practice Problems
section: What does this license you to claim?
text:
What does this license you to claim?
A hospital study reports: patients who received the new protocol had 2.1 fewer days in hospital, controlling for age, sex, comorbidity score, and whether the patient was discharged to home care.

“The protocol reduces stay by 2.1 days.”
Which of the four controls worries you, and why?
What would you need to believe for this to be causal?
The lead author adds: “we also controlled for total treatment cost, which strengthened the result.” What do you say?
How would you report this honestly in one sentence?








Discussion





7. No. It is an association among patients alike on four variables, and “reduces” is causal language.
8. Discharge to home care is plausibly a consequence of a shorter, better recovery—a mediator, or worse, a collider if it is also driven by things that affect length of stay. Age, sex and comorbidity are ordinary confounders and belong.
9. That every common cause of receiving the protocol and of length of stay is among the controls. Severity at admission almost certainly is not, and sicker patients plausibly got the older protocol—which would make 2.1 an overestimate.
10. Cost is downstream of length of stay: longer stays cost more. It is a collider or a mediator depending on the diagram, and either way “it strengthened the result” is a warning sign rather than support. A control that improves your finding deserves more scrutiny than one that weakens it.
11. “Among patients of similar age, sex and comorbidity, the new protocol was associated with 2.1 fewer days (95% CI …). This is causal only if severity at admission did not influence which protocol was used; if sicker patients received the old one, the true effect is smaller than 2.1.”

title: Practice Problems
text:
Bring to class

Break your own model. Take the model you fitted for Nov 2. Draw residuals against fitted, compute Cook’s distance, and compute a VIF for each predictor. Bring whichever plot is worst and be ready to say what it means.
Draw the diagram. For your project’s main relationship, write down what causes what—three or four variables is enough. Then mark each as confounder, mediator or collider relative to your question, and say which ones belong in the model. Bring the diagram, not the model.
Argue about this. “With enough controls, an observational study is as good as an experiment.” Use the collider simulation and the specification range from What Would License a Causal Claim, and decide what the strongest honest version of that sentence would be.

title: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests
text:
What is here
Monday, November 30
Post your questions on any of these pages by Monday at 12:00 noon, the morning of class.
The Standard Error of a Mean answered one question completely: how much would a sample mean move if you collected the data again? The answer was \sigma/\sqrt{n}, it came out of four lines of algebra, and everything since has been built on it. Confidence intervals, the denominator of every test statistic, the standard error printed beside every regression coefficient—all of it is that one derivation, reused.
Now look at the questions your project actually asks.
What is the median household income, give or take? How strongly are these two variables correlated, give or take? What is the 90th percentile of response time, and could it plausibly be under two seconds? Is the ratio of these two rates really 1.4, or could it be 1.0?
Not one of those is a mean, and \sigma/\sqrt{n} has nothing to say about any of them. The formula toolkit you have been handed covers a narrow strip of the questions people ask, and the strip is narrow for a historical reason: those are the cases somebody could do the algebra for, in an era when the alternative was a room full of human computers.
This week the alternative stops being expensive.
The substitution costs you something, and Why Resample is honest about what. But what it buys is large: the machinery no longer cares what statistic you chose. Median, correlation, 90th percentile, ratio of two trimmed means, the gap between two groups’ interquartile ranges—the code is the same four lines every time, and you never have to find out whether a formula exists.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests
text:
Why Resample



The gap, stated plainly. Why the toolkit only covers means, and a case where the formula does not exist at all. Then a case where the formula exists and is simply wrong—a t-interval at n = 8 on skewed data that covers the truth 73% of the time while claiming 95%. The plug-in idea, and the limit of it: the bootstrap quantifies sampling variability and cannot repair a biased sample.








The Bootstrap



The algorithm in four lines, then the trust-building move: bootstrap a mean and check the answer against s/\sqrt{n} from The Standard Error of a Mean. They agree. Then a median and a correlation, where no formula was available. Percentile intervals, how many resamples are enough, why the replacement is the whole mechanism—and the two places the bootstrap genuinely breaks.








Permutation Tests



The null hypothesis as a physical procedure: if the labels carry no information, shuffling them should change nothing—so shuffle them 10,000 times and look. A two-group comparison end to end, the p-value as a tail proportion, and the same data run through a t-test for comparison. If p-values felt mystical when you met them, this is the chapter where they stop being.








Inference for a Fitted Model



The two intervals people confuse—one for the average outcome at a given x, one for the next observation—and why only one of them shrinks to nothing. Then bootstrapping a regression coefficient, and a case where the formula’s standard error is fifteen percent too small while the output looks perfectly ordinary.








Practice Problems



Predict-before-you-run, resampling code that runs cleanly and answers a different question from the one asked, and judgment calls—including one where the bootstrap is the wrong tool and the right answer is to say so.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests
text:
How to read this week
Two procedures, and they are easy to confuse. Both call sample() in a replicate() loop, and on screen they look almost identical. They answer opposite questions:









Bootstrap
Permutation test




Resamples
observations, with replacement
labels, without replacement


Keeps fixed
the labels attached to each observation
the observations themselves


Distribution is centered at
roughly your observed statistic
zero—no effect


Answers
how much would my estimate move?
could this have happened by chance alone?


Produces
a standard error, a confidence interval
a p-value



If you can state which row you are in before you write the loop, you will not write the wrong loop. Every year some fraction of the class bootstraps when they meant to permute, gets a plausible-looking number, and reports it.
Predict first, as always. When The Bootstrap asks what happens if you drop replace = TRUE, write down your prediction before running the cell. That particular one is worth being wrong about once.






Due this week
