HW 7 is due at the start of class, and Monday’s lab is Bootstrapping your own project’s statistic—so come with a statistic in mind from your project data, ideally one that is not a mean. A median, a correlation, a percentile, a ratio, a difference between two groups. If the lab is going to be useful to you, bring the thing you actually need an interval for.
Post your reading questions by Monday noon.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Why Resample
text:
A number the mean cannot describe
Here is the honest position you are in after eleven weeks.
You can put a give-or-take on a mean. You can put one on a difference of two means, which is a mean in disguise. You can put one on a proportion, which is the mean of a column of zeros and ones. And in the modeling weeks you get standard errors for regression coefficients, which are weighted means of the outcome.
That is the list.
It is not a coincidence that the list is short. Every item on it is a mean, because the machinery of The Standard Error of a Mean—\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n—is a theorem about sums, and the central limit theorem that followed is a theorem about sums too. Sums are what the mathematics could reach.
The questions people ask are not confined to that list, and this chapter is about what happens when your question walks off the edge of it.
A small charity has 30 donations from its first campaign, in dollars.
Most gifts are between $10 and $45. A few are much larger, and one is $348.70. This is the shape almost every money variable has, and it is why Describing a Single Variable spent time on skew.
The mean is $57.19 and the median is $26.65. They differ by more than a factor of two, and only one of them describes a donor:
Eight of the thirty donors—27%—gave more than the average donation. If the director asks what does a typical supporter give?, the answer is $26.65 and it is not close. Reporting $57.19 would have the fundraising team writing appeals aimed at a donor who barely exists.
So you report the median. And then the director, who has been well trained, asks the Describing a Single Variable question:
You have nothing. There is no median row in the standard error table. What you can do is the thing you were taught, which is the wrong thing:
An interval from $28.09 to $86.30—for the mean, which is not the number you decided to report, and which is nearly useless anyway: drop the single $348.70 gift and s falls from 77.95 to 56.16, so a quarter of the width of that interval is one donor.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Why Resample
text:
If we ran the campaign again with 30 different donors, how different would that $26.65 be?










Two separate failures, and this chapter fixes both




The statistic you want has no formula. Median, correlation, 90th percentile, ratio of two rates, difference of two medians, interquartile range—no standard error in your toolkit, and for several of them no simple one exists at all.
Where a formula does exist, its assumptions can fail. The t-interval above is entitled to its 95% only under conditions this sample plainly does not meet. The next section measures exactly how badly.




“But surely there is a formula for the median”
There is, and looking at it is instructive. For a large sample from a population with density f, the standard error of the sample median is approximately
\operatorname{SE}(\text{median}) \approx \frac{1}{2f(m)\sqrt{n}}
where m is the population median and f(m) is the height of the population density at that point. Note what the formula needs: not the population variance, which you can estimate easily, but the population density at a single point, which you cannot. Estimating a density well is a harder problem than the one you started with, and it requires choices—bandwidths, kernels—that change the answer.
So the formula exists on paper and dissolves in your hands. That is the normal situation off the edge of the list, and it is worth knowing that the reason we teach means is not that means are the most useful summary. It is that means are the ones somebody could do the algebra for.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Why Resample
section: Where the formula exists and is still wrong
text:
Where the formula exists and is still wrong
Take the second failure on its own, because it is the one people do not expect.
Forget medians. Suppose you want the mean, the formula does apply, and you build a t-interval exactly as taught. How often does it actually contain the truth?
We can check, because we can be the population. Draw a sample of 8 from a skewed population whose true mean we know, build the 95% t-interval, and ask whether the truth is inside. Then do that 4,000 times and count.








72.9%. The procedure advertises 95% and delivers 73%. More than a quarter of the intervals miss, and a reader who took the interval at face value would be wrong about four times as often as they were told to expect.
This is not a bug in R and it is not a bad seed. Run the identical code on a Normal population:








94.75%, which is 95% to within simulation noise. The formula is fine. The formula’s assumptions were fine in the second case and not in the first, and nothing in the output of t.test() will ever tell you which case you are in.






Warning



This is what “the assumptions failed” means in practice. Not an error message. Not a warning. A number, printed confidently, whose stated properties are false.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Why Resample
text:
What we actually need
Step back from formulas and ask what the question is.
You have a statistic—call it \hat\theta, whether that is a mean, a median, a correlation, or anything else. It was computed from one sample. A different sample would have given a different value. The distribution of those values, across all the samples you might have drawn, is the sampling distribution, and every give-or-take in statistics is a summary of it: its spread is a standard error, its middle 95% is a confidence interval.
The Standard Error of a Mean obtained that distribution directly, by brute force:
```{r}
sample_means <- replicate(5000, mean(rnorm(n, mean = 100, sd = sigma)))
sd(sample_means)
```
Draw a fresh sample from the population, compute the statistic, repeat 5,000 times, look at the spread. No algebra, no assumptions, and it works for any statistic—swap mean for median and the code still runs:








There it is. The sampling distribution of the median of 30 donations sits at $37.82, against a true population median of $36.60, with a spread of $9.41—so a standard error for a median, obtained with no theory whatsoever.
And it is useless, because of one line: rlnorm(30, meanlog = 3.6, sdlog = 1.1). That line draws a fresh sample from the population. In this chapter we could write it because we invented the population. In your project you cannot. You have 30 donations and there is no going back to the well.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Why Resample
text:
The substitution
Here is the whole of confidence intervals.






The plug-in idea



We need to draw samples from the population, and we cannot.
But we have 30 observations that came from that population, and they are the only information about it in existence. So we use them as a stand-in: we treat the sample as though it were the population, and draw from that.
Drawing n observations from a pile of n observations, in a way that lets the same one come up more than once, is exactly sampling with replacement.


Compare the two lines directly:




The population version (The Standard Error of a Mean, impossible in practice)
The bootstrap version (available now)




Draw a sample
rlnorm(30, 3.6, 1.1)
sample(donation, 30, replace = TRUE)


Compute the statistic
median(...)
median(...)


Repeat
replicate(4000, ...)
replicate(4000, ...)


Read off the spread
sd(...)
sd(...)



One cell changed. Everything else is identical—and the one that changed is the one you could not run.
















So the charity’s answer is: the typical gift is about $27, and a repeat campaign of the same size would plausibly put that figure anywhere between $19 and $41. That is an honest sentence about a median, produced with no formula, no distributional assumption, and four lines of base R.
The details—why this works, how far to trust it, and where it fails—are 6.2. What matters here is that you can see where the idea came from: it is the The Standard Error of a Mean simulation with the one impossible step replaced by the best available substitute.






The name is Bradley Efron’s, from 1979, and it is a joke about pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps—getting something from apparently nothing. The something is not free, and the next section is the bill.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Why Resample
section: What the substitution buys, and what it does not
text:
What the substitution buys, and what it does not
The substitution is sample for population. Everything the bootstrap tells you is conditional on that swap being reasonable.
What you get. If your sample was drawn fairly from the population you care about, the empirical distribution of your data is a genuinely good stand-in for the population distribution, and it gets better as n grows. The variability you observe across resamples then really does approximate the variability you would see across fresh samples. That is a theorem, and it is why the bootstrap is not a trick.
What you do not get. Anything about whether you sampled the right people.
Watch this fail. A campus study advertises for volunteers, and—as volunteers do—only people at the higher end of the scale bother to respond.








The population mean is 100.04. The survey mean is 117.07—wrong by 17 points, and no analysis of these 60 numbers can know that.
Now bootstrap it, carefully and correctly:
















A 95% interval of (115.11, 119.16), four points wide, beautifully tight, and it does not contain the true mean of 100. It never will. Every resample is drawn from the same 60 volunteers, so every resample inherits their tilt, and running 100,000 resamples instead of 10,000 would narrow the interval further while leaving it centered on the wrong number.






The sentence to memorize



The bootstrap quantifies sampling variability. It does not detect, correct, or warn you about bias.
A tight bootstrap interval says your number is reproducible. It says nothing about whether your number is right.


This should feel familiar. It is the same warning attached to \sigma/\sqrt{n} in The Standard Error of a Mean—two million self-selected respondents give a gorgeous standard error and can be wrong by twenty points—and it is the same warning as the Aug 31 session on where the data came from. Selection bias, survivorship bias, and non-response are properties of how the rows got into your file. Resampling those rows cannot undo them, because the resampling never leaves the file.
So the Aug 31 questions do not go away this week; they get more important, not less. Who is missing from this sample? is the question no amount of computation answers, and a narrow interval around a biased estimate is worse than a wide one, because it is more persuasive.






 A narrow interval around the wrong number







A campus wellness study advertises on Instagram and collects 400 responses. The sample mean sleep duration is 7.6 hours. A bootstrap with 10,000 resamples gives a 95% percentile interval of (7.5, 7.7).
A colleague concludes: “The interval is narrow, so we can be confident the average student sleeps about 7.6 hours.”
What is wrong with that reasoning?

Nothing—the bootstrap makes no distributional assumptions, so the interval is valid whatever the data.The interval should have been computed with more resamples; 10,000 is too few for n = 400.The bootstrap resamples the 400 responses that were collected, so it describes how much the estimate would move under re-sampling of the same kind. If students who volunteer on Instagram sleep differently from students who do not, every resample inherits that tilt and the interval is narrow around the wrong number.The bootstrap is only valid for a mean, so the interval does not apply to sleep duration.



The bootstrap treats your sample as a stand-in for the population and then draws from it. Everything it tells you is downstream of that substitution.
If the substitution is good—if your 400 responses look like the population in the ways that matter—then the spread of the bootstrap distribution is a genuine estimate of how much your statistic would move if you collected the data again, and the percentile interval means what you want it to mean.
If the substitution is bad, the bootstrap does not notice. It cannot: the 400 responses are all the information it is given. A self-selected sample that runs half an hour high will produce resamples that all run half an hour high, and the interval will be tight around 7.6 when the truth is 7.1.






Important



The bootstrap quantifies sampling variability. It does not detect, correct, or warn you about bias.


This is the same lesson as \sigma/\sqrt{n} from Week 5, in new clothes. A survey of two million self-selected respondents has a beautiful standard error and can be wrong by twenty points. Narrowness is a statement about reproducibility, not about truth—and a narrow interval around a biased estimate is worse than a wide one, because it is more persuasive.
The remedy is never more resampling. It is the Aug 31 question: where did this data come from, and who is missing from it?
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Why Resample
text:
Exercises

Exercise: who is above average?















mean(donation > mean(donation))
= 8/30 = 0.2667. Equivalently sum(donation > mean(donation)) / length(donation).



Exercise: measure the coverage yourself
The chapter claimed a 95% t-interval covers only about 73% of the time on small skewed samples. Do not take it on faith—the function below runs one such study and reports whether its interval caught the truth.















```{r}
mean(replicate(4000, one_study()))
```
About 0.73. The gap between the claimed 0.95 and the delivered 0.73 is the entire motivation for this week.



Exercise: make the substitution
This is the move the whole week rests on. In 6.1 we wanted the sampling distribution of the median and could not draw fresh samples from the population. Do it with the sample instead.















```{r}
sd(replicate(4000, median(sample(donation, 30, replace = TRUE))))
```
About 5.3. Writing length(donation) in place of the hard-coded 30 is the better habit—the resample must be the same size as the original sample, and hard-coding that number is how it silently stops being true.



Exercise: what is this interval entitled to say?















answer <- "B"
The interval quantifies variability under repetition of this recruitment procedure. Repeating a tilted procedure gives a tilted answer every time, and tightly.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Why Resample
text:
Summary

The standard error machinery of The Standard Error of a Mean covers means and things that are means in disguise—proportions, differences of means, regression coefficients. Medians, correlations, percentiles, and ratios are outside it.
Formulas for those statistics either do not exist or need quantities you cannot estimate—the median’s standard error needs the population density at the median.
Where a formula does exist, its assumptions can fail silently. A 95% t-interval at n = 8 on a skewed population covered the truth 72.9% of the time; the same code on a Normal population covered 94.75%. Nothing in the output distinguishes the two cases.
What every give-or-take needs is the sampling distribution of the statistic. The Standard Error of a Mean built it by drawing many samples from a known population. You have one sample and no population.
The substitution: treat the sample as a stand-in for the population and draw from it—which is sampling with replacement, n at a time. One line of the The Standard Error of a Mean simulation changes; the rest is identical.
It works for any statistic, because nothing in the loop depends on which statistic you chose.
It quantifies sampling variability and nothing else. A bootstrap of a self-selected sample gave a 95% interval of (115.11, 119.16) around a true mean of 100. Narrow, reproducible, and wrong. Aug 31’s question—who is missing from this data?—is not answerable by resampling.

Next: the algorithm in full, checked against a case where we already know the right answer.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
text:
The algorithm
Why Resample argued for the substitution. This chapter does it properly: the algorithm, a check against a case where we already know the answer, two statistics no formula would have given us, and the places where the whole thing falls over.
Three details of step 1 matter and are worth stating before anything else runs.
The resample is the same size as the original sample, n. Not 1,000, not n/2. The bootstrap is imitating the act of collecting a sample of size n, and the width of a sampling distribution depends on n. Change the resample size and you are estimating the standard error of a study you did not run.
With replacement. Without it, drawing n from n just reorders the data and nothing varies at all. There is a section on this below, because it is the single most common bug in bootstrap code and it fails silently.
Whatever statistic is. Nothing in the loop knows or cares. That is the entire point of the week.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
text:
The bootstrap, in four steps



You have a sample x_1, \ldots, x_n and a statistic \hat\theta computed from it.

Draw n observations from your sample with replacement. Call it a resample.
Compute the statistic on the resample.
Repeat steps 1–2 B times, collecting B values \hat\theta^*_1, \ldots, \hat\theta^*_B.
The spread of those B values estimates the spread of the sampling distribution of \hat\theta.

In R, that is one line:
```{r}
boot <- replicate(B, statistic(sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE)))
```
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
text:
One resample, looked at closely
Forty-eight patients’ waiting times at a walk-in clinic, in minutes:
















Mean 11.45 minutes, and because this is a mean we already have its standard error from The Standard Error of a Mean: s/\sqrt{n} = 0.4714. Hold on to that number; it is the answer key.
Now draw one resample and look at it:
















Read that resample. 9.7 appears four times, 11.5 five times, and a substantial fraction of the original values do not appear at all—only 25 of the 48 distinct values made it in. The resample is not a copy of the data. It is the same data with the weights jostled, and its mean came out 11.38 rather than 11.45.
That jostling is the mechanism. Each observation is included a random number of times, so each resample is a slightly different “study”, and the variation across resamples stands in for the variation across studies.
How much of the data shows up in a typical resample?








About 63.6%, and not by accident. Any particular observation is missed on a single draw with probability 1 - 1/n, so it is missed by all n draws with probability (1-1/n)^n, which tends to e^{-1} \approx 0.368. So the expected fraction included is 1 - (1-1/n)^n \to 1 - 1/e = 0.632, essentially regardless of n. Roughly a third of your data sits out every resample, and that is by design.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
text:
Does it actually work?
Here is the move that should earn the bootstrap your trust, and it is worth doing before you use the method on anything you care about.
We are about to bootstrap a mean—a statistic whose standard error we already know from The Standard Error of a Mean. If the bootstrap is sound, it must reproduce s/\sqrt{n}. If it does not, nothing else it tells us is worth reading.








0.4634 against 0.4714, a ratio of 0.983. Two completely different routes to the same number: one is four lines of algebra about variances of sums, the other is a computer shuffling a vector ten thousand times and never touching a formula.






The 1.7% gap is not simulation noise—it is systematic and it is explicable. The bootstrap resamples from the empirical distribution, whose variance is \frac{n-1}{n}s^2 rather than s^2, so the bootstrap SE targets \sqrt{(n-1)/n}\cdot s/\sqrt n = 0.4665, about 1% below the formula. At n = 48 that is invisible in practice; at n = 6 it is not, which is one reason small samples appear in the failure list below.



Here is the bootstrap distribution:








Compare it, mentally, with the histograms in The Standard Error of a Mean. It is the same picture: a roughly Normal pile of statistic-values, centered on the estimate, whose width is the standard error. The difference is that 5.3 built it by going back to the population 5,000 times and this one never left the 48 observations.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
text:
The percentile interval
Once you have B bootstrapped values, an interval requires no further theory: take the middle 95% of them.








That is the percentile interval: (10.535, 12.354). Against the t-interval for the same data:








(10.502, 12.398). The two agree to within about four hundredths of a minute—two and a half seconds—on an interval nearly two minutes wide.
They differ slightly, and in a predictable direction: the bootstrap interval is a touch narrower, because the t-interval multiplies by t_{47,0.975} = 2.011 to account for having estimated \sigma from the data, while the percentile interval reads its endpoints off the resamples and inherits the same \sqrt{(n-1)/n} shrinkage noted above. At n = 48 that is a rounding error. At n = 10 it is not, and the t-interval is the safer choice whenever its assumptions hold.






Where both apply, use the formula. The bootstrap is not a replacement for t-intervals on well-behaved means; it is what you reach for when there is no formula, or when you have reason to believe the formula’s assumptions are false. Agreement on the easy cases is what licenses you to trust it on the hard ones.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
section: A median, where nothing else was available
text:
A median, where nothing else was available
Back to the 30 donations from Why Resample, and the question the director actually asked.
















A 95% interval of ($18.85, $40.85) for the median gift. Notice something the formula approach could never have produced:








The interval reaches $7.80 below the estimate and $14.20 above it. It is asymmetric, and it should be—the population is right-skewed, so the median of a resample can wander further up than down. Any interval of the form “estimate \pm 2\,\text{SE}” is symmetric by construction and would have got this wrong in both directions at once.
Look at the distribution and you can see why an interval is the right output here and a standard error alone is not:








It is lumpy. The median of 30 numbers is always the average of the 15th and 16th order statistics, so it can only take a limited set of values—the 10,000 resamples produced 99 distinct medians and no others. That granularity is real, not an artifact, and it is one more thing a smooth formula would have concealed.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
section: A correlation, and the trap in it
text:
A correlation, and the trap in it
45 students’ study hours and exam scores:








r = 0.7666. How precise is that?
There is a formula—Fisher’s z transformation, which cor.test() uses—and it requires the pair (x, y) to be bivariate Normal, an assumption almost nobody checks and which fails routinely for bounded scores and skewed predictors. Bootstrap it instead.
The trap: a correlation is a property of pairs. If you resample hours and score independently you destroy the pairing and measure the correlation of unrelated columns, which is zero by construction. So resample the row indices and carry both columns along:
















A 95% interval of (0.651, 0.856). And the formula’s answer, for comparison:








(0.610, 0.865). The same story—both say “strong, and pinned down to about \pm 0.1”—with the bootstrap interval slightly narrower on the low side. Two methods, one assumption-laden and one not, landing in the same place is the outcome you want to see, and when they disagree markedly you have learned something worth chasing.






Resample rows, not columns



Whenever your statistic involves more than one variable—a correlation, a regression slope, a difference of group means, a ratio of two totals—resample observations, not each column separately. The unit you resample must be the unit that was independently sampled in the first place.
This is the single most common conceptual error in student bootstrap code, and it does not throw an error. It quietly returns the sampling distribution of a statistic computed on data with the relationship torn out of it.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
text:
How many resamples?
B is not n, and confusing the two is the second most common error.
n is fixed by your data and determines how wide the bootstrap distribution is—that is the thing you are trying to measure. B is chosen by you and determines how precisely you have measured it. Raising B costs seconds and buys you a stabler answer to the same question; it does not buy you a better study.
Watch. Five independent runs of the same bootstrap at B = 200 and at B = 20{,}000, each reporting the upper endpoint of the 95% interval:












run 1
run 2
run 3
run 4
run 5
spread




B = 200
12.376
12.315
12.353
12.380
12.250
0.130


B = 20{,}000
12.354
12.352
12.350
12.363
12.348
0.015



Both rows sit at about 12.35, which is the honest answer given these 48 observations. The top row wobbles by 0.13 depending on nothing but the random seed; the bottom row wobbles by 0.015. That is the 1/\sqrt{B} from The Standard Error of a Mean again—a hundredfold increase in B divides the Monte Carlo error by ten.






Rules of thumb




B = 1{,}000 is plenty for a standard error, which is a summary of the bulk of the distribution.
B = 10{,}000 for a 95% interval, whose endpoints depend on the sparse tails and are noisier.
Report B alongside the interval, and use set.seed() so the number in your report is the number a reader reproduces.
If someone asks you to narrow an interval, more resamples is never the answer. More data is.









 Turning up B







You have n = 40 observations and you run a bootstrap with B = 1{,}000 resamples, getting a 95% percentile interval of width 3.2. Your colleague suggests raising B to 100,000.
What will that change?

The interval will get narrower, because more resamples means more information about the population.The interval will get wider, because more resamples reach further into the tails.The interval will stay about 3.2 wide, but its endpoints will stop wobbling from run to run. B controls how precisely you have measured the bootstrap distribution; n controls how wide that distribution is.Nothing at all—the percentile interval is a deterministic function of the data.



There are two sources of randomness here, and keeping them apart is the point of the question.
The sample size n sets how much the statistic really would move if the study were repeated. That is the quantity you are trying to estimate, and it is fixed the moment your data is collected. No amount of resampling improves it.
The number of resamples B sets how well you have measured that quantity. Each resample is one draw from the bootstrap distribution, and, as in Week 5, the Monte Carlo error in any summary of those draws falls like 1/\sqrt{B}.
So raising B from 1,000 to 100,000 divides the run-to-run wobble in the endpoints by ten, and leaves the width essentially where it was. If you want a narrower interval you need more data, not more resamples.
A practical rule: B = 1{,}000 is enough for a standard error, and B = 10{,}000 is comfortable for a 95% interval, whose endpoints depend on the sparse tails of the distribution and so are noisier than its middle. Resamples are cheap. Observations are not.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
section: Why the replacement is the whole mechanism
text:
Why the replacement is the whole mechanism
Predict this before you run it. The only change is replace = FALSE.








Exactly zero, and one distinct value. Drawing 48 items from a pile of 48 without replacement returns all 48 items in a new order. The mean does not look at order. So all 1,000 “resamples” are the same number, their standard deviation is 0, and the code cheerfully reports that your estimate has no uncertainty whatsoever.
No error. No warning. A perfectly formatted zero.






The check that catches it



A bootstrap standard error of exactly 0 is always a bug. So is one that is absurdly small compared with s/\sqrt{n}.
Better still, run the test from earlier in this chapter on your own data: bootstrap the mean and compare it with s/\sqrt{n}. If those two disagree badly, your bootstrap code is wrong, and you have found out before you trusted it with the statistic you actually care about.








 The missing argument







A student writes a bootstrap and forgets one argument:
boot <- replicate(2000, mean(sample(x, length(x), replace = FALSE)))
sd(boot)
x has 48 observations. What does sd(boot) print, and why?

Roughly s/\sqrt{48}, the same as with replace = TRUE—whether you sample with or without replacement makes little difference at this sample size.Exactly 0, because sampling 48 of 48 values without replacement can only reorder the data, and the mean does not care about order. All 2,000 “resamples” are the same 48 numbers.An error, because sample() cannot draw 48 values from a vector of length 48.Roughly s, the standard deviation of the data, because without replacement each resample is a fresh independent sample.



Drawing 48 items from a set of 48 without replacement is a shuffle. You get every observation back exactly once, in a new order, and every summary that ignores order—the mean, the median, the standard deviation, the correlation with a correspondingly shuffled partner—is bit-for-bit identical every time.
So the 2,000 replicates are 2,000 copies of one number, and their standard deviation is exactly 0. The code runs, prints something, and reports that your estimate has no uncertainty at all. That is the most dangerous kind of bug.
Replacement is not a technicality; it is the entire mechanism. With replacement, some observations appear twice or three times and others not at all—on average about 63% of the original values appear in any given resample. That reshuffling of weights is what makes one resample differ from the next, and the variation across resamples is the whole estimate.
The way to catch this in your own code is to check that your bootstrap standard error is not zero, and—better—to check the one case where you know the answer: the bootstrap SE of a mean should land close to s/\sqrt{n}.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
text:
Where the bootstrap breaks
It is a general method, not a universal one. Two failures are worth knowing by name, because both produce output that looks fine.

Very small n
The bootstrap can only ever redistribute the values you have. With five observations, there are only 126 distinct multisets of size 5 to draw, so the “sampling distribution” is a handful of points pretending to be a curve.
















10,000 resamples, 116 distinct answers. And the interval:








The percentile interval is (41.96, 54.62); the t-interval is (36.77, 57.35), more than 60% wider. The bootstrap interval is too narrow, and the reason is structural rather than random: the resamples can never contain a value more extreme than the largest observation, so at tiny n the tails of the true sampling distribution are simply unrepresented. There is nothing in the data to build them from.
Below roughly n = 20, be careful; below n = 10, the bootstrap is not rescuing you and you should say what your sample size is and let the reader discount accordingly.


Statistics that depend on the extremes
This one is more interesting, because it fails no matter how large n is.
Suppose you want the maximum of a population—the peak load a system has to survive, the largest claim an insurer might face. Forty observations from a population whose true maximum is 100:








The largest value we saw is 98. Bootstrap it:
















Look at what happened. The bootstrap distribution takes nine distinct values, 64% of them exactly 98, and the 95% interval is (90.8, 98.0). Its upper endpoint is the observed maximum—and it always will be, because no resample can contain a value larger than the largest observation. The true maximum of 100 lies outside the interval, and no increase in B or n will ever let the interval reach it.
That 64% is not a coincidence either: it is the 1 - (1-1/n)^n \approx 0.632 from earlier. The largest observation appears in about 63% of resamples, and whenever it does, the resample maximum is exactly it.






The general condition



The bootstrap works for statistics that are smooth functions of the data—means, medians, correlations, quantiles away from the edges, regression coefficients, ratios. Perturb the data slightly and the statistic moves slightly.
It fails for statistics that depend on the extreme order statistics: the maximum, the minimum, the range, the 99.9th percentile of 200 observations. For those, the empirical distribution is a bad stand-in exactly where it matters, because your sample has no information at all about the region beyond its own edge. Extreme-value theory exists for this reason.
It also fails when the observations are not independent—time series with autocorrelation, students clustered in classrooms, repeated measures on the same subject. Resampling individual rows destroys the dependence, and the resulting standard error is too small, in exactly the way Step 2 of the The Standard Error of a Mean derivation was too small. (There are block bootstraps for this; they resample contiguous chunks instead of rows.)
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
text:
The recipe
For anything you will meet this term:
```{r}
set.seed(6101)
B <- 10000
n <- length(x)

boot <- replicate(B, {
  i <- sample(n, n, replace = TRUE)   # resample ROW INDICES
  statistic(x[i])                     # ... or f(x[i], y[i]) for paired data
})

sd(boot)                              # standard error
quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))       # 95% percentile interval
```
Then, before you believe a word of it: run the same code with statistic set to mean and check it against sd(x)/sqrt(n).
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
text:
Exercises

Exercise: bootstrap a standard error















```{r}
sd(replicate(2000, mean(sample(wait, length(wait), replace = TRUE))))
```
About 0.46, against s/\sqrt{n} = 0.4714.



Exercise: break it on purpose
Predict the answer before you run this one. It is the same code as the last exercise with one argument changed.















```{r}
sd(replicate(2000, mean(sample(wait, 48, replace = FALSE))))
```
Exactly 0. Each “resample” is a permutation of the original 48 values, so every resample mean equals mean(wait).



Exercise: an interval for a statistic with no formula















```{r}
boot <- replicate(4000, quantile(sample(wait, length(wait), replace = TRUE), 0.9))
quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))
```
About (13.7, 17.2). The 90th percentile is far enough from the edge of the data that the bootstrap is comfortable here—unlike the maximum, which is at the edge.



Exercise: bootstrap a correlation















```{r}
sd(replicate(2000, {
  i <- sample(length(hours), length(hours), replace = TRUE)
  cor(hours[i], score[i])
}))
```
About 0.053. The single index vector i is what keeps each student’s hours attached to that same student’s score.



Exercise: two intervals, one dataset















answer <- "A"
Agreement where both methods are valid is the check that licenses the bootstrap elsewhere. Divergence is a prompt to ask which assumption is under strain.



Exercise: when not to bootstrap















answer <- "B"
The maximum is a function of the extreme order statistic, and the empirical distribution has nothing beyond its own largest value. Smooth statistics are fine; edge statistics are not.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: The Bootstrap
text:
Summary

The algorithm: resample n observations with replacement, compute the statistic, repeat B times, summarize the spread. One line of R, and indifferent to which statistic you chose.
About 63.2% of the original observations appear in a typical resample. That jostling of weights is the mechanism.
The trust check: bootstrapping a mean gave SE 0.4634 against the The Standard Error of a Mean formula’s 0.4714—agreement to within 2%, by two routes that share nothing. Run this check on your own data before believing anything else.
Percentile interval: the middle 95% of the bootstrap distribution. On the waiting times it matched the t-interval to within 2.5 seconds. On the donations it produced a properly asymmetric interval, ($18.85, $40.85) around a median of $26.65, which no \pm 2\,\text{SE} rule could give.
Resample rows, not columns. Resampling hours and score separately measures the wobble of a correlation of zero.
B is not n. n sets the width of the interval; B sets how precisely you have measured it, with Monte Carlo error falling like 1/\sqrt{B}. Use B = 10{,}000 for an interval and stop worrying about it.
Without replacement, everything collapses to a single number and the SE is exactly 0. Silently.
It breaks at very small n (five observations give 116 distinct resample means and an interval 60% too narrow), for statistics driven by the extremes (the bootstrap interval for a maximum has the observed maximum as its upper endpoint, always), and for dependent observations.

Next: the same resampling idea aimed at a different question—not how much would my estimate move? but could this have happened by chance?
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Permutation Tests
text:
The experiment
In the hypothesis-testing week you learned that a p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as yours, if the null hypothesis were true. That sentence is correct, and for most people it stays a sentence. The null hypothesis is somewhere off in the distance being true, a formula converts your data into a t, and a function returns a number.
This chapter removes the formula. The null hypothesis becomes something you can do—a physical operation on your own data, which you can watch, run ten thousand times, and count. Nothing here requires a distribution, a degrees of freedom, or an assumption about shape.
If p-values felt mystical in October, this is where they stop being.
A product team randomized 33 new users to the old onboarding flow or a redesigned one, and measured minutes of engagement in the first week.
The new flow is ahead by 10.9 minutes. Eighteen users and fifteen users, and group standard deviations of 12.3 and 9.4—so the groups overlap heavily and 10.9 is not obviously beyond what shuffling people around could produce.
That is exactly the question: could a gap this large have arisen with no real difference between the flows at all?
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Permutation Tests
section: The null hypothesis, as an instruction
text:
The null hypothesis, as an instruction
Say the null hypothesis out loud, carefully:

The redesign has no effect. Each user would have engaged for the same number of minutes whichever flow they had been assigned to.

Now notice what that implies about your data file. If a user’s outcome does not depend on their assignment, then the labels "old" and "new" are just tags that a randomizer stuck on afterwards. Any other assignment of those same 18 and 15 tags to those same 33 outcomes was equally likely to have happened.
That is not a metaphor. The randomization genuinely could have come out differently, and under the null the numbers would have been identical—only the tags would have moved. So we can generate the alternative worlds ourselves:
















In that particular alternative world, the “new” group came out 6.09 minutes worse. Nothing about the users changed. Only the labels moved.






The core move



sample(arm) shuffles the labels without replacement, so exactly 18 users are called "old" and 15 are called "new", as in the real study. The outcomes never move.
Do that ten thousand times and you have built, from your own data and with no theory at all, the distribution of results the null hypothesis predicts.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Permutation Tests
text:
Ten thousand alternative worlds








Two things to read off before going further.
It is centered at zero—to three decimal places. That is not luck; it is the null hypothesis made visible. Shuffling cannot create a systematic advantage for either label, so the average shuffled difference is zero by construction. This is the sharpest contrast with the bootstrap, whose distribution is centered at your observed statistic.
Its spread is 4.31 minutes. That is a standard error, obtained without a formula: it is how much a difference of means bounces around at these sample sizes and this variability, when nothing real is going on.
Here is the picture, with the observed difference marked:








Chance alone routinely produces gaps of 4 or 5 minutes and occasionally 12. Our 10.9 sits well out in the right tail. The whole question is how far out.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Permutation Tests
section: The p-value, as a counting exercise
text:
The p-value, as a counting exercise








100 out of 10,000, so p = 0.010.
Read that sentence again, because it is the definition of a p-value with the mathematics taken out: in one hundred of ten thousand worlds where the labels meant nothing, the gap was at least as big as the one we saw.
That is all a p-value has ever been. No t distribution, no degrees of freedom, no assumption about the shape of anything.






Two-sided, and why abs()



We counted shuffles where |{\text{difference}}| \geq |10.9|—that is, worlds where the gap was at least as extreme in either direction. That is the two-sided p-value, and it is what you want unless you genuinely committed, in advance, to caring only about one direction. Dropping the abs() roughly halves the p-value, and doing so after seeing which way the result went is one of the ways researchers fool themselves.








A permutation p-value is never exactly 0



If none of your 10,000 shuffles is as extreme as the observed value, the honest report is p < 0.0001, not p = 0. Some analysts use (1 + \#\{\text{as extreme}\})/(B+1) for this reason, which cannot return zero. The finite B has put a floor on the resolution, and that floor is your reporting limit.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Permutation Tests
section: The same data, through a t-test
text:
The same data, through a t-test
Now the comparison that matters, because it tells you what you have gained and what you have not.








The Welch t-test gives p = 0.0072. The permutation test gave p = 0.010. The same conclusion, from two procedures with almost nothing in common.









Permutation test
Welch t-test




p-value
0.010
0.0072


Null distribution
built by shuffling your data
assumed to be t with 30.8 df


Assumes near-Normality
no
yes, or a large n


Assumes equal variances
no
no (Welch)


Assumes exchangeability under the null
yes
implicitly


Works for the median instead
yes, unchanged
no



The agreement is the point, in the same way as 6.2’s mean check. Two methods that share no machinery landing on the same answer is what tells you the permutation machinery is sound—and once it is sound, you can point it at questions the t-test cannot reach.






Where the t-test’s assumptions hold, it is a fine tool and a great deal faster. The permutation test earns its keep when n is small, when the data are plainly not Normal, or when the statistic you care about is not a difference of means at all.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Permutation Tests
text:
What it assumes
“Assumption-free” is a slogan you will see attached to permutation tests, and it is not true. There is exactly one assumption, and it is a real one.






Exchangeability under the null



If the null hypothesis is true, then every relabelling you generate must have been equally likely to occur.
In a randomized experiment this is not an assumption at all—it is a description of what the experimenter did. That is why permutation tests and randomized experiments fit together so naturally: the test reruns the randomization.


Where it fails, it fails hard:

Paired or repeated measures. Thirty patients measured before and after treatment: shuffling all 60 labels freely asserts that patient 7’s “before” could have been patient 22’s “after”. It could not. The correct test flips a coin within each pair.
Clustered data. Students within classrooms, patients within hospitals. The unit that was randomized is the cluster, so the cluster is what you shuffle.
Non-random assignment. If the “new” arm is everyone who opted in to the beta, then the labels were never exchangeable in the first place. The permutation test will happily return a p-value that answers a question about randomization you never performed. This is Aug 31’s warning again: a clean computation on a self-selected comparison is still a self-selected comparison.

The general rule: shuffle only what the null says is interchangeable.






 What shuffling builds







In a permutation test comparing two groups, you shuffle the group labels 10,000 times and recompute the difference in means each time.
What is the resulting distribution of 10,000 differences?

The distribution of the true difference between the two groups.The sampling distribution of the difference in means, in the same sense as the bootstrap distribution.The set of differences you could have seen if the labels carried no information—that is, the null hypothesis, built out of your own data rather than assumed from a formula.The distribution of measurement error in the outcome variable.



This is the idea worth taking away from the whole chapter, because it turns the null hypothesis from a sentence into a procedure you can watch run.
“There is no treatment effect” says that a subject’s outcome would have been the same whichever arm they had been assigned to. If that is true, then the labels are just tags stuck on afterwards, and any other assignment of the same tags to the same outcomes was equally likely to have happened. Shuffling reproduces exactly those alternative worlds, and the histogram of shuffled differences is what “no effect” looks like at your sample size, with your data’s spread and your group sizes.
The p-value is then a counting exercise with no formula in it: what fraction of those null worlds produced a difference at least as extreme as the one you actually got?
Note what it is not. It is not a sampling distribution of your estimate—it is centered at zero by construction, not at the observed difference, so you cannot read a confidence interval off it. That is the bootstrap’s job. The two procedures look similar on screen and answer opposite questions: the bootstrap resamples observations with replacement, keeping labels attached, and asks how much the estimate would move; the permutation test reassigns labels without replacement, keeping the observations fixed, and asks what would happen if the labels meant nothing.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Permutation Tests
text:
Any statistic you like
Here is the payoff for the week. The engagement data is right-skewed and a couple of heavy users are pulling the means around, so suppose you would rather compare medians. There is no median t-test. There does not need to be:








Medians of 69 and 81, a gap of 12 minutes, p = 0.0157. One word changed in the code—mean became median—and the entire inferential apparatus followed.
The same substitution works for a difference of trimmed means, a ratio of medians, a difference in 90th percentiles, a difference in standard deviations, or a correlation. Choose the statistic that answers your question, then test it. That is the opposite of the usual order, in which people pick the question their software has a test for.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Permutation Tests
text:
A/B tests, revisited
A/B testing was built on the two-proportion test. Permutation handles it with the same three lines, and the labels are literally the randomization.
1,200 visitors, split evenly between two versions of a landing page; the outcome is whether they clicked.








B converted 7.83% against A’s 6.33%—a lift of 1.5 percentage points, which is nearly a quarter more conversions and would be a genuinely valuable result. Is it real?








p = 0.365. Reshuffling which visitors were called “B” produces a gap of 1.5 points or more about a third of the time. There is no evidence here at all.








The two-proportion test says 0.368, agreeing to the third decimal.






The A/B testing lesson, in numbers



The experiment saw 38 clicks and 47 clicks. A difference of nine events is what the whole decision rests on, and nine events is nothing. This is what an underpowered A/B test looks like from the inside: a headline lift of 24%, a plausible business story, and a p-value of 0.37.
The failure was not in the analysis, it was in the sample-size calculation before the test was launched—and the temptation now, to keep the test running until the gap looks convincing, is precisely the peeking problem. The permutation test is not a way around any of that. It is a better-behaved way of getting the same disappointing answer.








 Shuffling what you are not allowed to shuffle







Thirty patients each had their blood pressure measured before and after eight weeks on a drug. An analyst stacks the 60 measurements into one vector, labels each one "before" or "after", shuffles the 60 labels 10,000 times, and reports the resulting permutation p-value.
What is wrong with this?

Nothing—a permutation test makes no assumptions, so it is always safe.Shuffling all 60 labels breaks the pairing. A patient’s two readings belong together, and under the null the only thing that could have been swapped is the order within each patient—so the correct test shuffles the two labels separately inside each of the 30 pairs.The test is invalid because 10,000 shuffles is far fewer than the 2^{30} possible label assignments.Permutation tests require equal group sizes, and here both groups have 30, so the test is fine.



Permutation tests are assumption-light, not assumption-free. The one assumption they do make is exchangeability under the null: if the null hypothesis is true, every relabelling you are willing to generate must have been equally likely to occur.
Free shuffling of all 60 labels asserts that patient 7’s “before” reading was just as likely to have been patient 22’s “after” reading. It was not. Patients differ enormously from each other in baseline blood pressure, and that between-patient variation is exactly what the paired design was built to remove. Throwing all 60 readings into one pot puts that variation back into the null distribution, which becomes far too wide—and the test loses most of its power.
The fix keeps the structure the design gave you. Under the null “the drug does nothing”, each patient’s two readings could equally well have arrived in either order, so you flip a coin within each pair, 30 independent flips, and recompute the mean difference. That is a valid permutation test, and it is the resampling counterpart of the paired t-test.
The general rule: shuffle only what the null hypothesis says is interchangeable. Repeated measures, matched pairs, students clustered in classrooms, and readings from the same sensor over time all constrain what you are allowed to permute—the same structure that broke Step 2 of the Week 5 derivation breaks free shuffling here, and for the same reason.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Permutation Tests
text:
Bootstrap or permutation?
They look nearly identical on screen and answer different questions. Before you write the loop, decide which row you are in.









Bootstrap
Permutation test




The question
how much would my estimate move?
could this have happened by chance?


Resample
observations, with replacement
labels, without replacement


What stays fixed
which label each observation carries
the observed values


Centered at
your observed statistic
zero


Output
standard error, confidence interval
p-value


Typical use
“the median gift is $27 (95% CI $19–$41)”
“the redesign’s 10.9-minute gain has p = 0.01”



A useful habit: report both. An interval says how big the effect might be; a p-value says whether you can rule out zero. The interval is almost always the more useful of the two in a report, and the p-value is what a reviewer will ask for anyway.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Permutation Tests
text:
Exercises

Exercise: the observed statistic















mean(minutes[arm == "new"]) - mean(minutes[arm == "old"])
= 81.733 - 70.833 = 10.9.



Exercise: where is the null distribution centered?















```{r}
mean(replicate(5000, {
  s <- sample(arm)
  mean(minutes[s == "new"]) - mean(minutes[s == "old"])
}))
```
About 0. Under free shuffling neither label is favoured, so the null distribution is centered at zero.



Exercise: compute a permutation p-value
Different data this time—a small randomized trial with 20 subjects per arm.















```{r}
observed <- mean(resp[group == "treated"]) - mean(resp[group == "control"])

perm <- replicate(10000, {
  s <- sample(group)
  mean(resp[s == "treated"]) - mean(resp[s == "control"])
})

mean(abs(perm) >= abs(observed))
```
About 0.047, against t.test()’s 0.0469.



Exercise: change the statistic, keep the machinery















```{r}
observed_med <- median(minutes[arm == "new"]) - median(minutes[arm == "old"])

perm_med <- replicate(10000, {
  s <- sample(arm)
  median(minutes[s == "new"]) - median(minutes[s == "old"])
})

mean(abs(perm_med) >= abs(observed_med))
```
About 0.0157.



Exercise: what does 0.010 license you to say?















answer <- "C"
The p-value is a statement about data under an assumed null, not a probability attached to a hypothesis, and it is silent about effect size.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Permutation Tests
text:
Summary

A permutation test turns the null hypothesis into a procedure: if the labels carry no information, every reassignment of them was equally likely, so reassign them and look.
sample(arm) shuffles labels without replacement, keeping the group sizes fixed and leaving the outcomes untouched.
The permutation distribution is centered at zero, by construction. It is what “no effect” looks like at your sample sizes and your spread.
The p-value is a tail proportion: 100 of 10,000 shuffles reached 10.9 minutes or more in either direction, so p = 0.010. No formula, no degrees of freedom.
On the same data the Welch t-test gave p = 0.0072. Agreement where both apply is what licenses the method where only one does.
The one assumption is exchangeability under the null, and it is free in a randomized experiment. It fails for paired data, clustered data, and non-random assignment—shuffle only what the null says is interchangeable.
The statistic is yours to choose. Swapping mean for median gave p = 0.0157 for a comparison with no textbook test at all.
A/B tests are permutation tests. The landing-page experiment showed a 24% relative lift, nine extra clicks, and p = 0.365—which is what an underpowered test looks like from the inside, and no analysis method fixes it.
Bootstrap for intervals, permutation for p-values. With replacement and labels fixed, or without replacement and labels shuffled. Decide which before writing the loop.

Next: practice problems, and then bring a statistic from your own project to the lab.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Inference for a Fitted Model
text:
Two intervals, two questions
You can now fit a linear model and read the standard error printed beside each coefficient. That number came out of a formula, and the formula assumed things: that the errors have the same variance everywhere, and that they are independent. When those hold, it is the right answer and nothing here improves on it.
This chapter is for when they do not, and for one confusion that has nothing to do with assumptions at all—people asking a model for an interval and getting back a perfectly correct answer to a different question.
A fitted model at x = 5 gives you a number. There are two honest intervals you could put around it, and they differ by a factor of five.
Both are centered on the same fitted value. They answer different questions:
The second is wider because it carries two sources of uncertainty rather than one. The confidence interval only has to account for not knowing where the line is. The prediction interval has to account for that and for the fact that individual points scatter around the line by \sigma even if you knew the line exactly.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Inference for a Fitted Model
text:
Confidence interval for the fitted value. Where is the average y among all cases with x = 5? It is an interval for a property of the population—a point on the true regression line.
Prediction interval. Where will the next single observation with x = 5 land? It is an interval for one future draw.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Inference for a Fitted Model
section: The test that tells them apart
text:
The test that tells them apart
Watch what more data does.








The confidence interval collapses towards zero. The prediction interval does not. It converges to roughly 2 \times 1.96 \times 2.5 \approx 9.8, which is the irreducible scatter of individuals around the line.
That is the whole distinction, and it is the reason the confusion matters. With enough data you can know the average outcome to any precision you like. You will never know an individual outcome better than \sigma, no matter how much data you collect, because the uncertainty is in the world rather than in your estimate.






Which one does the question want?






“What is the average salary of graduates with five years of experience?” — confidence interval.
“What should I expect to be offered, with five years of experience?” — prediction interval.

A model quoted with a confidence interval where the reader wanted a prediction interval understates the uncertainty enormously, and it is the more common direction of the mistake because the narrower number looks better.









 Exercise: which interval





A hospital fits a model of length of stay on age. A ward manager asks: “A 72-year-old is being admitted this afternoon. How long should I plan for them to stay?”
Assign the letter, for example answer <- "A".















B.
D is the instructive wrong answer. The confidence interval does become arbitrarily narrow with enough data—that is exactly why it is the wrong tool here. An interval that shrinks to nothing cannot be describing a single patient’s stay, because single patients do not become more alike as you collect more of them. That is the same distinction as The Standard Error of a Mean between the SD of the data and the SE of the mean, arriving now with a model attached.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Inference for a Fitted Model
text:
Bootstrapping a coefficient
Now the assumptions. A slope is a weighted average of the outcome, so the bootstrap applies to it exactly as it applied to a median—resample rows, refit, collect the number.








They agree, and they should: the data were generated with exactly the constant variance the formula assumes. When the assumptions hold, the bootstrap earns you nothing. That is worth seeing before the case where it earns you a great deal.
Note what is being resampled. You draw whole rows—an x and its y together—which is the same rule as The Bootstrap: resample the unit that was sampled from the population, not the columns.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Inference for a Fitted Model
text:
When the formula is wrong
Here the spread of y grows with x. Everything else is unchanged, and the model is still correctly specified—the line really is 3 + 2x.








The fan shape is the diagnostic. Now compare what the two methods claim about the slope:








The bootstrap reports a noticeably larger standard error. One of them is right, and we can settle it by brute force—regenerate the world many times and measure how much the slope actually moves:








The bootstrap is close to the truth; the formula is too small. Its standard error is computed from a single pooled estimate of \sigma, so it averages the tight left-hand region together with the noisy right-hand one, and the noisy points sit where leverage is highest.
The consequence is the one that matters: a confidence interval built from the formula is too narrow, and a p-value computed from it is too small. You would overstate the evidence, and nothing in the output would look wrong.






 Exercise: bootstrap a slope





cars is built into R: speed in mph and dist, the stopping distance in feet, for 50 observations.
Bootstrap the slope of dist ~ speed with 2,000 resamples and return the bootstrap standard error—a single number.


















```{r}
sd(replicate(2000, {
  i <- sample(nrow(cars), replace = TRUE)
  coef(lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars[i, ]))[2]
}))
```
About 0.42, against summary(lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars))’s 0.4155.
The two agreeing is not a null result. It is evidence that the constant-variance assumption is tenable for these data, which you would otherwise be taking on faith.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Inference for a Fitted Model
text:
What resampling does not fix
The bootstrap corrects the standard error when the formula’s variance assumption fails. It corrects nothing else, and it is worth being explicit about what remains broken:

A missing confounder. Bootstrap a coefficient from a model that omits an important variable and you get an accurate interval around a biased estimate.
A wrong functional form. If the relationship curves and you fitted a line, resampling reproduces the line faithfully.
A biased sample. As Where the Data Came From argued, no computation performed on a sample can tell you about people who are not in it. Resampling a self-selected survey ten thousand times produces ten thousand self-selected surveys.

The bootstrap is a statement about sampling variability, and sampling variability is only one of the ways a number can be wrong. A narrow interval around the wrong number is still the wrong number, and it is now wearing a credential.






Check yourself






Which of the two intervals stops shrinking as n grows, and what is it converging to?
A colleague reports “we are 95% confident a customer will spend between £18 and £24.” Which interval did they most likely compute, and which did they need?
The bootstrap SE of a slope matches the formula’s SE. What have you learned?
Non-constant variance made the formula’s SE too small. Which direction does that push a p-value, and why is that the dangerous direction?
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Inference for a Fitted Model
text:
Where this goes next
You now have two routes to a standard error for the same quantity, and a way to tell whether they agree. That is the practical content of the whole part: the formulas are shortcuts for an experiment, and when you doubt a shortcut you can run the experiment.
The project asks you to state what your analysis does and does not support. These two chapters give you the vocabulary for the second half of that sentence—a coefficient with an honest standard error, an interval whose meaning you can name, and a clear-eyed account of the things resampling could not have fixed.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Practice Problems
text:
Predict before you run
None of these are graded and none of them are auto-checked. They exist so that you arrive on Monday with something to argue about.
The first section comes in two halves as usual: predict, then run. Write the prediction down before you press Run—resampling output is particularly easy to nod along with after the fact, because every number is plausible and none of them is checkable by eye.
This runs and is still wrong is the important half this week. Every cell in it executes cleanly, produces a well-formatted number, and is wrong. Resampling code fails silently more readily than almost anything else you will write: there is no formula to sanity-check against, no warning, and the output is always a nice small number that looks like a standard error.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Practice Problems
text:
A1. Which statistic is estimated most precisely?
Sixty salaries, heavily right-skewed. The same bootstrap is run three times, on the mean, the median, and the 10% trimmed mean.
Predict the ordering of the three standard errors before running, and say why.








Then answer: the median came out with a standard error about 25% smaller than the mean’s. Explain that in terms of what a resample does to a long right tail—which observations move the mean around, and how often do they appear in a resample? Then say why “the median is more precise” is nonetheless not a general reason to prefer medians, by naming a population where the ordering would reverse.


A2. The resample size is not a free parameter
x has 100 observations. Three bootstraps, differing only in how many observations each resample contains.
Predict all three numbers, at least as ratios, from \sigma/\sqrt{n}.








Then answer: only one of the first three is the standard error of your estimate. Say which, and say precisely what question the other two answer. Then explain why size_400 is not a way of getting a more precise result out of 100 observations, in a sentence you could say to a manager who suggests it.


A3. B and n do different jobs
Four bootstraps: two sample sizes crossed with two values of B.
Predict which of the four numbers are about equal to each other, and in what pattern, before running.








Then answer: the four numbers form two pairs, not four distinct values. Say what each of n and B controls, and what a hundredfold increase in B bought in each row. Then: if the numbers within a pair are not exactly equal, what is the size of that discrepancy a measurement of?


A4. Two ways to shuffle
A permutation test can shuffle the labels or shuffle the outcomes.
Predict whether the two p-values will differ.








Then answer: the two agree to within simulation noise, and there is a reason that is not a coincidence. State it. Then say what quantity the small remaining gap between 0.0466 and 0.0414 is measuring, and how you would make it go away.


A5. The bootstrap meets the minimum
Sixty measurements from a population whose true minimum is 5.
Predict the lower endpoint of the interval before running.








Then answer: the lower endpoint is 5.4 and the median of the bootstrap distribution is also 5.4. Explain both, and then state the general condition from The Bootstrap that this violates. Finally: the upper endpoint, 8.4, is a perfectly sensible number. Why does the interval fail on one side and not the other?
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Practice Problems
section: This runs, and it is still wrong
text:
This runs, and it is still wrong
Every cell below executes without an error or a warning. Find the problem, say what the number actually measures, and fix it.

B1. The correlation with a confidence interval around zero

Task: 50 stores’ advertising spend and sales. Report the correlation and a 95% bootstrap interval for it.

















The observed correlation is 0.8645 and the “95% interval” is (-0.275, 0.275)—an interval that does not contain the estimate, and that comfortably contains zero.
Answer: what is boot_r actually the sampling distribution of? Point at the exact line that causes it, say why the center came out at 0.0008 rather than 0.86, and write the corrected cell. Then say what feature of the output should have stopped the analyst before they read the interval at all.










B2. The suspiciously precise response time

Task: 80 API response times. Report the standard error of the mean.









3.621 milliseconds. And the correct answer:








Answer: name the single wrong number in the first cell. Then: the wrong answer is smaller than the right one by a factor of about 3.5. Predict that factor from \sigma/\sqrt{n} before checking it against 12.545/3.621, and say which study the 3.621 is the standard error of. Finally, the general rule from 6.2 that this breaks, in one sentence.


B3. The panel that answered

Task: estimate mean weekly grocery spending for a city. A loyalty-card panel yields 900 respondents; report the mean with a bootstrap interval.

















Answer: the bootstrap code is entirely correct and the reported interval misses the truth. Say what the interval is a valid statement about, and name the population it actually describes. Then: the analyst proposes raising the panel to 9,000 respondents. What happens to the interval, what happens to the error, and what would you spend the money on instead? Tie your answer to the Aug 31 material by name.


B4. Before and after

Task: 30 patients had blood pressure measured before and after eight weeks on a drug. Test whether the drug changed it.









An observed drop of 3.73 mmHg and p = 0.4644. Now the correct test, which shuffles only what the null says is interchangeable—the order within each patient:








Zero of 5,000.
Answer: the first test says nothing is happening and the second says the effect is overwhelming. Explain the gap in terms of what the free shuffle put into the null distribution that the paired shuffle kept out—compute sd(pre) and sd(d) if it helps. Which assumption from Permutation Tests did the first cell break? And, on reporting: the second test found 0 of 5,000, so what number goes in the paper?


B5. Yesterday looks a lot like today

Task: 400 daily readings from a sensor. Report the standard error of the mean daily level.

















The bootstrap and the formula agree beautifully, at about 0.106. Both are wrong. Here is the truth, available only because we know how the data was generated:








Answer: 0.329 against 0.106—the reported uncertainty is understated by a factor of three. Say why resampling individual days destroys the very feature of the data that makes the mean imprecise, and connect it to the step of the The Standard Error of a Mean derivation that fails here. Then: the bootstrap and the formula agreed, which 6.2 offered as a validity check. Why did that check not catch this, and what would you have had to look at instead?
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Practice Problems
text:
Judgment
No code. Bring written answers; we will disagree about these out loud.

C1. The wrong tool
A civil engineer has 150 annual peak river levels and needs the level that will be exceeded once in 200 years, for a flood defense specification. She bootstraps the 99.5th percentile of her 150 observations and reports a 95% interval.
Say what is structurally wrong with this, in terms of where the information for that number would have to come from. Then: is her problem the same as the maximum problem from The Bootstrap, or a different one? Finally, and most importantly, write the two sentences she should put in her report instead—remembering that “the data cannot answer this” is a finding, not a failure, and that a defense will be built either way.


C2. Which interval goes in the report?
You have n = 22 observations, mildly right-skewed. The t-interval is (41.2, 58.8). The bootstrap percentile interval is (42.6, 59.9).
Neither is obviously right. Argue for one, then argue for the other, then say what you would actually write—and what you would put in the methods section so that a reader could tell what you did. Then answer the question a colleague will ask: “Why not just report whichever is narrower?”


C3. The A/B test that nearly worked
6.3’s landing-page test gave a 24% relative lift, 38 clicks against 47, and p = 0.365. The product manager says: “The permutation test is more powerful than the old proportion test, so let’s rerun the analysis that way and see.”
Two things are wrong with that sentence. Name both. Then use \sigma/\sqrt{n} to estimate roughly how many visitors per arm would have been needed to detect a 1.5-point lift on a 6% base rate, and say what you would have told the team before launch. Finally, connect this to the peeking problem from A/B testing: what is the specific temptation created by a p-value of 0.365, and why does resampling do nothing about it?


C4. “Resampling makes no assumptions”
You will read this sentence in blog posts and hear it in interviews.
List what the bootstrap actually assumes, and what a permutation test actually assumes. For each, give a concrete situation from this week’s chapters where the assumption fails and the method returns a confident wrong answer. Then rewrite the sentence so that it is both short and true.


C5. Your own project statistic
This is the preparation for Monday’s lab, so do it in writing.
Pick one number from your project data that is not a mean—a median, a correlation, a percentile, a ratio of two rates, a difference between two groups, whatever your question actually needs.

Write the statistic as a one-line R expression on your data.
Say whether you need an interval or a p-value, and therefore whether you will bootstrap or permute. Justify the choice in one sentence.
Write down the check you will run first: bootstrap a mean from the same data and compare it with s/\sqrt{n}.
Name the one thing about how your data was collected that your interval will not account for. Every dataset has one.

Bring all four. Item 4 is the one we will spend the most time on.
crumbs: Resampling: the Bootstrap and Permutation Tests

title: Logistic Regression
text:
What is here
Monday, December 7
Post your questions on any of these pages by Monday at 12:00 noon, the morning of class.
A great many of the outcomes worth modeling are yes or no: converted, churned, defaulted, recovered, passed. Everything you have learned about coefficients, standard errors and intervals carries over to them—but the straight line does not, because probabilities are bounded and a line is not.
This week is the model that respects that bound, and the one place it reliably trips people: its coefficients are on a scale nobody has intuition about, and the two natural ways of describing them—odds and probabilities—are different things that get used interchangeably in print.
Nothing here is new machinery so much as the same machinery on a transformed scale. If you can read a regression table and say what a confidence interval claims, you can do this.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
Why Linear Regression Will Not Do



Sixteen percent of fitted values outside [0,1], all of them at the extremes where the model would be used. Variance that cannot be constant, and a relationship that must flatten at both ends.








The Logistic Model



Odds, log-odds, and the S-curve that comes back. glm(family = binomial), how to read its output, and why type = "response" is the argument to remember.








Odds Ratios and Their Intervals



Exponentiate to get something sayable—then the misreading. The same odds ratio of 2.21 moved probability by 0.115, 0.189 and 0.060 at three starting points. Odds are not chances, and the difference is not small.








Deviance and Checking



What replaces R^2, why pseudo-R^2 is not it, and thresholds as a business decision: moving from 0.3 to 0.7 took precision from 0.78 to 0.93 and recall from 0.92 to 0.77. Plus separation, and what an enormous coefficient is telling you.








Practice Problems



Including a 99%-accurate model that predicts zero events, and a bank report you cannot interpret without a number it does not give you.

title: Logistic Regression
section: The sentence this week is aiming at
text:
The sentence this week is aiming at
“Churn is 25% among free customers. Pro customers have 1.8 times the odds of churning (95% CI 1.2 to 2.8), which puts them at 38%.”
The baseline rate, the odds ratio with its interval, and the probability it implies. Give all three and the claim cannot be misread; give only the middle one and it almost always is.






Due this week



HW 8 is due at the start of class, and your project is presented on December 10. And as always, post your questions on these pages by Monday before.

title: Why Linear Regression Will Not Do
text:
It predicts probabilities outside [0, 1]
A great many outcomes are yes or no. Did the customer convert, did the patient recover, did the loan default, did the student pass.
You can code those as 0 and 1 and run lm(). R will not stop you, the output will look ordinary, and the model is called a linear probability model. It is not useless—for a rough first look at a common outcome it is often fine—but it fails in three ways, and the third is the one that decides the matter.
Sixty-four of the four hundred fitted values are impossible—probabilities below zero or above one. The line has no way to know it is predicting a proportion.
This is not a rounding problem. If the model is being used to make a decision at the extremes—flagging the riskiest loans, targeting the likeliest churners—the extremes are exactly where you were going to use it.
crumbs: Why Linear Regression Will Not Do

title: Why Linear Regression Will Not Do
section: The variance is not constant, by construction
text:
The variance is not constant, by construction
A binary outcome has variance p(1-p), which you met when deriving the standard error of a proportion. That depends on p, which depends on x. So the constant-variance assumption from Reading Residuals is violated by the nature of the outcome, not by bad luck.








Two stripes, because a residual can only be y - \hat y for y \in \{0, 1\}. No diagnostic plot will ever look right, and the reported standard errors are wrong.
crumbs: Why Linear Regression Will Not Do

title: Why Linear Regression Will Not Do
section: The relationship is not a straight line
text:
The relationship is not a straight line
This is the substantive objection, and the other two follow from it.
