A one-unit increase in x cannot add a constant amount to a probability, because probabilities are bounded. Moving someone from 0.50 to 0.60 is easy; moving them from 0.95 to 1.05 is impossible. Whatever the relationship is, it must flatten at both ends.
That is a statement about the world rather than about statistics. The natural shape is an S: slow at the bottom, steep in the middle, flat at the top. What logistic regression does is fit exactly that curve.






When the linear probability model is defensible





It is used in economics, and the defense is real: if all the fitted probabilities land between roughly 0.2 and 0.8, the S-curve is nearly straight over that range, and the coefficients have an easy reading as changes in probability.
Even then you need robust standard errors, and you have to check the fitted range. For anything involving rare events—fraud, churn, default, disease—the probabilities live at the flat end and the linear model is simply wrong.









 Exercise: how bad is it here?





y is binary and x is continuous. Fit a linear probability model and return the proportion of fitted values that are not valid probabilities.


















```{r}
f <- fitted(lm(y ~ x))
mean(f < 0 | f > 1)
```
0.16—one in six.
The useful habit is mean() of a logical vector, which turns any yes/no question about rows into a proportion in one call. And the useful observation is where the impossible values sit: at both extremes, which is precisely the region a targeting or screening model operates in.
crumbs: Why Linear Regression Will Not Do

title: Why Linear Regression Will Not Do
text:
Summary

A binary outcome coded 0/1 can be fitted with lm(), giving a linear probability model.
It predicts impossible values—16% of fitted values here were outside [0,1], all at the extremes.
Its variance cannot be constant, since a binary outcome has variance p(1-p), so the standard errors are wrong and no residual plot will look right.
Most importantly, the true relationship must flatten at both ends, because probabilities are bounded.
It is defensible when every fitted probability is mid-range. It is not defensible for rare events, which is most of the interesting cases.

Next: the curve that respects the bound.
crumbs: Why Linear Regression Will Not Do

title: The Logistic Model
text:
Odds, and log-odds
The requirement is a curve that stays between 0 and 1 and flattens at both ends. The logistic model gets one by modeling something unbounded and transforming back.
Start with odds: the probability of the event divided by the probability of its complement.
\text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p}
A probability of 0.5 is odds of 1. A probability of 0.9 is odds of 9—“nine to one on”. Odds run from 0 to infinity, so they have removed the upper bound but not the lower.
Taking logs removes the other one. Log-odds, or the logit, runs from -\infty to +\infty:
Note the symmetry: log-odds is 0 at p = 0.5, and p = 0.25 and p = 0.75 are mirror images at \mp 1.099.
That unbounded quantity is what the model puts a straight line through:
\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
Solving back for p gives the S-curve:
p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}}
which is plogis() in R.
Linear in the middle, flat at both ends, never leaving [0, 1]. The model is linear—just not on the scale of the outcome.

title: The Logistic Model
text:
Fitting it








glm with family = binomial is the whole change. Reading the output:
Estimate — coefficients on the log-odds scale. The slope of 0.793 says a one-unit increase in x adds 0.793 to the log-odds. That is not a number anybody has intuition about, which is what the next chapter is for.
Std. Error — as always, the standard deviation of the coefficient’s sampling distribution.
z value — estimate over standard error. It is a z rather than a t because the fitting method is maximum likelihood and the reference distribution is Normal in large samples, not because anything conceptual changed.
Deviance and AIC — measures of fit, covered in Deviance and Checking.
Note there is no R^2 and no residual standard error. Neither has a natural definition here, and the various “pseudo-R^2” substitutes do not mean what R^2 meant.

title: The Logistic Model
text:
Reading the fit as probabilities
Coefficients on the log-odds scale are for the model. Probabilities are for people.
















type = "response" is the argument to remember. Forgetting it returns log-odds, and a “probability” of -3.5 is the sign that you did.

title: The Logistic Model
text:
Maximum likelihood, in one paragraph
Least squares had a closed form. Logistic regression does not: R chooses the coefficients that make the observed pattern of zeros and ones most probable, by iterating until it converges.
Two practical consequences. Convergence can fail, and R will say so—warnings here are worth reading rather than suppressing. And the standard errors are large-sample approximations, so with very few observations, or very few events, treat them with more caution than the printout suggests.






 Exercise: from coefficients to a probability





Using the fitted model fit, return the predicted probability at x = 5.


















```{r}
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(x = 5), type = "response")
```
About 0.608.
Equivalently plogis(coef(fit)[1] + coef(fit)[2] * 5), which is worth computing once: predict(type = "response") is exactly the linear predictor passed through plogis(), and seeing that removes any mystery from the function.
Without type = "response" you get 0.440, the log-odds. A “probability” outside [0,1], or one suspiciously near zero for a common event, is almost always this mistake.

title: The Logistic Model
text:
Summary

Odds are p/(1-p); log-odds are unbounded, and that is what the model fits a straight line to.
Back-transformed, this gives the S-curve plogis()—linear in the middle, flat at both ends, always inside [0,1].
glm(y ~ x, family = binomial) fits it. Coefficients are on the log-odds scale; z values rather than t because the theory is large-sample.
predict(..., type = "response") gives probabilities. Forgetting it is the standard error.
There is no R^2 here, and fitting is by maximum likelihood, so convergence warnings matter.

Next: turning a log-odds coefficient into something you can say out loud.

title: Odds Ratios and Their Intervals
text:
Exponentiate
A coefficient of 0.793 on the log-odds scale is correct and unsayable. This chapter turns it into a sentence, and then guards the sentence against the misreading that follows it everywhere.
If \beta_1 is the change in log-odds per unit of x, then e^{\beta_1} is the factor by which the odds multiply.
The odds ratio on x is 2.21, with an interval of [1.92, 2.55].
Say it as: each additional unit of x multiplies the odds of the outcome by about 2.2, with a 95% interval from 1.9 to 2.6.
Three details.
Exponentiate the interval, do not build one around the odds ratio. Compute the interval on the log-odds scale where the sampling distribution is roughly Normal, then transform both endpoints. The result is asymmetric around 2.21, which is correct.
An odds ratio of 1 means no effect, because multiplying by 1 changes nothing. So the null value is 1 rather than 0, and an interval containing 1 is the one that fails to exclude no effect.
confint() versus confint.default(). The default method here uses profile likelihood, which is better in small samples; confint.default() uses the Wald interval, estimate \pm 1.96 \times \text{SE}. They agree in large samples. Either is fine; know which you used.

title: Odds Ratios and Their Intervals
text:
The misreading
An odds ratio of 2.2 does not mean the probability doubles. It usually does not even mean the probability rises by a constant amount.








The same odds ratio of 2.21 throughout. The change in probability is 0.115 low down, 0.189 in the middle, and 0.060 at the top.
That is the S-curve doing its job. Odds multiply by a constant; probabilities cannot, because they are bounded. A treatment that doubles the odds moves someone from 0.10 to 0.18, and someone from 0.90 to 0.95.






The sentence to avoid





“The odds ratio is 2.2, so the treatment doubles your chance.”
Odds are not chances. They coincide only when the outcome is rare—at p = 0.01, odds are 0.0101, and an odds ratio is close to a risk ratio. For a common outcome they diverge sharply, and in a population where the baseline is already 0.5 an odds ratio of 2.2 raises the probability to 0.69, not to 1.0.
Journalists make this error constantly, and so do papers. If your audience wants “how much more likely”, give them predicted probabilities at specific values, not the odds ratio.

title: Odds Ratios and Their Intervals
text:
Categorical predictors
With a factor, each odds ratio is against the baseline level—the same arrangement as linear models.








planpro at 1.81 says pro customers have about 1.8 times the odds of free customers. The baseline has no row, so a reader who does not know it is free cannot interpret anything—say which level is the baseline.
The intercept exponentiates to the odds for the baseline group, not a probability. Convert it: plogis(coef(fit2)[1]).

title: Odds Ratios and Their Intervals
text:
Reporting it properly
Give three things, in this order.

The odds ratio with its interval. The estimate of the effect.
Predicted probabilities at meaningful values of the predictor. This is what the audience wants and what they will otherwise infer wrongly.
The baseline rate. An odds ratio is meaningless without knowing what it is multiplying.









“Churn is 25% among free customers, 38% among pro and 61% among enterprise. Pro customers have 1.8 times the odds of churning that free customers do (95% CI 1.2 to 2.8).”
That sentence cannot be misread.






 Exercise: an odds ratio with its interval





mtcars again: model am (0 = automatic, 1 = manual) on wt. Return the odds ratio for wt—a single number.


















```{r}
exp(coef(glm(am ~ wt, data = mtcars, family = binomial))["wt"])
```
About 0.018.
An odds ratio below 1 is a negative association, and very small ones are hard to read. Invert: 1/0.018 \approx 56, so each additional 1,000 lb multiplies the odds of being automatic by about 56. Same fact, sayable.
The interval matters here as much as anywhere—with 32 observations it is wide, and exp(confint.default(...)) is worth computing before quoting the 56.

title: Odds Ratios and Their Intervals
text:
Summary

Exponentiate a coefficient to get an odds ratio; exponentiate the interval’s endpoints, not the ratio.
The null value is 1, not 0.
An odds ratio is not a risk ratio. The same 2.21 changed probability by 0.115, 0.189 and 0.060 at different starting points. They coincide only for rare outcomes.
With factors, each ratio is against a baseline that has no row—name it. The intercept exponentiates to odds, not a probability.
Report the odds ratio with its interval, predicted probabilities at meaningful values, and the baseline rate.

Next: whether the model fits at all.

title: Deviance and Checking
text:
What deviance is
Linear regression had R^2 and a residual standard error. Logistic regression has neither, and the substitute is deviance—which is less intuitive, more useful, and printed on every glm summary whether you read it or not.
Deviance measures how far a model’s fitted probabilities are from the observed zeros and ones. Lower is better, it is on an arbitrary scale, and only differences between deviances mean anything.
Two are reported.
The drop between them is what your predictors bought.
A drop of 244 for one degree of freedom. Under a null of “this predictor does nothing”, that drop follows a \chi^2 distribution with 1 df, where anything above about 3.8 is significant. So this is decisive.
That is the logistic analogue of the F-test, and it generalizes: to compare two nested models, fit both and compare their deviances against a \chi^2 with df equal to the number of extra parameters.
Adding noise drops the deviance a little—it always does, exactly as R^2 always rose—and the \chi^2 test correctly declines to be impressed.
AIC does the same job with a penalty built in, so it is comparable across non-nested models. Lower is better, and a difference of less than about 2 is not worth acting on.

title: Deviance and Checking
text:
Null deviance — the fit of a model with only an intercept: one probability for everybody.
Residual deviance — the fit of your model.

title: Deviance and Checking
text:
There is no R^2
Several “pseudo-R^2” measures exist—McFadden’s, Nagelkerke’s, Cox–Snell—and they are not the proportion of variance explained, because a binary outcome has no variance to apportion in that sense. They are monotone transformations of the deviance drop, they are not comparable across datasets, and quoting one as if it were R^2 misleads.
If you want a summary of how well the model separates the classes, use a classification measure and say what threshold you used.

title: Deviance and Checking
text:
Classification is a separate decision
The model returns probabilities. Turning them into predictions requires a threshold, and that threshold is a business choice, not a statistical one.








Moving the threshold from 0.3 to 0.7 raises precision from 0.78 to 0.93 and drops recall from 0.92 to 0.77. Nothing about the model changed—only the cut-off, and which error you preferred to make.
Those two words are the ones you met in Conditional Probability and Bayes: precision is P(\text{event} \mid \text{flagged}), recall is P(\text{flagged} \mid \text{event}), and which matters depends on the cost of a false alarm against the cost of a miss.






Accuracy is a bad summary





Here the outcome occurs 56% of the time, so predicting “yes” for everyone gets 56% accuracy with no model at all. For a rare event it is far worse: at 1% prevalence, predicting “no” always is 99% accurate and completely useless.
Always report the base rate next to any accuracy figure, and prefer precision and recall—or the interval on a coefficient, if the question was inferential rather than predictive.

title: Deviance and Checking
text:
Separation
The failure mode particular to logistic regression: if a predictor separates the outcome perfectly, the likelihood has no maximum and the coefficients run away.








A coefficient of 23.6 with a standard error of 58,059. R warns that fitted probabilities of 0 or 1 occurred, and that warning is the diagnosis.
What it means: the data say the effect is infinite, because they contain no case that contradicts a perfect rule. Usually the cause is a predictor that encodes the outcome—a variable recorded after the event, or a proxy for it.
What to do: look for the leak first. If the separation is genuine and the sample is simply small, penalized methods such as Firth logistic regression give finite estimates.






 Exercise: did the predictor earn its place?





Fit am ~ wt on mtcars with family = binomial and return the drop in deviance from the null model to the fitted one.


















```{r}
g <- glm(am ~ wt, data = mtcars, family = binomial)
g$null.deviance - g$deviance
```
24.05 on one degree of freedom, against a \chi^2 cutoff near 3.84. Decisive.
anova(g, test = "Chisq") reports the same drop with its p-value, and is the form to use when you have several predictors and want them assessed in turn.

title: Deviance and Checking
text:
Summary

Deviance replaces R^2: lower is better, the scale is arbitrary, and only differences matter.
The drop from null to residual deviance is a \chi^2 test on the predictors— 244 on 1 df here. anova(fit, test = "Chisq") does it; AIC compares non-nested models.
Pseudo-R^2 is not R^2. Do not quote it as though it were.
Classification needs a threshold, which is a business decision. Moving it from 0.3 to 0.7 took precision from 0.78 to 0.93 and recall from 0.92 to 0.77.
Accuracy needs its base rate beside it, or it is meaningless.
Separation produces enormous coefficients and standard errors, and usually means a predictor is leaking the outcome.

Next: the practice problems, and then putting the whole term into one analysis.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Predict the output
Not graded, not auto-checked. Bring your answers and your disagreements.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Discussion





1. 0.793 on the log-odds scale, 2.21 as an odds ratio. Same fact, and only the second is sayable.
2. The probability change is largest in the middle and smallest at the ends, though the odds ratio is constant everywhere. That is the S-curve, and it is why “the odds double” and “the chance doubles” are different sentences.
3. 0.608 against 0.440. The second is a log-odds and is not a probability at all—though it looks like one, which is what makes the mistake survive.

title: Practice Problems
section: This runs and is still wrong
text:
This runs and is still wrong































Discussion





4. Accuracy is about 0.99 and the model predicts zero events. Always saying “no” is equally accurate. The base rate is doing all the work, which is why accuracy without prevalence is not a report.
5. A coefficient of 23.6 with a standard error of 58,059. This is separation—the data contain no case contradicting a perfect rule—and the first thing to suspect is that the predictor encodes the outcome.
6. The odds ratio is about 3.3 and the probability goes from 0.71 to 0.89. Tripling the odds raised the chance by 18 points, not by 200%. For a common outcome the two are nowhere near each other.

title: Practice Problems
section: What does this license you to claim?
text:
What does this license you to claim?
A bank reports: a logistic model of default on income, employment length and credit utilization. The odds ratio on utilization is 1.9 (95% CI 1.6 to 2.3) per 10 percentage points. Accuracy is 96%.

“Raising utilization by 10 points nearly doubles the chance of default.”
“The model is 96% accurate, so it is good.”
What single number would you ask for first?
The bank wants to use it to decline applications. What changes about how you would evaluate it?
Employment length has an odds ratio of 0.98 with an interval of 0.93 to 1.04. What do you report?








Discussion





7. No—odds, not chance. If baseline default is 2%, an odds ratio of 1.9 takes it to about 3.7%, which nearly doubles it. If baseline were 40% it would take it to 56%. The claim depends entirely on the base rate, which the sentence omits.
8. Default is rare, so 96% accuracy is probably worse than predicting “no default” for everyone. Ask for the prevalence.
9. The base rate of default. Nothing in the report is interpretable without it.
10. It becomes a classification problem with a threshold, and the threshold is a policy decision balancing declined-good-customers against accepted-bad-ones. Precision and recall at the chosen cut-off, not accuracy—and a fairness review, since the model is now making decisions about people.
11. That the data are consistent with no effect of employment length, and also with a 7% reduction and a 4% increase in the odds per unit. Not “employment length does not matter”—that is the misreading from October.

title: Practice Problems
text:
Bring to class

Fit one on your project data. If your outcome is not binary, make one— above/below a meaningful threshold. Report the odds ratio with its interval and predicted probabilities at two or three values that mean something.
Write the sentence. One sentence reporting your main coefficient, with the baseline rate in it, that a non-technical reader could not misinterpret as a risk ratio. Bring it written down.
Argue about this. “Since we are going to threshold the probabilities anyway, we may as well use a classifier and skip the inference.” Work out what you would lose, using Deviance and Checking and Odds Ratios and Their Intervals, and when the argument is actually right.

title: From Question to Report
text:
What is here
Wednesday, December 9 (Designated Monday, the last teaching session)
Post your questions on any of these pages by Monday at 12:00 noon, the morning of class.
Every week this term taught one move. This one puts them in order.
The main chapter is a complete analysis on data you can run yourself—airquality, built into R, 153 rows and messy in the ways real data is messy. It stops at each point where the term supplied a decision: a quarter of the outcome is missing and June is 70% absent, the outcome is skewed and the residuals fan out until it is logged, the diagnostics pass and get reported anyway, and the finished claim is a sentence with four clauses each of which is load-bearing.
Seven steps, and only one of them is the model. That proportion is the point of the course.
The rest of the part is about getting it onto paper and defending it out loud, which is what your project asks and what a job will ask more often than it asks you to fit anything.

title: From Question to Report
text:
One Analysis, End to End



The whole term, in order, on airquality. Missingness first, then exploration, a scale decision with a reason, the fit, the checks, the coefficient said properly, and four specific limitations.








Writing the Report



Five sections, and the two everybody skips. How to write a result so it cannot be misread, what a figure caption is for, and why numbers in your prose should come from your code.








Defending It Out Loud



Questions are individual and grades can differ within a team. The five questions you will actually be asked, why “I don’t know” is a complete sentence when followed by something, and the one-minute version that is all most people will ever hear.








Project Clinic



A checklist to run before the session, and four things worth bringing—including “my result is boring”, which is a better use of the hour than it sounds.

title: From Question to Report
section: The habit the course was for
text:
The habit the course was for
Say what you found, say how precisely, and say what would change your mind.
Everything technical this term—standard errors, intervals, diagnostics, randomization, resampling—exists to let you say those three things honestly about a particular dataset. The tools change every few years. That obligation does not.






Due



Project presentations are Thursday, December 10, at a time announced during the term. The written report, the repository and the AI disclosure are due with them.

title: One Analysis, End to End
text:
1. Look at what you have before anything else
Every chapter this term taught one move. This one does a whole analysis, in order, on data you can run yourself—and stops at each point where the term supplied a decision.
The dataset is airquality: daily air quality measurements in New York, May to September 1973. It is built into R, it is small, and it is messy in the ways real data is messy.
The question: how is ground-level ozone related to temperature, and what can we say about how much?
Thirty-seven of 153 ozone readings are missing, nearly a quarter, plus seven solar readings. Before touching a model, ask the question from Where the Data Came From: is that missingness random?
It is not. June is 70% missing where every other month is around 16%. That is a pattern, not noise, and it changes what the analysis can claim: whatever we conclude will rest almost entirely on May, July, August and September.
That single line is the difference between an analysis and a report. Nothing downstream fixes it, and nothing downstream reveals it either.
We keep 111 of 153 rows. Write that number down; it goes in the report.

title: One Analysis, End to End
text:
2. Explore before modeling








Two things are visible and both matter. Ozone is strongly right-skewed, and the relationship with temperature curves upward and fans out—the spread at high temperatures is much larger than at low ones.








Skew of 1.23 raw, -0.54 logged. This is the log-normal shape—a positive quantity built from effects that multiply—and taking logs is not a trick to make a plot look nicer. It is a claim that the mechanism is multiplicative, which for a pollutant concentration is reasonable.

title: One Analysis, End to End
text:
3. Fit, and check the fit








The raw-scale residuals fan out badly; the logged ones are far more even. Put numbers on it rather than trusting the eye:








On the raw scale the residual spread runs 15.1, 11.7, 27.1 across terciles—a clear violation of constant variance, which means every standard error from that model is wrong. On the log scale it settles down considerably.
We keep the log model, and we say why in the report.








Largest Cook’s distance 0.362, well under 1, so no single day is running the fit. VIFs near 1.4, so the predictors are not standing in for each other. Both checks passed, and both get one sentence in the report—a check you ran and did not report is a check the reader cannot credit.

title: One Analysis, End to End
text:
4. Read the coefficients








The coefficient on Temp is 0.0492 on the log scale, which is not sayable. Exponentiating turns it into a percentage:








Each additional degree Fahrenheit is associated with about 5.0% more ozone, with a 95% interval from 3.8% to 6.3%, comparing days with the same wind and solar radiation.
Every clause is load-bearing: associated with declines the causal claim, comparing days with the same wind and solar radiation names what was held fixed, and the interval is the honest precision.

title: One Analysis, End to End
section: 5. Say what it does not support
text:
5. Say what it does not support
Four limitations, and none of them are hedging—each is a specific fact a reader needs.
Missing data. A quarter of ozone readings are absent and June is 70% missing. The estimate describes the days that were recorded, and if readings failed more often on extreme days the relationship on those days is unknown.
Not causal. Temperature is not randomly assigned. Hot days differ from cool days in many ways—more sunlight, less wind, different traffic—and although wind and solar are in the model, the October argument applies: adjustment reaches the variables we recorded.
One place, one summer. New York, May to September 1973. Nothing here generalizes to another city or another decade without an argument.
Interpolation only. Temperatures ran from 57 to 97°F. The model says nothing about 110°F, however confidently it would answer.






 Exercise: the effect of wind, said properly





Using the same log model, return the percentage change in ozone associated with a one-mph increase in wind, holding temperature and solar radiation fixed.


















```{r}
100 * (exp(coef(lg)["Wind"]) - 1)
```
About -6.0\% per mph, comparing days at the same temperature and solar radiation.
Worth noticing why this strengthens the whole analysis: the sign has an obvious mechanism—wind disperses pollutants—so the model is behaving as physics would predict. A coefficient you can explain is evidence the model is tracking something real; one you cannot is a prompt to look for the reason before publishing it.

title: One Analysis, End to End
text:
Summary

Look at missingness before anything else. A quarter of ozone readings were absent and June was 70% missing—a fact no later step would have surfaced.
Skew of 1.23 became -0.54 under a log, and the residual fan disappeared with it. Choosing a scale is a modeling decision, not cosmetics.
Checks that pass still get reported: Cook’s distance 0.36, VIFs near 1.4.
The result, said properly: about 5.0% more ozone per degree, 95% interval 3.8% to 6.3%, comparing days alike in wind and solar radiation.
Four limitations, each specific: missingness, no randomization, one place and one summer, and no extrapolation past 97°F.

Next: getting that onto paper.

title: Writing the Report
text:
The structure
The analysis is done. What remains is the part your grade and your career actually turn on, because an analysis nobody can follow is indistinguishable from one that was never done.
This chapter is the structure, and then the sentences.
Five sections. Anything you cannot fit into one of them probably belongs in an appendix.
1. The question. One paragraph. What you asked, why it matters, and what would count as an answer. If a reader stops here they should know what you were trying to find out.
2. The data. Where it came from, how many rows you started with, how many you used, and what you lost. This is where the missingness discussion goes, and it is the section most often skipped and most often decisive.
3. What you did. The analysis, in the order you did it, including the decisions—why a log scale, why those predictors, which model you settled on and what you tried first. Reproducible: someone with your repository can rerun it.
4. What you found. Estimates with intervals. Figures with captions that say what the reader should notice.
5. What it does and does not support. The limitations, specific enough to argue with.
A reader in a hurry reads sections 1 and 4. A reader who is going to act on it reads 2 and 5. Section 3 is for the person checking your work, which includes you in six months.

title: Writing the Report
text:
Writing a result
The single most useful habit of the term, applied to a sentence:

Among days with the same wind and solar radiation, each additional degree Fahrenheit was associated with about 5.0% more ozone (95% CI 3.8% to 6.3%).

Four things are doing work.
“Among days with the same…” names what was held fixed. Without it, “holding everything else constant” is a claim about the world rather than about your model.
“was associated with” declines the causal claim. If you have an experiment, say caused. If you do not, do not.
“about 5.0%” is the estimate, on a scale a reader can use.
“(95% CI 3.8% to 6.3%)” is the precision. A number without one is a number whose reliability the reader must guess at.






Report the interval, not the p-value





By now this should be a reflex. The interval contains everything the p-value contains and adds the effect size and the precision. Include the p-value if a convention demands it; lead with the interval.

title: Writing the Report
text:
Figures
Three rules cover most of it.
Every figure has a caption saying what to notice. “Ozone against temperature” is a title. “Ozone rises with temperature, and its spread rises too—which is why the analysis is on a log scale” is a caption.
Label axes with units. Temp is a column name. “Temperature (°F)” is a label.
A figure that needs three paragraphs to explain is two figures.
Use ggplot2 for anything going in the report, and remember that facet_wrap() is usually the answer when a single panel is getting crowded.

title: Writing the Report
text:
Reproducibility
The repository is a deliverable, not a formality.

It runs from a clean session. The two-computer test: a stranger clones it and gets your numbers.
No absolute paths. /Users/you/Desktop/final_v3.csv breaks for everyone else.
A seed anywhere there is randomness. Bootstrap, permutation, sampling.
Numbers in the text come from the code, via inline expressions, not typed by hand. Typed numbers go stale the moment the data changes, and they always change.

title: Writing the Report
text:
The AI disclosure
Your report includes a prompt log and a critique. Two things make the difference between a disclosure that earns marks and one that does not.
Be specific about what it got wrong. “The assistant suggested a linear model on the raw scale, which the residual plot showed was untenable” is a critique. “The assistant was mostly helpful” is not.
Say what you checked. The value of the disclosure is evidence that you verified rather than accepted. Naming the check is the evidence.

title: Writing the Report
text:
The final read
Before you submit, read the report and ask three questions.
Would a stranger know what I did? Not “could they reconstruct it from the code”—would they know from the prose.
Is every number in the results section attached to an interval or a count?
Have I said what would change my conclusion? If nothing would, the conclusion is not empirical.






The one thing that separates a good report





Not the model. Every report in the class will have a model, and most of them will be reasonable.
What distinguishes the good ones is section 5: a specific, honest account of what the analysis cannot say. Reports that claim less are believed more, and markers—like employers—can tell immediately whether the author knows where the weak points are.

title: Writing the Report
text:
Summary

Five sections: question, data, method, findings, limitations. Section 2 and section 5 are the ones that get skipped and the ones that matter.
Write results as: among cases alike in X, a one-unit change in Y was associated with Z (95% CI …). Every clause earns its place.
Figures need captions that say what to notice, and axis labels with units.
The repository must run from a clean session with no absolute paths, seeds set, and numbers generated by code rather than typed.
The AI disclosure is graded on the specificity of the critique.
Claiming less is believed more.

Next: defending it out loud.

title: Defending It Out Loud
text:
The talk
Presentation questions are answered individually, and members of one team may receive different grades. That is in the syllabus, and this chapter is what it means in practice.
It is also the closest thing in the course to a job interview, and the skill is the same one: explaining a decision you made to somebody deciding whether to trust you.
Assume the audience has not read your report and will not.
Open with the question and the answer. Not the data, not the methods—the question and what you found. Everything after that is support for a claim they already have in mind, which is far easier to follow than a mystery.
One idea per slide. If a slide needs a paragraph of narration, it is two slides.
Show the figure that made you believe it. Not every figure you produced—the one that changed your mind. If none did, that is worth knowing before you present.
End on the limitation. Finishing with what the analysis cannot say is counter-intuitive and works, because it pre-empts the first question and signals you know where the weak points are.

title: Defending It Out Loud
text:
What you will be asked
The questions are individual and they are mostly the same five, in some form. None of them are traps.
“Why did you choose that model?” Have a reason that is about the data or the question. “It had the highest R^2” is not one; “the outcome is a positive skewed quantity and the residuals fanned out on the raw scale” is.
“What does that coefficient mean?” Say the careful sentence. Name what was held constant, use associated with unless you randomized, and give the interval.
“What would change your conclusion?” The best question in the set. A good answer names something specific—a variable you could not measure, a subgroup you could not observe, a range you did not cover.
“Why should I believe this is not confounded?” For observational data the honest answer is usually “you should not, entirely”—followed by which confounders you handled, which you could not, and which direction the most likely one would push your estimate. Signing the bias is worth far more than denying it exists.
“What did your teammate do?” Because the grades are individual. Know the whole analysis, not only your part.

title: Defending It Out Loud
text:
Answering well
Answer the question asked. The commonest failure is answering an adjacent question you prepared for.
“I don’t know” is a complete sentence when it is followed by something. “I don’t know—we did not test that, and it would need X” is a good answer. Inventing one is the only response that costs marks.
Do not defend a decision you now think was wrong. “Looking at it again, I would use a log scale for the reason you are pointing at” demonstrates judgment. Arguing for a choice you no longer believe demonstrates the opposite.
Numbers with their uncertainty. If you say “5%” and the interval was 3.8 to 6.3, say so. It takes three extra words and it is the entire difference between a result and an assertion.






The one-minute version





Be able to give the whole thing in a minute: question, what you did, what you found, what it does not support.
That version is what someone repeats to a colleague after you have left the room, and it is the only part of your work most people will ever encounter. Write it down and practice it.

title: Defending It Out Loud
text:
Before the day

Rehearse with the slides you will actually use, out loud, timed.
Have the repository open in case someone asks to see a figure or a number.
Know your own limitations section well enough to state it without reading.
Agree who answers what, and then be prepared to answer anything anyway.

title: Defending It Out Loud
text:
Summary

Questions are individual; teammates can receive different grades, so know the whole analysis.
Open with the question and the answer. End on the limitation.
Five questions come up: why that model, what does the coefficient mean, what would change your conclusion, why is it not confounded, what did your teammate do.
Sign the bias rather than denying it. “The most likely omitted variable would push this up, so treat it as an upper bound” is the strongest thing you can say about observational data.
“I don’t know” plus what it would take beats a fabricated answer every time.
Practice the one-minute version. It is the part that travels.

title: Project Clinic
text:
The checklist
The last session is a clinic. Bring the project in whatever state it is in—the useful version of this is not a polished presentation but the part you are stuck on.
Work through the checklist below first. Most of it takes minutes and every item has caught somebody out.

title: Project Clinic
text:
Data

How many rows did you start with, and how many did you use? Both numbers, in the report.
What is missing, and is it missing at random? Cross-tabulate missingness against something—a group, a time period. If it is patterned, say so. See Where the Data Came From.
Who is not in this data at all? Selection, survivorship, convenience.
Every variable’s type and range checked—no -999, no dates in 1900, no percentages above 100.



Analysis

Does the outcome’s scale make sense? Skewed positive quantities usually want a log. Look at the histogram before deciding.
Residuals against fitted, plotted and looked at. A curve or a funnel means stop.
Cook’s distance computed. If anything is above 1, refit without it and report both.
VIFs, if you have several predictors that could overlap.
For each control: is it a confounder, a mediator, or a collider? See What Would License a Causal Claim.
Every seed set, if there is any randomness.



Reporting

Every estimate has an interval.
Every coefficient is written the careful way: among cases alike in X, associated with, give or take.
Every figure has a caption that says what to notice and axis labels with units.
Limitations are specific. “Our sample was small” is not a limitation; “the interval runs from a 2% to a 40% improvement, so the study cannot distinguish a trivial effect from a large one” is.
Numbers in the prose come from the code, not typed.
AI disclosure includes the prompt log and a critique naming something specific.



Repository

Runs from a clean session, on a machine that is not yours.
No absolute paths.
A README saying what to run and in what order.
The data is either in the repository or the script downloads it.

title: Project Clinic
text:
Bring one of these
Whichever is true. All four are good uses of the session.
“I do not know whether this is a real finding.” Bring the estimate and its interval, and we will work out together what it supports.
“My model fails a diagnostic and I do not know what to do.” Bring the residual plot. This is the most common one and usually the most fixable.
“I cannot decide what to control for.” Bring the causal diagram rather than the model—three or four variables and arrows between them. The argument is about the diagram, and the model follows.
“My result is boring.” Bring it. A precisely estimated null is a genuine finding, and “we can rule out anything larger than 2%” is a sentence with content. A boring result honestly reported beats an interesting one that does not survive a question.






What not to bring





A finding you went looking for after the analysis did not work.
If you tested twelve subgroups and are presenting the one that came out, that is the multiplicity problem and the honest move is to report all twelve and label the finding exploratory. You will be asked how many comparisons you made, and the answer “I don’t know” is worse than any number.

title: Project Clinic
text:
Summary

Run the checklist before the clinic; most items take minutes.
The two sections that decide a report are what you lost from the data and what the analysis cannot say.
Bring the thing you are stuck on, not the thing that is finished.
A precisely estimated null is a finding. Report it as one.

title: Interview Questions
text:
How they are marked
These are the questions this material turns into when somebody is deciding whether to hire you.
Every part of the course has a page here, in the order the course covers them. The questions are the same material as the notes, asked the way an interviewer asks it: out loud, under time, with a follow-up waiting.
None are trick questions, and none are attributed to a company. Attributions to named firms are usually wrong, stale, or under NDA, and a wrong attribution misleads whoever is preparing. What each question carries instead is the role and stage it belongs to—phone screen, technical round, hiring manager—because that is what actually determines what a good answer sounds like.
Each question opens with a difficulty pill and a row of tags naming the concepts it tests. Every tag links to the chapter that covers it, so a question you cannot answer is one click from the material that answers it.
warm-up you should be able to answer this after reading the chapter once · core the version most often actually asked · hard the follow-up that separates candidates
Questions are ordered by difficulty within each page, so working top to bottom is working from what you know toward what you do not.

title: Interview Questions
text:
How to use them
Answer out loud before you read anything. The model answers are written the way you would say them, not the way you would write them, because the failure mode in an interview is not ignorance—it is knowing the material and producing a disorganised three-minute version of it under pressure.
The single most useful thing you can do with this section is work through it with another person, one asking and one answering, and swap. Holding the question is the harder seat: knowing what a good answer contains is a different skill from producing one, and it is the skill that makes you useful in a code review.
That is also exactly the format of the first half of every lab, which is not a coincidence.

title: Lab 1

Part A—Discussion
Getting messy data into shape, and asking who is missing from it.

title: Lab 1
text:
First half






 B1. Take inventory before you touch anything








Produce one table with a row per column of clinic giving its type, its number of missing values, and its number of distinct values.
Do not clean anything yet. The point is to know what you have.












```{r}
inventory <- data.frame(
  type    = sapply(clinic, function(x) class(x)[1]),
  missing = sapply(clinic, function(x) sum(is.na(x))),
  unique  = sapply(clinic, function(x) length(unique(x[!is.na(x)])))
)
```
Two things should stop you. site has five distinct values for what is obviously two sites. And patient has fewer unique values than rows, which means the identifier is not identifying.










 B2. The identifier that is not one








Return the number of patient values that appear more than once.
Then, before you touch it: decide as a group whether a repeated patient ID is a duplicate row to delete, or a patient with two visits. Your answer determines what you do next, and the data cannot tell you which it is.












```{r}
n_repeated <- sum(table(clinic$patient) > 1)
```
Five. duplicated() would tell you how many rows are repeats; this tells you how many patients are.
The judgment is the point. If these are duplicate exports, drop them. If they are second visits, dropping them removes exactly the patients who came back—the sickest, or the least satisfied—which is a selection bias you introduced yourself.










 B3. Five sites that are two








Create clinic$site_clean, a factor with exactly two levels, north and south.












```{r}
clinic$site_clean <- factor(tolower(trimws(clinic$site)))
```
trimws() then tolower(). "North " needs both; doing only one leaves three levels and the error is easy to miss because table() prints them adjacently.
This is the cheapest bug in the whole lab and the one most likely to reach production, because nothing errors—you simply get results for three sites and a sentence about the north that is wrong.










 Checkpoint



Stop typing. I will ask one question and call on someone at random.
Confer first: you found four defects in this file. Which one would have been hardest to notice if you had gone straight to computing the average wait time—and which would have done the most damage?

title: Lab 1
text:
Second half






 B4. Sentinels are not data








age contains impossible values. Create clinic$age_clean with those converted to NA, and return nothing else changed.
Decide as a group what counts as impossible before you look at how many rows it removes.












```{r}
clinic$age_clean <- ifelse(clinic$age > 0 & clinic$age < 120, clinic$age, NA)
```
The -999s are a missing-value code from a system that could not store NA; the 201 is a typo or a different unit.
The order matters more than the code. mean(clinic$age) before this step returns a number, prints no warning, and is wrong by several years. Nothing tells you.










 B5. What did the cleaning cost








Return the proportion of rows that are complete on age_clean, wait_min and score—a number between 0 and 1.












```{r}
kept <- mean(complete.cases(clinic[, c("age_clean", "wait_min", "score")]))
```
mean() of a logical vector is the proportion of TRUEs, which turns any yes/no question about rows into a percentage in one call.
About one row in seven is gone, and none of it announced itself.










 B6. Who did you lose








The last question is the one that matters and it has no single right answer.
Compare the rows you kept with the rows you dropped. Are they alike? Use whatever comparison you think is fair—by site, by age, by wait time.
Then write one sentence, as a comment, that you would be willing to put in a report.












One defensible approach:
```{r}
complete <- complete.cases(clinic[, c("age_clean", "wait_min", "score")])
round(rbind(
  kept    = c(n = sum(complete),  mean_wait = mean(clinic$wait_min[complete], na.rm = TRUE)),
  dropped = c(n = sum(!complete), mean_wait = mean(clinic$wait_min[!complete], na.rm = TRUE))
), 2)
prop.table(table(clinic$site_clean, complete), margin = 1)
```
A sentence that would survive review:

Of 240 records, 203 were complete on age, wait time and satisfaction. The dropped records were not evenly distributed across sites, so results below describe the completed records rather than all visits.

Note what it does not claim. It does not say the missingness was harmless, and it does not quantify a bias it cannot measure. It tells the reader what to be careful about, which is all an honest limitation ever does.










Before you leave



You did no statistics today. You did the part that decides whether the statistics will mean anything—and every decision you made in Part B was a judgment the data could not make for you.
That is the shape of the term.
